1A. CASE INFORMATION
If you need information regarding your case—including contacting the other party, accessing pleadings or orders, or reviewing hearing dates—please visit www.BrowardClerk.org.
To register for e‑filing, please visit:
https://www.17th.flcourts.org/self-rep-lit-efiling/
1B. LABELING YOUR FILINGS IN CMS/RETURN OF SERVICE
When a Plaintiff’s firm has served a Defendant, you should pick Summons Returned Served in the Dropdown Menu when filing the return of service. We have a lot of problems with this issue. The Clerk’s Office indicates it does not force the Filer to follow any particular label or pick any particular label. But when reviewing the case to see if service has taken place within 120 days of the Statement of Claim filed, everyone looks for the magic docket entry Summons Returned Served. Seeing things like Notice of Filing or Affidavit, will cause issues, because most staff are not trained to look through those items. Yes, effectively a Return of Service is an affidavit from the process server. However, not every affidavit is a return of service. Yes if you file something, you could call it a Notice of Filing. However, not every notice of filing is a return of service. Yet Summons Returned Served, is exactly what it says it is. These other labels (Notice of Filing, Affidavit) however, may end up getting the case accidentally dismissed because personnel are not trained to look through every docket entry, hunting for the Return of Service. It is better that you label it right away from the beginning to avoid confusion. 
2A. COMMUNICATION WITH THE JUDGE (Call or Email)
Before Calling  
* Please review these procedures, as many common questions are answered here.
Division and Judicial Email
* Communication with Chambers should not be used in lieu of filing a proper request or motion in writing. 
* Communication with Chambers, must not be unilateral or one-sided, you must include the emails of all parties involved in the case, you cannot communicate with the Court without the other side being made aware of what is being discussed. 
* If you find yourself asking if the Court can take an action on something, that should be in the form of a motion, not an email. 
* All communications to the judicial office must be submitted by email to: div102@17th.flcourts.org.
* The subject line must include the case number, case name, and the specific matter (e.g., COCE26-03457682024 –30 minute Hearing Requested). 
* No exceptions: you must include the opposing party on all emails. 
* ALL MOTIONS AND REQUESTS MUST BE FILED WITH THE CLERK.
Ex Parte Communications
* All communications with the judicial office must comply with Canon 3 of the Code of Judicial Conduct, which prohibits a judge from initiating, permitting, or considering ex parte communications, or considering communications outside the presence of the parties regarding a pending or impending matter, unless permitted by law.
* All parties must be copied on any email directed to the judicial office unless an ex parte communication is legally authorized.
* The judge and judicial assistant is not permitted to provide legal advice.
Unsolicited Communications
* Parties may contact the judicial office only in accordance with these procedures.
* Unsolicited communications from non‑parties will not be considered by the Court.
Communications After Difficulties
* If you experience any technical difficulties, unexpected or unforeseeable lateness, or unexpected or unforeseeable absences, call Chambers right away at 954-831-7322, do not just simply assume we will excuse your lateness, technical difficulty, or absence (after more than 24 hours has elapsed), unless you let us know there was a problem contemporaneously or at the time you are scheduled for court whether in-person or by Zoom. Leave a message or send an email to div102@17th.flcourts.org if you cannot speak with someone right away. Also call and email the opposing party too, because ex parte communications are not permitted. If you end up wasting the time of others, and do not reach out, do not expect this does not impact the time of the Court and the time of others. It does, and your lack of diligence may impact the outcome. 
Other Communication Procedures
* Any email sent to or received from the judicial office may constitute a public record subject to disclosure under applicable law.
Some Defendants may choose to proceed as unrepresented or without an attorney. The Court cannot give legal advice, and is not telling anyone to proceed unrepresented or not. However, if a Defendant continues as self-represented,they are encouraged to utilize the e-Filing Portal by registering at: www.myflcourtaccess.com. 
Although it is not required, registering at the e-Filing Portal provides the parties with the convenience of filing documents with the Clerk of Court without having to physically come to the courthouse or mail documents. The e-Filing Portal also ensures e-service of all documents to all registered parties. The Help Desk Line is: (850) 577-4609.
2B. STANDARD GOVERNING “EMERGENCY” MOTIONS
The Court emphasizes that the designation of a motion as an "emergency" does not, standing alone, establish an entitlement to immediate judicial intervention or expedited consideration. Pursuant to Seventeenth Judicial Circuit Administrative Order 2021-51-CO, a genuine emergency is one in which irreparable harm, death, or manifest injury will result unless immediate relief is afforded. Matters falling outside this definition do not constitute emergencies merely because a party considers the requested relief urgent, important, or time-sensitive.
The Fourth District Court of Appeal has expressly cautioned that improperly designated emergency motions disrupt court procedures and interfere with the orderly consideration of matters already pending before the Court. USAA Casualty Insurance Co. v. Pembroke Pines MRI, Inc., 24 So. 3d 588, 589 (Fla. 4th DCA 2009).
An impending trial date, dissatisfaction with a scheduling order, an approaching discovery deadline, or a party's belated recognition of the need to pursue available procedural remedies does not, without more, establish a genuine emergency. A party's lack of diligence or failure to pursue available remedies in a timely manner does not ordinarily justify bypassing established procedures or obtaining preferential treatment over other pending matters.
The Court must independently determine whether the circumstances presented warrant emergency consideration. Absent a sufficient showing of immediate and irreparable harm or other qualifying injury, the matter shall proceed in the ordinary course, subject to the Court's discretion to provide expedited consideration where otherwise appropriate. Denial of emergency consideration does not necessarily constitute a denial of the underlying motion on its merits.
3. STATUS OF AN ORDER
Orders submitted electronically on active cases (pre post judgement) are generally reviewed within 3–7 business days, unless the Court is in recess, on vacation, observing a holiday, or attending judicial education. The Court does not provide individual status updates on pending orders. All pending matters are addressed through the Court’s normal review process.
Motions which are merely filed, but with no Orders actually submitted, will not be considered unless Orders are submitted to the queue for the Judge to review and grant or deny, if the Order does not require a hearing. Motions which require a hearing before a ruling, must be scheduled for a hearing, to be considered. It is not upon the Judge to set your case for a hearing to obtain a result on your motion. It is the party’s responsibility to do so. 
All motions which do not comply with these directions, will not be acted upon, and will be considered abandoned after the elapse of time. This applies whether a party is represented or acting pro se.  
All time frames are calculated in business days from the date the order is submitted to the Court Management System, not from the date it was e‑filed.
Please see # 14 with regard to Emergency Motions and Emergency Requests. 
4.  ADMINISTRATIVE ORDER FOR DIVISION  
Administrative Order No. 2025-41-CO ADMINISTRATION OF SMALL CLAIMS CREDIT CARD CASES AND AUTOMATIC INVOCATION OF CERTAIN FLORIDA RULES OF CIVIL PROCEDURE IN SMALL CLAIMS CREDIT CARD CASES ASSIGNED TO COUNTY CIVIL DIVISIONS 47, 101, AND 102  Here is the link: https://www.17th.flcourts.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/AO-2020-82-CO-Amendment-1.pdf 
5.  REQUESTING  A CONTINUANCE OF A HEARING OR TRIAL
Before filing a Motion for Continuance, you must first contact the opposing party to determine whether they object. Your motion must include the name of the individual you contacted and the date(s) you attempted or completed contact.
* If the opposing party objects, you must set the Motion for hearing pursuant to Florida Rule of Judicial Administration 2.545(e).
* If all parties agree to the continuance, you may submit an agreed order electronically. Please note that the Court does not automatically grant joint or agreed Motions for Continuance of a Pretrial Conference, Mediation, or Trial. Each request is evaluated on a case‑by‑case basis.
* If your case is set for Trial, you must remain mindful of all deadlines contained in the Order Setting Non‑Jury Trial.
* Please be advised that e‑filing a Motion or submitting a Motion and proposed order through the Court Management System (CMS) does not excuse appearance. Appearance is excused only if and when the Court enters an order granting the continuance.
* If you miss any conference, hearing, or trial, you must call the Judge’s Chambers as soon as possible after the missed hearing, if you are claiming that the lack of attendance is a circumstance out of your control. 
* Do not email the Division 102 email account to request a continuance of a hearing, trial, or mediation. All such requests must be made by written motion only
6.  COURT INTERPRETERS AND ADA ACCOMMODATIONS AT HEARINGS
Interpreters
The Court does not provide interpreters for county civil cases. It is the responsibility of the party requiring interpretation to bring an interpreter who is certified, language‑skilled, provisionally approved, or registered with the Office of the State Courts Administrator, as required by Rules 2.560 and 2.565 of the Florida Rules of Judicial Administration.
Parties who are unable to obtain a certified interpreter must bring someone who can assist them in understanding the proceedings. The Court will determine whether that individual is qualified to interpret the proceedings.
ADA Accommodations
If you require an ADA accommodation, please contact 954‑831‑7721 at least 7 days before your scheduled court appearance, or immediately upon receiving notice if your appearance is scheduled in fewer than 7 days.
Information regarding ADA accommodations is available at: https://www.17th.flcourts.org/the-americans-with-disabilities-act-ada/
7.  DIVISION 102 - ZOOM LINK AND APPEARANCE
IF AND ONLY IF the Court has expressly authorized a Zoom appearance, you must use the following link:
Join Zoom Meeting  
https://17thflcourts.zoom.us/j/85713920051  
Meeting ID: 857 1392 0051
If no Zoom language appears in the Notice of Order Setting Hearing you MUST appear in person. While we may allow Zoom for parties that are in other parts of the state or other states or countries, if you live and/or work in Miami-Dade County or Palm Beach County, do not assume this is sufficiently far away enough to use Zoom. We require tri-county parties to come in person as required.
8.  WAIVER OF APPEARANCE AT PRETRIAL CONFERENCE, RESET, and DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
Pretrial Conferences
Mandatory mediations take place at the pretrial conference. The filing of an answer, responsive paperwork, motions, and so forth, cannot change the required appearance at the pretrial conference appearance except as indicated below, when both sides are represented by counsel per the Small Claims Rules. 


No one may attend a pretrial conference (PTC) by Zoom or telephone. The logistics of pretrial conferences do not permit it: cases are called rapidly, the parties confer, mediations take place, the court is not set up for this during such a pretrial conference calendar. Requests or motions to appear by Zoom or telephone at a pretrial conference will be denied, in most cases. The solution is to secure an alternative. The Court will consider for those special cases where a remote appearance is necessary (disability, injury, hospital stay, military service, being abroad and unable to immediately return, etc.), to schedule the person to an alternative date and time where Zoom will be possible (motion calendar, case management conference, etc.). However, mediations are not easily rescheduled, and due to case timing, may have to be waived. 


“If you are a person with a disability who needs any accommodation in order to participate in this proceeding, you are entitled, at no cost to you, to the provision of certain assistance. Please contact the ADA Coordinator, Room 20140, 201 S.E. Sixth Street, Fort Lauderdale, Florida 33301, 954-831-7721 at least 7 days before your scheduled court appearance, or immediately upon receiving this notification if the time before the scheduled appearance is less than 7 days.  If you have a hearing or voice disability you can contact the court through the Florida Relay Service by calling 711.”
Waiver of Appearance at Pretrial Conference
When all parties are represented by counsel, the attorneys may agree to waive personal appearance at the initial Pretrial Conference. A written agreement of waiver, signed by all attorneys, must be submitted to the Court. The agreement must include:
* A brief statement of the disputed issues of fact and law
* The number of witnesses expected to testify
* An estimate of the time needed to try the case
* Any stipulations of fact
The Joint Stipulation to Waive Appearance at the Pretrial Conference and the proposed Order must be submitted through the Court Management System (CMS) before 12:00 p.m. (noon) on the business day prior to the scheduled Pretrial Conference. If the Joint Stipulation is not yet reflected on the docket, counsel must submit a copy that includes the e‑filing number at the top.
Upon approval of the waiver, the Court will set the trial as required by Rule 7.090(d) and may refer the case to expedited mediation. Any mediation arising from a waived Pretrial Conference is at the parties’ expense.
Please note: Filing a Motion to Continue, a Joint Stipulation, and a proposed order with the Court does not excuse any party from appearing unless and until the Court enters the order granting the request.
Demand for Jury Trial
If a Demand for Jury Trial is timely filed, the case will be randomly reassigned by the Clerk to a judge in the County Civil Jury Division.
To waive appearance at the Pretrial Conference, you must submit the Order of Transfer along with the Demand for Jury Trial directly to the Court Management System (CMS) before 12:00 p.m. (noon)  two (2)  business days prior to the scheduled Pretrial Conference or you will be required to appear in person. 
Please note: Filing a demand for jury and submitting an  Order of Transfer to the Court does not excuse any party from appearing unless and until the Court enters the order granting the request


9.  ORDERS SUBMITTED ELECTRONICALLY TO “CMS” (Court Management System) 
E‑Filing Pleadings
Please be advised:
* If the case is CLOSED  you MUST  contact the Clerk to reopen or it will be rejected.
* When a Motion or Pleading is e‑filed with the Clerk, the Judge does not automatically receive a copy.
* When you file a pleading it is not viewable in the docket until the Clerk processes it
* Simply e‑filing a Motion does not excuse any deadline
* Submission of a Motion and proposed Order through CMS does not excuse appearance unless the Court has entered an order granting the requested relief.
Submission of Orders
All Orders must be submitted electronically through the Court Management System (CMS):
https://cms.17th.flcourts.org/auth/login
Supporting Documentation Requirement
When submitting a proposed Order, parties must upload the referenced Motion, Stipulation, Affidavit, and/or other supporting documents, each showing the e‑filing number, under the Supporting Documentation tab in CMS.
If these documents are not uploaded, the Order will be rejected.
10.  HEARINGS THAT MUST BE SET EXCLUSIVELY THROUGH THE JUDICIAL ASSISTANT
The following types of hearings may only be scheduled through the Judicial Assistant by submitting an email request to DIV102@17th.flcourts.org.


Important Notice:  
All motions must be e‑filed and viewable in the Clerk’s docket before a hearing may be scheduled.
Hearings set without compliance will be canceled.
Additionally, any of the hearings listed below that are scheduled without coordination with the Judicial Assistant will be canceled:
* Special set hearings longer than fifteen (15) minutes
* All Claim of Exemption, Garnishment, and Post‑Judgment hearings
* Evidentiary hearings
* Attorney fee hearings
* Hearings scheduled before the Pretrial Conference
11.  ACCESSING COURT MANAGEMENT SYSTEM ONLINE SCHEDULER FOR "MOTION CALENDAR/SPECIAL SET HEARINGS" 
* Parties shall not set or use the online scheduler to schedule any motions prior to the Pretrial Conference.
* The Pretrial Conference must occur first before any hearing may be set using the online scheduler.
* Failure to comply will result in cancellation of the hearing.
* You may access the Court Management System Online Scheduler at: https://cms.17th.flcourts.org/auth/
* All motions must be filed and visible on the Clerk’s online docket before scheduling a hearing.
* A Notice of Hearing must accompany every motion when setting a hearing.
* Failure to file the Notice of Hearing will result in the case being omitted from the docket.
* If a case has been disposed of, it must be reopened with the Clerk of Court and placed in active status before a motion may be set for hearing.  You may contact the County Clerk at 954‑831‑5622 for assistance.
* If a party fails to appear after proper notice, the matter may proceed in their absence.
* No more than two (2) total cases may be noticed by any law firm—including all attorneys affiliated with the firm—on any given day, unless leave of Court is obtained.
* If more than two cases are scheduled in violation of this procedure, the Judicial Assistant may cancel the hearing.
* Counsel may not “squeeze” a hearing into a time slot that does not provide adequate time for resolution.
* No “add‑ons” are permitted without Court approval.
* If the matter cannot be resolved within the allotted time, the parties must request additional hearing time.
12.  NOTICES OF HEARING AND COURTESY COPIES
A copy of the Notice of Hearing must be timely e‑filed. The Notice of Hearing must include:
* The name of the person with whom the hearing was coordinated
* The date the motion was filed
* All requirements of Local Rule 11
You must provide at least 5 business days’ notice if the Notice of Hearing is e‑served, or 10 business days’ notice if served via U.S. Mail.
Mandatory Coordination (Local Rule 11)
All special set hearings must include the following certification in the body of the Notice of Hearing:
“I hereby certify that I have made a good faith attempt to resolve this matter by having direct communication about the matter with all parties, prior to my noticing this motion for hearing.”
Failure to comply with these procedures may result in the hearing being stricken from the docket or the imposition of other sanctions as the Court deems appropriate. (See Local Rule 11)
Hearing times must be cleared with opposing counsel or pro se parties. Good‑faith cooperation is expected from attorneys, their staff, and self‑represented litigants. If counsel, staff, or a pro se litigant fails to respond within three (3) business days, or refuses to cooperate in coordinating a hearing, the difficulty should be specifically described in the motion or in the Notice of Hearing.
Non‑Responsive Party When Coordinating a Hearing
If you have made a good‑faith effort to coordinate a hearing and have not received a response from the opposing party within three full business days, you may set the hearing unilaterally.
The Notice of Hearing must clearly state:
“Set Unilaterally Pursuant to Judge Clermont’s Procedures.”
Non‑Jury Trial Requirements and Deadlines
If your case is set for a Non‑Jury Trial, you must review and comply with all deadlines in the Order Setting Trial.
Many litigants underestimate the inherent risks associated with proceeding to trial. It is a common misconception that a case is a "slam dunk" simply because one side feels morally or factually justified. However, courtroom outcomes are governed by procedural rules, evidentiary standards, and burdens of proof. Critical pieces of evidence may be excluded if not properly disclosed, authenticated, or supported by a valid hearsay exception. Similarly, essential testimony may be missing because a party did not realize it was required to prove specific legal elements of their claim or defense. These pitfalls often arise unexpectedly. This is precisely why experienced attorneys and seasoned litigators frequently choose to settle cases: because trial outcomes carry significant uncertainty, and even strong cases can be derailed by technical omissions, evidentiary rulings, or procedural errors. All parties should carefully weigh these risks as they prepare for trial.
Whether arguing a motion, evidentiary hearing, nonjury trial, jury trial, this warning applies particularly to pro se litigants: "I don't know," "I have never done this before," "I was unaware" and so forth, are not valid excuses because Florida courts have repeatedly held that self-represented litigants are subject to the same procedural standards as represented parties. In Walker v. Estate of Yee, 376 So. 3d 758, 758 (Fla. 4th DCA 2024), the Fourth District reiterated that the principles governing proper presentation of a case apply equally to pro se litigants. See also Kohn v. City of Miami Beach, 611 So. 2d 538, 539-40 (Fla. 3d DCA 1992) (holding that self-representation does not relieve a party from complying with applicable rules of civil procedure); Anderson v. School Board of Seminole County, 830 So. 2d 952, 953 (Fla. 5th DCA 2002) (stating that pro se litigants are not to be treated differently from similarly situated represented litigants); Barrett v. City of Margate, 743 So. 2d 1160, 1162 (Fla. 4th DCA 1999) (recognizing that a court may not assist a pro se litigant to the detriment of the opposing party).
You must be prepared to present your case, including all witnesses and evidence, on the hearing or trial date. These rules apply whether you are a plaintiff or defendant, represented or unrepresented. Likewise, being unknowledgeable of the law is no excuse, if you choose to stay unrepresented, you must follow all applicable statutes, rules, and orders pertaining to your hearing or trial. I cannot give legal advice, so please do not ask, “Please Judge, tell me what I should do?”
13.  CANCELLATION OF A SPECIAL SET HEARING OR TRIAL
Cancellation of Hearings and Notice to the Court
Hearings scheduled on the Motion Calendar docket may only be canceled with Court approval.(See Local Rule 11.)
If the parties reach an agreement, an agreed order resolving the matter must be submitted to the Court prior to the hearing time and entered by the Court.
If an agreed order has been entered, counsel must promptly notify the Judicial Assistant so that any previously scheduled hearing dates may be canceled. This courtesy allows the Court to make those time slots available for other matters.
Settlement or Voluntary Dismissal — Required Notice to the Court
The Plaintiff must immediately notify the Court by emailing DIV102@17th.flcourts.org and attaching a copy of the e‑filed:
* Notice of Settlement
* Stipulation for Settlement
* Voluntary Dismissal
If the pleading is not yet reflected on the docket, it must include the e‑filing number.
The deadline to submit the Stipulation for Settlement, Notice of Settlement, and/or Voluntary Dismissal to the Court is 5:00 p.m. the day before trial/hearing.
Failure to meet this deadline will require the parties to appear at the hearing or trial.
The Plaintiff must also simultaneously email the Notice of Voluntary Dismissal and/or Settlement to DIV102@17th.flcourts.org so that future dates may be removed from the docket. This courtesy allows other matters to be scheduled.
Important Warning
A Notice of Cancellation or Notice of Settlement does not cancel the hearing. Court approval is required.  
Failure to appear may result in sanctions.
14.  MISCELLANEOUS RULES ABOUT COURT
Actions Not Authorized, Lack of Foresight, and Proper Planning
Zoom is provided for those who are authorized. The Zoom is de-activated during any hearing unauthorized or the pretrial conference as no one is permitted to be on the Zoom during this time. In addition, the Division procedures indicate not to use the Zoom unless a person has been authorized to use the Zoom. 
Please be advised that the parties are expected to comply with all applicable rules of procedure, local requirements, and Division 102 procedures. The Court cannot consider informal email requests for substantive relief. Any request for relief must be filed as a proper motion, must be served on all parties, and must be set for hearing when a hearing is required. Filing a motion does not automatically cancel, continue, stay, or excuse attendance at any scheduled court event.


The Court notes the following procedural concerns:
First, a party may not file motions and then assume that the requested relief has been granted before the Court has ruled. A pending motion does not excuse a party’s absence from a scheduled hearing, case management conference, pretrial conference, mediation, or other court proceeding unless and until the Court enters an order granting such relief.
Second, motions must be filed with sufficient time for the opposing party to respond and for the Court to address the matter in an orderly fashion. Last-minute motions, especially those filed so close to a scheduled court event that the Court and the opposing party have insufficient time to review them, do not automatically create good cause to cancel or continue the proceeding.
Third, parties are responsible for timely setting appropriate motions for hearing in advance when a hearing is necessary. The filing of a motion alone does not place the matter on the Court’s calendar, does not require immediate action by the Court, and does not suspend existing deadlines or court appearances.
Fourth, parties shall not engage in ex parte communications with the Court. Communications seeking substantive relief, discussing the merits of the case, requesting a continuance, requesting cancellation of a hearing, or otherwise asking the Court to take action must not be sent directly to the judge outside the presence of all parties. Any such request must be made by proper filing and service.
Fifth, emails sent directly to the judge are not a substitute for filing a motion through the Clerk of Court. The Court will not grant relief based upon informal email communications. Any future communications must comply with the applicable rules, must copy all parties, and must not seek ex parte consideration of disputed matters.
Sixth, parties are further advised that the Court should not be copied or “looped in” on email communications concerning disputes between the parties. The Court does not supervise informal disagreements between litigants by email. If the parties have a dispute, they are expected to communicate with each other in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures. If the issue cannot be resolved, the proper course is to file the appropriate motion, serve it on all parties, and set the matter for hearing so it may be addressed in court, not through informal email exchanges involving the Court.
Seventh, the Court also takes a dim view of a party attempting to convert that party’s lack of planning into an emergency for the Court. Illness, disability, scheduling conflicts, travel issues, and other claimed impediments must be raised as soon as they are known or reasonably should have been known. When a party has had notice of a hearing or court event for an extended period of time, the Court is unlikely to view favorably a last-minute motion filed on the eve of the proceeding, particularly where the issue could have been raised weeks or months earlier. A party who allows substantial time to pass should not expect the Court, opposing party, or court staff to expedite review or rearrange the Court’s calendar because of the party’s own lack of foresight, planning, or preparation. 
Accordingly, unless and until the Court enters a written order granting relief, all parties remain obligated to comply with existing deadlines, attend scheduled proceedings, and follow Division 102 procedures.
Dress Code and Demeanor in Court
You may be asked to remove items like masks, sunglasses, scarves, and any other items that obscure your face. You should not wear a hat in court without good cause (medical purpose, alopecia, religious reasons), as these items may contain weapons or recording devices, and may obscure your face. You should not consume alcohol or narcotics prior to coming to the courtroom. You should not bring weapons of any kind, including batons, nightsticks, mace, or any firearm into the courtroom. You should not bring alcohol, narcotics or contraband of any kind into the courtroom. You should be dressed appropriately, and this includes sensible tops, bottoms, and footwear. Men laypersons should wear a shirt with a collar and long pants. (Jeans are acceptable).  Women laypersons should wear a dress, or a blouse and skirt or long pants. (Jeans are acceptable).  None of your clothing should be revealing of any breasts, private parts, sexual organs, or other nudity, whole or in part.
Attorneys should be dressed in formal business wear for men and women – in particular suits and ties for men. Female attorneys should wear suits, whether pantsuits or skirt suits, in neutral colors. Pair these with a crisp blouse and closed-toe shoes. Keep jewelry minimal and tasteful.
Whether attorney or layperson, you should avoid:
·       Shorts, tank tops, ball caps, or T-shirts
·       Flip-flops, sneakers, or revealing clothing
·       Low necklines, tight jeans, or sleeveless shirts
·       Hats or caps unless for religious purposes
Electronic Device Use in Court
You should not bring Android phones, smartphones, iPhones, Galaxy phones, or cellular telephones, pagers, and other sound emitting devices into the courtroom. If you must have such devices on you, they should be turned off. The worst case scenario is that they should be silenced completely so that they do not emit a sound. You should likewise not be cautious with tablets, laptops, notebooks, webbooks, or other electronic devices which you plan to use for court, because the glare of the screen may become disruptive, and the sounds may also become disruptive. Such devices should be powered off; worst scenario they should either be muted or volume level turned down to 0. Electronic devices that make distracting lights and sound may not be permitted in the courtroom without good cause and are prohibited. You may be permitted to use such devices, with good cause, for medical issues, disability, and language issues.
American with Disabilities Act (ADA)
The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was enacted on July 26, 1990, and later amended with changes effective January 1, 2009. The ADA provides comprehensive federal civil rights protections in employment, governmental services and programs, public accommodations, transportation and telecommunications to qualified persons with disabilities.
The Chief Judge of the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit signed AO 2018-10-GEN (Amendment 1) which requires that all communications noticing court proceedings or services in the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit include the following language pursuant to Florida Rule of Judicial Administration 2.540 (See ADA Administrative Order link at https://www.17th.flcourts.org/the-americans-with-disabilities-act-ada/).
“If you are a person with a disability who needs any accommodation in order to participate in this proceeding, you are entitled, at no cost to you, to the provision of certain assistance. Please contact the ADA Coordinator, Room 20140, 201 S.E. Sixth Street, Fort Lauderdale, Florida 33301, 954-831-7721 at least 7 days before your scheduled court appearance, or immediately upon receiving this notification if the time before the scheduled appearance is less than 7 days.  If you have a hearing or voice disability you can contact the court through the Florida Relay Service by calling 711.”
ADA Coordinator:
Taiwo Akinkunmi
ADA Hotline:
954 831-7721
Address:
Office of the Court Administrator
201 SE 6th Street, Room 2
Fort Lauderdale FL 33301
Picture Taking/Video Taking/Media Recording
Under Florida law, the courtroom is open to the public. Barron v. Florida Freedom Newspapers, Inc., 531 So. 2d 113 (Fla. 1988). No non-media, laypersons, parties, or attorneys should be recording in the courtroom at any time. This is regardless of whether the recording is audio only, video only, or a combination of both. The court has proceedings in place to capture the audio of criminal or traffic proceedings, which must be recorded according to the criminal rules. Any mediapersons should observe all administrative orders regarding recording court proceedings and you may not begin recording without going through the appropriate court personnel at all times. This includes AO 2021-74-GEN, 2022-8-GEN, 2018-4-GEN, 2022-37-GEN, 2018-14-CRIM, 2019-82-CRIM, 2018-42-GEN, and any other AOs not mentioned here, but which are relevant.
An obvious exception is when a private party in a civil case has hired a court reporter to record the proceedings to preserve a record.
You have the same First Amendment right to attend all stages of criminal trials as you do in federal court. See Richmond Newspapers, Inc. v. Virginia, 448 U.S. 555, 580(1980); see also Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Lewis, 426 So. 2d 1, 3 (Fla. 1982). This includes the preliminary hearing and the jury selection process.
You may be denied access to the courtroom if there would otherwise be a serious and imminent threat to the administration of justice. For example, the court may exclude you if the media's presence will deprive the defendant of her right to a fair trial because media coverage will influence the jury. However, if the trial court closes the proceeding, the closure must be no broader than necessary to protect the interest of the accused and closure must be an effective way to protect the accused's rights. There must be no alternative available other than change of venue. See generally Press-Enterprise Co. v. Superior Ct., 478 U.S. 1 (1986); Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Lewis, 426 So. 2d 1, 6 (Fla. 1982).
Article I, Section 21, of the Florida Constitution provides access to courts. Article I, Section 24, of the Florida Constitution allows access to open meetings and records. Fla. R. Gen. Prac. & Jud. Admin has several rules on the subject such as Technology in the Courtroom (2.450), Access to Electronic Devices (2.451), and Public Access to Judicial Branch Records (2.420). You should be familiar with all relevant rules, statutes, and administrative orders. More often than not, there may be a single video feed used for media, and thus you will participate in a media pool. For more information see: https://www.17th.flcourts.org/media-relations/.  
All matters concerning media should be directed to:
Sallie James
Public Information Officer
Seventeenth Judicial Circuit of Florida
(954) 831-7559
sjames@17th.flcourts.org  
15.  MOTIONS FOR REHEARING/RECONSIDERATION
Parties must review Administrative Order No. 2022‑5‑Gen regarding Motions for Rehearing (“AO”). Upon review of the motion, the Judge may grant, deny, or set the matter for hearing at the Court’s discretion.
These motions may not be set for hearing by the parties without prior permission of the Court.
Strict compliance with the Administrative Order is required.
To access Administrative Order No. 2022‑5‑Gen, click here.
16.  POST JUDGMENT AND GARNISHMENT PROCEEDINGS
The Judicial Assistant may only schedule post judgment and garnishment hearings.  Please email your post judgment hearing request to div102@17th.flcourts.org. 
Please do not use the online scheduler to set these types of hearings or they will be canceled.
Garnishment related orders shall be electronically submitted via the Court Management System “CMS”.  DO NOT MAIL PHYSICAL ORDERS TO THE COURT
When submitting your proposed Orders, please include the following as your supporting documentation:
1.             A copy of the Final Judgment or Default Final Judgment with e-filing number
2.             A copy of the Motion with the e-filing #
3.             Notice of Garnishment to Defendant and Answer with e-filing # (if applicable) 
4.     Proof of payment that the Writ Fee has been paid to the Clerk 
17.  SUBMISSION OF EXHIBITS FOR TRIAL OR EVIDENTIARY HEARING
Parties represented by Counsel must upload their exhibits through the Court Management System “CMS”, and provide a copy of the same to the opposing party at least five (5) days prior to trial. Exhibits must be numbered and, if there are photographs, ensure color copies are provided. If the exhibits exceed (25) pages, copies must be provided to the Court on the day of trial.
Self-represented litigants shall file their exhibits with the Broward County Clerk, and provide a copy of the same to the opposing party at least five (5) days prior to trial. Exhibits must be numbered and, if there are photographs, ensure color copies are provided. If the exhibits exceed (25) pages, copies must be provided to the Court on the day of trial.

19.  USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN COURT FILINGS
Administrative Order 2026-03-Gen (Amendment 1) USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN COURT FILINGS and any other subsequent or relevant rules and orders. 
1. AI Use in Legal Work:
AI may assist in researching, drafting pleadings, documents, filings, and discovery. All AI-generated content must be supervised by a human who verifies citations, factual claims, and conclusions. Users must guard against plagiarism, confidentiality breaches, inaccuracies, false information, and inappropriate language. 
2. Attorney Responsibility:
Lawyers may use AI only if they can reasonably ensure compliance with ethical obligations. Attorneys remain fully responsible for their work product and must follow Florida law and the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar, including rules on competence, confidentiality, candor to the tribunal, and supervision of others.
3. Pro Se Litigant Responsibility:
Individuals representing themselves must be cautious, ensuring AI does not generate fictitious legal authorities or misleading information. They must follow all procedural rules and accept responsibility for any procedural mistakes, inaccuracies, or AI “hallucinations.”
4. Confidentiality and Authenticity:
All users of AI must verify the authenticity and accuracy of information generated by AI. They must take reasonable steps to prevent AI errors, protect confidential information, and comply with legal, procedural, and ethical rules.
5. Certification Requirement:
   1. Must comply with the Florida Rules of Civil Procedure, The Florida Rules of General Practice and Judicial Administration as well as any particular Florida Supreme Court’s rule that applies to the subject. 
   2. Must comply with any local Seventeenth Judicial Circuit Administrative Orders and Local Rules on the subject. . 
6. Definition of AI:
AI refers to computer systems that mimic human intelligence to generate text, images, audio, and synthetic media. AI can perform tasks such as language interpretation, problem-solving, citation generation, and document drafting. Common tools include but are not limited to ChatGPT, Legora, Spellbook, Anthropic Claude, Harvey AI, Eve Legal, Seedance, DeepSeek, NotebookLM, Nano Banana, Adobe Firefly, Grammarly, Perplexity, Harvey AI, Lexis+AI, AI.Law, Westlaw Drafting Assistant, Co-Counsel by Thomson Reuters, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot.
7. Sanctions:
Improper AI use or submitting false or misleading AI-generated content may result in sanctions. Potential sanctions include contempt, striking pleadings, dismissal of actions, fines, attorney’s fees, and referral to The Florida Bar for disciplinary proceedings. As the Florida Supreme Court ordered in SC2026-0673, “Given the demonstrated risks of generative AI and to promote the accuracy and integrity of court filings, we amend rule 2.515(d)(2) to require the signer of a filing to represent that the legal authorities identified in that filing ‘exist and are accurately cited.’  
This requirement applies both to filings prepared by attorneys and to filings prepared by unrepresented parties.  We also amend rule 2.515(d)(2) to provide that the court may ‘impose sanctions for any filing inconsistent with this representation after providing the signer notice and an opportunity to be heard.’  And we amend rule 2.515(d)(2) to specify that ‘[s]uch sanctions may include reprimand, contempt, striking of the document, dismissal of proceedings, costs, attorneys’ fees, or other sanctions.’”  In re Amendments to Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.515, No. SC2026-0673, 2026 WL ___ (Fla. May 28, 2026).
This Court still holds filers accountable for matters more than just filings which contain nonsupportive, irrelevant, nonexistent, or miscited legal authorities. Any word or sentence which is contained in a filing, used in support of a request, objection, pleading, answer, motions, or any other legal document filed within a court case, which contains proposed relief, points of law, arguments, reasoning, advocacy, representation on behalf of a client, which was generated with the use of AI, is subject to similar scrutiny, and the signer is responsible for it, and may be sanctioned with any the methods previously described in this paragraph, should the use of generative AI lead to misleading, misinforming, misrepresenting by omission, or perpetrating fraud on this Court.

21.  FLA. R. CIV. P. 1.202(c) AND CONFERRAL
Is it on the Rule 1.202(c) exemption list?
   * Yes → No conferral required
   * No → Conferral required
Are both parties represented?
   * If not → No conferral required
Is the certificate present and meaningful?
   * If not → deny without prejudice or set for compliance
Motions That Do NOT Require Conferral
Under subdivision (c) of the rule 1.202, you do not have to confer before filing these types of motions:
   * Motions for default
   * Motions for injunctive relief
   * Motions for judgment on the pleadings
   * Motions for summary judgment
   * Motions to dismiss for failure to state a claim
   * Motions to involuntarily dismiss
   * Motions to dismiss for failure to prosecute
   * Motions to permit maintenance of a class action
   * Motions for directed verdict and motions under Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.530
   * Motions for writ of possession under Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.580
   * Motions for garnishment, attachment, or other enforcement under Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.570
   * Motions filed in summary procedure cases under Florida Statutes § 51.011
   * Motions that, by law, do not require notice to the other side
   * Any motion where one or more parties are self-represented (pro se)
In short, dispositive motions and enforcement-type motions are generally excluded from the conferral requirement.
Motions That Do Require Conferral
Everything else generally requires a good-faith conferral before filing. Although see any AO’s or 17th Judicial Circuit Local Rules as well that may modify this. Common examples include:
   * Motions to compel discovery
   * Motions for protective order
   * Motions to continue (unless otherwise specifically exempted)
   * Motions to strike (not listed as exempt)
   * Motions to amend pleadings
   * Motions to extend deadlines
   * Motions regarding case management disputes
   * Motions to compel better discovery responses
   * Motions for sanctions (unless enforcement-type under Rule 1.570)
The rule requires not just a conversation, but a real effort to resolve or narrow the issue, and then a certificate of conferral included with the motion.
If conferral fails, the moving party must state in the motion:
   * The date of the conference or attempts,
   * The method (phone, Zoom, in person, etc.), and
   * Whether the other side agreed, partially agreed, or refused.
The Governing Principle (Rule 1.202)
   * Conferral IS required for most non-dispositive motions.
   * A certificate of conferral (or non-requirement) must be included in the motion.
   * No conferral required if either side is pro se.
Discovery Motions and Pre-Filing Requirements with Local Rule 11A
Before filing any motion relating to discovery, the parties must comply with Local Rule 11A of this Circuit. The purpose of this rule is to encourage the resolution of discovery disputes without court intervention whenever possible.
Prior to filing a motion to compel, motion for protective order, or any other motion relating to discovery, the moving party must confer in good faith with the opposing party to attempt to resolve or narrow the dispute. If the parties are unable to resolve the dispute, they must jointly prepare and submit to the Court a short written statement identifying the discovery issues that remain unresolved. The Court will review the submission and determine whether the matter can be resolved without a formal motion, whether a hearing is required, or whether formal motion practice will be permitted.
A motion filed without compliance with this procedure may be denied or stricken without a hearing. Compliance with this process is required for both attorneys and self-represented parties.
Parties are reminded that this pre-motion procedure is in addition to the conferral requirement set forth in the Florida Rules of Civil Procedure and is designed to promote efficient case management and reduce unnecessary litigation.
22.  COURT’S STANDING ORDER
ORDER REGARDING MANDATORY APPEARANCE AT PRE-TRIAL CONFERENCE
THIS CAUSE is before the Court to clarify the obligations of all parties with respect to attendance at the Pre-Trial Conference. This is a STANDING order of the Court. All litigants must observe this standing order. The Court, being fully advised, hereby ORDERS as follows:
   1. Mandatory Appearance Required
All Defendants are required to appear in person at the scheduled Pre-Trial Conference. Attendance is mandatory.
   2. Filing an Answer Does Not Excuse Appearance
The filing of an Answer, Affirmative Defenses, or any other written response does not excuse a party from attending the Pre-Trial Conference.
   3. Motions Are Not Automatically Heard
The filing of a motion does not place the matter before the Court for hearing. Any party seeking relief by motion must properly schedule and calendar the motion for hearing in accordance with applicable rules and procedures.
   4. Continuances and Zoom Requests
Motions for continuance or requests to appear via Zoom are not automatically granted. Such requests must be set for hearing and ruled upon by the Court. A Zoom request is never heard at a pretrial conference; all pretrial conferences must be attended in person and never over Zoom. 
All trials are conducted in person and are not held via Zoom absent a specific Court order entered in advance of the hearing.
   5. Failure to Appear Is Not Excused by Filing
The Court handles a high volume of filings. A party’s belief that the mere filing of a motion or document has “notified” the Court does not excuse failure to appear.
Unless and until a party receives a Court order granting relief from attendance, the obligation to appear remains in full force and effect. This will not be grounds for excusable neglect. This instruction is clear, and there can be no confusion regarding it, regardless whether or party is represented or is acting pro se. 
   6. Consequences of Non-Appearance
Failure to appear at the Pre-Trial Conference may result in the entry of a default, dismissal, or other appropriate sanctions.
   7. Due Diligence
Due diligence means that you shall call Chambers immediately 954-831-7322 if a deadline or hearing is missed for any reason and speak to someone as soon as possible. At a bare minimum leave a voice mail message and email message to div102@17th.flcourts.org. 
   8. No Ex Parte
You may not email the judge directly at his email address. This is not permitted, period. 
It is so ORDERED and ADJUDGED.
Signed this 9th day of April, 2026 in Broward County, Florida,
/s/ Woody R. Clermont
Honorable Woody R. Clermont
County Court Judge
  

ORDER REQUIRING MEET AND CONFER BEFORE CASE MANAGEMENT CONFERENCES
THIS CAUSE is before the Court upon review of the file and the Court’s procedures for case management conferences. The Court finds that meaningful case management requires the parties to communicate before appearing before the Court, narrow the issues to be addressed, and be prepared to advise the Court of the status of the case. Accordingly, it is hereby:
ORDERED AND ADJUDGED as follows:
      1. Meet and Confer Required. Whenever a case management conference is scheduled in this matter, the parties shall meet and confer no later than five (5) days before the scheduled case management conference.

      2. Plaintiff Must Initiate the Conference. Because Plaintiff is prosecuting the litigation, the burden is on Plaintiff to initiate the meeting and confer with Defendant or defense counsel. Plaintiff shall make a good faith effort to contact Defendant or defense counsel in sufficient time to comply with this Order.

      3. Purpose of Meet and Confer. The parties shall make an earnest attempt to resolve the matter, narrow the issues, discuss any pending disputes, and identify any matters that must be addressed by the Court.

      4. Settlement Case Management Conferences. If the case management conference concerns settlement, then all settlement paperwork shall be completed and ready for the judge to review and sign at the case management conference. This includes any stipulation for dismissal, proposed order, satisfaction, release-related filing, or other appropriate closing document.

      5. Fraud or Identity Theft Case Management Conferences. If the case management conference concerns allegations of fraud, unauthorized charges, or identity theft, Plaintiff shall be prepared to report the results of any investigation to Defendant and to the Court. The plaintiff shall be prepared to state whether the case will be dismissed, whether additional investigation is needed, or whether the matter remains contested and must be resolved by trial.

      6. Bankruptcy Case Management Conferences. If the case management conference concerns bankruptcy, Defendant shall ensure that a proper suggestion of bankruptcy has been filed in the court file before the case management conference. The filing shall include the federal bankruptcy case number, the federal court in which the bankruptcy is pending, the chapter under which bankruptcy relief is sought, and any other relevant information needed for the Court to determine whether a stay of proceedings is required.

      7. Trial Issues and Stipulations. At a minimum, the parties shall discuss any issues affecting trial, including witnesses, exhibits, contested facts, legal issues, evidentiary issues, damages, and any stipulations that may reduce the time needed for trial.
      8. Preparation for the Court. The parties shall appear at the case management conference prepared to advise the Court of:
a. whether the parties met and conferred;
b. who participated in the meet and confer;
c. what issues were resolved;
d. what issues remain pending;
e. whether the case can be settled, dismissed, stayed, or must proceed to trial; and
f. what specific action the Court is being asked to take.

      9. Failure to Comply. Failure to comply with this Order may result in the Court continuing the case management conference, setting the matter for trial, dismissing the case, entering default where legally appropriate, imposing sanctions, or entering any other order deemed appropriate under the circumstances.

      10. A case management conference is not intended to be the first time the parties discuss the issue that caused the conference to be set. The parties are expected to make a meaningful, good faith effort to address the issue before appearing before the Court.
It is so ORDERED and ADJUDGED.
Signed this 15th day of May, 2026 in Broward County, Florida,
/s/ Woody R. Clermont
Honorable Woody R. Clermont
County Court Judge

Accordingly, we affirm the judgment, . . . .” ).

items.summary:
Practically, when a dealer breaches the conditions of its written contract and the auction operator that handled the wholesale transaction loses money as a result, the auction operator is among those who can claim against the dealer's bond, so the surety cannot avoid liability merely because the claimant is the auction house rather than a retail buyer.

Holding: A motor vehicle auction operator qualifies as a 'person in a wholesale transaction who suffered a loss as a result of the failure of the dealer to comply with the conditions of its written contract' and is therefore entitled to recover under the dealer's bond.

Disposition: Affirmed

citations.quote:
DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA  
FOURTH DISTRICT  
 
COASTAL BUILDING CONTRACTORS, LLC, 
Appellant, 
 
v. 
 
ABRAHAM CALIXTE and DOROTHY DROUILLARD 
a/k/a DOROTHY CALIXTE, 
Appellees. 
 
Nos. 4D2025-2593 and 4D2025-3611 
 
[November 4, 2026] 
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit, St. 
Lucie County; Steven J. Levin, Judge; L.T. Case Nos. 
562023CA002443AXXXHC and 562023CA002748AXXXHC. 
 
Lawrence S. Klitzman of Klitzman Law Group, PLLC, Sunrise, Robert J.  
Powell, Matthew M. Couch, and Ethan C . Gibson of Moorhead Law Group, 
Pensacola, for appellant. 
 
Abraham Calixte, Port St. Lucie, pro se. 
 
Dorothy Drouillard a/k/a Dorothy Calixte, Port St. Lucie, pro se.  
No brief filed for appellees. 
 
L
OTT, J. 
 
Coastal Building Contractors, LLC (“Coastal”), a subcontractor, tried to 
record a lien after a payment dispute arose with the Calixtes for work 
which Coastal had performed on their home.  
 
But Coastal made one mistake—a mistake that was consequential for 
this appeal.  
 
Coastal completed its work by December 1, 2022.  But its recorded 
notice of lien erroneously stated that the date of completion was October 
21, 2022.  The notice , filed on February 16, 2023, needed to be filed within 
90 days of completion of the work, so it appeared on its face untimely, even 
though it was actually timely.   
2 
  
The trial court dismissed Coastal’s claim of lien as untimely.  The trial 
court reasoned that because the notice was not timely amended to reflect 
the correct completion date, the notice remained untimely on its face, 
invalidating the claim of lien. 
 
But that was not the correct inquiry, for which reversal is required.  The 
notice was timely because it was recorded within 90 days of the actual 
completion of the work—the notice  just contained an erroneous 
description of the completion date.  On remand, the trial court should 
assess whether that error prejudiced the homeowners.  If no prejudice 
occurred, then the error falls within the statutory safe harbors and the lien is valid.   
 
Background 
 
The Calixtes hired a general contractor, Port St. Lucie Properties, Inc. 
(“PSL”), to construct a single-family residence. PSL subcontracted with 
Coastal to perform masonry, carpentry, and slab work.  The project was 
delayed because required drywall materials were unavailable, and the 
remaining work was completed on or about December 1, 2022.1 
 Coastal recorded its original claim of lien on February 16, 2023.  The 
recorded document incorrectly listed the completion date as October 21, 2022.  On September 28, 2023 and October 24, 2023, Coastal recorded 
an Amended Claim of Lien and Second Amended Claim of Lien, respectively, to reflect a December 20, 2022 completion date.  
 
The Calixtes initiated an action for slander of title and a declaratory 
judgment to invalidate the lien, later depositing cash security to secure the 
Second Amended Claim of Lien.  Coastal filed a consolidated foreclosure 
action objecting to the cash deposit.  The trial court entered summary 
judgment for the Calixtes, finding that because the original lien was 
untimely, the amendments were invalid, and the Calixtes suffered legal 
prejudice.  The trial court released the cash security deposit and awarded 
the Calixtes $80,000 in attorney’s fees.  
 
 
1 Coastal  admits that a dispute exists about  the date , and that some record 
evidence shows it to be December 9, 2022 , while other evidence  shows it to be  
December 20, 2022.  That distinction is immaterial , inasmuch as all are within 
90 days of February 16, 2023.  
3 
 Analysis 
 
“We review de novo an order granting summary judgment.”  Kincaid v. 
Walmart, Inc., 430 So. 3d 141, 146 (Fla. 4th DCA 2026)  (setting out 
standard for summary judgment). 
 
Section 713.08, Florida Statutes (2022), sets out the requirements for 
a contractor to make a claim of lien for work performed.   
 
Among other things, the claim of lien must state “[t]he time when the 
first and the last item of labor or service or materials was furnished.”  Id. 
§ 713.08(1)(f). 
 
Section 713.08 provides that “[t]he claim of lien may be recorded at any 
time during the progress of the work or thereafter but not later than 90 days after the final furnishing of the labor or services or materials by the lienor.”  § 713.08(5).  Further, “[a]ny claim of lien recorded as provided in 
this part may be amended at any time during the period allowed for 
recording such claim of lien,” that is, 90 days after the final furnishing.  § 
713.08(4)(b).   
 
The statute contains two “safe harbor” provisions for errors in the 
notice.  First, “the negligent inclusion or omission of any information in 
the claim of lien which has not prejudiced the owner does not constitute a default that operates to defeat an otherwise valid lien.”  § 713.08(3).  
Second, “[t]he omission of any of the foregoing details or errors in such 
claim of lien shall not, within the discretion of the trial court, prevent the 
enforcement of such lien as against one who has not been adversely 
affected by such omission or error.”  § 713.08(4)(a).   
 
The trial court reasoned that the lien was untimely filed because, on its 
face, the lien stated that the final furnishing was on October 21, 2022.  
The court further reasoned that the attempted amendment was invalid 
because it was filed more than 90 days after the corrected completion date 
of December 20, 2022.  The court concluded the lien was facially untimely 
and remained so, rendering it unenforceable.  The court alternatively 
found that the Calixtes were prejudiced because the lien impaired their 
property rights. 
 The trial court was, to be sure, correct in finding that Coastal’s attempts 
to amend the lien months down the road were improper and thus those 
amended notices are nullities.  See § 713.08(4)(b), Fla. Stat. ( 2022) (“Any 
claim of lien recorded as provided in this part may be amended at any time 
4 
 during the period allowed for recording such claim of lien[.]  [i.e., 90 days 
from final furnishing].”).   
 
But the trial court erred in finding that the erroneous lien, left 
unamended, was fatally deficient and incurable.  Even though error 
caused the lien to appear untimely, the question of timeliness turns on 
whether the lien was, in fact , untimely.  And it is undisputed that the lien 
was not untimely, because the final work was performed within 90 days of 
the date of recording.2  
 Although the lien notice included erroneous information (the wrong 
date) and excluded correct information (the right date), section 713.08  
contains two safe-harbor provisions that might salvage the claim from 
such mistakes.  First, “the negligent inclusion or omission of any 
information in the claim of lien which has not prejudiced the owner does not constitute a default that operates to defeat an otherwise valid lien.”  § 
713.08(3), Fla. Stat. ( 2022).  And second, “errors in such claim of lien shall 
not, within the discretion of the trial court, prevent the enforcement of 
such lien as against one who has not been adversely affected by such 
omission or error.”  § 713.08(4)(a). 
 The question for the trial court, then, is whether the error, that is, the 
wrong date recited in the notice, “prejudiced the owner” or otherwise 
“adversely affected” the Calixtes.  §§ 713.08(3), (4)(a), Fla. Stat (2022).  
 
The trial court did not reach that question.  The court instead held that 
the failure to cure the error through amendment ended the inquiry.  But 
that ignored the safe harbor provisions. 
 
The trial court alternatively held that the error prejudiced the Calixtes 
by causing an otherwise invalid lien on their property to be valid and thus 
encumber their property.  But that asked the wrong question of “what” 
prejudiced the Calixtes.  Of course the lien prejudiced the Calixtes: that’s 
the point of a lien.   
 
The safe harbor analysis instead must ask whether the error prejudiced 
the owner.  In a counterfactual world where no error occurred and the 
correct information was included, would things have played out differently 
for the Calixtes?  For example, did the error prevent them from 
 
2 At least, it appears to be undisputed.  The Calixtes did not file an answer brief.  
If the trial court on remand finds a genuine dispute of material fact on the 
question of whether the work were  in fact completed within 90 days of the 
recording of the lien, then the court should  proceed accordingly.  
5 
 understanding the claim and defending their rights with respect to it?  Did 
they in good faith rely to their detriment on the erroneous information, or 
did they know the information was wrong, cross their fingers, and hope 
they had drawn bank error in their favor?   
 
Along such lines, in McCown v. Pierce Const ruction, Inc., 552 So. 2d 
940, 941 (Fla. 4th DCA 1989), we reversed a dismissal where the claim of 
lien failed to provide a proper description of the subject property.  We noted 
that the “record reveals nothing to indicate that Pierce would have been 
exposed to any prejudice had the trial court followed that course” and that  
prejudice appeared absent where “[i]t is unlikely that [lienee] was unable 
to identify the subject property; it defended the action from the start.”  Id.  
Accord Johnson & Bailey Architects P.C. v. Se. Brake Corp., 517 So. 2d 776, 
778 (Fla. 2d DCA 1988) (“We note also that as the lien did reference the 
contract from which it arose, it is unlikely that Southeast was unable to 
identify the subject property.”); Premier Finishes, Inc. v. Maggirias, 130 So. 
3d 238, 243 (Fla. 2d DCA 2013) (prejudice unlikely shown where, even 
with errors, “it is unlikely that Mr. Maggirias would be unable to deduce the relationship between Premier Finishes and PFI Construction”). 
 The trial court erred in distinguishing our decision in O’Brian 
Associates of Orlando, Inc. v. Tully, 184 So. 2d 202 (Fla. 4th DCA 1966) —
that case is materially similar.  In O’Bria n, which concerned a 
substantively similar statute (then section 84.041), the contractor filed a 
claim of lien that was facially untimely.  Id. at 204.  Then the contractor  
sought to amend its claim of lien to show that the wrong date had been 
listed for the furnishing of materials and that the lien was in fact timely 
recorded.  Id.  We held that the lien could not be amended because the 
window for amending the claim had passed.  Id. (“The amended claim of 
lien was filed long after ninety days from the final furnishing of the materials by O’Brian so the amendment could not be permitted under the 
provisions of that portion of the statute.”).  However, we continued: 
 
Having determined that the claim of lien may not be amended, 
the question remaining is whether the lien may be enforced under the theory that the date set forth in the claim of lien on 
which the first materials were supplied was, in fact, erroneous 
and that the materials were, in fact, supplied within forty-five 
days.  Section 84.081(4)(a) provides that the omission of any 
of the details or errors in a claim of lien shall not, within the 
discretion of the trial court, prevent the enforcement of such 
lien as against one who has not been adversely affected by 
such omission or error.  We feel that neither party has shown 
an absence of a material issue of fact on the issue of whether 
6 
 or not the owners have not been adversely affected by the 
alleged error in the claim of lien.  The statements contained in 
the proof submitted in support of summary judgment by each party on this issue are conclusions and not facts admissible 
as evidence and they are, therefore, insufficient to serve as a 
basis for summary decree.  After full evidentiary hearing, the 
trial court will be in a position to exercise its discretion in 
determining whether or not the error in the claim of lien 
should prevent the enforcement of the lien.  To permit 
enforcement the court must determine that the owners have 
not been adversely affected by the error. 
 
Id. at 204–05 (cleaned up). 
  So too, here.  Accord McCown, 552 So. 2d at 941  (where claim was 
defective for failure to identify property, “the trial court should have permitted McCown to rely on the original claim of lien which was timely 
recorded” and assessed whether lienee suffered prejudice from omission); 
Royal Ambassador Condo. Ass’n, Inc. v. E. Coast Supply Corp., 495 So. 2d 932, 934–35 (Fla. 4th DCA 1986) (“While the adjudication against the 
entire property is overbroad and contrary to statute, unless a unit owner 
can demonstrate he was prejudiced by the overly broad description of the 
property liened, the lien should be effective against the respective units  
according to their proportionate shares of the common expenses.”); Sam 
Rodgers Props., Inc. v. Chmura , 61 So. 3d 432, 441 (Fla. 2d DCA 2011) 
(“Even assuming that the trial court was correct in rejecting the amended 
claim of lien as untimely filed or that it was for work that was done for the 
wrong purpose, the trial court erred in determining that the amended 
claim of lien rendered the initial claim of lien unenforceable.”). 
 
On remand, the trial court should consider whether the error 
prejudiced the owners, such that the error did or did not fall within section 
713.08’s safe harbor provisions.   
 We leave this determination to the trial court’s discretion.  And we leave 
all other matters, including all issues pertaining to fees, for the trial court 
to consider on remand in light of this opinion.  Cf. McCown, 552 So. 2d at 
941 (“Further proceedings will determine the prevailing party entitled to 
fees and costs . . . .”). 
 Reversed and remanded. 
 
L
EVINE  and K LINGENSMITH , JJ., concur. 
 
7 
 *            *            * 
 
Not final until disposition of timely-filed motion for rehearing.

items.summary:
Practically, a contractor whose lien recites the wrong completion date but was actually recorded within 90 days of finishing the work does not automatically lose the lien: the homeowner cannot defeat it merely because the lien clouds title, but must show the misstatement itself harmed their ability to understand or defend the claim or caused detrimental reliance; absent such prejudice the safe harbors keep the lien enforceable and foreclosure may proceed.

Holding: A claim of lien is timely if recorded within 90 days of the actual final furnishing of labor, services, or materials, measured by that actual completion date and not by a completion date mistakenly recited on the lien; an amendment is permitted only within the 90-day recording window, so a late amendment is a nullity; and the statutory safe harbors in section 713.08(3) and (4)(a) preserve an otherwise valid lien against non-prejudicial negligent errors, the controlling question being whether the error itself adversely affected or prejudiced the owner rather than whether the lien encumbers the owner's property.

Disposition: Reversed and remanded

MARIBEL MONTES ,

November 6, 2026  
   
PER CURIAM.  
 
 Maribel Montes appeals a non- final order denying her motion to enforce the 
trial court’s order compelling arbitration.   We lack jurisdiction to consider this 
appeal because the non -final order being appealed involves the denial of a request 
to enforce a pr ior order, not an order determining entitlement to arbitration.   Fla. R. 
App. P. 9.130(a)(3)(I) (permitting review of non- final orders which “determine the 
entitlement of a party to arbitration . . . ”); see Cohen v. D.R. Horton, Inc. , 121 So. 
3d 1121, 1123 (Fla. 5th DCA 2013) (concluding it lacked jurisdiction to consider 
2 
 appeal of non- final order seeking relief from prior order compelling arbitration 
because it did not involve entitlement to arbitration); Henderson v. Tandem Health 
Care of Jacksonville, Inc. , 898 So. 2d 1191, 1192 (Fla. 1st DCA 2005) (concluding 
rendition of new order requiring rescheduling and active participation in arbitration 
was not appealable as order determining entitlement to arbitration, which had been 
determined in earlier order tha t was not appealed).  
 DISMISSED.  
 
NARDELLA, SMITH and MIZE , JJ., concur.

 No Appearance for Appellee.

items.summary:
Practically, a party cannot manufacture an immediate appeal by moving to enforce an earlier order that already compelled arbitration; because entitlement to arbitrate was settled in that earlier, unappealed order, the denial of the enforcement motion is not independently appealable under rule 9.130, so the appeal is dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Holding: Interlocutory review under rule 9.130(a)(3)(I) lies only from a non-final order determining a party's entitlement to arbitration; an order denying a motion to enforce a prior order that had already compelled arbitration does not determine entitlement to arbitration-because that question was resolved in the earlier order that was not appealed-so the appellate court lacks interlocutory jurisdiction over such an appeal.

Disposition: Dismissed

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 28, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D26 -1965  
Lower Tribunal No. 24-7333 -FC-04 
________________  
 
 
Dimo Veselinov  Panov , 
Petitioner,  
 
vs. 
 
Irina Panova , 
Respondent.  
 
 
 
 A Case of Original Jurisdiction – Prohibition . 
 
 Dimo Veselinov Panov, in proper person . 
 
 No appearance , for respondent.  
 
 
Before  FERNANDEZ, MILLER, and LOBREE,  JJ.  
 
 MILLER, J.  
 Petitioner, Dimo Veselinov Panov, the former husband, seeks a writ of 
prohibition disqualifying the assigned trial judge from further presiding over 
 2 his post -decretal dissolution proceedings.  The trial court denied petitioner’s 
verified motion for disqualification “on  its merits .”  Panov correctly posits that 
this ruling “looked beyond the mere legal sufficiency of prejudice,” which 
would ordinarily warrant disqualification , in and of itself, regardless of the 
sufficiency of the underlying motion.1  See Bundy v. Rudd , 366 So. 2d 440, 
442 (Fla. 1978) (“When a judge [looks beyond the mere legal sufficiency of 
a motion for disqualification], he has then exceeded the proper scope of his 
inquiry and on that basis alone established grounds for his disqualification.”); 
MacKenzie v. Super Kids Bargain Store, Inc. , 565 So. 2d 1332, 1339 (Fla. 
1990)  (“Although we have concluded that the ground for disqualification 
asserted in the initial motion was legally insufficient, we agree with the 
decision below that  [the] . . . subsequent motion for disqualification should 
have been granted.  . . . In ruling on [the] motion for disqualification, [the 
judge] went beyond a mere determination of the legal sufficiency of the 
motion and passed upon the truth of the facts alleged. ”).  Yet seven days 
 
1 There is no indication that the judge was a successor , as defined under the 
Florida Rules of General Practice and Judicial Administration .  See Fla. R. 
Gen. P rac. & Jud. Adm in. 2.330(i)  (“If a judge has been previously 
disqualified on motion  for alleged prejudice or partiality under subdivision (e), 
a successor judge cannot be disqualified based on a successive motion by 
the same party unless the successor judge rules that he or she is in fact not 
fair or impartial in the case. Such a successor judge may rule on the t ruth of 
the facts alleged in support of the motion.” ). 
 
 3 after denying the motion , the trial judge was reassigned to a different division .  
Under our precedent, reassignment of the judge to a different division 
renders the issue of disqualification moot.  See Polanco v. Citizens Prop.  Ins. 
Corp. , 271 So. 3d 1117, 1118 (Fla. 3d DCA 2019) (“Because the trial court 
has been reassigned to a different division, we dismiss , as moot, that portion 
of the petition .”); Reiser v. State , 894 So. 2d 302, 302 (Fla. 4th DCA 2005) 
(“Because the trial judge has been reassigned to a different  division, we find 
that the issue of disqualification and transfer is moot .”).  Accordingly , we 
dismiss  the petition.  
 Petition d ismissed .

items.summary:
Practical effect: a judge ruling on a motion to disqualify must confine the inquiry to the legal sufficiency of the motion, or the ruling itself creates a ground for that judge's disqualification; but once the judge is reassigned to a different division the disqualification issue is moot, so prohibition lies only while that judge remains on the case. Arose in post-decretal dissolution proceedings but announces general judicial-disqualification and mootness doctrine. Not final pending any timely rehearing motion.

Holding: On an original petition for prohibition, a trial judge who, in ruling on a motion to disqualify, looks beyond the mere legal sufficiency of the motion and passes upon the truth of the alleged facts exceeds the proper scope of inquiry and thereby establishes grounds for the judge's own disqualification, unless a successor-judge rule would permit a truth inquiry. Where, however, the judge is reassigned to a different division after ruling, the disqualification issue is moot and the petition must be dismissed.

Disposition: Petition for writ of prohibition dismissed as moot.
