Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 28, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D24 -1000  
Lower Tribunal No. 14-22252 -CA-01 
________________  
 
 
Homeowners Choice Property & Casualty Insurance 
Company , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Sandra Moise , 
Appellee.  
 
 
 An Appeal from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, Migna 
Sanchez -Llorens , Judge.  
 
 Butler Weihmuller Katz Craig , LLP, and Mihaela Cabulea (Tampa) , for 
appellant.  
 
 Alvarez , Feltman , Da Silva & Costa, P.L., and Paul B. Feltman , for 
appellee.  
 
 
Before  SCALES, C.J., and MILLER and BOKOR , JJ.  
 
 BOKOR, J . 
 2  After a verdict in favor of the insured, Homeowner’s Choice Property & 
Casualty Insurance Company appeals the denial of its motion for summary 
judgment on the issue of exclusion for damages under the insurance policy’s 
earth movement and settlement provisi ons. The insured’s expert report 
claimed damage to the property from vibrations “without displacement of the 
earth.” The insured also provided deposition testimony that she felt vibrations 
and shaking during the event caused by heavy construction equipment  at 
the adjacent property.  The trial court denied summary judgment for the 
insurer, concluding that the earth movement and settlement exclusions didn’t 
encompass damages caused from vibrations without earth movement. For 
the reasons that follow, we affirm the orders on review.   
I 
This appeal challenges a final judgment in favor of the insured in an 
action for breach of a home insurance policy.  The insurer provided coverage 
for the home , located  in Miami , Florida . The applicable policy, which became 
effective May 8, 2013, provides that direct physical losses to the subject 
property occurring within the policy period are covered except where 
otherwise excluded. Relevant here, the  policy excludes damages “caused 
directly or indirectly by any of the following  . . . regardless of any other cause 
or event contributing concurrently or in any sequence to the loss,” including:   
 3 b. Earth Movement and Settlement, meaning:   
 
(1) Earthquake, including land shock waves or tremors before, 
during or after a volcanic eruption;   
 
(2) Landslide;   
 
(3) Mine subsidence;   
 
(4) Mudflow or mudslide;   
 
(5) Any other earth movement including “Sinkhole Loss”, 
“Sinkhole Activity”, earth sinking, rising or shifting;   
 
(6) Clay shrinkage or other expansion or contraction of soils or 
organic materials;   
 
(7) Decay of buried or organic materials;   
 
(8) Settling, cracking or expansion of foundations;   
 
(9) Erosion or movement resulting from improper compaction, 
site selection or any other external forces [.] 
 
The policy also excludes damages for losses “involving collapse” or caused 
by “[s]ettling, shrinking, bulging or expansion, including resultant cracking, of 
pavements, patios, foundations, walls, floors, roofs or ceilings.”  
The insured brought the initial complaint on August 27, 2014, alleging 
that the insurer failed to cover damages to the property that occurred on 
March 1, 2014. Specifically, the insured claimed that the property incurred 
cracking and related damage to the floors, walls and ceiling because of  
vibrations from demolition activity at a neighboring house. In response to the 
 4 claim, the insurer commissioned an inspection from Bracken Engineering, 
Inc., which inspected the property on May 6, 2014 , and concluded that the 
damages were caused by material shrinkage or settlement. The insurer’s 
field adjuster also inspected the property on May 20, 2014 , and denied the 
insured’s claim on June 6, 2014, concluding that the damages were excluded 
as being caused by material shrinkage or settlement rather than vibrations.  
The operative third amended complaint stylized the claim as a 
declaratory judgment action rather than a breach of contract claim, though 
the complaint still sought “damages attributable to the Loss, if covered.” In 
response, the insurer filed an answer and affirmative defenses, including 
several defenses claiming that the insured failed to fulfill her post -loss 
obligation to timely report the loss, protect the property, and provide records. 
The insurer also claimed that the damages were excluded under the ea rth 
movement and settlement provisions of the policy because they were caused 
by cracking or settling of the foundations as a result of vibrations. The insurer 
subsequently moved for summary judgment on its sixth and seventh 
affirmative defenses, arguing that recovery was barred under the earth 
movement and settlement exclusions.  
In support of summary judgment, the insurer proffered reports and 
deposition testimony from the insured’s expert, Alfredo Brizuela, who 
 5 inspected the property on July 24, 2014. Brizuela’s report concluded that the 
damages were caused by “the vibration created by the impact of the heavy 
construction equipment” at the adjacent property which “travelled through the 
lime rock subsoil strata an d induced vibration s into the property foundation 
structure.” He also attested  that the damages were caused by “vibrations 
from the heavy machinery working in the vicinity of the property,” which 
entered the frame of the property in the form of an energy wave and caused 
it to resonate, damaging rigid wood and tile structures. In his affidavit 
describing the report, Brizuela also clarified that the vibration was the sole 
case of the damages and “[t]he vibrations damaged the property without 
displacement of the earth. ” (emphasis added). The insured had also testified 
at her deposition that she was in the property during the demolition, felt 
vibrations and observed picture frames shifting and shaking during the event, 
and first noticed the damage  on March 3, 2014, a few days after the 
demolition  next door . After a hearing, the court denied summary judgment 
for the insurer on December 6, 2019, in a brief order that also found that 
damage caused by “vibrations” was not among the exclusions under the 
policy’s earth movement and settlement provisions.  
Subsequently, the insured also moved for summary judgment as to the 
five affirmative defenses relating to the alleged failure to comply with post -
 6 loss obligations (affirmative defenses 2, 3, 4, 5, and 14), alleging that those 
defenses were waived by denying coverage on the basis of the cause of the 
damages. The insured’s motion also argued that several other affirmative 
defenses predicated on differ ent policy exclusions were inapplicable, relying 
on additional deposition testimony and an affidavit from David Compton, the 
president of Bracken Engineering, who testified that the cause of the 
damages was soil movement in the foundations resulting from v ibration. The 
court granted summary judgment as to those defenses on January 10, 2020.  
Prior to trial, the insured moved in limine to exclude all testimony 
relating to both the post -loss obligations and “that vibration is an excluded 
loss under the policy’s earth movement and settlement provision,” pursuant 
to the court’s December 6, 2019 order finding that vibration was not an 
excluded cause of loss. The court granted these motions. The case 
ultimately proceeded to a jury trial from November 7 –18, 2022, and the jury 
returned a verdict finding that the damages were not excluded under the 
policy. Final judgment was entered May 1, 2024. The insurer timely 
appealed . 
II 
 The insurer first claims that the trial court erred by denying summary 
judgment under the earth movement and settlement provision, as well as 
 7 ruling that “vibrations” were not an excluded cause of loss and limiting 
admission of related evidence at trial.  We review the trial court’s summary 
judgment order de novo. Fla. Bar v. Greene , 926 So. 2d 1195, 1200 (Fla. 
2006).  We review the trial court’s discretionary rulings on the motions in 
limine for abuse of discretion. Patrick v. State , 104 So. 3d 1046, 1056 (Fla. 
2012).  
 The insurer relies on  Hernandez v. Citizens Property Insurance Corp. , 
306 So. 3d 137, 138 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020), which affirmed summary judgment 
for the insurer under a similar policy containing an earth movement provision 
that excluded coverage for losses “caused directly or indirectly by any of the 
following,” including “Ea rth sinking, rising or shifting” or “settling, cracking, or 
expansion of foundations .” There  though, the insurer’s engineer attested that 
the damages were “caused by the off -site blasting vibrations [that] led to the 
house shifting, resulting in cracks in walls and flooring .” Id. at 139.  The losses  
in Hernandez  were unambiguously excluded under the plain terms of the 
policy. Id.; see also  State Farm Fire & Cas. Co. v. Castillo , 829 So. 2d 242, 
247 (Fla. 3d DCA 2002) (“Castillo I ”) (directing summary judgment for insurer 
and finding that the earth movement and settlement provision at issue there 
unambiguously excluded damages caused by earth movement resulting 
from blasting) ; Castillo v. State Farm Florida Ins. Co. , 971 So. 2d 820 , 822 –
 8 23 (Fla. 3d DCA 2007)  (“Castillo II ”) (finding no exclusion under similar policy 
that involved allegations that “vibrations and shockwaves caused by blasting 
and without displacement of the earth resulted in damage to an insured 
dwelling” ). Here, relying on materially identical policy language and like 
Castillo II , the insured’s expert opined that the damage was caused not by 
earth movement, settling, or any other excluded cause, but by 
“vibrations  . . . without displacement of the earth.”  
 This court also dealt with a similar situation more recently in Tower Hill 
Prime Ins urance  Co. v. Bermudez , 388 So. 3d 165 (Fla.  3d DCA 2023). In 
Bermudez , this court  affirmed the denial of the insurer ’s motion for directed 
verdict (the trial equivalent of summary judgment) where the insured ’s expert 
testified that the damage was caused by “land shock waves from blasting ” at 
a nearby quarry, not by soil or earth movement. Id. at 170. The court held 
that the case presented a battle of the experts, and that a directed verdict in 
favor of the insured was not appropriate where the  jury could reasonably 
have concluded that shock waves  alone  caused the damage . Id. at 171.   
More recently, in  Izquierdo v. Universal Ins urance  Co. of N orth 
America , 429 So. 3d 1122 , 1124  (Fla. 3d DCA  2026), this court  reaffirmed 
this principle  and reversed summary judgment in favor of the insurer where 
a factual dispute existed as to whether “ the cracking damage was caused by 
 9 land shock waves, without attendant earth movement .” Under such 
circumstances, like here, if a jury were to make such a finding, then  “the 
subject earth movement exclusion will not apply. ” Id. Here, t he parties 
presented conflicting evidence, with the insurer’s expert indicating that the 
damage was  caused by material settlement or other preexisting conditions, 
and the insured’s expert attesting that the damages were caused solely by 
vibration.  
The insurer next argues that notwithstanding the summary judgment 
ruling, the trial court reversibly  erred in granting a motion in limine limiting 
the presentation of evidence  at trial  related to vibration , effectively preclud ing 
the insurer from arguing the applicability of the earth movement and 
settlement provision at all. However,  this overstates the impact of the court’s 
ruling . The court’s ruling only held that “vibration ,” specifically , was not 
among  the exclusions, and the court did not limit other evidence relating to 
the earth movement provision generally. Moreover, the insurer’s position 
throughout the case was not that vibration did not occur at all, but that soil 
settlement was the cause of loss,  rather than vibrations alone. The insurer’s 
expert, Mr. Compton , testified to this effect at trial as the insurer’s only expert 
witness, agreeing that vibration occurred but that “vibration did not cause this 
damage.” Other than identifying a possibly overbroad ruling in limine, t he 
 10 insurer does not identify either how its defense was limited or  any evidence  
or testimony  it was unable to present because of  these rulings . Even if the 
court erred in limiting hypothetically relevant evidence or testimony , it does 
not appear that the insurer was prejudiced by such  exclusion. A nd an error 
is harmless when there is no reasonable possibility it contributed to the 
verdict. See, e.g. , Special v. W. Boca Med. Ctr. , 160 So. 3d 1251, 1256 (Fla. 
2014).  
The insurer then argues that the court improperly granted partial 
summary judgment as to the affirmative defenses relating to the post -loss 
obligations. But “[a]n insurer’s repudiation of coverage waives the insurer’s 
right to insist upon the insured’s compliance with policy conditions, such as 
filing a proof of loss.” Goldberg v. Universal Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. , 302 So. 
3d 919, 925 (Fla. 4th DCA 2020)  (“Here, by failing to pay any amount for the 
personal property loss, Universal effectively denied coverage for that loss. 
Such a denial of coverage waives the insurer’s right to insist upon the 
insured’s compliance with policy conditions, such as submittin g 
supplemental claims.”) . The parties do not dispute that the damages 
occurred on March 1, 2014, that the insured made the claim and submitted 
proofs of loss on April 22, 2014,  that the insurer inspected the property on 
May 6, 2014, and that the insurer denied the claim on June 6, 2014. While 
 11 the denial letter indicated that there was additional documentation not 
received, the letter was a “declination of coverage” based on a substantive 
determination that specifically indicated that “there is no coverage for the 
cracking/settlement damage because the causes for the damage determined 
by Bracken are specifically excluded under your policy,” citing both the earth 
movement and settlement provision and separate provisions for preexisting 
damages and regular wear and tear.  
The denial letter included an additional section indicating that the 
insured had not yet received all requested documentation from the insured, 
as well as boilerplate language indicating that the insured does not intend to 
waive any of its rights under the  policy; however, even that disclaimer 
language specifically described the letter as a “declination of coverage.” The 
inclusion of this language referencing the post -loss obligations and 
reservation of rights was likely not sufficient to avoid a finding  of waiver for 
denying the claim. See, e.g. , Castro v. Homeowners Choice Prop. & Cas. 
Ins. Co. , 228 So. 3d 596, 599 (Fla. 2d DCA 2017) (“When an insurance 
carrier investigates a claim of loss and denies coverage because it concludes 
that a covered loss has not occurred, the insurance carrier cannot assert the 
insured’s failure to comply with the po licy’s conditions precedent to filing suit 
as a basis for summary judgment.”).  
 12 Finally, we note that the court did not err by awarding money damages 
in the judgment. The insurer claims that because the third amended 
complaint was stylized as a declaratory judgment action, the trial court 
improperly granted relief not requested by the parties by also award ing the 
insured the $240,000 in damages found by the jury verdict, plus prejudgment 
interest. However, as the insured notes, the complaint here also claims that 
the insurer improperly denied coverage and requests money damages 
“attributable to the Loss, if  covered.” Moreover, “ [a] money judgment may be 
obtained for damages sought as incidental or supplemental relief pursuant 
to a declaratory decree.” McAllister v. Breakers Seville Ass’n, Inc. , 41 So. 3d 
405, 408 (Fla. 4th DCA 2010) (quotation omitted); see also  § 86.061, Fla. 
Stat. (“Further relief based on a declaratory judgment may be granted when 
necessary or proper.”). Because monetary damages were sought in the 
operative complaint, we affirm this aspect  of the judgment as well.  
III 
 For the reasons explained above, we affirm the orders on appeal in 
all respects.  
 Affirmed.

items.summary:
Coverage judgment affirmed against the homeowner insurer: expert testimony that vibrations without displacement of the earth caused the cracking put the earth-movement/settlement exclusion out of reach as a battle-of-experts jury question; the insurer's substantive denial of coverage forfeited its post-loss-obligation defenses; the jury's damages plus prejudgment interest was proper supplemental relief even though the operative complaint was styled as declaratory; and the in limine limits on the insurer's proof were harmless and non-prejudicial.

Holding: Summary judgment for a homeowner insurer is improper under an earth movement/settlement exclusion where the insured's expert opines that the damage was caused by vibrations or shock waves without displacement of the earth, because whether the loss falls within the exclusion then presents a battle-of-experts fact question for the jury; separately, an insurer's repudiation or substantive denial of coverage waives its right to insist on the insured's compliance with post-loss conditions precedent, and boilerplate reservation-of-rights or non-waiver language in the declination is generally insufficient to preserve them; and a money judgment may be granted as further or supplemental relief under a declaratory decree (section 86.061) when damages were requested in the operative complaint.

Disposition: Affirmed.

vs. 
J&J 111 Associates, Inc., 
Appellee. 
An Appeal from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, Peter R. 
Lopez, J udge . 
ROSENBAUM INTERNATIONAL LAW FIRM, P.A., and Michael 
Rosenbaum; Jeffery P. Shapiro, P.A.,  and Jeffery P. Shapiro, for appellant. 
EGOZI & BENNETT, P.A., a nd Bernard L. E gozi a nd B randen J. 
Stillman,  for appellee. 
Before FERNANDEZ, GORDO and BOKOR, JJ. 
P
ER CURIAM.  
 2 Affirmed.   See  All-Dixie Ins. Agency,  Inc. v. Moffatt , 212 So.  2d 347, 
350 (Fla. 3d DCA 1968)  (It is a “well -established rule that where the parties 
to a contract have selected the language contained therein, and where that 
language is clear and unambiguous, the courts are without authority to 
rewrite the terms of the agreement to give them a meaning other than the 
one expressed. ”); accord Antoniazzi  v. Wardak , 259 So.  3d 206, 211 (Fla. 
3d DCA 2018) ( “If a contract is clear, complete and unambiguous, there is 
no need for judicial construction.” ); see Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.510(a)  (“The court 
shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a 
matter of law. ”); Star Cas. Ins. Co.  v. Gables Ins. Recovery, Inc., 346 So.  3d 
1244, 124 6 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022) (citing Anderson  v. Liberty Lobby,  Inc., 477 
U.S. 242, 251 (1986)) (“ An issue of fact is ‘genuine ’ . . . when a reasonable 
jury could potentially return a verdict in favor of the non- moving party  . . . 
[and] ‘material ’ when it may affect the outcome of the case under the 
applicable substantive law. ”); see Pan Am.  W., Ltd. v. Cardinal Com. 
Dev., LLC, 50 So.  3d 68, 71 (Fla. 3d DCA 2010) (“ Where a contractual 
provision is unambiguous, no issue of fact is presented as to the meaning of 
the language or the parties ’ intent, and the moving party is entitled to 
judgment as a matter of law. ”); accord  Dirico v. Redland Ests ., Inc., 154 
 3 So. 3d 355, 359 (Fla. 3d DCA 2014)  (“Absent ambiguity, there were no 
genuine issues of material fact that precluded summary judgment here. ”).

items.summary:
Clear contract language is enforced as written on summary judgment; because an unambiguous agreement leaves nothing to construe, a dispute over its meaning is decided as a question of law rather than submitted to a factfinder.

Holding: Where the parties have selected clear and unambiguous contract language, courts may not rewrite the agreement to give it a meaning other than as expressed and no judicial construction is needed; an unambiguous provision raises no genuine issue of material fact, so under rule 1.510(a) the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.

Disposition: Affirmed

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 28, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D25 -1982  
Lower Tribunal No. 23-11400 -CA-01 
________________  
 
 
Amanda Miguel Collado Laguna , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
The Berry Farm, LLC , 
Appellee.  
 
 
 
An Appeal from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, Javier A. 
Enriquez , Judge.  
 
Eaton & Wolk, PL and Daniel R. Schwartz  and Douglas F. Eaton , for 
appellant.  
 
AndersonGlenn LLP , and John J. Glenn and Amanda N. Rumker 
(Boca Raton) , for appellee.  
 
 
Before  MILLER, LOBREE and GOODEN , JJ. 
 
LOBREE, J.  
 2 Amanda Miguel Collado Laguna (“Collado”)  appeals a final summary 
judgment entered in favor of The Berry Farm, LLC (“Berry”) in this negligence 
action in which Collado seeks damages for the personal injuries she suffered 
when using a slide located on Berry’s premises.  The trial court entered 
summary judgment for Berry on the basis that it was immune from liability 
under section 570.88(1), Florida Statutes (2021).   We conclude  that the trial 
court erred in granting summary judgment because there are genuine issues 
of material fact as to Berry’s compliance with the posting and notice 
requirements of section 570.89, Florida Statutes (2021) , which are 
necessary to invoke the privilege of immunity provided by section 570.88(1).  
BACKGROUND  
Berry is a working farm located in Miami.  On October 10, 2021, 
Collado visited Berry  with her three year old son  to attend Berry’s annual 
Harvest  Festival .  While there, Collado fractured her right ankle when her 
feet hit the ground after going down a slide in the children’s playground area. 
Collado subsequently filed an amended complaint for negligence against 
Berry alleg ing that it: (1) failed to maintain reasonable care of its premises 
and allowed a dangerous condition to be on its premises for an unreasonable 
amount of time, causing her to fall, and that Berry  had a duty to warn her 
about the dangerous conditions; and (2) failed in its obligation to implement 
 3 proper safety protocols when operating the slide and failed in its obligation 
to ensure that the slide was operated in a safe manner.  Berry answered and 
raised numerous affirmative defenses, including that it was immune from 
liability under section 570.88 , Florida Statutes .  
Berry moved for summary judgment, arguing in part that as an 
“agritourism operator” as defined by section 570.86(2), Florida Statutes 
(2021) , it was shielded from liability for Collado’s injury under section 
570.88(1)  because Collado’s injury resulted from an inherent risk of an 
agritourism activity,  and on the date of the incident it had posted “at its 
entrance and next to the playground area” signs  containing the notice of 
inherent risk as required by section 570.89.   In support , Berry relied on the 
affidavit of Karl Wiegandt, the owner and managing member of Berry.  
Wiegandt attested that Berry’s premises includes playground areas to 
provide entertainment and recreational activities for children , and those 
playgrounds have slides for use by children.  Wiegandt further attested that 
on October 11, 2021, Berry had “several signs posted on the property 
containing the notice of inherent risk specified in Section 570.89, Florida 
Statutes, including at its entrance and next to the playground area where 
Plaintiff was allegedly  injured.”  The body of the  affidavit included three  
 4 photos of “ examples” of the signs that were posted “throughout The Berry’s 
Farm’s property .”  
Collado responded in opposition to Berry’s summary judgment motion.  
Relevant here, Collado asserted that there is a genuine issue of material fact 
as to whether any signs  were posted in accordance with section 570.89 on 
the date of the incident because: (1) the photos that Berry relies on to show 
that the signs were posted  on October  21, 2021, have a date stamp of June 
15, 2022 ; (2) Wiegandt was unable to testify in his deposition as to when the 
signs were put up; (3) a screenshot  from Berry’s Instagram account  six days 
before the incident show s only one sign posted in the playground , and an 
inspection of the premises on May 8, 2025, showed that sign stated  that 
parental supervision is required for use of  the playground ; and (4) Collado 
testified  in her deposition  that she did not see a sign at the entrance of the 
property or at the playground site.  In support of her response , Collado relied 
on: Wiegandt’s deposition; a photograph of a sign  stating that parental 
supervision is required for use of the playground ; her own deposition; 
photographs  of warning signs  provided by Berry;  screenshot s from Berry’s 
Instagram account from August 1, 2021 , September  15, 2021 , and October 
4, 2021 .   
 5 Collado testified  in her deposition  that she did not recall what the 
entrance to Berry looks like and she did not remember any signs outside the 
entrance.  When asked if she noticed “any warning signs on the day of the 
incident before you slid down the slide,” Collado responded that “[t]her e was 
nothing there.”  Collado was then shown a defense exhibit of images of two 
warning signs.  When asked if she had seen the signs on the day of the 
incident, Collado answered that she had not, and then testified that the signs 
were “not present on the day” of the incident and “[t]hey were nowhere 
inside.”   In his deposition, Wiegandt testified about  the photographs  of the 
signs  date stamped  June 15, 2022.   He stated  that the signs are located to  
the right and left of the main pavilion , and that the signs were placed on the 
property  before  Berry’s first opening.  
After a hearing, the trial court granted summary judgment for Berry.  As 
to the  requirement s of section 570.89, the trial court found that Weigant’s 
“unrebutted” affidavit  showed “ that signs compliant with Section 570.89, 
Florida Statutes, were posted at the entrance and by the playground as early 
as 2020.”  The trial court found that Collado “presented no admissible 
evidence showing that such signs were not posted on the date of th e 
incident.”  Specifically, Collado ’s “inability to recall seeing a sign,” and 
reliance on Instagram images that do not depict the entire premises or 
 6 playground area, did not create a genuine issue of material fact.  The trial 
court concluded that  because Collado was injured while participating in an 
agritourism activity which had an inherent risk and Berry posted warning 
signs in accordance with section 570.89 , Berry’s liability for Collado’s injury 
was precluded under section 570.88 .  Thereafter , the trial court entered final 
judgment for Berry.  
STANDARD OF REVIEW  
“The court shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows that 
there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled 
to judgment as a matter of law. ” Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.510 (a).  “Accordingly, ‘the 
correct test for the existence of a genuine factual dispute is whether “the 
evidence is such that a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the 
nonmoving party. ”’” Feldman v. Schocket , 366 So. 3d 1104, 1107 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2022) (quoting In re Amends. to Fla. Rule of Civ. Proc. 1.510 , 317 So. 
3d 72, 75 (Fla. 2021) ); see also  Ortega v. JW Marriott Inv., LLC , 405 So. 3d 
473, 477 (Fla. 3d DCA 2025)  (“Properly understood, summary judgment is 
akin to a pre -trial directed verdict. ” (quoting CG Tides LLC v. SHEDDF3 VNB, 
LLC, 388 So. 3d 1081, 1084 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024) ). 
Because  Berry raised section 570.88 as an affirmative defense , it has 
the burden of proof at trial to show its entitlement to  immunity from liability 
 7 under that section.   See Custer Med. Ctr. v. United Auto. Ins. Co. , 62 So. 3d 
1086, 1096 (Fla. 2010) .  Where  the party  moving for summary judgment has 
the burden of proof at trial,  “the movant must affirmatively show the absence 
of a genuine issue of material fact: it must support its motion with credible 
evidence that would entitle it to a directed verdict if not controverted at trial. ”  
K & M Elec. Supply, Inc. v. Brown Elec. Sols., LLC , 432 So. 3d 1045, 1049 
(Fla. 4th DCA 2026) ; see also  United States v. Four Parcels of Real Prop. in 
Greene & Tuscaloosa Ctys. in State of Ala. , 941 F.2d 1428, 1438 (11th Cir. 
1991)  (stating that when the party moving for summary judgment has the 
burden of proof at trial, it “ must show that, on all the essential elements of its 
case on which it bears the burden of proof at trial, no reasonable jury could 
find for the nonmoving party.   If the moving party makes such an affirmative 
showing, it is entitled to summary judgment unless the nonmoving party, in 
response, ‘come[s] forward with significant, probative evidence 
demonstrating the existence of a triable issue of fact. ’” (cleaned up) (quoting 
Chanel, Inc. v. Italian Activewear of Fl a., Inc. , 931 F.2d 1472, 1477 (11th Cir. 
1991) )).  “The evidence in the summary judgment record is interpreted in the 
light most favorable to the non -moving party.” CG Tides LLC , 388 So. 3d at 
1085.  
ANALYSIS  
 8 Collado argues that the trial court erred in entering summary judgment  
for Berry  because genuine issue s of material fact exist as to whether on the 
day of her injury Berry was in compliance with the notice and posting 
requirements of 570.89 .  Specifically, Collado contends that the trial court 
disregarded her deposition testimony that there were no warning signs 
present on the day of the incident.  We agree.  
Sections 570.85 –89, Florida Statutes, govern agritourism in Florida.   
Section 570.88 affords a limitation on legal liability to an agritourism operator 
where a plaintiff’s injur y resulted from the inherent risks of an agritourism 
activi ty.  That section provides as follows, in part:  
(1) Except as provided in subsection (2), an agritourism operator, 
his or her employer or employee, or the owner of the underlying 
land on which the agritourism occurs is not liable for injury or 
death of, or damage or loss to, a participant resulting from  the 
inherent risks of agritourism activities  if the notice of risk required 
under s. 570.89 is posted as required.  Except as provided in 
subsection (2), a participant, or a participant ’s representative, 
may not maintain an action against or recover from an 
agritourism operator, his or her employer or employee, or the 
owner of the underlying land on which the agritourism occurs for 
the injury or death of, or damage or loss to, an agritour ism 
participant resulting exclusively from any of the inherent risks of 
agritourism activities.  
 
§ 570.88(1), Fla. Stat. ( emphasis added) .  In order to “invok[e] the privileges 
of immunity provided by this section,” an “agritourism operator . . .  or the 
owner of the underlying land on which the agritourism occurs” must comply 
 9 with sections 570.89(1),(2).  § 570.89(3), Fla. Stat.  Those sections provide 
as follows:  
(1)(a) Each agritourism operator shall post and maintain signs 
that contain the notice of inherent risk specified in subsection (2) . 
A sign shall be placed in a clearly visible location at the entrance 
to the agritourism location and at the site of the agritourism 
activity . The notice of inherent risk must consist of a sign in black 
letters, with each letter a minimum of 1 inch in height, with 
sufficient color contrast to be clearly visible.  
 . . . . 
(2) The sign and contract required under subsection (1) must 
contain the following notice of inherent risk:  
 
WARNING  
 
Under Florida law, an agritourism operator is not liable for injury 
or death of, or damage or loss to, a participant in an agritourism 
activity conducted at this agritourism location if such injury, 
death, damage, or loss results from the inherent risks of  the 
agritourism activity. Inherent risks of agritourism activities 
include, among others, risks of injury inherent to land, equipment, 
and animals, as well as the potential for you to act in a negligent 
manner that may contribute to your injury, death, da mage, or 
loss. You are assuming the risk of participating in this agritourism 
activity.  
§ 570.89(1)(a),(2), Fla. Stat. (emphasis added).  
Here, the trial court found that Wiegandt’s affidavit demonstrated “ that 
signs compliant with Section 570.89, Florida  Statutes, were posted at the 
entrance and by the playground as early as 2020 .”  The trial court then found 
that Collado’s “inability to recall seeing a sign, or pointing to photos that 
simply do not capture signage” did not create a genuine issue of material fact 
 10 on the issue of Berry compliance with section 570.89, and concluded that 
Weigandt’s testimony was “undisputed and unrebutted.” In so concluding, 
the trial court failed to consider the entirety of Collado’s deposition testimony.  
Although Collado testified that she did not remember any signs outside the 
entrance to Berry, she further testified that warning signs were not present 
at Berry on the day of incident  and that “they were nowhere inside.”  
Credibility determinations are for the jury, and a reasonable jury could 
conclude that Collado’s testimony was more believable than Weingardt’s 
statement that signs containing the notice requirement of section 570.89 
were posted at Berry’s entrance and the  playground area. “ While ‘[t]he n ew 
Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.510 indubitably endows the trial court with 
considerably broader authority to resolve a case on summary judgment,  the 
general rule remains intact: credibility determinations and weighing the 
evidence are jury functions, not those of a judge. ’” Katha, LLC v. SHEDDF3 -
AE, LLC , 394 So. 3d 707, 710 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024)  (cleaned up) (quoting 
Navarro v. Borges , 388 So. 3d 1044, 1047 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024)).   Additionally , 
the three images of “example” signs contained in the body of Wiegandt’s 
affidavit do not contradict Collado’s testimony that there w ere no sign s the 
day of the incident .  Two of the images reflect a June 2022 date , which is 
eight months after the incident,  and the location of the third, undated 
 11 “example” of a sign is unclear as to its location.  See, e.g. , Del Rio v. Russell 
Eng’g, Inc. , 351 So. 3d 1180, 1183 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022)  (reversing summary 
judgment entered in favor of defendant where neither party’s photograph 
established how or where relevant manhole appeared on date of accident 
and therefore photographic evidence did not contradict plaintiff’s testimony 
as to manhole’s location; “[Plaintiff]’s  testimony was sufficient to establish a 
disputed issue of material fact concerning the location of the manhole cover.  
The photographic evidence produced did not definitively disprove [plaintiff]’s  
testimony.  Rather, when  [plaintiff] 's testimony and the photographic 
evidence at issue are taken together, it is clear they present an issue of fact 
for a jury to decide. ”). 
Viewing the record in the light most favorable to the non -movant , there 
remains a triable issue of fact as to  whether Berry was in compliance with 
section 570.89 on the day of the incident such that a reasonable jury could 
return a verdict for Collado.1  See Chowdhury v. BankUnited, N.A. , 366 So. 
3d 1130, 1134 (Fla. 3d DCA 2023) (“Our new summary judgment standard 
mirrors the standard for a directed verdict such that the inquiry focuses on 
 
1 As we reverse on this single basis , we do not reach Collado’s alternative  
contention that the trial court erred in entering summary judgment because  
her injury did not result from  “inherent risks of agritourism activities.”  § 
570.88(1), Fla. Stat. (2021).  
 12 ‘whether the evidence presents a sufficient disagreement to require 
submission to a jury or whether it is so one -sided that one party must prevail 
as a matter of law.’” (quoting In re Amends. to Fla. Rule of Civ. Proc. 1.510 , 
309 So. 3d 192, 192 (Fla. 2020))) .  We therefore  find that the trial court erred 
in granting summary judgment for Berry as a matter of law.  Accordingly, we 
reverse the summary judgment entered in Berry’s favor and remand for 
further proceedings.  
Reversed and remanded .

items.summary:
Practical effect: an agritourism operator cannot obtain summary judgment on statutory immunity when the injured participant testifies that the required inherent-risk warning signs were absent on the day of injury; because the operator raised immunity as an affirmative defense it carries the trial burden and must negate that dispute, and credibility and weighing remain jury functions under the directed-verdict-like Rule 1.510 standard. Not final pending any timely rehearing motion.

Holding: Agritourism immunity under section 570.88 is conditioned on compliance with the posting and notice requirements of section 570.89 (clearly visible, format-compliant signs at the entrance and at the activity site). Where the defendant raises that immunity as an affirmative defense, it bears the burden of proof at trial, so on summary judgment it must affirmatively establish the absence of a genuine issue of material fact with credible evidence that would entitle it to a directed verdict, viewing the record in the light most favorable to the non-movant. Because the plaintiff's deposition that no compliant signs were present on the day, corroborated by date-stamped photographs and social-media screenshots, presented a genuine dispute that the operator's affidavit of (later-dated, unclearly located) example signs did not conclusively negate-and because credibility and weighing are jury functions-summary judgment for the operator was improper.

Disposition: Final summary judgment in favor of the defendant reversed and remanded.

Author: Judge Lobree

BD FL Notes, LLC, 136NW 126 ST Project, LLC, Hernando 
Anthony Ca rrillo, Sherry Johnson Carrillo, and   
Capital Holdings Funding, LLC , 
Appellees.  
 
 
  An Appeal from  a non -final order  from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Robert T. Watson, Judge . 
  Vogel Law Firm,  PLLC,  and David Michael Vogel  and Hal S. Vogel  
(Davie) , for appellants.  
 
 2 COHN & DUSSI, LLC, and James J. Webb (Boston, MA.), for appellee  
BD FL Notes, LLC . 
 
Before LOGUE, GORDO and GOODEN , JJ.  
 
 GOODEN, J . 
 The Appellants are contract p urchasers of pre- construction 
condominium units at Wynwood Atriums, which were being constructed by 
the Appellee Developer, 136 NW 126 ST Project, LLC.    They appeal an 
order granting in part and denying in part their motion to intervene.   The 
Purchasers assert that the order effectively denied their motion.1   
For the purchase and construction of Wynwood Atriums , the Developer 
executed a mortgage with Triumph Capital Partners .  The mortgage stated:  
Section 2.4  Liens . Mortgagor shall not, directly or indirectly, 
create or suffer or permit to be created, or to stand, against the 
Property . . . any lien, charge, mortgage, deed of trust, adverse 
claim or other encumbrance . . . whether senior or junior in lien to this Mortgage. . . .  
. . . 
 Section 5.4  Subordinate Financing . If Mortgagor, without the 
prior written consent of Mortgagee, executes or delivers any pledge, security agreement, mortgage or deed of trust covering all or any portion of the Property . . . Mortgagee may . . . declare the Obligation to be immediately du e and payable.  
 
 
1 We review this order for an abuse of discretion.  See Mendoza v. Kendall 
Park Plaza, Ltd. , 429 So. 3d 1082, 1084 (Fla. 3d DCA 2026).   
 3  To purchase the units, the Purchasers executed purchase agreements 
with the Developer.  These agreements  contained a s ubordination clause : 
18. Subordination of Purchase Agreement to Mortgage Liens : 
The Purchaser agrees that all terms and provisions of this 
Agreement are, and shall be, subject and subordinate to the lien of any mortgage heretofore or hereafter made or placed Upon the subject property, subject lands, or the Condominium, and to any advances heretofore or hereafter made thereon, to the full 
extent thereof, without the execution of any further legal 
documents by the Purchaser.  Nothing by reason of the 
execution of this Agreement shall be construed as giving or 
granting unto the Purchaser any lien upon the Unit, Purchaser 
hereby expressly waiving and relinquishing any lien or lien rights, 
legal or equitable, which might otherwise accrue or be available to Purchaser by operation of law or otherwise.  
 
 The Developer did not complete construction by the mortgage’s 
maturity date .  Triumph Capital extended the maturity date of the loan , but 
ultimately initiated foreclosure in February 2022.  During that litigation, 
Triumph Capital assigned its interest to the Appellee, BD FL Notes.  
Thereafter, by way of an agreement, BD FL Notes allowed the Developer to 
continue to close on units to  pay down the m ortgage.   The Developer , 
however, failed to c lose on the agreed upon  number of units .  Thus, BD FL 
Notes declared the agreement  in default .  The trial court entered final 
judgment of foreclosure on July 6, 2023 . 
 4  Soon  after, the Purchasers moved to intervene.  They sought  to vacate 
the foreclosure so that they  could close on their units.2  The trial court 
conducted five evidentiary hearings.  It granted the Purchasers’ request in  
part, finding that  they had a junior interest and adding them as parties to the 
post-foreclosure judgment.   
The Purchasers argue that they should have been added as junior 
lienholders.  Post-judgment intervention is permitted only in rare 
circumstances, when the proposed intervenor demonstrates a sufficient 
interest in the property .  See Wags Transp. Sys., Inc. v. City of Miami Beach , 
88 So. 2d 751, 752 (Fla. 1956) (permitting post -judgment intervention by 
non-party because “the petition to intervene showed such an interest in the 
res that the ends of justice require that it be granted”) . 
 But this argument fails because their purchase agreements expressly 
disclaim and waive any lien rights .  In the purchase agreement, the 
Purchasers agreed:  “Nothing by reason of the execution of this Agreement 
shall be construed as giving or granting unto the Purchaser any lien upon the Unit, Purchaser hereby expressly waiving and relinquishing any lien or lien rights, legal or equitable, which might otherwise  accrue or be available 
 
2 While not raised in their m otion to intervene, the Purchasers later stipulated 
that they were aware of the litigation since October 2022 —nine months 
before the stipulated final judgment of foreclosure.  
 5 to Purchaser by operation of law or otherwise. ”  “We are bound to give effect 
to that agreement. ”  Summit Aviation, Inc. v. MSP Recovery Aviation, LLC, 
51 Fla. L. Weekly D1815 , *2 (Fla. 3d DCA Sept. 2, 2026) .  See Barakat v. 
Broward Cnty. Hous. Auth. , 771 So. 2d 1193, 1195 (Fla. 4th DCA 2000)  (“A 
fundamental tenet of contract law is that parties are free to contract, even 
when one side negotiates a harsh bargain. ”).   
 Because the Purchasers expressly waived the lien rights on which their 
claim to junior  lienholder status depends, they failed to establish the property 
interest necessary to warrant post -judgment intervention.   See Dickinson v. 
Segal , 219 So. 2d 435, 436 –37 (Fla. 1969) ; Lewis v. Turlington , 499 So. 2d 
905, 907 (Fla. 1st DCA 1986) ; Idacon, Inc. v. Hawes , 432 So. 2d 759, 761 
(Fla. 1st DCA 1983) .  Accordingly, t he trial court did not abuse its discretion.  
 Affirm ed.

items.summary:
Pre-construction condominium purchasers whose purchase agreements expressly waive any lien rights cannot establish the property interest needed to intervene post-judgment in the developer's mortgage foreclosure, so the trial court's refusal to let them intervene (here to vacate the foreclosure and close) is affirmed; reviewed for abuse of discretion, and courts enforce harsh but bargained-for contract terms.

Holding: Post-judgment intervention is allowed only in rare circumstances where the proposed intervenor demonstrates a sufficient interest in the property such that the ends of justice require intervention; because the purchasers' agreements expressly disclaimed and waived all lien or lien rights, they could not show the property interest on which junior-lienholder intervention depends, so denying intervention was not an abuse of discretion.

Disposition: Affirmed.

SIXTH DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
Case No. 6D2025-2288  
Lower Tribunal No. 2022 -CA-003712  
_____________________________  
 
RICHARD VAUGHAN , 
Appellant,  
v. 
USMI  PROPERTIES FIVE, LLC , 
Appellee.  
_____________________________  
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for Polk County . 
Michael P. McDaniel , Judge . 
 
November 6, 2026  
 
MIZE , J. 
 
Appellant, Richard Vaughan (“Vaughan”), appeals from a final judgment 
entered in favor of Appellee, USMI Properties Five, LLC (“USMI”), following the 
trial court grant ing USMI’s motion for judgment on the pleadings.  Vaughan 
brought a claim against USMI for negligence after a decayed tree located on 
USMI’s property fell over and landed on Vaughan’s house, causing significant 
damage.  The trial court granted USMI’s motion for judgment on the pleadings 
based on its conclusion that USMI did not owe Vaughan any legal duty to prevent 
2 
 the decayed tree on USMI’s property from causing harm on Vaughan’s property.  
Because the trial court erred in concluding that USMI owed no legal duty to 
Vaughan when USMI was aware of the  decayed condition of the tree, we reverse 
the final judgment and the trial court’s order granting the motion for judgment on 
the pleadings . 
Background and Procedural History 
Vaughan’s complaint filed in the trial court alleged that Vaughan and USMI 
own adjacent properties that share a boundary line.   In 2022,  a large, rotten oak 
tree on USMI’s property fe ll over and onto Vaughan’s house, causing significant 
damage.  The complaint alleges that USMI “knew that the tree was rotten for years prior to the tree falling into [Vaughan’s] property” and that the tenant that resides 
at USMI’s property in fact complained to USMI several times about falling limbs  
before the tree ultimately fell  on Vaughan’s house .  Vaughan’s house was in a 
location at which it was reasonably foreseeable to USMI that the house could be damaged  by the rotten tree. Vaughan alleged that, based on those allegations, 
USMI owed a legal duty to Vaughan and that USMI breached that duty by failing to remove the tree, thereby causing Vaughan to suffer damages to his home and his 
home -based business.  
3 
 In his complaint, Vaughan asserted a claim against USMI for negligence .1  
After filing its answer, USMI filed a motion for j udgment on the p leadings.  In the 
motion, USMI argued that, based on the allegations of the complaint, even if the 
rotten  tree created a foreseeable zone of risk, USMI did not owe a legal duty to 
Vaughan to prevent  the tree  from causing harm on Vaughan’s property .  
Specifically, USMI argued that Florida had adopted a categorical rule mandating 
that an owner of land is not liable when a tree on his land causes harm on adjacent  
property, even when the tree is diseased , the owner has knowledge that the tree is 
diseased,  and it is reasonabl y foreseeable that the tree will cause harm on an 
adjacent property.   For this purported rule, USMI cited Gallo v. Heller, 512 So. 2d 
215 (Fla. 3d DCA 1987),  and Scott v. McCarty , 41 So. 3d 989 (Fla. 4th DCA 
2010).   USMI argued that these cases provide a special exception to the normal 
rule of foreseeability for determining whether a defendant owes a legal duty to a plaintiff.   
In response, Vaughan argued that under Florida’s negligence jurisprudence, 
where a landowner has actual knowledge that a tree on his property is diseased, the landowner has a duty to exercise reasonable care to prevent the  diseased tree  from 
causing harm to adjoining property owners.  Vaughan further argued that Gallo  
 
1 Vaughan also asserted a claim for “negligence per se” based on  USMI’s 
alleged violation of a statute.  The trial court granted summary judgment on the 
“negligence per se” claim and Vaughan does not appeal that ruling.  
4 
 and Scott  only adopted a rule by which landowners could not be held liable when  
the limbs or vegetation of healthy  trees grow onto or over a neighbor’s property, 
and that these cases had no applicability to a diseased tree where it is reasonabl y 
foreseeable that the tree will cause harm on a neighbor’s property.  
After a hearing, the trial court entered an order adopting the position of 
USMI and granting the motion for judgment on the pleadings.  Vaughan moved for 
reconsideration, which the trial court summarily denied.  The trial court then 
entered final judgment in favor of USMI, and this appeal followed.    
Analysis  
 On appeal, the parties make the same arguments to us that they made to the 
trial court.  As explained below, w e disagree with the trial court that Gallo  and 
Scott  carved  out an exception to Florida’s negligence law and created a categorical 
rule that an owner of land is not liable when a tree on his land causes harm on adjacent property, even when the tree is diseased, the owner has knowledge that the tree is diseased, and it is reasonably foreseeable that the tree will cause harm on 
an adjacent property.  Instead, as Vaughan argues, Gallo  and Scott merely adopted 
the so -called “Massachusetts rule,” which provides that landowners are not liable 
when the limbs or vegetation of healthy  trees grow onto or over a neighbor’s 
property.  Because the Massachusetts rule  adopted by Gallo  and Scott  is not 
applicable to the facts of this case and do es not support the trial court’s decision to 
5 
 grant the motion for judgment on the pleadings, we need not and do not decide 
whether we agree with our sister courts that Florida law recognizes the  rule.  
Rather, we only decide that : (1) the common law of negligence as applied in 
Florida imposed a duty on USMI to exercise reasonable car e to prevent the tree 
that it (as alleged in the complaint) knew was rotten from causing harm  on adjacent 
propert ies such as  Vaughan’s; and (2) w ith there being no “ exception” that negates  
this duty, the trial court erred in granting the motion for judgment on the pleadings 
on the ground that USMI owed no duty to Vaughan.  
I. Standard of Review  
The standard of review for an order granting a motion for judgment on the 
pleadings is de novo.  Henao v. Pro.  Shoe Repair, Inc. , 929 So. 2d 723, 725 (Fla. 
5th DCA 2006).   “A motion for judgment on the pleadings is governed by the same 
legal test as a motion to dismiss for failure to state a cause of action. ” Id.  Thus, “a 
motion for judgment on the pleadings must be determined only on the pleadings 
and without the aid of outside matters such as affidavits, depositions or other 
showings of fact.”  Salazar v. Ortiz , 431 So. 3d 566, 570 (Fla. 6th DCA 2026)  
(quoting Turner v. Turner , 599 So. 2d 765, 766 (Fla. 5th DCA 1992)).  Further, 
“[w]here a defendant moves for judgment on the pleadings, a court must take as 
true all of the material allegations in the plaintiff ’s complaint and must disregard 
all of the denials in the defendant ’s answer. ” Talcott Reso l. Life Ins. Co. v. 
6 
 Novation Cap.  LLC, 261 So. 3d 580, 584 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018) (quoting Miller v. 
Finizio & Finizio, P.A. , 226 So.  3d 979, 982 (Fla. 4th DCA 2017) (emphasis 
removed)).   A judgment on the pleadings should be granted “ only if the pleadings 
establish that the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. ” Perez 
Escalona v. City of Miami Beach , 227 So. 3d 722, 724 (Fla. 3d DCA 2017).  
II. Negligence and the Element of Duty 
To state a claim for negligence, a plaintiff must allege  ultimate facts which 
establish  that: (1) the defendant owed a  legal duty to the plaintiff; (2) the defendant 
breached that duty; (3) the plaintiff was injured as a result of the defendant ’s 
breach of duty; and (4) the injury caused the plaintiff damage s. Jackson v. Sweat , 
783 So. 2d 1207, 1207 (Fla. 1st DCA 2001); Graulau Maldonado v. Orange Cnty. 
Pub. Libr . Sys., 273 So. 3d 278, 279- 80 (Fla. 5th DCA 2019).   
Whether a duty exists in a negligence case is a matter of law to be decided 
by the court, not a jury. Sierra Orlando Props. , Ltd. v. Allen , 419 So. 3d 283, 286 
(Fla. 6th DCA 2025) (citing McCain v. Fla . Power Corp. , 593 So. 2d 500, 504 
(Fla. 1992)).  The standard for determining when a defendant owe s a common law 
duty to a plaintiff was set forth by the Florida Supreme Court in Mc Cain . 593 So. 
2d at 503.   In McCain , the Court held that “ a legal duty will arise whenever a 
human endeavor creates a generalized and foreseeable risk of harming others.” Id.  
“The McCain  court described ‘ reasonable, general foresight ’ as the core of the duty 
7 
 element and instructed that the focus is ‘whether the defendant ’s conduct 
foreseeably created a broader “zone of risk”  that poses a general threat of harm to 
others. ’” Sierra Orlando Props ., 419 So. 3d at  286 (quoting McCain , 593 So. 2d at 
503).   “[T]he zone of risk created by a defendant defines the scope of the 
defendant ’s legal duty and the scope of the zone of risk is in turn determined by the 
foreseeability of a risk of harm to others.” Id.  (quoting Smith v. Fla. Power &  Light 
Co., 857 So. 2d 224, 229 (Fla. 2d DCA 2003) ).  “[T] he duty then placed upon the 
defendant is to either lessen the risk or see that sufficient precautions are taken to 
protect others from the harm that the risk poses. ” Id.; see also  McCain , 593 So. 2d 
at 503 (“ Where a defendant ’s conduct creates a foreseeable zone of risk, the law 
generally will recognize a duty placed upon defendant either to lessen the risk or see that sufficient precautions are taken to protect others from the harm that the 
risk poses.” (quoting Kaisner v. Kolb , 543 So.  2d 732, 735 (Fla. 1989))); Williams 
v. Davis , 974 So. 2d 1052, 1056 (Fla. 2007) (“[W]here a person’ s conduct is such 
that it creates a ‘ foreseeable zone of risk’  posing a general threat of harm to others, 
a legal duty will ordinarily be recognized to ensure that the underlying threatening 
conduct is carried out reasonably. ”).  The McCain  standard has been applied “to a 
countless variety of factual circumstances  in order to determine the existence of a 
duty under our negligence law ,” including numerous cases concerning whether 
landowners owed a duty arising from  conditions on their property that created a 
8 
 risk to persons or property outside  their property.2 Williams , 974 So. 2d at  1056 -
57, 1057- 60 (discussing cases where the McCain  standard was applied in such 
cases) ; see also Hardin v. Jacksonville Terminal Co. , 175 So. 226, 228 ( Fla. 1937) 
(“[T]here is no liability on the part of a landowner to persons injured outside his 
lands . . . , unless the owner has done or permitted something to occur on his lands 
which he realizes or should realize involves an unreasonable risk of harm to others 
outside his land, and therefore imposes on him, as an owner or possessor of the 
land, the duty of abating or obviating the use or condition from which the risk is 
encountered.”).  
In this case, USMI does not  dispute that knowingly maintaining a large 
rotten oak tree on its property foreseeably created a zone of risk of harm to its 
neighbors , and it is obvious that it did so.   Thus, under the McCain  standard, 
Vaughan’s complaint adequately alleged that USMI owed a common law duty to 
Vaughan to exercise reasonable care to prevent the rotten tree from causing harm 
on Vaughan’s property.  Having not disputed that the McCain  standard is satisfied 
 
2 In line with our sister courts, w e find McCain ’s articulation of the standard 
by which to determine whether a legal duty exists in a negligence case to be a 
holding that is generally applicable to common law negligence actions in Florida, 
as the Florida Supreme Court decided the proper standard to resolve the issue of 
when a duty is owed in a negligence action and then applied that standard on a 
chosen decisional path that led from the facts of the case to the judgment, thereby 
making the standard a holding applicable to the cause of action of common law 
negligence. See Crecelius v. Rizzitano , 430 So. 3d 268, 286- 87 (Fla. 6th DCA 
2026) (Gannam, J., concurring).  
9 
 by Vaughan’s complaint,  USMI’s sole argument is that the rule recognized in 
Gallo  and Scott  created an exception to the McCain  standard in the form of a 
categorical rule that an owner of land is not liable when a tree on his land causes 
harm on adjacent property, even when the tree is diseased, the owner has 
knowledge that the tree is diseased, and it is reasonably foreseeable that the tree 
will cause harm on an adjacent property.  Thus, we turn to the supposed exception.  
III. The Massachusetts rule and alternative  rules recognized by other states.  
In beginning our discussion of the Massachusetts rule, we  note that both 
parties to this appeal addressed the rule in their briefing by doing what  we have 
repeatedly cautioned litigants not to do  – both parties assumed that we would 
follow our sis ter courts ’ decisions  recogni zing th e Massachusetts rule without 
addressing whether our  sister courts’ decisions were correct.  The parties argue 
over the correct scope of the Massachusetts rule  and whether it applies to this case , 
but neither party addressed whether Florida law in fact recognizes the 
Massachusetts rule , “despite our repeated statements that we will only follow the 
decisions of our sister courts when those decisions are correct. ” Ruffenach v. 
Deutsche Bank Nat ’l Tr. Co. as Tr. for Ameriquest Mortg . Sec. Inc., Asset -Backed 
Pass -Through Certificates Series 2005- R8, 431 So. 3d 1055, 1072 (Fla. 6th DCA 
2026) (Mize, J., concurring) (collecting cases in which the Sixth District has stated 
that it will only follow the decisions of our sister courts when those decisions are 
10 
 correct ).  Litigants should take this opinion as yet another cautionary statement  that 
parties cannot assume we will follow decisions of our sister courts with no 
examination  of whether those decisions are correct.  See Pardo v. State , 596 So. 2d 
665, 667 (Fla. 1992) (“[A]s between District Courts of Appeal, a sister district ’s 
opinion is merely persuasive.”) (quoting State v. Hayes , 333 So. 2d 51, 53 (Fla. 4th 
DCA 1976)).  
As to the scope of the Massachusetts rule, Vaughan is correct  that the rule 
simply does not encompass diseased trees.  In our own review of jurisprudence 
throughout the United States, we have found numerous special rules various states 
have adopted governing a landowner’s liability to adjacent property owners for 
harm or encroachments caused by trees on the landowner’s property.  There are at 
least five such rules: the Massachusetts rule, the Virginia rule, the Hawaii r ule, the 
Pennsylvania rule, and the Restatement rule. See Michalson v. Nutting , 175 N.E. 
490, 491 (Mass. 1931) (recognizing the Massachusetts rule in Massachusetts); 
Hasapopoulos v. Murphy , 689 S.W.2d 118, 119- 21 (Mo. Ct. App. 1985)  
(discussing the Restatement rule and then adopting the Massachusetts rule); Lane 
v. W.J. Curry & Sons , 92 S.W.3d 355, 356- 64 (Tenn. 2002) (discussing the 
Restatement rule, the Virginia rule, the Hawaii rule, and the Pennsylvania rule before adopting the Hawaii rule); Jones v. Wagner , 624 A.2d 166, 171 (Pa. 1993)  
(adopting the Pennsylvania rule); Melnick v. C.S.X. Corp. , 540 A.2d 1133, 1136 -38 
11 
 (Md. 1988) (discussing the Restatement rule, the Virginia rule, and the Hawaii rule 
before adopting the Massachusetts rule).   Without going into unnecessary detail, 
the rules vary in what liability they impose  (or do not impose ) depending on 
various factors.  For example, under the Restatement rule, liability turns on 
whether the tree is natural to the land or artificial in the sense of having been 
planted or influenced by human activity  in some way . Lane , 92 S.W.3d at 361- 62; 
Melnick , 540 A.2d at  1136.   Under the Virginia rule, liability depends on whether a 
tree is “noxious” and causes actual harm to an adjoining property. Lane , 92 S.W.3d 
at 362; Melnick, 540 A.2d at 1137 .  Under the Hawaii rule, liability turns  on 
whether the tree causes actual harm or poses an imminent danger of actual harm to adjoining property other than casting shade or dropping leaves, flowers or fruit. 
Lane , 92 S.W.3d at 362- 63; Melnick , 540 A.2d at  1137 .  Under the Pennsylvania 
rule, it appears that a landowner bears liability for any encroachment by a tree on his property onto an adjoining property, even in the absence of any actual harm to the adjoining property. Lane , 92 S.W.3d at 363 (citing Jones , 624 A.2d at  171).  
The Massachusetts rule originated in Michalson v. Nutting . In Michalson, 
the plaintiff alleg ed that the roots from a tree on the defendant’s property had 
penetrated the plaintiff’s land and caused damage to plaintiff’s house, including 
damaging the foundation and the sewer and drain pipes.  175 N.E. at 490.  The 
plaintiff sought injunctive relief and damages. Id.  Despite the trial judge finding 
12 
 that the facts were just as the plaintiff alleged, he found the defendant was not 
liable for any damage caused by the defendant’s tree to the plaintiff’s property, nor 
was the defendant required to remove the roots  from the plaintiff’s property. Id.   
On appeal, the appellate court affirmed the trial court’s ruling, reasoning that 
an owner of a property i s entitled to grow trees anywhere on his property, and the 
growth of trees naturally will result in the extension of branches and roots over and 
into adjoining properties. Id.  “ It would be intolerable to give an action in the case 
of an innoxious tree whenever its growing branches extend so far as to pass beyond the boundary line and overhang a neighbor’ s soil. It would be equally intolerable 
where roots penetrate the neighbor’ s soil. ” Id. (quoting Countryman v. Lighthill , 24 
Hun 405, 407 (N.Y. 1881) (internal quotations omitted)).  While the plaintiff had 
no cause of action, he was not without a remedy. Id.  The court stated that property 
owners such as the plaintiff are entitled to engage in self -help and cut  off any 
branches or roots that grow over or into their  property from a tree on an adjoining 
property. Id. at 490- 91.  The court concluded that:  
The common sense of the common law has recognized that it is wiser 
to leave the individual to protect himself, if harm results to him from 
this exercise of another’ s right to use his property in a reasonable way, 
than to subject that other to the annoyance, and the public to the burden, of actions at law, which would be likely to be innumerable 
and, in many instances, purely vexatious.  
Id. at 491.  
13 
 Michalson  involved a healthy tree, and the court’s stated reasoning was 
expressly limited to healthy, or “ innoxious,” trees and relied on a landowner’s right 
to use his property in a “reasonable way” to grow healthy trees.  Thus, the holding 
of Michalson – the Massachusetts rule – is that a landowner cannot be held liable 
when the branches or roots of a healthy tree on the  landowner’s property encroach 
over or onto an adjoining property. See Crecelius , 430 So. 3d at  274 (“The holding 
of a case consists of those propositions along the chosen decisional path or paths of 
reasoning that (1) are actually decided, (2) are based upon the facts of the case, and 
(3) lead to the judgment.” (quoting Pedroza v. State , 291 So. 3d 541, 547 (Fla. 
2020) (internal quotations omitted))).  
Numerous courts that have adopted the Massachusetts rule have made clear 
that it applies only to healthy trees.3 See, e.g.,  Hasapopoulos, 689 S.W.2d at 121; 
 
3 Multiple courts have  also noted that a plaintiff asserting a claim based on 
an allegation  that a diseased or decayed tree on the  defendant’s property caused 
harm on the plaintiff ’s adjoining property must establish that the defendant knew 
or should have known that the tree was diseased or decayed.  Pesaturo v. Kinne , 20 
A.3d 284, 289 (N.H. 2011) (“[A] landowner who knows or should know that his 
tree is decayed or defective has a duty to maintain the tree to eliminate this 
dangerous condition. . . . [T] he manifestation of the tree ’s decay must be readily 
observable in order to require a landowner to take reasonable steps to prevent harm .” (quoting Ivancic v. Olmstead , 488 N.E.2d 72, 74  (N.Y. 1985) (internal  
quotations,  alterations omitted))); Klein v. Weaver , 593 S.E.2d 913, 914 (Ga. Ct. 
App. 2004) (“In regard to liability for a defective tree the ordinary rules of 
negligence apply. The owner of a tree is liable for injuries from a falling tree only if he knew or reasonably should have known the tree was diseased, decayed or 
otherwise constituted a dangerous condition.”  (quoting Willis v. Maloof, 361 
S.E.2d 512, 513 (Ga. Ct. App. 1987) )); Meyers v. Delaney , 529 N.W.2d 288, 290 
14 
 Ivancic v. Olmstead , 488 N.E.2d 72, 73  (N.Y. 1985) (“[I]t is established that no 
liability attaches to a landowner whose tree falls outside of his premises and injures 
another unless there exists actual or constructive knowledge of the  defective 
condition of the tree .” (emphasis added)); Schwalbach v. Forest Lawn Mem ’l Park , 
687 S.W.2d 551, 552 (Ky. Ct. App. 1985) (adopting the Massachusetts rule and 
stating that “W e are not confronted with a dead tree which is likely to fall and 
cause serious injury.  A claim for damages or removal of such a tree might be 
based on the theory of negligence  . . . .”).   
And indeed, the Florida cases that adopted the Massachusetts rule  and on 
which USMI relies , Gallo and Scott , both involved healthy trees and articulated the 
rule as applying to healthy trees.   In Gallo , the plaintiff alleged that the branches 
and roots from a tree on the defendant’s property caused the plaintiff’s driveway and walkway to crack, damaged the plaintiff’s roof, and dropped leaves onto the 
plaintiff’s property that caused the plaintiff’s dog to have allergies. Gallo , 512 So. 
2d at 216.  In upholding the trial court’s dismissal of the plaintiff’s complaint, the 
 
(Iowa 1995) (“[W]e limit liability to those situations in which it is established that 
the tree’ s owner had actual or constructive notice of the tree ’s defective 
condition .”); see also Rowe v. McGee , 168 S.E.2d 77, 81 (N.C. Ct. App. 1969) 
(“[W]here a landowner knows that he has a tree on his property which is in a 
dangerous condition and which is likely to fall and injure the property of an 
adjoining landowner, he has a duty to eliminate such danger.”); Vann v. Bailey, 
709 So. 2d 615, 61 5 (Fla. 5th DCA 1998) (“The record in the instant case contains 
sufficient evidence of actual or constructive knowledge regarding the defective or 
rotten condition of the laurel oak tree.”).  
15 
 Third District Court of Appeal stated that “ the rule at common law and the 
majority rule in this country, which is followed in Florida, is that a possessor of 
land is not liable to persons outside the land for a nuisance resulting from trees and 
natural vegetation growing on the land.”4 Id. (emphasis added).  Quoting 
Michalson , the court stated that the underlying rational e for this rule is that: 
[I]t is wiser to leave the individual to protect himself, if harm results 
to him from this exercise of another’ s right to use his property in a 
reasonable way, than to subject that other to the annoyance, and the 
public to the burden, of actions at law, which would be likely to be innumerable and, in many instances, purely vexatious.  
Id. (quoting Michalson , 175 N.E. at 491 (emphasis added)).  Thus, the Gallo  court 
articulated the holding of Michalson  – the Massachusetts rule –  as applying to the 
natural growth of trees (i.e., healthy trees  that are growing)  and relying on a 
landowner’s right to use his property in a “reasonable way” to grow such trees.  
The Gallo  court  did not articulate the Massachusetts rule as applying to rotten trees 
 
4 While the Gallo  court  cited multiple c ases from other states to support its 
adoption of the Massachusetts rule, the court  did not engage in any examination of 
the common law of England to determine that the Massachusetts rule was  in fact  
“the rule at common law ,” nor did the court  show that enough states had adopted 
the Massachusetts rule to establish that the rule was “the majority rule in this 
country.”  Gallo , 512 So. 2d at  216.  The only Florida case that Gallo  cited was 
Richmond v. Gen eral Engineering  Enter prises Co., a previous Third District case 
which adopted the Massachusetts rule but expressly stated  that “there is substantial 
authority to the contrary, which may indeed represent the majority rule .” 454 So. 
2d 16, 17 (Fla. 3d DCA 1984).   Like Gallo  and Scott , Richmond  involved a healthy 
tree. Richmond , 454 So. 2d at 17.  
16 
 or as protecting a defendant that unreasonably allows a rotten tree to sit on his  
property until it falls over and causes harm  on an adjoining property.5 
The material facts of Scott  were the same as Gallo  except the plaintiff in 
Scott  exercised her self -help option to remove the portions of her neighbor ’s tree 
that intrud ed on her property and then sought damages for the cost of that removal 
in addition to damages for the harm caused by the tree’s encroaching branches and 
roots before she removed them. Scott , 41 So. 3d at 989.  Just like Gallo , nothing in  
the Fourth District’s articulation of the Massachusetts rule in Scott  indicated that 
the rule applies to rotten trees or protects a defendant that unreasonably allows a rotten tree to sit on his property until it falls over and causes harm on an adjoining 
property.
6 
 
5 While this case involves alleged property damage, USMI’s counsel 
conceded at oral argument that under USMI’s proposed interpretation of the 
Massachusetts rule, a defendant that knowingly allows a rotten tree to sit on his 
property until it falls over and causes harm on an adjoining property would also be 
immunized from liability for any injuries or deaths caused by the falling tree.  
6 In Balzer v. Ryan , the First District Court of Appeal referenced  the self -
help portion of the Massachusetts rule  in deciding that a trial court did not depart 
from the essential requirements of law by finding that a n adjoining property owner 
that exercised their self -help remedy and cut off roots encroaching from a tree on 
their neighbor’s property was not liable to the owner of the tree for damage to the 
tree that resulted  from the removal of the roots.  263 So. 3d 189, 191 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2018).  In doing so, the First District articulated the rule as apply ing to healthy 
trees. Id. (“Under Florida law, it is well- established that an owner of a healthy tree 
is not liable to an adjoining property owner for damage caused by encroaching tree branches or roots, but the adjoining property owner is privileged to trim back, at 
his own expense, any encroaching tree roots or branches which has grown onto his 
17 
 In sum, the Massachusetts rule adopted in Scott  and Gallo  simply does not 
apply to the facts of this case as they are alleged in Vaughan’s complaint , i.e., 
where an owner of land had actual knowledge that a tree on his property was rotten 
and dangerous, the owner took no action to address the danger, and the tree fell 
over and caused damage on an adjoining property.  
IV. We do not decide whether Florida recognizes the Massachusetts rule or 
any alternative tree related rule.  
Since the Massachusetts rule, by its own terms, does not apply to the facts of 
this case, we need not decide whether Florida recognizes the  Massachusetts rule as 
an exception to the duty normally imposed by the common law of negligence ( now 
governed by the McCain  framework).7  To make such a decision would require 
significant historical research and would seem to hinge on whether the common 
law and statute laws of England recognized the Massachusetts rule (in some  form 
previously articulated) as an exception to the general law of negligence as of July 
 
property.”  (quoting Gallo , 512 So. 2d at  216 (internal quotations, alterations 
omitted))).  
7 While McCain  is the Florida’s Supreme Court’s most recent holding 
articulating the standard for determining when a defendant owes a common law duty in a negligence case, the common law of negligence long predates  McCain  as 
well as any states’ adoption of the Massachusetts rule or any of the other special 
tree related rules other states have adopted. See Warren v. Ind.  Tel. Co. , 26 N.E.2d 
399, 403 ( Ind. 1940)  (“Actions for injuries to the person caused by the negligence 
of another were known under the common law of England, and triable by jury.”).  
18 
 4, 1776.8 See § 2.01, Fla. Stat. (2024) (“The common and statute laws of England 
which are of a general and not a local nature  . . . down to the 4th day of July, 1776, 
are declared to be of force in this state . . . . ”).  Given that neither party provided 
any briefing concerning whether the Third and Fourth District were correct to 
adopt the Massachusetts rule , and the significant historical research that would be 
required to determine whether they were correct to do so, we exercise our 
discretion not to decide this issue when it is not necessary to decide this case.  
We have a duty to affirm the trial court’s ruling if there is any theory or 
principle of law in the record which would support the ruling.  Caballero -Quinones 
v. Wilder , 435 So. 3d 129, 138- 40 (Fla. 6th DCA 2026), reh’g denied , (June 19, 
2026). Therefore, if any of the other tree related rules –  the Virginia rule, the 
Hawaii rule, the Pennsylvania rule, and the Restatement rule – would support the 
trial court’s ruling if recognized as an exception to the McCain  framework, then 
we would have a duty to determine if Florida law recognized such a rule.  However, none of the special tree related rules recognized by other states would 
result in an affirmance of the trial court’s order even if they were recognized  in 
Florida .
9  Therefore, just like the Massachusetts rule, we need not decide whether 
 
8 Of course, any relevant  holdings of the Florida Supreme Court concerning 
the common law of negligence or section 2.01, Florida Statutes, would also be 
crucial to answering this question.  
9 The allegations in Vaughan’s complaint facially establish that the Virginia 
rule, the Hawaii r ule, and the Pennsylvania rule , if they were recognized  in Florida , 
19 
 Florida recognizes any of these rules as an exception to the common law rule for 
determining when a defendant owes a duty in a negligence case.  
Conclusion  
Under the McCain  framework, Vaughan’s complaint adequately alleged that 
USMI owed a common law duty to Vaughan to exercise reasonable care to prevent 
the rotten tree on USMI’s property from causing harm on Vaughan’s property.  
The trial court erred in determining that the allegations of the complaint 
established that an exception applied which negated th at duty.  Accordingly, the 
trial court’s final judgment and order granting USMI’s motion for judgment on the 
pleadings are reversed, and this case is remanded to the trial court for further 
proceedings consistent with this opinion.  
REVERSED and REMANDED for further proceedings.  
PRATT, J., and BEAMER, D. K., Associate Judge,  concur.  
 
 
 
would not bar Vaughan’s negligence claim.  The only special tree rule that the 
complaint does not facially establish would not apply is the Restatement rule, as 
nothing in the complaint indicates whether the rotten tree on USMI’s property was 
“natural” or “artificial. ”  However, the complaint states a cause of action for 
negligence and does not establish that the Restatement rule would apply  to negate 
the duty element .  Therefore, construing the allegations of the complaint in the 
light most favorable to Vaughan, the complaint would not fail to state a cause of 
action for negligence based on the Restatement rule. See  Laguerre v. City of Coral 
Springs, 673 So. 2d 60, 61 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996) (“A motion to dismiss must be 
considered in the light most favorable to appellant. ”); Henao, 929 So. 2d at  725 
(“A motion for judgment on the pleadings is governed by the same legal test as a 
motion to dismiss for failure to state a cause of action. ”). 
20 
 Daniel F. Pilka, of Pilka Adams  & Reed, P.A., Brandon , for Appellant . 
 
Willia m S. Chambers, IV, of Campbell Trohn Tamayo & Aranda, P.A., Lakeland, 
for Appellee.

AND DISPOSITION THEREOF IF TIMELY FILED

items.summary:
Practically, a neighbor whose home is damaged by a landowner's tree that the owner knew was rotten can survive judgment on the pleadings, because the duty-negating Massachusetts rule shields only healthy trees whose branches or roots encroach, not a known-decayed tree that falls and causes foreseeable harm; so long as the complaint pleads the owner's knowledge and the foreseeable risk, the negligence claim states a duty, though the court declined to settle whether Florida actually adopts the Massachusetts rule because no tree-rule variant would have saved the judgment.

Holding: An order granting a motion for judgment on the pleadings is reviewed de novo under the same standard as a motion to dismiss for failure to state a cause of action-the court considers only the pleadings, accepts the plaintiff's material allegations as true, disregards the defendant's denials, and grants relief only if the pleadings establish that the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Whether a negligence duty exists is a question of law governed by the McCain foreseeable-zone-of-risk standard, under which a duty arises whenever conduct creates a generalized, foreseeable risk of harm; the Massachusetts rule adopted in Gallo and Scott, which shields a landowner from liability for encroachment by a healthy tree's branches or roots onto adjoining property, does not extend to a diseased or rotten tree, so a landowner who knows or should know that a tree is decayed owes reasonable care to prevent foreseeable harm to adjacent property, and neither that rule nor the alternative tree rules recognized elsewhere would negate the duty on these pleadings. The court expressly declined to decide whether Florida recognizes the Massachusetts rule or any alternative tree rule because none would support affirmance.

Disposition: Reversed and remanded

 PER CURIAM.  
 2  Affirmed.  See Villars v. Buckley Towers Condo. Inc., 433 So. 3d 1021,
