items.summary:
Practical effect: a pro se condominium owner who failed to answer the complaint cannot relitigate questions of law already resolved in an earlier appeal of the same case (law of the case), and a judgment resting on that default together with the association's affidavit-and-attachment proving the outstanding assessments will stand. Per curiam citation affirmance; opinion not final pending any timely rehearing motion.

Holding: Affirming on the law-of-the-case doctrine and the prior appeal's holding, the court applies the rule that when successive appeals arise in the same case, questions of law decided on a prior appeal govern the same court and the trial court through all subsequent stages; consistent with the earlier decision, the owner failed to file a responsive pleading, received notice and an opportunity to be heard, and the association established the outstanding assessments by affidavit with an attachment, leaving no reversible error.

Disposition: Nonfinal order affirmed per curiam.

DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA  
FOURTH DISTRICT  
 
COASTAL BUILDING CONTRACTORS, LLC, 
Appellant, 
 
v. 
 
ABRAHAM CALIXTE and DOROTHY DROUILLARD 
a/k/a DOROTHY CALIXTE, 
Appellees. 
 
Nos. 4D2025-2593 and 4D2025-3611 
 
[November 4, 2026] 
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit, St. 
Lucie County; Steven J. Levin, Judge; L.T. Case Nos. 
562023CA002443AXXXHC and 562023CA002748AXXXHC. 
 
Lawrence S. Klitzman of Klitzman Law Group, PLLC, Sunrise, Robert J.  
Powell, Matthew M. Couch, and Ethan C . Gibson of Moorhead Law Group, 
Pensacola, for appellant. 
 
Abraham Calixte, Port St. Lucie, pro se. 
 
Dorothy Drouillard a/k/a Dorothy Calixte, Port St. Lucie, pro se.  
No brief filed for appellees. 
 
L
OTT, J. 
 
Coastal Building Contractors, LLC (“Coastal”), a subcontractor, tried to 
record a lien after a payment dispute arose with the Calixtes for work 
which Coastal had performed on their home.  
 
But Coastal made one mistake—a mistake that was consequential for 
this appeal.  
 
Coastal completed its work by December 1, 2022.  But its recorded 
notice of lien erroneously stated that the date of completion was October 
21, 2022.  The notice , filed on February 16, 2023, needed to be filed within 
90 days of completion of the work, so it appeared on its face untimely, even 
though it was actually timely.   
2 
  
The trial court dismissed Coastal’s claim of lien as untimely.  The trial 
court reasoned that because the notice was not timely amended to reflect 
the correct completion date, the notice remained untimely on its face, 
invalidating the claim of lien. 
 
But that was not the correct inquiry, for which reversal is required.  The 
notice was timely because it was recorded within 90 days of the actual 
completion of the work—the notice  just contained an erroneous 
description of the completion date.  On remand, the trial court should 
assess whether that error prejudiced the homeowners.  If no prejudice 
occurred, then the error falls within the statutory safe harbors and the lien is valid.   
 
Background 
 
The Calixtes hired a general contractor, Port St. Lucie Properties, Inc. 
(“PSL”), to construct a single-family residence. PSL subcontracted with 
Coastal to perform masonry, carpentry, and slab work.  The project was 
delayed because required drywall materials were unavailable, and the 
remaining work was completed on or about December 1, 2022.1 
 Coastal recorded its original claim of lien on February 16, 2023.  The 
recorded document incorrectly listed the completion date as October 21, 2022.  On September 28, 2023 and October 24, 2023, Coastal recorded 
an Amended Claim of Lien and Second Amended Claim of Lien, respectively, to reflect a December 20, 2022 completion date.  
 
The Calixtes initiated an action for slander of title and a declaratory 
judgment to invalidate the lien, later depositing cash security to secure the 
Second Amended Claim of Lien.  Coastal filed a consolidated foreclosure 
action objecting to the cash deposit.  The trial court entered summary 
judgment for the Calixtes, finding that because the original lien was 
untimely, the amendments were invalid, and the Calixtes suffered legal 
prejudice.  The trial court released the cash security deposit and awarded 
the Calixtes $80,000 in attorney’s fees.  
 
 
1 Coastal  admits that a dispute exists about  the date , and that some record 
evidence shows it to be December 9, 2022 , while other evidence  shows it to be  
December 20, 2022.  That distinction is immaterial , inasmuch as all are within 
90 days of February 16, 2023.  
3 
 Analysis 
 
“We review de novo an order granting summary judgment.”  Kincaid v. 
Walmart, Inc., 430 So. 3d 141, 146 (Fla. 4th DCA 2026)  (setting out 
standard for summary judgment). 
 
Section 713.08, Florida Statutes (2022), sets out the requirements for 
a contractor to make a claim of lien for work performed.   
 
Among other things, the claim of lien must state “[t]he time when the 
first and the last item of labor or service or materials was furnished.”  Id. 
§ 713.08(1)(f). 
 
Section 713.08 provides that “[t]he claim of lien may be recorded at any 
time during the progress of the work or thereafter but not later than 90 days after the final furnishing of the labor or services or materials by the lienor.”  § 713.08(5).  Further, “[a]ny claim of lien recorded as provided in 
this part may be amended at any time during the period allowed for 
recording such claim of lien,” that is, 90 days after the final furnishing.  § 
713.08(4)(b).   
 
The statute contains two “safe harbor” provisions for errors in the 
notice.  First, “the negligent inclusion or omission of any information in 
the claim of lien which has not prejudiced the owner does not constitute a default that operates to defeat an otherwise valid lien.”  § 713.08(3).  
Second, “[t]he omission of any of the foregoing details or errors in such 
claim of lien shall not, within the discretion of the trial court, prevent the 
enforcement of such lien as against one who has not been adversely 
affected by such omission or error.”  § 713.08(4)(a).   
 
The trial court reasoned that the lien was untimely filed because, on its 
face, the lien stated that the final furnishing was on October 21, 2022.  
The court further reasoned that the attempted amendment was invalid 
because it was filed more than 90 days after the corrected completion date 
of December 20, 2022.  The court concluded the lien was facially untimely 
and remained so, rendering it unenforceable.  The court alternatively 
found that the Calixtes were prejudiced because the lien impaired their 
property rights. 
 The trial court was, to be sure, correct in finding that Coastal’s attempts 
to amend the lien months down the road were improper and thus those 
amended notices are nullities.  See § 713.08(4)(b), Fla. Stat. ( 2022) (“Any 
claim of lien recorded as provided in this part may be amended at any time 
4 
 during the period allowed for recording such claim of lien[.]  [i.e., 90 days 
from final furnishing].”).   
 
But the trial court erred in finding that the erroneous lien, left 
unamended, was fatally deficient and incurable.  Even though error 
caused the lien to appear untimely, the question of timeliness turns on 
whether the lien was, in fact , untimely.  And it is undisputed that the lien 
was not untimely, because the final work was performed within 90 days of 
the date of recording.2  
 Although the lien notice included erroneous information (the wrong 
date) and excluded correct information (the right date), section 713.08  
contains two safe-harbor provisions that might salvage the claim from 
such mistakes.  First, “the negligent inclusion or omission of any 
information in the claim of lien which has not prejudiced the owner does not constitute a default that operates to defeat an otherwise valid lien.”  § 
713.08(3), Fla. Stat. ( 2022).  And second, “errors in such claim of lien shall 
not, within the discretion of the trial court, prevent the enforcement of 
such lien as against one who has not been adversely affected by such 
omission or error.”  § 713.08(4)(a). 
 The question for the trial court, then, is whether the error, that is, the 
wrong date recited in the notice, “prejudiced the owner” or otherwise 
“adversely affected” the Calixtes.  §§ 713.08(3), (4)(a), Fla. Stat (2022).  
 
The trial court did not reach that question.  The court instead held that 
the failure to cure the error through amendment ended the inquiry.  But 
that ignored the safe harbor provisions. 
 
The trial court alternatively held that the error prejudiced the Calixtes 
by causing an otherwise invalid lien on their property to be valid and thus 
encumber their property.  But that asked the wrong question of “what” 
prejudiced the Calixtes.  Of course the lien prejudiced the Calixtes: that’s 
the point of a lien.   
 
The safe harbor analysis instead must ask whether the error prejudiced 
the owner.  In a counterfactual world where no error occurred and the 
correct information was included, would things have played out differently 
for the Calixtes?  For example, did the error prevent them from 
 
2 At least, it appears to be undisputed.  The Calixtes did not file an answer brief.  
If the trial court on remand finds a genuine dispute of material fact on the 
question of whether the work were  in fact completed within 90 days of the 
recording of the lien, then the court should  proceed accordingly.  
5 
 understanding the claim and defending their rights with respect to it?  Did 
they in good faith rely to their detriment on the erroneous information, or 
did they know the information was wrong, cross their fingers, and hope 
they had drawn bank error in their favor?   
 
Along such lines, in McCown v. Pierce Const ruction, Inc., 552 So. 2d 
940, 941 (Fla. 4th DCA 1989), we reversed a dismissal where the claim of 
lien failed to provide a proper description of the subject property.  We noted 
that the “record reveals nothing to indicate that Pierce would have been 
exposed to any prejudice had the trial court followed that course” and that  
prejudice appeared absent where “[i]t is unlikely that [lienee] was unable 
to identify the subject property; it defended the action from the start.”  Id.  
Accord Johnson & Bailey Architects P.C. v. Se. Brake Corp., 517 So. 2d 776, 
778 (Fla. 2d DCA 1988) (“We note also that as the lien did reference the 
contract from which it arose, it is unlikely that Southeast was unable to 
identify the subject property.”); Premier Finishes, Inc. v. Maggirias, 130 So. 
3d 238, 243 (Fla. 2d DCA 2013) (prejudice unlikely shown where, even 
with errors, “it is unlikely that Mr. Maggirias would be unable to deduce the relationship between Premier Finishes and PFI Construction”). 
 The trial court erred in distinguishing our decision in O’Brian 
Associates of Orlando, Inc. v. Tully, 184 So. 2d 202 (Fla. 4th DCA 1966) —
that case is materially similar.  In O’Bria n, which concerned a 
substantively similar statute (then section 84.041), the contractor filed a 
claim of lien that was facially untimely.  Id. at 204.  Then the contractor  
sought to amend its claim of lien to show that the wrong date had been 
listed for the furnishing of materials and that the lien was in fact timely 
recorded.  Id.  We held that the lien could not be amended because the 
window for amending the claim had passed.  Id. (“The amended claim of 
lien was filed long after ninety days from the final furnishing of the materials by O’Brian so the amendment could not be permitted under the 
provisions of that portion of the statute.”).  However, we continued: 
 
Having determined that the claim of lien may not be amended, 
the question remaining is whether the lien may be enforced under the theory that the date set forth in the claim of lien on 
which the first materials were supplied was, in fact, erroneous 
and that the materials were, in fact, supplied within forty-five 
days.  Section 84.081(4)(a) provides that the omission of any 
of the details or errors in a claim of lien shall not, within the 
discretion of the trial court, prevent the enforcement of such 
lien as against one who has not been adversely affected by 
such omission or error.  We feel that neither party has shown 
an absence of a material issue of fact on the issue of whether 
6 
 or not the owners have not been adversely affected by the 
alleged error in the claim of lien.  The statements contained in 
the proof submitted in support of summary judgment by each party on this issue are conclusions and not facts admissible 
as evidence and they are, therefore, insufficient to serve as a 
basis for summary decree.  After full evidentiary hearing, the 
trial court will be in a position to exercise its discretion in 
determining whether or not the error in the claim of lien 
should prevent the enforcement of the lien.  To permit 
enforcement the court must determine that the owners have 
not been adversely affected by the error. 
 
Id. at 204–05 (cleaned up). 
  So too, here.  Accord McCown, 552 So. 2d at 941  (where claim was 
defective for failure to identify property, “the trial court should have permitted McCown to rely on the original claim of lien which was timely 
recorded” and assessed whether lienee suffered prejudice from omission); 
Royal Ambassador Condo. Ass’n, Inc. v. E. Coast Supply Corp., 495 So. 2d 932, 934–35 (Fla. 4th DCA 1986) (“While the adjudication against the 
entire property is overbroad and contrary to statute, unless a unit owner 
can demonstrate he was prejudiced by the overly broad description of the 
property liened, the lien should be effective against the respective units  
according to their proportionate shares of the common expenses.”); Sam 
Rodgers Props., Inc. v. Chmura , 61 So. 3d 432, 441 (Fla. 2d DCA 2011) 
(“Even assuming that the trial court was correct in rejecting the amended 
claim of lien as untimely filed or that it was for work that was done for the 
wrong purpose, the trial court erred in determining that the amended 
claim of lien rendered the initial claim of lien unenforceable.”). 
 
On remand, the trial court should consider whether the error 
prejudiced the owners, such that the error did or did not fall within section 
713.08’s safe harbor provisions.   
 We leave this determination to the trial court’s discretion.  And we leave 
all other matters, including all issues pertaining to fees, for the trial court 
to consider on remand in light of this opinion.  Cf. McCown, 552 So. 2d at 
941 (“Further proceedings will determine the prevailing party entitled to 
fees and costs . . . .”). 
 Reversed and remanded. 
 
L
EVINE  and K LINGENSMITH , JJ., concur. 
 
7 
 *            *            * 
 
Not final until disposition of timely-filed motion for rehearing.

items.summary:
Practically, a contractor whose lien recites the wrong completion date but was actually recorded within 90 days of finishing the work does not automatically lose the lien: the homeowner cannot defeat it merely because the lien clouds title, but must show the misstatement itself harmed their ability to understand or defend the claim or caused detrimental reliance; absent such prejudice the safe harbors keep the lien enforceable and foreclosure may proceed.

Holding: A claim of lien is timely if recorded within 90 days of the actual final furnishing of labor, services, or materials, measured by that actual completion date and not by a completion date mistakenly recited on the lien; an amendment is permitted only within the 90-day recording window, so a late amendment is a nullity; and the statutory safe harbors in section 713.08(3) and (4)(a) preserve an otherwise valid lien against non-prejudicial negligent errors, the controlling question being whether the error itself adversely affected or prejudiced the owner rather than whether the lien encumbers the owner's property.

Disposition: Reversed and remanded

1 Appellee was precluded from filing an answer brief  after failing to heed our

 2  MILLER, J.  
 In this eviction dispute, a ppellant, Maria Gimenez, the tenant, appeals 
from a  final judgment of removal r endered in favor of appellee,  Bargain 
Properties, Inc., the landlord .2  We have jurisdiction.   See Fla. R. App. P.  
9.030(b)(1)(A) .  The tenant raises two issues on appeal.  First, she contends 
the trial court erred in granting removal because she filed a viable answer 
and counterclaim; second, she asserts she established she was entitled to

For the reasons below, we disagree and affirm.   
I 
 In April  2025, the landlord filed an eviction lawsuit against the tenant.  
The landlord attached a three -day notice of nonpayment, and the complaint 
alleged the tenant failed to pay past due rent  for a four -month period.   
The tenant  filed a  document titled  “Answer  Counterclaim  
Recoupment ,” alleging  that her rent was current and  the landlord’s  neglect 
rendered the premises uninhabitable.  The trial court scheduled a rent 
determination hearing.  In lieu of proceeding forward on the hearing , the 
parties entered into a negotiated partial settlemen t.  The tenant  would be 
 
2 Given our decision, we summarily deny review of the denial of the tenant’s  
motion to stay.  
 3 permitted to reside in the premises, rent free, until July 12, 2025 .  On that 
date, she would voluntarily vacate the property and the landlord, in turn, 
would file a voluntary dismissal.  The parties also agreed that the tenant  
would amend her counterclaim within twenty days.  The trial court ratified the 
stipulation.  
 Rather than fil e an amended counterclaim  within the pr escribed period, 
the tenant filed her “Amended Answer. ”  But c ontrary to the title, she sought  
two forms of affirmative relief: (1) to recoup past paid rent under a theory of 
retaliatory conduct; and (2) to remain in possession of the premises until  
December 2025.   
The landlord  moved to dismiss, contending that the pleading  failed to 
state a cause of  action and violated the expedited procedures set forth in the 
summary eviction procedure statutes .  The trial court granted the motion, 
without prejudice, and authorized  further amendment within fifteen days.   
The tenant  again amended, this time filing an Amended Answer and 
Counterclaim , alleging substantially similar theories.   
On July 13, 2025 , the day after the tenant agreed to vacate the 
property, the  landlord  filed a motion for f inal judgment of removal .  The 
motion  sought immediate possession and included an  affidavit of 
noncompliance .  The affidavit stated that the tenant refused to relinquish 
 4 possession of the property, contrary to the terms of the settlement 
agreement.  The tenant filed an emergency motion to extend the previously 
agreed upon habitation period.  The trial court summarily entered a  final 
judgment for removal .  This appeal ensued . 
II 
A 
In enacting t he Florida Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (the “Act”), 
the legislature made an express decision to provide  an expedited process 
for determining  the right of possession.   § 51.011, Fla. Stat.  (2025 ); ch. 83, 
Fla. Stat. ( 2025 ).  The right of possession is paramount, operating essentially 
in a vacuum “without the necessity of deciding all  other  issues between the 
parties. ”  Camena Invs. & Prop. Mgmt. Corp. v. Cross , 791 So. 2d 595, 597 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2 001).  Unless the tenant interposes the defense of payment,  
the failure to deposit the amount of rent alleged as unpaid in the complaint  
in the court registry serves as  a waiver of  all defenses to possession.  
§ 83.232(1), Fla . Stat.    
The tenant correctly posits that section  83.64, Florida Statutes, 
prohibits “retaliatory conduct ,” and provides that it is a valid defense to 
possession.  Among the  retaliatory  acts prohibited  are decreases in services 
or increases in rent precipitated by tenant complaints to the landlord .  Id. 
 5 § 83.64(1).  But the Act further provides that this defense is inapplicable  “if 
the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause.”   Id. § 83.64(3).   
“Good cause ” includes “good faith actions for nonpayment of rent.”   Id. 
B 
Here, the tenant timely alleged  in her Amended Answer and 
Counterclaim that  she paid  her rent  but that the landlord retaliated against 
her for complaining about the condition of the property and improperly raised 
her rent.  But that does not end our analysis.  Rather than proceed with the 
evidentiary hearing on the  amount of rent, if any, that should be paid into the 
court registry during the pendency of the case, the tenant agreed to 
relinquish possession on the specified date.  In so doing, she waived any 
defenses to possession.   
Her subsequent failure to abide by the terms of  the agreement did not 
revive her affirmative defenses .  See Scarborough Assoc. v. Fin. Fed. Sav. 
and Loan Ass’n of Dade Cnty., 647 So. 2d 1001, 1003 –1004 (Fla. 3d DCA 
1994)  (holding that a superseding modification agreement waived 
preexisting defenses) .  It instead  entitled the landlord to immediate relief, 
enforcing the bargain ed-for terms.  
 
   
 6 C 
To the extent that the tenant  claims the trial court erred  in rejecting her 
contention that the agreement was the product of duress or coercion, this 
issue evades our review .  She has failed to provide us with any transcripts 
of the proceedings or establish any  error on the face of the  orders under 
review .  See Applegate v. Barbett Bank of Tallahassee , 377 So. 2d 1150, 
1152 ( Fla. 1979)  (“Without a record of the trial proceedings, the appellate 
court can not properly resolve the underlying factual issues so as to conclude 
that the trial court’s judgment is not supported by the evidence or by an 
alternative theory.  Without knowing the fa ctual context, neither can an 
appellate court reasonably conclude that the trial judge so misconceived the 
law as to require reversal.”) .3  Accordingly, we affirm  the order under review . 
Affirmed.  
 
3 Despite the tenant’s contention to the contrary, the judgment does not 
reach the counterclaim ; it expressly  self-limits to removal.

items.summary:
In a summary residential eviction the tenant forfeits the case by skipping procedure: absent a payment defense she must deposit the claimed unpaid rent into the registry or waive all possession defenses, and a ratified stipulation to vacate waives her earlier defenses, which do not revive when she later breaches—so removal enforcing the bargained-for terms is affirmed, and her duress claim is unreviewable for want of a transcript; her motion-to-stay review is summarily denied.

Holding: In a summary residential eviction the right to possession is resolved summarily and, absent a payment defense, the tenant's failure to deposit the claimed unpaid rent into the court registry waives all defenses to possession; the statutory retaliatory-conduct defense is unavailable where the landlord evicts for good cause, which includes a good-faith nonpayment action; a tenant who agrees in a ratified stipulation to surrender possession waives preexisting defenses, which do not revive upon her later breach, entitling the landlord to enforce the bargained-for terms; and without a transcript the appellate court cannot find error (Applegate).

Disposition: Affirmed.

[October 28, 2026]

and Eric C. Hayden of Zoeller, Hayden & Thron, PLLC, West Palm Beach, 
and Kevin C. Smith of Lytal, Reiter, Smith, Ivey & Fronrath, West Palm

Dinah S. Stein and Michael J. Byrne of Hicks, Porter & Stein, P.A., 
Miami, for appellees Merrill W. Reuter, M.D., Advanced Orthopedics, Inc. 
d/b/a Spine/Orthopedics, Broward Outpatient Medical Center, LLC, Palm 
Coast Anesthesia Group, LLC, Premier Orthopedic and Neurosurgical 
Group, LLC, Central Spine and Orthopedics Centers, LLC d/b/a 
Interoperative Monitoring, Two and Two, LLC, Complete Rehab and 
Medical Center of Plantation, Inc., Kendall Spine and Orthopedics, LLC, Medassist Surgical, LLC, Prestige Orthopedics, LLC, Orthopedic and Spine 
Center of South Florida, LLC, Universal Mediquip, Inc., Broward 
Outpatient Urgent Care, LLC, Center for Neurosurgical Excellence, LLC, Complete Rehab and Medical Centers of Pompano, Inc., Complete Rehab 
and Medical Centers of West Palm Beach, Inc., Hollywood Rehab and 
Medical Center, LLC, Brian Bauer, individually, and Craig Bauer, 
individually.  
 Jim White of White Russell, P.A., Palm Beach for appellees Merrill W. 
Reuter, M.D., and Advanced Orthopedics, Inc. 
 Ryan M. Sanders of Lubell & Rosen, LLC, Fort Lauderdale, and Rolando 
A. Diaz of DLG Lawyers, Miami, for appellee Beth Israel Outpatient Surgical Center, LLC d/b/a Broward Outpatient Surgical Center. 
 
M
AY, J. 
 
 The record is 22,060 pages long, not counting the supplemental record, 
and this case has not gotten beyond a motion to dismiss.  Forty-one  
plaintiffs were given six attempts to plead a cause of action.  The forty-one 
plaintiffs now appeal the dismissal with prejudice of their 1,492-page 
Fourth Amended Complaint, containing 7,803 paragraphs, and alleging 
nine causes of action against twenty-two defendants.  They argue the trial 
court erred in dismissing each count of their complaint with prejudice.  We disagree and affirm. 
3 
 • The Facts 
 
o The Background of the Underlying Litigation.  
 
 This is a novel piece of litigation spanning over a decade and featuring 
three primary chapters.  This appeal involves chapter three.  
Chapter One 
 
 The plaintiffs were involved in a variety of incidents, including car 
accidents, slip and falls, and others.  They were initially represented by 
the Fenstersheib Law Group (“FLG”).  The FLG referred the plaintiffs to one 
or more of the defendants in connection with their personal injuries, 
pursuant to letters of protection.  The plaintiffs were treated by one or more of the defendants.   
  The plaintiffs pursued their personal injury claims, seeking damages 
for, among other things, medical expenses incurred because of their alleged injuries.  Ultimately, the plaintiffs settled their respective personal 
injury claims.  
Chapter Two 
  During the resolution of the personal injury claims, an FLG employee 
embezzled money from the FLG trust accounts.  This resulted in the FLG 
failing to pay the medical providers (currently the defendants) for the 
services rendered despite the letters of protection.  Seventeen medical 
entities—all owned by Craig and Brian Bauer—sued the FLG and plaintiffs 
to recover payment for services rendered (the “Theft Lawsuits”).
1   The Theft 
Lawsuits ultimately settled and were dismissed in May 2021. 
 
 
 
1 According to a counterclaim filed in this case, attorney Fenstersheib reported 
the employee theft to the Florida Bar, which opened an investigation.  The 
counterclaim alleged that Fenstersheib and the FLG devised a scheme to pressure 
the medical providers to back off their collection efforts by claiming the  medical 
providers were engaged in fraudulent practices and perform ed “fake” surgeries.   
 
 Specifically, the counterclaim alleged the p laintiffs had injuries requiring  
minimal ly invasive surgical  treatment  and they sought  compensation for th e 
surgeries in their personal injury litigation .  The plaintiffs  submitted the bills for 
those surgeries  and medical care and were paid for those expenses when settling 
their claims.  But neither the FLG nor the plaintiffs ever paid the medical 
providers.  
4 
 Chapter Three 
 
 This brings us to the current lawsuit and this appeal.   
  In October 2021, the plaintiffs filed a 325-page, forty-five-count 
complaint against the same medical providers that had previously sued 
them, including the Bauers individually, Dr. Reuter, the orthopedic surgeon, and Dr. Reuter’s surgical assistant, Dr. Metzger.  The original 
complaint alleged medical malpractice claims against all defendants 
except the Bauers, and claims for fraud, negligent misrepresentation, 
breach of fiduciary duty, accounting, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligent infliction of emotional distress, violation of 
the Florida RICO statute, civil conspiracy, and deceptive and unfair trade 
practices.  
 The next month, the plaintiffs filed an amended complaint alleging 
similar claims.  The defendants moved to dismiss.    
 While those motions were pending, the trial court entered an order on 
a motion for leave to amend the complaint in a similar case that had been 
filed earlier by a different plaintiff (Harris) , alleging similar claims.  In that 
March 2022 order in the Harris case,  the trial court found that the 
complaint read “more like an introductory statement of a John Grisham 
novel, rather than a legally based short concise statements of facts, with 
lack of specificity regarding Counts of Civil RICO, Fraud, IIED, ‘crime schemes’, etc.”   
  The plaintiffs, now including Harris, filed a Second Amended 
Complaint.  The defendants moved to dismiss and sever counts in the 
Second Amended Complaint.  After a lengthy hearing, the trial court once again dismissed the complaint without prejudice.  The dismissal order 
identified numerous deficiencies in each count of the Second Amended 
Complaint.   
 
 The plaintiffs’ Third Amended Complaint was nearly twice the length of 
the Second Amended Complaint and attached over 400 pages of medical 
bills.  The defendants again moved to dismiss.  The trial court held another 
lengthy hearing and dismissed the Third Amended Complaint without prejudice.  This time the trial court warned the plaintiffs that it was their  
final opportunity to plead their case. 
 
o The Fourth Amended Complaint 
 
5 
  After five attempts to plead their claims, all of which resulted in 
dismissals, the plaintiffs filed their Fourth Amended Complaint, alleging 
medical malpractice, vicarious liability for medical malpractice, fraud, 
negligent misrepresentation, violation of the civil RICO Act, and civil 
conspiracy. 
  The complaint now contained 129 paragraphs of general allegations, 
followed by 1,763 paragraphs of plaintiff-specific allegations.  The plaintiffs 
incorporated all 129 general allegations into each of the nine counts for 
each of the 41 plaintiffs, regardless of whether the allegations were 
connected to the claim or the defendant named in the count.  The 
defendants filed motions to dismiss, which the trial court granted.  In 
doing so, the trial court noted this was the sixth complaint and “attempt 
to adequately and sufficiently state a cause of action.”  
 In essence, the Fourth Amended Complaint alleged the plaintiffs were 
“all involved in either a motor vehicle accident, slip and fall, or other such event” and sustained injuries.  The plaintiffs presented to the chiropractic 
Bauer defendants (Brian and Craig Bauer) and their entities
2 as well as 
medical defendants (Reuter and Metzger) for treatment of these injuries.   
 
 The plaintiffs alleged the defendants “worked together to fake the 
performance of a medically necessary and beneficial surgical procedure for 
the purpose of collecting extra monies from [p]laintiffs’ personal injury 
settlements.”  According to the complaint, the defendants were alleged to 
have “lied to [p]laintiffs, put them under general anesthesia, and then 
‘operated’ on them by cutting them open and sewing them back up without 
performing any medically beneficial surgery at all.” 
 
 The dismissal order stated, in part, “[t]he convoluted nature of the 
pleading renders it impossible for [d]efendants to adequately frame an 
Answer [because] the allegations repeatedly comingle conclusions against 
separate individuals and entities without discerning how, or why, or who 
did what on which occasion that would subject each to collective or 
vicarious liability under any” cause of action alleged.  The plaintiffs filed 
two motions for rehearing and reconsideration.  Both were denied. 
 
 
2 Defendant entities included Beth Israel, Broward Medical, Palm Coast 
Anesthesia, Central Spine, Premier Orthopedic, Two and Two, Complete Rehab 
Plantation, Kendall Spine, MedAssist , Prestige, Orthopedic and Spine, Universal 
Mediquip, Broward Urgent, Neurosurgical Excellence, Complete Rehab Pompano, 
Complete Rehab West Palm, and Hollywood Rehab.  
6 
  From the dismissal order and the orders denying the motions for 
rehearing and reconsideration, the plaintiffs now appeal.   
 
• The Analysis 
 
 We begin with Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.110, which provides 
that “[a] pleading which sets forth a claim for relief . . . must state a cause 
of action and must contain:  . . . (2) a short and plain statement of the 
ultimate facts showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.”   
 
 Subsection (f) provides “[e]ach claim founded on a separate transaction 
or occurrence” must “be stated in a separate count . . . when a separation 
facilitates the clear presentation of the matter set forth.”  Fla. R. Civ. P. 
1.110(f).  “[G]eneral, vague and conclusory statements are insufficient to 
satisfy the requirement that a pleader allege ‘a short and plain statement 
of the ultimate facts showing the pleader is entitled to relief. . . .’” Jordan 
v. Nienhuis, 203 So. 3d 974, 976 (Fla. 5th DCA 2016) (quoting Fla. R. Civ. 
P. 1.110(b)).  
 “The complaint must [also] set out the elements and the facts that 
support them so that the court and the defendant can clearly determine 
what is being alleged.”  Barrett v. City of Margate, 743 So. 2d 1160, 1162 
(Fla. 4th DCA 1999).  “It is not permissible for any litigant to submit a 
disorganized assortment of allegations and argument in hope that a legal premise will materialize on its own.”  Id. at 1163. 
  Despite these pleading requirements, the plaintiffs’ attempts to comply 
with the trial court’s direction and the rules of civil procedure  ran afoul of 
both.  As the trial court’s August 2023 dismissal order correctly observed, the complaint failed to allege who “made the initial referral and who (which 
defendants) referred plaintiffs to Dr. Reuter. . . .  There are many conclusory statements lumping multiple defendants together with no 
connectivity.”    
 Regarding the fraud and negligent misrepresentation claims, the trial 
court commented:  “the complaint suffers from a lack of specificity (ie: who, 
what, when and where).”  The complaint failed to describe what false 
statement was made, what reliance had occurred, and what damages 
patients had sufferred.    
 Concerning the RICO allegations, the trial court found the plaintiffs had 
“failed to define the timeframe” and which defendants were engaged and 
at what times.  Regarding the civil conspiracy claim, the trial court found 
the complaint failed to allege an agreement between two or more parties 
7 
 and each defendant’s role in the conspiracy.  The trial court refused to 
“take notice of what may or may not be found in discovery.”  Because the 
trial court determined the plaintiffs had failed to sufficiently plead an 
actionable underlying tort or wrong, dismissal of the conspiracy claims 
was required as well.  See City of Miami  v. Alvarez, 421 So. 3d 802, 806 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2025) (citing Raimi v. Furlong, 702 So. 2d 1273, 1284 (Fla. 
3d DCA 1997)).  
 
 The trial court provided an example in the order dismissing the Fourth 
Amended Complaint.  “[I]n reference to the allegations of taking kickbacks 
or engaging in other acts by the ‘surgeon group’, [d]efendants identify 328 
references to possibly ‘other members’ thereof (not Dr. Reuter) without 
identifying which ‘other’ [d]efendants or possibly non-party persons they 
are alleging engaged in such conduct.”   
 
 In each count, the plaintiffs incorporated 129 general allegations, 
ranging from a description of corporate structures to billing practices, self-
referrals and kickback violations, “faked” surgeries, and battery, into each 
of the nine counts for each of the forty-one plaintiffs.  This indiscriminate 
incorporation of random allegations rendered each count defective under 
Rule 1.110(b).  See Gerstein v. Int ’l Asset Value Grp., LLC, 199 So. 3d 979, 
981―82 (Fla. 4th DCA 2016) (affirming dismissal with prejudice where trial court took issue with complaint’s incorporation of thirty-three  
introductory paragraphs into all counts). 
 
 We also note that plaintiff Tamonica Allen’s specific allegations appear 
on pages thirty-four to forty-four of the complaint (at pages 14792 to 
14802 of the record), but the allegations of Allen’s medical negligence claim 
do not appear until page 423 of the complaint, 361 pages later.  And even 
then, they shed little light on plaintiff Allen’s theory.  
 
 In the specific section, plaintiff Allen alleges that she “underwent . . . 
orthopedic spine ‘surgery,’” and that defendant Reuter concealed the “true 
nature” of the surgery, which had no medical benefit.  A reader cannot 
discern whether the claim is that defendant Reuter  negligently 
recommended and performed a procedure that was not indicated, recommended the correct procedure but performed a different procedure, 
or was simply negligent in performing the procedure. 
 
 Perhaps the most conspicuous void in the plaintiffs’ complaint is the 
lack of causation to any actual damage.  The complaint fails to allege how 
the plaintiffs suffered any damage from the alleged fraudulent medical 
bills.  No plaintiff was alleged to have paid a fraudulent bill.  In fact, the 
8 
 complaint indicates the bills were used to corroborate the plaintiffs’ claims 
in their personal injury actions, which were then settled.  
 
 The complaint also failed to identify any claimed injuries from alleged 
felonious touching as opposed to medical malpractice.  The plaintiffs’ 
allegations that defendant Reuter’s surgeries caused them to have 
additional medical care are too tenuous to support a claim for civil RICO.   
See Bortell v. White Mountains Ins. Grp., Ltd., 2 So. 3d 1041, 1047 (Fla. 4th 
DCA 2009) (plaintiff who suffered financial harm through lost 
commissions due to defendants’ unauthorized sale of insurance was 
precluded from asserting RICO claims because illegal activity was directed 
toward the state, and plaintiff’s lost commission was only indirectly related 
to the improper conduct). 
   As the trial court appropriately noted, “damages are not fungible when 
there are approximately forty individual [p]laintiffs alleging approximately forty separate and individual claims resulting from separate and distinct . 
. . facts.”  Because the complaint failed to articulate the causal link 
between the alleged misrepresentations and any specific injury, dismissal 
of those claims was warranted. 
 
• Conclusion 
 
 This is a case where it is impossible to find a life raft―“a short and plain 
statement of the ultimate facts showing that the pleader is entitled to 
relief”―in a vast ocean.  One thing is certain:  the trial court here patiently waded multiple times through a sea of allegations in an ocean of pages 
and provided the plaintiffs with numerous opportunities to state a claim 
that could be answered by the defendants.  The plaintiffs simply failed to 
do so.   
 
 We have similarly spent days wading through the treacherous waters 
of this complaint and reached the same conclusion.  The Fourth Amended Complaint neither complies with the Florida Rules of Civil Procedure nor the trial court’s direction.  As the trial court’s order stated: “[t]here is 
simply a point in litigation when defendants are entitled to be relieved from the time, effort, energy, and expense of defending themselves against 
seemingly vexatious claims.”  Kohn v. City of Miami Beach, 611 So. 2d 538, 
539 (Fla. 3d DCA 1992) (citing Feigin v. Hosp. Staffing Servs. , Inc., 569 So. 
2d 941 (Fla. 4th DCA 1990)). 
 
 Affirmed. 
 G
ROSS and C IKLIN, JJ., concur. 
9 
  
*            *            * 
 
Not final until disposition of timely-filed motion for rehearing.

items.summary:
A sprawling multi-plaintiff suit against medical providers asserting malpractice, fraud, civil RICO, and conspiracy was properly dismissed with prejudice after six pleadings: indiscriminate incorporation of hundreds of conclusory allegations into every count for every plaintiff violated Rule 1.110, no causal damage from the allegedly fraudulent bills was pleaded, indirect or derivative harm cannot support civil RICO, and conspiracy fails without an actionable predicate tort; defendants may be relieved from vexatious, unanswerable pleading after ample amendment chances.

Holding: Rule 1.110 requires each count to state its elements and supporting ultimate facts in a short and plain statement and to separate claims by transaction; indiscriminate incorporation of general allegations into every count for every plaintiff, coupled with conclusory groupings of multiple defendants, is insufficient. Dismissal with prejudice is proper after repeated failed opportunities to amend where the pleading remains so disorganized that defendants cannot frame an answer. A civil RICO claim requires a causal link between the alleged pattern of racketeering and the plaintiff's own injury, so harm that is only indirect or derivative is insufficient. Civil conspiracy cannot survive without a properly pleaded actionable underlying tort and an allegation of the agreement and each defendant's role in it.

Disposition: Affirmed.

DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA  
FOURTH DISTRICT  
 
TAPLIN FALLS, LTD., and 
TAPLIN MEADOWS DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION, 
Appellants, 
 
v. 
 
JASON BROWN and GENELLE GORDON, 
Appellees. 
 
No. 4D2025-3894 
 
[October 28, 2026] 
 
Appeal from the County Court for the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit, 
Broward County; Kathleen E. Angione, Judge; L.T. Case No. 
062025CC016224AXXXNO. 
 
Warren E. Friedman of Friedman Sklar PLLC, Boca Raton, for appellant 
Taplin Falls, Ltd. 
 
No appearance for appellees. 
 K
LINGENSMITH , J. 
 Appellant Taplin Falls, Ltd., appeals from orders striking a provision of 
a final judgment and denying its motion for attorney’s fees and costs 
against Appellees Jason Brown and Genelle Gordon.  The trial court struck 
the provision from the final judgment on its own initiative nearly three 
months after entering the final judgment, concluding that the provision 
allowing extended time for filing the attorney’s fees motion was legally 
erroneous.  Because a perceived error of law did not authorize the trial 
court to revise the final judgment after the time for rehearing had expired, 
we reverse and remand for reinstatement of the provision and consideration of Taplin Falls’s request for attorney’s fees and costs on the 
merits. 
 
The underlying proceeding was an uncontested landlord-tenant action.  
In August 2025, the trial court entered a final judgment awarding Taplin Falls $10,233.  The judgment expressly reserved jurisdiction to award 
attorney’s fees and costs.  Paragraph 4 of the final judgment further 
provided that Taplin Falls had “forty-five (45) days from the date of this 
2 
 Final Judgment to pursue attorney’s fees and costs.”  Taplin Falls filed its 
motion seeking attorney’s fees and costs on the forty-fifth day after entry 
of the final judgment. 
 
In November 2025, three months after the entry of the final judgment, 
the trial court held a hearing on that motion.  At that hearing, the court 
sua sponte entered an order striking paragraph 4.  As a result, the trial 
court denied the attorney’s fees motion as untimely in a separate order,  
citing Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.525 and Barco v. School Board of 
Pinellas County, 975 So. 2d 1116 (Fla. 2008). 
 
Taplin Falls sought rehearing or reconsideration, arguing that the trial 
court lacked authority to substantively modify the final judgment months 
after its entry and that they were entitled to rely on the forty-five-day 
period expressly stated in the judgment to file their motion.   The trial court 
denied relief, reasoning that the issue was “very well established black 
letter law, and all parties to this action should well have been aware of the 
state of the law on the timing for filing a motion for attorney’s fees and 
costs.”  This appeal followed. 
 
Whether the trial court had authority to modify the final judgment 
presents a question of law reviewed de novo.  See Fetchick v. Fetchick, 346 
So. 3d 209, 211 (Fla. 5th DCA 2022); see also Perez v. Maldonato, 324 So. 
3d 1011, 1013 (Fla. 3d DCA 2021) (“A trial court’s interpretation and application of Florida law is reviewed de novo.” (citation omitted)).  The 
issue presented here is not whether the trial court correctly selected the 
time period stated in paragraph 4 when the trial court entered the final 
judgment.  The issue is whether the trial court could later strike that 
substantive provision through the procedure which it used. 
 
“When a trial court renders a final judgment in an action, its 
jurisdiction over that action is terminated, except that it retains continuing 
jurisdiction to enforce its judgment.”  Fetchick, 346 So. 3d at 211 (quoting 
Kozel v. Kozel, 302 So. 3d 939, 945 (Fla. 2d DCA 2019)).  A trial court’s 
authority to revise a final judgment is governed by Florida Rules of Civil 
Procedure 1.530 and 1.540.  Thus, “[e]xcept as provided by Rules 1.530 
and 1.540, Florida Rules of Civil Procedure, the trial court has no authority 
to alter, modify or vacate an order or judgment.”  Shelby Mut . Ins. Co. of 
Shelby, Ohio v. Pearson, 236 So. 2d 1, 3 (Fla. 1970).  The reservation of 
jurisdiction to decide attorney’s fees and costs only allowed the trial court 
to resolve that remaining matter.  The reservation did not confer 
continuing authority to rewrite substantive terms of the final judgment. 
 
3 
 The trial court’s sua sponte November order that revised the final 
judgment was entered well beyond rule 1.530’s period for relief.  Rule 
1.530 provides that motions and petitions for correction of error by the 
trial court must be made within ten days after rendition of the final 
judgment or order.  Id.  “Unless a proper motion or petition is filed within 
the allotted time, the judgment or order of the trial court becomes 
absolute.”  Id.  Because rule 1.530’s time limit had expired after ten days, 
the substantive amendment required a basis under rule 1.540. 
 
 Rule 1.540(a) permits a trial court to correct clerical mistakes and 
errors arising from oversight or omission, including on its own initiative.  
However, nothing in the record here supported the trial court’s action under rule 1.540(a) either.  The order did not identify a clerical mistake, 
nor did the order merely correct the written expression of a ruling.  The 
trial court’s only stated concern was the provision’s legal correctness.  The 
trial court’s revision eliminated the then- existing provision granting Taplin 
Falls forty-five days to pursue attorney’s fees and costs.  As a result, the 
trial treated the attorney’s fees motion filed within that forty-five day period 
as untimely.  That change was not ministerial. It substantively and 
materially altered the final judgment’s legal effect.  
 
Likewise, rule 1.540(b)(1) also did not authorize the amendment.  
Although rule 1.540(b)(1) permits relief for mistake, inadvertence, 
surprise, or excusable neglect, rule 1.540(b)(1) does not permit correction 
of judicial error arising from a trial court’s mistaken view of the law.  See 
Curbelo v. Ullman, 571 So. 2d 443, 445 (Fla. 1990) (“[J]udicial error such as a ‘mistaken view of the law’ is not one of the circumstances 
contemplated by the rule.” (citing Fiber Crete Homes, Inc. v. Div. of Admin, 
315 So. 2d 492, 493 (Fla. 4th DCA 1975)).  Any such error must be 
addressed through timely rehearing or appellate review, rather than by sua sponte using rule 1.540 as a substitute for those procedures.  Id. at 
444–45.  Thus, even if the trial court erred by including the forty-five-day 
provision in the judgment, the trial court’s later acknowledgement about 
the flawed legal basis for that provision did not supply proper grounds to 
strike the provision. 
 
The trial court’s order denying Taplin Falls’s motion for attorney’s fees 
and costs followed the unauthorized deletion of paragraph 4 and denied effect to the time period which paragraph 4 expressly provided.  Taplin 
Falls timely filed its motion within that period.  Therefore, the denial of the 
motion cannot stand on the premise that the trial court could retroactively 
remove the provision from the final judgment. 
 
4 
 We reverse the order striking paragraph 4 from the final judgment, as 
well as the order denying Taplin Falls’s motion for attorney’s fees and 
costs.  On remand, the trial court shall reinstate paragraph 4, determine 
entitlement to attorney’s fees and costs pursuant to Taplin Falls’ motion 
and, if entitlement is established, the amount to be awarded.  We express 
no view on either entitlement or amount.  
 
Reversed and remanded with instructions. 
 
GERBER , C.J., and W HITE, REBECCA , Associate Judge, concur. 
 
*            *            * 
 
Not final until disposition of timely-filed motion for rehearing.

items.summary:
A final judgment that reserved jurisdiction and gave the prevailing party 45 days to seek attorney's fees could not be rewritten sua sponte nearly three months later. Because the trial court's jurisdiction to revise the judgment ended after rule 1.530's ten-day window and rule 1.540 did not authorize undoing a substantive term based on a perceived legal error, the orders striking the 45-day provision and denying the timely fee motion are reversed and the provision reinstated so entitlement and amount can be considered on the merits.

Holding: A trial court's jurisdiction over an action terminates when it renders a final judgment, except for continuing jurisdiction to enforce it; after rule 1.530's ten-day window the court may alter, modify, or vacate the judgment only under rule 1.540, and a reservation of jurisdiction to award attorney's fees permits resolving that pending matter but not rewriting the judgment's substantive terms. Rule 1.540(a) reaches only clerical mistakes or errors of oversight or omission, and rule 1.540(b)(1) cannot be used to correct a judicial mistaken view of the law, which must instead be addressed by timely rehearing or appellate review; the court therefore cannot sua sponte strike a substantive 45-day fee-filing provision from a final judgment months after entry.

Disposition: Reversed and remanded with instructions.

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 28, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.

No. 3D26 -0944  
Lower Tribunal No. 23-28062 -CA-01

Victoria Friend LLC , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Tamiami Airport Service Center, Inc., et al. , 
Appellee s. 
 
 
 An Appeal from  a non -final order from the  Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Charles Kenneth Johnson , Judge.  
 
 Saltiel Law Group , and Matthew Carcano, and Hubert Menendez, for 
appellant.  
 
 Shutts & Bowen  LLP, and Michelle G. Hendler, and Julissa Rodriguez ; 
Shutts & Bowen LLP , and Erik R. Matheney  (Tampa) , for appellee s. 
 
 
Before  FERNANDEZ, LOGUE, and MILLER,  JJ.  
 
 PER CURIAM.  
 2  Appellant, Victoria Friend LLC, challenges an order denying its 
renewed motion for leave to amend to assert a claim for punitive damages.1 
After considering competing submissions, the trial court denied the motion 
on the discrete ground that the proffered conduct did not “rise[] to the level 
of punitives in terms of shocking, outrageous, and [ im]moral.”  The punitive 
damages statute conditions leave upon “a reasonable showing by evidence 
in the record or proffered by the claimant which would provide a reasonable 
basis for recovery of such damages.”  § 768.72(1), Fla. Stat. ( 2025).  
Consistently, the Florida Supreme Court has confirmed that the sufficiency 
of such a showing turns upon whether “a reasonable person could conclude, 
based on the claimant’s evidence, that the defendant committed ‘intentional 
misconduct’ or ‘gross negligenc e,’ as defined in section 768.72(2).” 
Perlmutter v. Fed. Ins. Co. , 434 So. 3d 681, 688 (Fla. 2026).  Recognizing 
that the trial court did not have the benefit of Perlmutter  at the time the order 
was rendered, we nonetheless conclude the procedure was defective and 
the court measured the proffer against a standard the statute does not 
prescribe.  See Bric McMann Indus. Inc. v. Regatta Beach Club Condo. 
Ass’n , 378 So. 3d 652, 655 (Fla. 2d DCA 2023) (“Under the revised statute, 
a plaintiff seeking to recover punitive damages under a theory of intentional 
 
1 We have jurisdiction. See Fla. R. App. P. 9.130(a)(3)(G).  
 3 misconduct need only proffer evidence of ‘intentional misconduct’ as defined 
in subsection 768.72(2)(a).”); see also  Perlmutter , 434 So. 3d at 691 
(quashing and remanding for reexamination of the proffer under the 
announced construction of the statute).   Accordingly, we reverse and remand 
for reconsideration of the motion.  
 Reversed and remanded.

items.summary:
Practical effect: a court may not deny leave to amend for punitive damages by applying a heightened "shocking, outrageous, and immoral" gloss; the statutory gatekeeper test is whether the proffered evidence would let a reasonable person find intentional misconduct or gross negligence as defined in section 768.72(2), so a proffer measured against the wrong standard is remanded for reconsideration (notably where the order predates the governing construction). Nonfinal appeal; opinion not final pending any timely rehearing motion.

Holding: Section 768.72(1) conditions leave to assert punitive damages on a reasonable evidentiary showing-provided by the record or the claimant's proffer-supplying a reasonable basis for recovery, which turns on whether a reasonable person could conclude from that evidence that the defendant committed intentional misconduct or gross negligence as defined in section 768.72(2). The trial court erred by denying leave on the discrete ground that the conduct was not sufficiently shocking, outrageous, and immoral, a standard the statute does not prescribe, so the order is reversed and remanded for reconsideration under the correct statutory standard.

Disposition: Nonfinal order denying the renewed motion for leave to amend to assert punitive damages reversed and remanded (appeal under Rule 9.130(a)(3)(G)).

items.summary:
Practical effect: an opposing party that obtains privileged material through the other side's inadvertent disclosure and then resists curing it, exploiting the unfair tactical advantage gained, can face counsel disqualification without the movant having to prove prejudice. Per curiam citation affirmance; opinion not final pending any timely rehearing motion.

Holding: Affirming on cited authority, the court applies the rule that where a party receives privileged material through the opposing party's inadvertent disclosure and then refuses to rectify the disclosure, gaining an unfair tactical advantage, a properly pleaded motion to disqualify may be granted without any requirement to demonstrate prejudice.

DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA  
SECOND DISTRICT  
 
 
DIAMOND EDGE CONSTRUCTION , LLC , 
 
Appellant , 
 
v. 
 
THE MOORINGS OF PINELLAS COUNTY CONDOMINIUM ASSOCIATION, 
INC., a Florida not -for-profit corporation; C.F. TUOHEY CONSTRUCTION, 
INC. d/b/a DIAMOND EDGE CONSTRUCTION; and ROBERT J. 
JACKSON, individually,  
 
Appellee s. 
 
No. 2D2026 -0713  
 
October 30, 2026  
 
Appeal pursuant to Fla. R. App. P. 9.130 from the Circuit Court for 
Pinellas County; Michael F. Andrews, Judge.  
 
Matthew J. Brinzo, Thomas E. Bishop, and Alexander T. Briggs of Bishop 
& Page, PLLC, Jacksonville, for Appellant.  
 
Gregory S. Grossman and Scott M. Gross of Greenberg Nikoloff, P.A., 
Dunedin, for Appellee The Moorings of Pinellas County Condominium 
Association, Inc.  
 
No appearance for remaining Appellees.  
 
GUARD , Judge . 
 Diamond Edge Construction, LLC appeals the denial of its motion 
to compel arbitration in a construction related  dispute with The Moorings 
of Pinellas County Condominium Association, Inc.   Because we conclude 
 
2 
 that the trial court was correct in determin ing Diamond Edge failed to 
prove  there was an enforceable agreement, we affirm.  
I. 
 Moorings is a condominium association located in Pinellas County, 
Florida.  On September 26, 2024, at least forty of its units were damaged 
by Hurricane Helene when the hurricane skirted Florida's west coast 
before making landfall near Perry, Florida.  The appendix  submitted by 
Diamond Edge  does not detail the extent of that damage.  
 At some point in time, Moorings began negotiating with Diamond 
Edge for Diamond Edge to provide construction related services to 
"[f]inish out work for 40 Hurricane Effected Units " at Moorings.  On June 
2, 2025, Diamond Edge provided Moorings with a Construction Services 
Agreement ( the Agreement) signed by its Chief Executive Officer.   On its 
first page, the Agreement indicate d Diamond Edge ha d a Florida general 
contractor  license  and provided  a license number .  But Diamond Edge 
was an unlicensed contractor , and the license number on the Agreement 
was a State of Florida fictitious name registration number.   The 
Agreement d id not contain a construction  price.  The Agreement d id not 
contain a scope of work to be performed.  The Agreement d id provide:  
Upon execution of this [Agreement], Diamond [Edge] will 
inspect the site where the work is to be performed and 
provide an initial scope to [Moorings] and its insurance 
adjuster for review.  After review of the scope, the parties 
shall mutually develop and agree upon, by execution of a 
Change Order in accordance with Section 2.7 herein, the 
scope of Work and cost ("Contract Price").  For all work 
covered by Company's flood insurance policy, the total 
Contract Price shall reflect the portion of proceeds [Moor ings] 
receives from its insurance carrier less an amount equal to 
[Moorings]'s public Adjuster's fee (the "Discount").  The 
Discount shall not exceed 8% of Diamond's total Contract 
Price for such Work.  
 
3 
 The Agreement provided for payment of an initial deposit but again d id 
not provide an amount.  Finally, the Agreement contain ed an arbitration 
provision : 
The Parties shall, for at least 15 days before any formal 
action, make a good faith effort to resolve any dispute.  
Should such efforts fail, the Parties agree that all disputes 
will be resolved by arbitration as provided by the Federal 
Arbitration Act, in  accordance with the Construction Industry 
Arbitration Rules of the AAA.  
The Agreement was unsigned by Moorings.  
 At some point between June 2, 2025, and August 2 8, 2025, 
Moorings remitted $818,266.02 to Diamond Edge.  It is unclear wh y 
these monies were remitted .  As the complaint here alleges , it was "to 
finish work in forty (40) hurricane effected units within [Moorings]. "  It 
does not appear that the parties ever agreed to a scope of work.  There 
does not appear to have been an agreed -to construction price or anything 
that looks like a contract price or discount as detailed in the Agreement.  
Sometime before  August 28, 2025 , Moorings learned that Diamond Edge 
was an unlicensed contractor .  On that day, Moorings, through its 
counsel, sent a letter to Diamond Edge terminating, to the extent that 
there was a contract, the Agreement and demanding certain records to 
account for the $818,266.02.  Th at letter reveal ed that work may have  
started  on the project and an amount of materials may have been  
procured.  But nothing in the appendix provide d us with the amount of 
work completed , supplies procured , or whether that work or those 
supplies were part of the scop e of the project .  Nor is there any  mention 
of building permits being obtained.  
At some point in time, Moorings also learned that Diamond Edge 
had entered into a Joint Venture Agreement with another company , 
Bosch Brothers Industries, LLC.   And that Bosch was transferre d 
 
4 
 $350,000 of the monies that Moorings remitte d Diamond Edge.  The joint 
venture was terminated after a dispute arose between Bosch and 
Diamond Edge related to a third company, C.F. Tuohey Construction, 
Inc.  Bosch later returned $350,000 to Moorings.  
 On September 22, 2025, Moorings sued Diamond Edge, Diamond 
Edge's Chief Executive Officer , Bosch, and Tuohey.   Moorings asserted 
claims for (1) declaratory relief  seeking a  declar ation that  the Agreement 
was void and unenforceable, (2) fraud in the inducement against 
Jackson, (3) fraud in the inducement against Tuohey, (4) fraud in the 
inducement against Diamond Edge,1 and (5) unjust enrichment against 
Diamond Edge.  Diamond Edge moved to compel arbitration under  the 
Agreement.  The trial court denied the motion to compel, concluding that 
"Diamond Edge has not met its burden to prove that there was an 
enforceable agreement to arbitrate  as there was no evidence beyond the 
unsigned contract, and contents of the Complaint submitted into the 
Court evidencing [Moorings] agreement to arbitrate any claim. "  Diamond 
Edge timely appealed that nonfinal order.  
II. 
As we have said multiple times, "Florida favors arbitration. "  
Kennedy v. Slockett , 414 So. 3d 318, 320 (Fla. 2d DCA 2025)  (citing UATP 
Mgmt., LLC v. Barnes , 320 So. 3d 851, 857 (Fla. 2d DCA 2021) ).  We 
review orders denying motions to compel arbitration de novo.  The Hillier 
Grp., Inc. v. Torcon, Inc. , 932 So. 2d 449, 452 (Fla. 2d DCA 2006) .  In 
ruling on a motion to compel arbitration, a court must consider three 
elements : (1) whether a valid agreement to arbitrate among  the parties 
 
1 Moorings pled two counts of fraud in the inducement  against 
Diamond Edge .  One count is against the Appellant Diamond Edge.  The 
other count is against Diamond Edge as a fictitious entity owned by 
Jackson and Tuohey . 
 
5 
 exists , (2) whether the issue litigated is arbitrable , and (3) whether the 
party seeking to compel arbitration waived that right.  Jackson v. 
Shakespeare F ound. , Inc., 108 So. 3d 587, 593 (Fla. 2013)  (citing Seifert 
v. U.S. Home Corp. , 750 So. 2d 633, 636 (Fla. 1999) ).  An arbitrator , not a 
court , considers the validity of a contract under state or federal law.  See 
Buckeye Check Cashing, Inc. v. Cardegna , 546 U.S. 440 , 445-46 (2006)  
("[U]nless the challenge is to the arbitration clause itself, the issue of the 
contract's validity is considered by the arbitrator in the first instance "); 
Sachse Constr. & Dev. Corp. v. Affirmed Drywall , Corp. , 251 So. 3d 1005, 
1011 -12 (Fla. 2d DCA 2018) (revers ing an order denying a contractor's 
motion to compel arbitratio n concluding invalidity under Florida law was 
an issue for an arbitrator ); Charles Boyd Constr ., Inc. v. Vacation Beach, 
Inc., 959 So. 2d 1227, 1228 -29 (Fla. 5th DCA 2007)  (holding similarly).  
In this case, the parties' arguments focus ed solely on whether an 
agreement to arbitrate exists.   Initiall y, Moorings argue d that there was 
no agreement to arbitrate because it never executed the Agreement.  We 
and other district courts have rejected such arguments and concluded 
that whether a valid agreement exists does not necessarily require an 
arbitration agreement to be executed.   Hayslip v. U.S. Home Corp. , 276 
So. 3d 109, 113 (Fla. 2d DCA 2019) ; GMRI, Inc. v. Brautigan , 392 So. 3d 
1098, 1102 -04 (Fla. 1st DCA 2024) ; Jean v. Bayview Loan Servicing, LLC , 
352 So. 3d 908, 909 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022) ; CEFCO v. Odom , 278 So. 3d 
347, 351 (Fla. 1st DCA 2019) ; Fi-Evergreen Woods, LLC v. Robinson , 135 
So. 3d 331, 335 (Fla. 5th DCA 2013) ; Santos v. Gen. Dynamics Aviation 
Servs. Corp. , 984 So. 2d 658, 660 (Fla. 4th DCA 2008) .  For example, in 
Hayslip , we concluded that home buyers "acquiesced " to an arbitration 
provision when they were on notice of the provision and took title and 
possession of a home.  276 So. 3d at 113.  We stated that "a party's 
 
6 
 conduct can demonstrate intent to be bound by the agreement."  Id.  
Similarly, in Santos , the Fourth District held in absence of a signed 
agreement a court is to consider the "party's words and conduct to 
determine whether the party assented to the agreement. "  984 So. 2d at 
661.   
Diamond Edge counters , relying almost solely on allegations in 
Moorings' complaint.  For example , it relies on the Moorings ' allegation  
that "[o]n June 2, 2025, the Association [Moorings] entered into a 
Construction Services Agreement ."  The problem with Diamond Edge's 
argument is it assumes that these allegations are  admissions  rather than 
statements made in "preliminary pleadings" which are not treated as 
admissions.   Brown v. Colonial Penn Ins ., 666 So. 2d 226, 227 (Fla. 2d 
DCA 1995); Vann v. Hobbs , 197 So. 2d 43, 45 (Fla. 2d DCA 1967).   In 
Vann , we stated that:  
Admissions made in the complaint and answer, upon which 
issue is finally joined, are accepted as facts without the 
necessity of supporting evidence.    The litigants are bound by 
these admissions.  However, they are not bound by 
admissions made in preliminary pleadings that have been  
successfully attacked by the opposing party, nor by 
admissions made in one of several separate and inconsistent 
defenses.  
Id. (citing to Olin's, Inc. v. Avis Rental Car Sys. of Fla ., Inc., 104 So. 2d 
508 (Fla. 1958)).  
 This case is not at issue.   There is no answer even filed .  It is 
unclear  whether the allegations in the complaint will be attacked by 
Diamond Edge.  It is also not clear whether any attack will be successful.  
There are allegations in the complaint and their attachments that 
contradict that there was an agreement  among st these parties .  Moorings 
stated also multiple causes of action in its complaint against Diamond 
Edge, one of which is inconsistent with a contract being formed.  A 
 
7 
 litigant can plead in the alternative both an unjust enrichment count and 
a count based on an express contract.  See Scott v. Acuity Real Est. 
Servs ., LLC , 359 So. 3d 881, 881 (Fla. 2d DCA 2023) (reversing a 
judgment that awarded monies on an unjust enrichment theory after 
finding that a contract existed);  Haskel Realty Grp ., Inc. v. KB Tyrone, 
LLC, 253 So. 3d 84, 86 (Fla. 2d DCA 2018) (stating that unjust 
enrichment is an alternative to a breach of contract claim); Diaz v. Cat 
Cay Holdings JHR, LLC , 51 Fla. L. Weekly D1635 (Fla. 3d DCA Aug. 12, 
2026) (stating that a plaintiff may plead a breach of contract and unjust 
enrichment counts in the alternative but cannot recover for both) .  Under 
these circumstances, the "entered into a contract " allegation in the 
complaint is not, at this stage, an admission  that can be held against 
Moorings .  
That said, the attachment of the unsigned contract to the 
complaint is evidence that Moorings  had notice of the arbitration 
provision.  If Diamond Edge could show "acquiescence " to or acceptance 
of the Agreement, then we could conclude a  contract  existed  and the 
arbitration provision would apply .  The closest conduct to acceptance 
that exists is Moorings remitting  $818,266.02 "to finish work in forty (40) 
hurricane effected units within the Association. "  The problem is that 
there is nothing in the appendix  connecting the $818,266.02 to the 
Agreement.  Nowhere in the Agreement is a construction price given.  
Nowhere in the Agreement is there an initial scope of work.  Nowhere in 
the Agreement is $818,266.02 listed, whether a deposit, full payment, or 
otherwise.   It is unclear what the $818,266.02 was for, when it was paid, 
or why it was paid .  Without any connection between the remitted 
amount and the contract itself, it cannot be treated as acquiescence to  
the contract.   
 
8 
 We are then only left with the unsigned Agreement.  Our review of 
that Agreement convinces us that the parties had not  agreed on essential 
terms, namely the scope of the work to be performed and the 
construction price to be paid .  In such circumstances, we have concluded 
that an agreement is not enforceable as the agreement was simply , at 
best, an agreement to agree.  Certified Motors, LLC v. Aventine Hill, LLC , 
369 So. 3d 1254, 1257 (Fla. 2d DCA 2023) ( "Failure to include essential 
terms is generally fatal to a contract's enforceability. " (citing Davis v. 
Hearthstone Senior Cmtys., Inc. , 155 So. 3d 1232, 1234 (Fla. 2d DCA 
2015)).   
 Accordingly, we affirm the trial court's denial of Diamond Edge's 
motion to compel arbitration.  
Affirmed.  
 
NORTHCUTT  and KHOUZAM , JJ., Concur.  
 
 
Opinion subject to revision prior to  official publication.

items.summary:
Confirms that Florida's strong policy favoring arbitration does not compel arbitration where the movant cannot prove formation. A court may deny a motion to compel (and the denial be affirmed) when the only evidence of agreement is an unsigned construction-services contract that omits essential terms, the claimant's large payments cannot be linked to that document, and the movant relies on the opponent's pre-answer complaint allegations that are not yet admissions. The opinion is marked subject to revision prior to official publication.

Holding: On a motion to compel arbitration, the proponent bears the burden of proving that a valid agreement to arbitrate exists-a threshold formation question for the court, distinct from challenges to a contract's overall validity, which generally go to the arbitrator unless aimed at the arbitration clause itself. An arbitration agreement need not be signed to bind a party: a party's words and conduct, including acquiescence while on notice of the clause, can show intent to be bound. But formation still requires agreement on essential terms, so an unsigned document that leaves essential terms (here, scope of work and construction price) open is at most an unenforceable agreement to agree, and a payment not connected to that document cannot establish acquiescence. Allegations that a party entered into a contract, made in preliminary pleadings before issue is joined, are not judicial admissions binding that party, particularly where breach-of-contract and unjust-enrichment counts are pleaded in the alternative.

Disposition: Nonfinal order denying the motion to compel arbitration affirmed (appeal under Rule 9.130).

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed  October 29, 2026.

________________ 
 
No. 3D26 -0143  
Lower Tribunal No. 25-7170- CA-01 
________________ 
 
 
Heather S. Maloney , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
A Better Blind, Inc. , 
Appellee.  
 
 
  An Appeal  from a non -final order  from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Javier  A. Enriquez , Judge.  
 
 Cornell & Associates, P.A., and Ware Cornell, Jr.  (Weston) , for 
appellant.  
 
 Berger Singerman LLP, and Anthony Carriuolo , for appellee.  
  Before  FERNANDEZ, LINDSEY and REBULL, JJ.  
  PER CURIAM.  
 2  Affirmed.  Int'l Univ. of Health Scis. Ltd., Inc. v. Abeles , 299 So. 3d 405, 
408 (Fla. 4th DCA 2020) (“ [R]eview of a nonfinal order on a motion to dismiss 
for lack of personal jurisdiction or improper service is de novo as to the 
court's legal rulings.”) ; McNae v. Fitzgerald , 400 So. 3d 748, 752 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2024)  (“Florida has held that in addition to the forum clause, there must 
be some independent basis for state jurisdiction in order to bring a 
nonresident into our courts. The additional basis in this case is [the 
defendant's alleged] breach of contract in Flori da by failing to [meet his 
contractual obligations] here.”  (quoting Desai Patel Sharma, Ltd v. Don Bell 
Indus., Inc. , 729 So. 2d 453, 454 (Fla. 5th DCA 1999) )); Machtinger v. Inertial 
Airline Servs. , Inc. , 937 So. 2d 730, 734 (Fla. 3d DCA 2006)  (“However, 
where the trial court's decision is based on live testimony, the appellate court 
defers to the trial court's determination of the facts [,]” which are reviewed for 
competent substantial evidence.) ; Intego Software, LLC v. Concept Dev., 
Inc., 198 So. 3d 887, 893 (Fla. 1st DCA 2016)  (“If a defendant's affidavits 
supporting dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction merely assert legal 
conclusions or otherwise fail to controvert the pertinent factual allegations of 
a complaint, the burden of proof on the existence or nonexistence of 
jurisdiction does not shift back to the plaintiff.” ).

items.summary:
Practical effect: personal-jurisdiction challenges to a nonresident turn on an independent jurisdictional basis rather than a contractual forum clause, and a movant whose supporting affidavits do not genuinely dispute the complaint's jurisdictional facts will not shift the burden; the legal rulings are reviewed de novo while live-testimony fact findings receive deference. Per curiam citation affirmance; opinion not final pending any timely rehearing motion.

Holding: Affirming a nonfinal order, the court restates the framework for a motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction or improper service: legal rulings are reviewed de novo, while factual findings based on live testimony are deferred to and reviewed only for competent substantial evidence; a forum-selection clause alone is insufficient to bring a nonresident into Florida courts, which requires an independent jurisdictional basis such as an alleged breach of contract committed in the state; and where the moving party's supporting affidavits merely assert legal conclusions or fail to controvert the complaint's pertinent factual allegations, the burden on the existence of jurisdiction does not shift to the plaintiff.

Disposition: Nonfinal order affirmed per curiam.

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed  November 4, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D25 -2106  
Lower Tribunal No. 25-13939 -CA-01 
________________
