Appellant s, 
 
vs. 
 
Cattleya PTC , 
Appellee.  
 
 
 An Appeal from  a non -final order from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Jason Emilios Dimitris , Judge.  
 
 Zimmerman, Kiser & Sutcliffe, P.A., and Ernest H. Kohlmyer , III, 
(Orlando) , for appellant s. 
 
 Gelber Schachter & Greenberg, P.A., and Barbara Llanes and Daniel 
R. Walsh , for appellee.  
 
 
Before  SCALES, C.J., and LOGUE and LOBREE , JJ.  
 
 LOGUE, J.  
 2 Appellants Rafael Lopes Brasileiro Martim (“R.  Martim”) and MME 
Martim, LLC ( “Martim, LLC ”) appeal the trial court’s order denying their 
motion to dismiss and compel arbitration. We dismiss part of their appeal for 
lack of jurisdiction and affirm the rest.  
In the case below, Cattleya PTC, a Swiss private trust company , sued 
Martim, LLC and R. Martim , its chief executive officer,  for conversion, unjust 
enrichment, and imposition of a constructive trust.  It alleged R.  Martim , who 
is a citizen of Brazil,  is a resident of Florida , and Martim, LLC is a Florida 
limited liability company . Cattleya PTC further alleged it had transferred 
$10,000,000 that it owned to R.  Martim and Martim, LLC to be invested on 
its behalf  and that R. Martim and Martim, LLC  had failed to provide proceeds 
from the investment, failed to account for the funds, and failed to return the 
funds on demand.  
R. Martim and Martim, LLC moved to dismiss and to compel arbitration.     
They moved to dismiss based on (1) lack of standing; (2) failure to join an 
indispensable party; (3) forum non conveniens; (4) improper venue based on 
a forum selection clause in a contract; and (5) an agreement to arbitrate.  
They filed no affidavits or testimony in support . Instead, they asked the trial 
court to take judicial notice of two pleadings from a lawsuit that Cattleya PTC 
had filed in federal court against R.  Martim and Martim, LLC on very similar 
 3 grounds.  The first was Cattleya  PTC’s federal compl aint, which allegedly 
contained conflicting averments. The second was R. Martim and Martim, 
LLC’s motion to dismiss . Attached to the motion to dismiss was a contract 
between Nervis Gerardo Villalobos  Cardenas  (the sole owner of Cattleya 
PTC) and Martim, LLC (signed by R.  Martim) , which provided for the transfer 
of $10,000,000 to M artim,  LLC and mandate d disputes be submitted to an 
arbitration proceeding by the International Chamber of Commerce in 
London . The contract was not attached to Cattleya PTC’s federal complaint. 
The arguments raised in their federal motion to dismiss largely  track the 
arguments they make here except , in their federal motion to dismiss , they 
argued the federal court lacked diversity jurisdiction to hear the case. 
Cattleya PTC voluntarily dismissed that federal suit and filed this one in its 
stead. After extensive briefing and arguments, the trial court denied the 
motion to dismiss , and this appeal followed.  
The denial of a motion to dismiss is a non -final order . This Court has 
jurisdiction to hear appeals of non-final orders only where the Florida 
Supreme Court has authorized such appeals by rule. Art. V, § 4(b)(1) , Fla. 
Const.  (“[District courts ] may review interlocutory orders in such cases to the 
extent provided by rules adopted by the supreme court. ”). No rules provid e 
this Court with jurisdiction to hear an appeal of a non -final order denying a 
 4 motion to dismiss for lack of standing or for failure to join an indispensable 
party. “Without jurisdiction, there is only one action we can take: we must 
dismiss.”  Fisher v. Hous. Auth. of the City of Key W. , 424 So. 3d 1017, 1022 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2025) . We therefore dismiss that part of the appeal.  
An interlocutory appeal of an order denying a motion to dismiss based 
on forum non conveniens, however, is authorized by rule. Fla. R. App. P. 
9.130 (a)(3)(C)(viii). The merits of the forum non conveniens analysis turns 
on the four factors set forth in Kinney System, Inc. v. Continental Insurance 
Co., 674 So. 2d 86, 94 (Fla. 1996), codified in Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 
1.061(a) .  “The burden of persuasion for each factor is on the moving party.” 
de Holguin v. Godin , 367 So. 3d 1286, 1289 (Fla. 3d DCA 2023).  
Generally, the party seeking a dismissal of a suit for forum non 
conveniens “must support the motion by affidavit or other evidence offered 
under oath.” Ground Improvement Techs., Inc. v. Merchs. Bonding Co. , 707 
So. 2d 1138, 1139 (Fla. 5th DCA 1998). “The only exception would be where 
the complaint itself shows on its face that a forum non conveniens  transfer 
is warranted.” Id. R. Martim and Martim , LLC failed to attach any affidavit or 
sworn evidence to their motion. See Reiber v. Yamasaki , 382 So. 3d 798, 
803 (Fla. 5th DCA 2024) (“ A trial court generally cannot conduct a 
‘meaningful analysis ’ under Kinney  if the defendant has not put forth any 
 5 evidence or proof in support of the motion to dismiss. ”).1 The unsworn 
statements of fact in the federal compl aint and motion to dismiss do not 
provide the necessary facts to even support a finding that an arbitration 
proceeding by the International Chamber of Commerce in London  is an 
adequate alternative forum because prior unsworn pleadings “may not 
[ordinarily ] be used by an opposing party as proof of an issue.” Hernandez 
v. CGI Windows & Doors, Inc. , 347 So. 3d 113, 118 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022) 
(quoting Hines v. Trager Constr. Co. , 188 So. 2d 826, 829 (Fla. 1st DCA 
1966)).  
We are left with only the allegations in the complaint  in this case . The re 
are no allegations in the complaint that the parties are bound to submit to an 
arbitration proceeding by the International Chamber of Commerce in 
London , much less that such a proceeding provides the jurisdiction over the 
parties, discovery , and access to witnesses sufficient to make it an adequate 
alternative forum . Moreover, the allegations aver that the defendants are 
residents of the current forum —Miami -Dade County. Exceptions exist but 
normally, “the fact that the defendants are all located in Miami -Dade County, 
 
1 R. Martim and Martim LLC’s argument that they should have had a hearing 
also fails, as this Court has previously held that “[t]he lack of affidavits . . . 
effectively negate [s] the [d]efendants’ argument on appeal that they should 
have received an evidentiary hearing” on the motion to dismiss for forum non 
conveniens. Navas v. Brand , 130 So. 3d 766, 770 (Fla. 3d DCA 2014).  
 6 Florida is an indication that it would be less burdensome for them to defend 
the lawsuit here.” Ryder Truck Rental, Inc. v. Adams , 401 So. 3d 430, 435 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2024) ; Taurus Int’l Mfg., Inc. v. Friend , 217 So. 3d 1133, 1134 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2017) (“[A] forum non conveniens argument coming from a 
party sued where he resides is both puzzling and strange .” (quoting Cardoso 
v. FPB Bank , 879 So. 2d 1247, 1250 (Fla. 3d DCA 2004) )). Based on the 
record before the trial court, therefore , we find no basis to hold the trial court 
committed revers ible error on this point.  
 The Florida Supreme Court has authorized i nterlocutory appeal s of 
order s denying a motion to dismiss based on a forum selection clause or a 
contract to arbitrate. Fla. R. App.  P. 9.130 (a)(3)(A), (I). However, 
Plaintiff/Appellee Cattleya PTC and Defendant/Appellant R.  Martim were not 
parties to the contract . “As a general rule, a contract cannot be enforced 
against a person who is not a party to the contract and has not otherwise 
agreed to its terms.”  Sifaco Grp., S.A. v. Margioukla , 51 Fla. L. Weekly 
D1440, at *4 (Fla. 4th DCA July 15, 2026).  Nervis Gerardo Villalobos 
Cardenas , the actual party to the contract with R.  Martim and Martim, LLC , 
is not a party to the litigation.  
While there might be  circumstances such as piercing the corporate veil 
that could overcome  these gaps, the facts necessary to do so do not appear 
 7 in this record, where, as indicated above, the Appellants submitted no 
affidavits or testimony in support of their motion. In fact, Appellants argue 
Cattleya PTC lacks standing to bring this action because it was not a party 
to the contract.  In these circumstances, given this record, we again are left 
with no basis to find the trial court committed error.  
Appeal dismissed in part; affirmed in part.

items.summary:
Practically, a defendant cannot convert a routine motion-to-dismiss denial into an appeal on standing or indispensable-party grounds, and to win dismissal or compel arbitration abroad it must actually produce sworn proof of the Kinney factors and show that the party resisting arbitration is bound by the clause; on this record the foreign-forum and arbitration arguments failed and the case proceeded in Florida.

Holding: No rule authorizes interlocutory review of an order denying dismissal for lack of standing or failure to join an indispensable party, so that portion is dismissed; forum non conveniens and forum-selection/arbitration denials are reviewable under rule 9.130, but the forum non conveniens movant bears the burden on each Kinney factor (codified in rule 1.061(a)) and must supply sworn evidence because unsworn prior pleadings are not proof; and absent record-supported grounds such as piercing the corporate veil, a forum-selection or arbitration clause generally cannot be enforced against a person who is not a party to the contract.

Disposition: Appeal dismissed in part; affirmed in part

Author: Judge Logue

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed  November 4, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D24-2069 
Lower Tribunal No.  20-8909 -CA-01 
________________  
 
 
JB Green Estate, LLC, et al. , 
Appellant s, 
 
vs. 
 
Fredric N. Karlton , et al. , 
Appellee s. 
 
 
 
 An Appeal from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, Thomas J. 
Rebull , Judge.  
 
 Sanchez -Medina, Gonzalez, Quesada, Lage, Gomez & Machado  LLP, 
and Gustavo D. Lage and Augusto R. Lopez , for appellant s. 
 
 Lerman & Whitebook , P.A., and Carlos D. Lerman (Hollywood) ; Law 
Offices of Victor K. Rones , P.A., and Victor K. Rones , for appellee s Fredric 
N. Karlton and Beneficial Funding Corp . 
 
 
Before  SCALES , C.J. , and BOKO R and GOO DEN , JJ.  
 
 SCALES, C.J.  
 2  
 JB Green Estate, LLC , William Holly and KLIP Associates, Inc.  
(collectively, “JB Green”)  appeal a n October 24, 2024 final judgment of 
foreclosure in favor of appellees Fredric N. Karlton and Beneficial Loan Corp.  
(together, the “Lender”), entered after a two-week  bench trial. We write only 
to address JB Green’s  central argument on appeal:  that the trial court’s 
factual findings  – notably, its finding that William  Holly  executed the subject 
loan documents  on behalf of JB Green  – were not supported by competent, 
substantial evidence .   
JB Green  first suggests that the trial court erred by not accepting  its 
handwriting expert’s testimony  that Holly’s signatures on the loan documents 
were forged . While a trial judge sitting as a fact -finder may not arbitrarily  
disregard the testimony of an expert witness, the judge may disregard an 
expert’s testimony if the judge provides a reasonable  explanation for doing 
so. See Coday v. State , 946 So. 2d 988, 1005 (Fla. 2006) (“While we have 
given trial judges broad discretion in considering unrebutted expert 
testimony, we have always required that rejection to have a rational basis. 
For example, the expert testimony could be rejected because of conflict with 
other evidence, credibility or impeachment of the witness, or other 
reasons.”); see also  Da Silva v. Labriola , 51 Fla. L. Weekly D1478, 2026 WL 
2104174, at *8 -9 (Fla. 3d DCA July 22, 2026).  
 3  Here, the trial court gave two quite  reasonable explanations  for 
disregarding the testimony of JB Green’s  expert witness: (i) the expert’s 
testimony was contradicted by the notary who testified that he actually 
witnessed the signatures in question ;1 and (ii) contrary to industry standards, 
the expert reviewed only photocopies, rather than  available originals, of the 
relevant loan documents.  
JB Green  also argue s that approximately two dozen  of the factual 
findings made by the trial court were unsupported by competent, substantial 
evidence ; therefore, cumulatively, they warrant reversal . We disagree. The 
trial court entered a comprehensive, detailed final judgment adjudicating 
several claims, counterclaims, and cross -claims. As the Lender’ s briefing 
notes, each of the trial court ’s factual findings  – including those challenged 
by JB Green – are supported by record evidence.  
JB Green misconstrues our standard of review  by suggesting that the 
trial court’s factual findings are not properly supported because JB Green  
adduced competing evidence  at trial . It is not within our purview to reweigh 
the evidence. Keys Country Resort,  LLC v. 1733 Overseas Highway, LLC , 
324 So. 3d 988, 988 (Fla. 3d DCA 2021) (“[I]t is not our function to conduct 
 
1 A different notary also witnessed Holly’s  signature s on an earlier set of loan 
documents that the Lender’s counsel had rejected.  
 4 a de novo review of the evidence , but simply to determine whether there 
exists in the record competent substantial evidence to support the judgment 
of the trial court[.]” (quoting Morey v. Everbank , 93 So. 3d 482, 489 -90 (Fla. 
1st DCA 2012) )). Indeed, when conducting a review of whether factual 
findings are supported by competent, substantial evidence, the reviewing 
court looks only at the evidence supporting th e findings , without regard to 
competing evidence. See State , Dep’t of Highway Safety & Motor Vehicles 
v. Wiggins , 151 So. 3d 457, 464 (Fla. 1st DCA 2014) (“The sole starting (and 
ending) point is a search of the record for competent substantial evidence 
supporting the decision.”).  We do not disturb factual findings , such as those 
made by the trial court below, that  are supported by competent, substantial 
evidence . Mowder v. Smith , 390 So. 3d 106, 109 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024).    
Affirmed.

items.summary:
Practically, a foreclosure borrower cannot overturn a bench-trial judgment by re-offering its own side of the evidence: the appellate court asks only whether competent, substantial evidence supports the trial court's findings and whether the court reasonably explained discounting the borrower's handwriting expert, so a well-supported final judgment is affirmed.

Holding: A trial judge sitting as factfinder may reject otherwise unrebutted expert testimony if the rejection has a rational basis, such as conflict with other evidence, credibility or impeachment, or the expert's methodology; and on review, findings supported by competent, substantial evidence are affirmed without the appellate court reweighing the evidence or weighing competing evidence, looking only to the evidence that supports the findings.

Disposition: Affirmed

Author: Chief Judge Scales

SIXTH  DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
Case No. 6D2025- 3091  
Lower Tribunal No. 2025- CA-007446 -O 
_____________________________  
 
BRAD HATCHER and AUDREY HATCHER , 
Appellant s,  
v. 
RESTORICAL , LLC  d/b/a  SYDONIE MANSION , 
Appellee . 
_____________________________  
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for Orange  County.  
Michael Deen , Judge.  
 
October 30, 2026  
 
GANNAM, J.  
 
Bradley and Audrey Hatcher appeal a temporary injunction obtained by their 
neighbor, Restorical , LLC, enjoining the Hatchers ’ noisy disruptions of weddings 
and other events hosted by Restorical. Because  there was not competent , substantial 
evidence supporting the likelihood of irreparable harm to Restorical absent the 
injunction, we reverse.  
I 
Restorical owns the historic Sydonie Mansion in Mount Dora, where it hosts 
weddings and other events. Restorical ’s owners, Clark and Amy Frogley, also live 
in the mansion. The Hatchers own and live on the neighboring property, where they 
2 have dogs, boats, various motor vehicles, and a shooting range. At the time of suit, 
Restorical had hosted weddings at the mansion for around nine years, averaging two 
to three weddings per week during its  September -to-May busy season.  
Restorical  claims  that, prior to 2025, the Hatchers sporadically disrupted its  
wedding events by, for example, playing loud music on speakers aimed at the 
mansion and letting their dogs run free on the mansion grounds. The  disruptions  
intensified  in 2025 with the Hatchers’  intentionally and repeatedly disrupting 
weddings with, for example, loud gunfire and revving chainsaw and airboat engines.  
Restorical sued the Hatchers on private nuisance and other grounds and sought 
a temporary injunction to immediately halt their disruptions. Following an 
evidentiary hearing at which the Frogleys  and Hatchers testified, the trial court 
entered a temporary injunction order  finding Restorical likely to succeed on the 
merits of its private nuisance claim that the Hatchers ’ “disruptive conduct during 
[Restorical ’s] scheduled events, including rapid gunfire, revving engines, use of 
airboats, operation of chainsaws, and release of dogs, all timed to coincide with 
wedding ceremonies, ” “has caused continuing disruption to [Restorical ’s] business, 
. . . threatening the loss of goodwill and the viability of the venue. ” The court found 
“[t]hose injuries are irreparable and not adequately compensable by monetary 
damages, ” and that “ [t]he public  interest is served by both the lawful enjoyment of 
property and the maintenance of order and civility between neighbors. ” The order 
prohibits the Hatchers from disrupting Restorical’s events  and requires  Restorical to 
provide  the Hatchers  written , twenty -four hour noti ce of its events.  
3 II 
To obtain a temporary injunction, a party must prove (1) a substantial 
likelihood of success on the merits, (2) the unavailability of an adequate remedy at 
law, (3) a likelihood of irreparable harm absent the  injunction, and (4) the injunction 
serves the public interest. Fla. Dep’t of Health v. Florigrown, LLC,  317 So. 3d 1101, 
1110 (Fla. 2021) ; Lusby v. Canevari , 363 So. 3d 233, 235 (Fla. 6th DCA 2023).  
Failure to prove any element requires denial  of the temporary injunction. 
Florigrown, LLC , 317 So. 3d at 1111. Even if all elements are proved, however, 
whether to grant the injunction remains within the trial court’s discretion.  Vinci v. 
Lake Lizzie Reserve Homeowners Ass’n, Inc. , 438 So. 3d 690, 691 n.2 (Fla. 6th DCA  
2026) (citing Geise v. Fleck, 433 So. 3d 931, 939 (Fla. 6th DCA 2026)) . Any order 
granting the injunction must contain “[c]lear, definite, and unequivocally sufficient 
factual finding s” on each  element . City of Jack . v. Naegele Outdoor Advert. Co. , 634 
So. 2d 750, 754 (Fla. 1st DCA 1994), approved sub nom.  Naegele Outdoor Advert. 
Co. v. City of Jack. , 659 So. 2d 1046 (Fla. 1995), as modified on reh’ g (Aug. 24, 
1995) ; see also  Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.610 (c) (“Every injunction shall specify the reasons 
for entry  . . . .”). We review a trial court ’s findings on each element  for competent, 
substantial evidence, its legal conclusions de novo, and its ultimate decision to grant 
or deny the injunction for an abuse of discretion.  Florigrown, LLC , 317 So. 3d at 
1110; Geise , 433 So. 3d at  939.1 
 
1 The trial court’ s likelihood of success finding includes its conclusion that 
section 823.16,  Florida Statutes,  providing certain legal immunities for gun range 
4 The Hatchers challenge the temporary injunction on several grounds, but we 
only address irreparable harm and inadequate remedy at law. We consider these 
elements together because, though distinct requirements  for injunctive relief, 
“[i]rreparable harm and an inadequate remedy at law are two sides of the same coin.”  
Park Crossing Homeowners Ass ’n, Inc. v. Suarez , 415 So. 3d 676, 691 n.3 (Fla. 4th 
DCA 2025) ; accord Fla. Ass’n of Realtors v. Orange Cnty. , 350 So. 3d 115, 130 
(Fla. 5th DCA 2022)  (“The concepts of irreparable harm and no adequate legal 
remedy are distinct prongs of the temporary injunction test, but they are related to 
one another. ”); Logan v. Logan, 397 So. 3d 1144, 1149 ( Fla. 2d DCA 2024) (same); 
Hamad v. Sarsour , 405 S o. 3d 334, 337 (Fla. 3d DCA 2025) (“Irreparable injury and 
no adequate remedy at law are distinct, but interrelated, prongs.”) . 
 
noise, provides the Hatchers no immunity from Restorical’ s nuisance claim  because 
it is unconstitutional . The trial court relied on  Gartman v. Southern Tactical Range, 
LLC, in which the First District held section 823.16 violated the plaintiff’s  right of 
access to the courts under article I, section 21 of the Florida Constitution. 417 So. 
3d 449, 459 (Fla. 1st DCA 2025)  (citing Kluger v. White , 281 So. 2d 1, 2 (Fla. 1973)  
(“We hold, therefore, that where a right of access to the courts for redress for a 
particular injury has been provided by statutory law predating the adoption of the 
Declaration of Rights of the Constitution of the State of Florida, or where such right 
has become a part of the common law of the State pursuant to Fla.  Stat. s 2.01, 
F.S.A., the Legislature is without power to abolish such a right without providing a reasonable alternative to protect the rights of the people of the State to redress for 
injuries, unless the Legislature can show an overpowering public neces sity for the 
abolishment of such right, and no alternative method of meeting such public 
necessity can be shown. ”)). Gartman is under review in the Florida Supreme Court, 
Southern Tactical Range, LLC v. Gartman, No. SC2025- 1259, and oral argument 
occurred on May 7, 2026.  Because we reverse on the irreparable harm element, we 
need not address likelihood of success on the merits , and so we do  not address the 
constitutionality of section 823.16.  
5 For temporary injunction purposes, an injury is irreparable whe n it has no 
adequate remedy at law —i.e., when it is not compensable by money damages . 
Hamad, 406 So. 3d at 337 (“Whether an injury is irreparable within this context is 
wholly dependent on the existence of an adequate remedy at law.”) ; Fla. Ass ’n of 
Realtors , 350 So. 3d at 130 (“ ‘Irreparable’ means an injury cannot be adequately 
repaired or redressed in a court of law by an award of money damages.”);  Landmark 
at Crescent Ridge LP v. Everest Fin., Inc. , 219 So. 3d 218, 220 (Fla. 1st DCA 2017)  
(“The law governing the irreparable harm required for injunctive relief is instructive; 
there is no irreparable harm for the purpose of a temporary injunction where the 
harm can be adequately compensated for by a monetary award.”  (cleaned up)) .2 
III 
Florida appellate decisions indicate a party  can show irreparable harm  or an 
inadequate remedy at law  justifying a temporary injunction in several ways.  A 
common example is cases where damages  cannot be  quantified . See, e.g. , Lincoln 
Tower Corp. v. Richter ’s Jewelry Co. , 12 So. 2d 452, 452–54 (Fla. 1943) ( “It appears 
 
2 Given that irreparable harm and inadequate remedy at law remain distinct 
requirements for a temporary injunction under binding precedent,  see Florigrown, 
LLC, 317 So. 3d at  1110, we do not hold that either or both could never be 
independently significant. But see Douglas Laycock, The Death of the Irreparable 
Injury Rule , 103 Harv. L. Rev. 687, 694 (1990) (“ The irreparable injury rule has two 
formulations. Equity will act only to prevent irreparable injury, and equity will act only if there is no adequate legal remedy. The two formulations are equivalent; what 
makes an injury irreparable is that no other reme dy can repair it . Attempts to 
distinguish the two formulations have produced no common usage. ” (footnote 
omitted)) ; Park Crossing Homeowners , 415 So. 3d at  691 n.3 ( quoting same ). 
6 that it would be impractical, if not impossible, to establish the damage to the lessor, 
or the lessees, resulting from a breach of the covenant and that the remedy at law 
would, therefore, not be adequate. ”); Zimmerman v. D.C.A. at Welleby, Inc. , 505 So. 
2d 1371, 1373 (Fla. 4th DCA 1987) (“The remedy at law, an action for damages, 
would be inadequate because of the difficulty in determining how many sales were 
lost and what the profit on each such lost sale would have been. Thus damages are 
said to be speculative and unascertainable. The harm is therefore irreparable and the 
remedy at law inadequate.”); Thompson v. Plan.  Comm’n of City of Jack ., 464 So. 
2d 1231, 1237 (Fla. 1st DCA 1985) (“Given these factors, calculations of appellants’ 
money damages would be speculative, thereby establishing the inadequacy of a legal 
remedy.”);  Liza Danielle, Inc. v. Jamko, Inc. , 408 So. 2d 735, 738–39 (Fla. 3d DCA 
1982)  (“We recognize that impossibility of ascertaining the amount of plaintiff's 
legal damages may establish inadequacy of the legal remedy so as to support an 
award of injunctive relief , and additionally, may establish the requisite irreparable 
character of the injury  . . . .”  (citations omitted)) .3 
 
3 Actual injury for which the calculation of damages is speculative, which is 
irreparable  harm , must be distinguished from speculative injury, which is no harm  
at all.  See Liza Danielle, Inc. , 408 So. 2d at  739 (“[A]n injury is irreparable where 
the damages are estimable only by conjecture, and not by any accurate standard. But 
mere difficulty in proving injury does not establish irreparable injury. One must 
distinguish between the difficulty of proving that an injury exists and the difficulty 
of measuring the amount or extent of a proven injury. ” (alteration  in original) 
(quoting 42 Am.  Jur. 2d Injunctions § 49 (now  42 Am. Jur. 2d Injunctions §§ 34, 36, 
Westlaw (database updated Aug. 2026) )); Biscayne Park, LLC v. Wal -Mart Stores 
E., LP , 34 So. 3d 24, 26 (Fla. 3d DCA 2010)  (“Because the alleged injury is 
7 Under  another line of cases, the total destruction of a business may be  
irreparable harm. See, e.g. , XIP Techs., LLC v. Ascend Glob. Servs ., LLC , 253 So. 
3d 1183, 1187 (Fla. 2d DCA 2018) ( “[T]he unrefuted evidence below was that these 
actions by XIP would result in the total destruction of Ascend’ s business. This was 
sufficient to establish irreparable harm without an adequate legal remedy. ”); U.S. 1 
Off. Corp. v. Falls Home Furnishings, Inc. , 655 So. 2d 209, 210 (Fla. 3d DCA 1995) 
(“[E]vidence of the potential destruction of a business, without a track record from 
which to calculate the potential loss and with harm of a continuing nature, may in 
some cases provide sufficient indicia of irrepa rable harm to support temporary 
injunctive relief.”); Richard v. Behav.  Healthcare Options, Inc. , 647 So. 2d 976, 978 
(Fla. 2d DCA 1994)  (“The record of the evidentiary hearing indicates BHO made an 
adequate showing for relief . . . . BHO argued that irreparable injury would occur if 
Richard, and other physicians if they knew that BHO permitted Richard to proceed, 
continued to collect receivables. BHO contended the irreparable injury would be the 
destruction of its business. ”). 
On the other hand, the  loss of some business , without more,  is not irreparable  
harm . See State Agency for Health Care Admin. v. Cont ’l Car Servs ., Inc. , 650 So. 
2d 173, 175–76 (Fla. 2d DCA 1995) (“[T]he trial court erred in concluding that Continental would suffer irreparable injury. Other than money damages and loss of 
 
speculative, we conclude that it is insufficient to meet the irreparable injury 
standard. ”). 
8 business to a competitor, Continental provided no evidence of irreparable injury or 
injury for which there was no adequate remedy at law.”);  State Dep ’t. of Transp. v. 
Kountry Kitchen of Key Largo, Inc. , 645 So. 2d 1086, 1086 (Fla. 3d DCA 1994)  
(“On the issue of irreparable injury, appellee Kountry Kitchen merely alleged that it 
will suffer harm if the sign is removed because the sign generates most of its 
business. However, an alleged loss of business will not support a finding of 
irreparable injury. ”); Tamiami Trail Tours, Inc. v. Greyhound Lines, Inc., S. 
Greyhound Lines Div. , 212 So. 2d 365, 366 (Fla. 4th DCA 1968) (“In order to 
support the granting of a temporary injunction it is also necessary for plaintiff to 
demonstrate irreparable injury; injury which cannot be redressed in a court of law. 
Mere loss of business because of a competitor will not suffice. Any loss Greyhound 
might suffer as a result of Tamiami’ s operation over the route in question could be 
easily documented by ticket sales and use, and damages assessed after final hearing.” (footnotes omitted)) . 
Finally, harm may be  irreparable if it is compensable by money damages but 
recurring with such frequency that a multiplicity of suits would be required to redress 
it. See, e.g. , City of Jack.  v. Giller , 135 So. 549, 551 (Fla. 1931)  (“The action of 
trespass in such cases is not a plain, complete, and adequate remedy at law, because it might require a multiplicity of actions to successfully recover for the damage done 
9 by repeated acts of usurpation over the land involved and a continued interference 
with and destruction of complainant ’s business  . . . .”).4 
Here, there is  not competent , substantial evidence to support a finding that  the 
Hatchers’ conduct is likely to irreparabl y harm Restorical  absent an injunction.5 The 
 
4 There may be other ways for a business to show irreparable harm or an 
inadequate remedy at law supporting a temporary injunction. W e do not attempt to 
catalogue them all here.  
5 At the  conclusion of the temporary injunction hearing, the trial court gave 
the parties the option to file post -hearing affidavits or declarations on matters 
discussed at the hearing, citing Bee Line En tertainment Partners v. State , in which 
the Fifth District agreed with several federal decisions holding  “that the court may 
rely on hearsay evidence and may even give inadmissible evidence some weight”  at 
a noticed and contested evidentiary hearing on a motion to dissolve a t emporary 
injunction. 791 So. 2d 1197, 1205–06 (Fla. 5th DCA 2001)  (internal quotation marks 
omitted) . This Court has not decided  that the Florida Evidence Code, ch. 90, Fla. 
Stat., including its mandate that affidavits and other hearsay  are not admissible 
absent an applicable exception , does not apply in a noticed and contested evidentiary 
hearing on a temporary injunction motion . See Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.610(a)(2) (“ No 
evidence other than the affidavit or verified pleading shall be used to support the 
application for a temporary injunction unless the adverse party appears at the 
hearing or has received reasonable notice of the hearing. ” (emphasis added)); 
§ 90.102, Fla. Stat. (“ This chapter shall replace and supersede existing statutory or 
common law in conflict with its provisions. ”); § 90.103(2), Fla. Stat. (“ This act shall 
apply . . . to civil actions and all other proceedings pending on or brought after 
October 1, 1981. ”); see also  Robinson v. State , 707 So. 2d 688, 691 (Fla. 1998)  
(holding “ affidavit proffered . . .  is nothing more than hearsay, i.e., an out -of-court 
statement offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted, which is inadmissible ”); 
Sasser v. Sasser , 437 So. 3d 529, 534 (Fla. 6th DCA 2026)  (“The affidavit was not 
admitted into evidence. If Jolene had tried to admit it into evidence, it would have 
been subject to a hearsay objection. ”); Reese v. Reese, 363 So. 3d 1202, 1210 n.6 
(Fla. 6th DCA 2023)  (“The admission of a financial affidavit into evidence is subject 
to the Florida Evidence Code, including [its hearsay provisions] .”); cf. Holland M. 
Ware Charitable Found. v. Tamez Pine Straw LLC , 343 So. 3d 1285, 1290 (Fla. 1st 
DCA 2022)  (Rowe, C.J., concurring) (“ In a contested hearing on a motion for 
temporary injunction, a trial court must take evidence. ”); Concerned Citizens for 
Jud. Fairness, Inc. v. Yacucci , 162 So. 3d 68, 72 (Fla. 4th DCA 2014)  (“At a 
contested hearing, the party opposing an injunction has the opportunity to cross 
10 trial court found the Hatchers’ conduct “ has caused continuing disruption to 
[Restorical’s]  business,  interfering with ceremonies and threatening the loss of 
goodwill and the viability of the venue .” And there was creditable testimony that 
Amy Frogley feared  Restorical  would lose wedding business  and would lose the 
historic Sydonie Mansion without wedding revenue to maintain it. But there was n o 
testimony  or other evidence  of cancelations  or lost bookings  showing that any loss 
of business  had occurred or was imminent , or evidence as to why an y actual loss of 
business would not be quantifiable  given  Restorical’s  nine-year track record  of 
even ts. Nor was there  testimony or other evidence of the likely total destruction of 
Restorical’s wedding and event  business absent an injunction.  At the time of the 
hearing, Restorical was still booking  weddings and was not informing customers of 
the Hatchers’ disruptions. True, there was testimony that a particular disruption 
required Restorical to partially refund a  single  wedding fee , but the refund is 
 
examine witnesses and challenge the allegations of the complaint. ”); Thomas v. 
Osler Med., Inc. , 963 So. 2d 896, 899–900 (Fla. 5th DCA 2007)  (“[I]in certain 
circumstances, a temporary injunction may be granted on an ex parte basis without 
notice and an evidentiary hearing.  In this instance, the trial court decides whether to 
issue the temporary injunction based on the pleadings and affidavits before it. Conversely, notice followed by an evidentiary hearing may precede the issuance of a temporary injunction, and in such an instance, the trial court relies on the testimony 
presented along with other appropriate evidence  to determine whether to grant or 
deny the injunction. ” (emphasis added) (citation omitted)) ; Hunter v. Dennies 
Contracting Co. , 693 So. 2d 615, 616 (Fla. 2d DCA 1997) (“ [A]t the hearing on the 
motion to dissolve . . .  an ex parte  temporary injunction, the party who obtained the 
injunction bears the burden of going forward with evidence . . . .”). We do not decide 
the issue here because the Hatchers did not object to the trial court’s consideration of the post -hearing affidavits or  declarations  on hearsay grounds  and, as a result, the 
issue is not preserved for our review . 
11 calculable, and there was no evidence  that the need to issue  refunds  will recur , much 
less recur in a manner that would result in unquantifiable damages  or the total 
destruction of Restorical’s business . Thus, the trial court ’s finding that Restorical 
would suffer irreparable harm absent the entry of a preliminary injunction was not 
supported by competent, substantial evidence.  
IV 
All told, there was competent , substantial evidence to support a finding that 
the Hatchers’ conduct is a harmful nuisance , but the harm is not self -evidently 
irreparable, and Restorical did not prove its irreparability . This is not to say 
Restorical cannot prove irreparable harm , but only that, on the record before us, there 
is no t competent , substantial evidence to support a finding that Restorical is likely 
to suffer irreparable harm without an injunction against the Hatchers’ nuisance 
conduct. W e reverse the temporary injunction and remand for further proceedings 
consistent with this opinion.  
REVERSED and REMANDED.  
STARGEL , J., concur s. 
MIZE, J., concurs, with opinion.  
_____________________________________ 
 
NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE MOTION FOR REHEARING 
AND DISPOSITION THEREOF IF TIMELY FILED .   
____________________________________ 
 
MIZE, J., concurring.  
 
12 I fully concur in the well- reasoned majority opinion.  I write separately to 
address what appears to be some tension in Florida jurisprudence concerning the 
irreparable harm requirement for injunctions.   
On the one hand, Florida courts have universally held that an injury causes 
irreparable harm only when it is not compensable by money damages. See, e.g. , 
Holland M. Ware Charitable Found. v. Tamez Pine Straw LLC , 343 So. 3d 1285, 
1289 (Fla. 1st DCA 2022)  (“Irreparable injury is defined as injury that cannot be 
cured by money damages, and the test for unavailability of adequate remedy at law is whether a judgment can be obtained, not whether it will be collectible once 
obtained. ”); Landmark at Crescent Ridge LP v. Everest Fin., Inc. , 219 So. 3d 218, 
220 (Fla. 1st DCA 2017)  (“The law governing the irreparable harm required for 
injunctive relief is instructive; t here is no irreparable harm for the purpose of a 
temporary injunction where the harm can be adequately compensated for by a monetary award.”  (cleaned up)); City of Miami Springs v. Steffen , 423 So. 2d 930, 
931 (Fla. 3d DCA 1982)  (“There is no irreparable harm for the purpose of a 
temporary injunction where the harm can be adequately compensated for by a 
monetary award. ”); Lutsky v. Schoenwetter , 172 So. 3d 534, 534 (Fla. 3d DCA 2015)  
(“[I]rreparable injury is injury that cannot be cured by money damages. ”); S. Fla . 
Limousines, Inc. v. Broward Cnty. Aviation Dept. , 512 So. 2d 1059, 1062 (Fla. 4th 
DCA 1987)  (“Irreparable injury will not be found if money damages are available 
as a remedy. ”); Bautista REO U.S., LLC v. ARR Invs. , Inc. , 229 So. 3d 362, 365 (Fla. 
4th DCA 2017)  (“Irreparable harm is not established if the harm can be adequately 
13 compensated by a monetary award. ”); Fla. Ass’n of Realtors v. Orange Cnty. , 350 
So. 3d 115, 130 (Fla. 5th DCA 2022)  (“‘Irreparable’ means an injury cannot be 
adequately repaired or redressed in a court of law by an award of money damages.”).   
In another line of cases, however, some district courts have stated that the total 
destruction of a business is sufficient to show irreparable harm. See, e.g. , XIP Techs., 
LLC v. Ascend Glob. Servs. , LLC , 253 So. 3d 1183, 1187 (Fla. 2d DCA 2018) 
(“[T]he unrefuted evidence below was that these actions by XIP would result in the 
total destruction of Ascend’s  business. This was sufficient to establish irreparable 
harm without an adequate legal remedy.”); Richard v. Behavioral Healthcare 
Options, Inc. , 647 So. 2d 976, 978 (Fla. 2d DCA 1994)  (“The record of the 
evidentiary hearing indicates BHO made an adequate showing for relief . . . .  BHO 
argued that irreparable injury would occur if Richard, and other physicians if they 
knew that BHO permitted Richard to proceed, continued to collect receivables. BHO 
contended the irreparable injury would be the destruction of its business. ”).  This 
line of cases appears to be irreconcilable with the rule that an injury causes irreparable harm only when it is not compensable by money damages.  Obviously, 
the destruction of a business can be compensable by an award of money damages 
equal to the value of the business.  Thus, assuming the value of a business can be 
calculated, the total destruction of a business will never be an injury that is not 
compensable  by money damages.   
At least some cases stating that the destruction of a business can cause 
irreparable harm seem to acknowledge that the destruction of a business can only 
14 constitute irreparable harm where the value of the business cannot be calculate d. See 
State, Dep’t of Health v. Bayfront HMA Med. Ctr., LLC , 236 So. 3d 466, 475 (Fla. 
1st DCA 2018)  (“[E]vidence of the potential destruction of a business, without a 
track record from which to calculate the potential loss  and with harm of a continuing 
nature, may in some cases provide sufficient indicia of irreparable harm to support 
temporary injunctive relief.”  (quoting U.S. 1 Off. Corp. v. Falls Home Furnishings, 
Inc., 655 So. 2d 209, 210 (Fla. 3d DCA 1995)  (emphasis added)) ).  Such a caveat 
resolves the tension but also means that any rule that the total destruction of a 
business is sufficient to show irreparable harm would really just be a specific 
application of the broader rule that an injury can cause irreparable harm where the 
damages from the injury cannot be quantified. See, e.g. , Lincoln Tower Corp. v. 
Richter ’s Jewelry Co. , 12 So. 2d 452, 452–54 (Fla. 1943) (“ It appears that it would 
be impractical, if not impossible, to establish the damage to the lessor, or the lessees, 
resulting from a breach of the covenant and that the remedy at law would, therefore, 
not be adequate. ”); Zimmerman v. D.C.A. at Welleby, Inc. , 505 So. 2d 1371, 1373 
(Fla. 4th DCA 1987) (“The remedy at law, an action for damages, would be inadequate because of the difficulty in determining how many sales were lost and 
what the profit on each such lost sale would have been.  Thus  damages are said to 
be speculative and unascertainable. The harm is therefore irreparable and the remedy 
at law inadequate.”); Thompson v. Planning Com m’n of City of Jacksonville , 464 
So. 2d 1231, 1237 (Fla. 1st DCA 1985) (“Given these factors, calculations of appellants’ money damages would be speculative, thereby establishing the 
15 inadequacy of a legal remedy.”); Liza Danielle, Inc. v. Jamko, Inc. , 408 So. 2d 735, 
738–39 (Fla. 3d DCA 1982)  (“We recognize that impossibility of ascertaining the 
amount of plaintiff ’s legal damages may establish inadequacy of the legal remedy 
so as to support an award of injunctive relief , and additionally, may establish the 
requisite irreparable character of the injury  . . . .” (citations omitted)).  
To the extent district court cases hold that the destruction of a business can 
constitute irreparable harm, without any requirement that the value of the business 
be incalculable, such a holding must be wrong.  If, as Florida courts have universally 
held, an injury causes irreparable harm only when it is not compensable by money 
damages, then the destruction of a business, on its own without evidence that the 
value of the business cannot be calculated, cannot be sufficient to show irreparable 
harm.  However , as the majority opinion rightly concludes, there was no evidence 
presented in this case that Restorical’s business would be destroyed in the absence of an injunction.  Therefore, this tension in Florida jurisprudence concerning the 
irreparable harm requirement for injunctions need not be resolved in this case.  
________________________________  
 
Lindsay C.T. Holt, of Crawford, Modica & Holt, Chartered Attorneys at Law, 
Tavares,  for Appellants.  
 
Jonathan M. Sykes  and Keenan D. Smith, of Nardella & Nardella, PLLC, Orlando, 
for Appellee.

items.summary:
A business seeking a temporary injunction cannot rely on a bare fear that nuisance conduct will cost it goodwill or bookings; absent evidence of actual or imminent lost business, unquantifiable damages, or likely destruction of the enterprise, irreparable harm is unproven and the injunction must be reversed, leaving the claimant to its damages remedy.

Holding: To obtain a temporary injunction a movant must prove a substantial likelihood of success on the merits, the unavailability of an adequate remedy at law, a likelihood of irreparable harm absent the injunction, and the public interest, with failure on any element requiring denial; findings on each element must rest on competent, substantial evidence. Irreparable harm and inadequate remedy at law are distinct but interrelated prongs, and an injury is irreparable only when it is not compensable by money damages. Loss of some business is not by itself irreparable harm; a business may satisfy the prong where damages cannot be quantified, where the record shows likely total destruction of the business without a track record from which to calculate the loss, or where harm recurs so frequently that a multiplicity of suits would be needed to redress it. On this record, generalized fears of lost goodwill and viability, without evidence of cancellations, lost bookings, or unquantifiable damages, did not support a finding of irreparable harm.

Disposition: Reversed and remanded

Author: Judge Gannam

FIRST DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
No. 1D2026 -1153  
_____________________________  
 
HERITAGE PROPERTY & 
CASUALTY INSURANCE COMPANY , 
 
Petitioner,  
 
v. 
 
JEFFREY A. RAPKIN , VIRGINIA M. 
RAPKIN , FLORIDA DEPARTMENT 
OF FINANCIAL SERVICES , 
FLORIDA PENINSULA INSURANCE 
COMPANY , EDISON INSURANCE 
COMPANY , BENJAMIN MANDELL , 
and J ORDAN LEE, 
 
Respondents.  
_____________________________  
 
No. 1D2026 -1171  
_____________________________  
 
FLORIDA PENINSULA INSURANCE 
COMPANY  and E DISON 
INSURANCE COMPANY , 
 
Petitioners,  
 
v. 
 
FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF 
FINANCIAL SERVICES , HERITAGE 
PROPERTY & CASUALTY 
INSURANCE COMPANY , JEFFREY 
2 A. RAPKIN , VIRGINIA M. RAPKIN , 
BENJAMIN MANDELL , and 
JORDAN LEE, 
 
Respondents.  
_____________________________  
 
 
Petition s for Writ of Certiorari—Original Jurisdiction.  
  
November 4, 2026  
  
P
ER CURIAM . 
 
Heritage Property & Casualty Insurance Company, Florida 
Peninsula Insurance Company, and Edison Insurance Company 
seek certiorari review of an Order for Pre-Hearing Process that 
compels them to disclose sealed records to two public-records 
requestors before the trial court determines whether the records 
are exempt. Because that ruling causes irreparable harm and 
departs from the essential requirements of law, we grant the 
petitions and quash the order.  
 
This consolidated certiorari matter arises from public-records 
requests tied to a Florida Department of Financial Services investigation into insurers’ claim-handling practices. Three suits 
followed: the insurers sought declaratory and injunctive relief to 
prevent disclosure of records concerning claimed  trade secrets, 
Florida Peninsula and Edison in one action and Heritage in another, while Jeffrey and Virginia Rapkin petitioned for a writ of 
mandamus to compel disclosure.  The court consolidated all three 
and abated the Rapkins’ mandamus suit pending resolution of the 
insurers’ claims that the records are exempt. Benjamin Mandell and Jordan Lee, the requestor-intervenors, filed public- records 
requests of their own and were granted intervention in the lower 
proceeding.  
 
Under a joint litigation plan the court adopted, the 
Department was to submit redacted and unredacted records to the 
3 court under seal, after which the court would conduct an in camera  
review and hold an evidentiary hearing on trade-secret status. The 
Department submitted the records under seal, but the court then 
conducted a mere “initial review,” which did no more than identify 
which of the 878 sealed pages carried a claimed exemption.  
 
On March 26, 2026, the court entered the Order for Pre-
Hearing Process , which states that the court “will not conduct the 
hearing in camera.” Instead, it directs that the sealed records be 
provided to the requestor-intervenors, who may “participate fully” 
in the evidentiary hearing and engage in discovery, subject to a 
confidentiality order. The day after the order was entered, Lee, 
who is also engaged in separate litigation against Heritage, served discovery requests on Florida Peninsula and Edison, and later 
noticed the deposition of Heritage’s corporate representative. The 
insurers moved for reconsideration, a protective order, and a 
temporary stay; on April 16, 2026, the court only granted a 
temporary stay. These petitions followed. 
 
To obtain certiorari relief from a nonfinal order, a petitioner 
must establish “(1) a departure from the essential requirements of 
the law, (2) resulting in material injury for the remainder of the 
case (3) that cannot be corrected on postjudgment appeal.”  
Lacaretta Rest. v. Zepeda, 115 So. 3d 1091, 1092 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2013). The latter two elements constitute irreparable harm, a 
jurisdictional condition precedent evaluated first. Id.  
 
Certain information may reasonably cause material injury of 
an irreparable nature, such as “cat out of the bag” material that could be used by an unscrupulous litigant to injure another person or party outside the litigation. Martin-Johnson, Inc. v. Savage, 509 
So. 2d 1097, 1100 (Fla. 1987) , superseded by statute on other 
grounds, § 768.72, Fla. Stat. The petitioners have made that 
showing: the sealed records are claimed to hold such material. And, although irreparable harm generally cannot be speculative, 
an exception applies to the premature dissemination of such 
information because “once the documents are disseminated, a 
privacy or trade secret interest has been invaded which cannot be 
remedied on direct appeal.” Wal-Mart Stores E., L.P. v. Endicott, 
81 So. 3d 486, 49 0–91 (Fla. 1st DCA 2011); see also Allstate Ins. 
Co. v. Langston, 655 So. 2d 91, 94 (Fla. 1995). The Order for Pre-
4 Hearing Process threatens this harm by requiring the sealed 
records to be produced to the requestor-intervenors.  
 
The confidentiality order the trial court contemplated does not 
avoid that result. A protective order permitting trade- secret or 
confidential material to be shared is not always sufficient to 
prevent harm . See Endicott, 81 So. 3d at 491; Am. Express Travel 
Related Servs., Inc. v. Cruz, 761 So. 2d 1206, 1209 (Fla. 4th DCA 
2000). “[O]nce the information becomes public, its confidentiality is lost forever.” Shands Teaching Hosp. & Clinics, Inc. v. Beylotte, 
357 So. 3d 307, 309 (Fla. 1st DCA 2023). The risk here is not 
hypothetical.  Lee served discovery the day after the order 
permitting his participation, confirming that the requestor-
intervenors are positioned to obtain and use the claimed-exempt 
materials outside the context of the litigation. Ordering production 
before a trade-secret determination forecloses  the exemption 
question  and inflicts injury that cannot be remedied on appeal. See 
Coventry First, LLC v. State, Off. of Ins. Regul., 30 So. 3d 552, 558–
61 (Fla. 1st DCA 2010)  (recognizing a vested property right in “the 
continuing confidentiality and exemption of [a provider’s] trade 
secrets and other work papers already submitted to the OIR,” and that disclosure of such records causes “legal and financial 
detriment”).  
 In any event, at this stage the petitioners need not establish 
that the records are, in fact, trade secrets. A prima facie showing 
of irreparable harm is enough to invoke certiorari review. 
Commonwealth Land Title Ins. Co. v. Higgins, 975 So. 2d 1169, 
1176 (Fla. 1st DCA 2008). That threshold is met, and certiorari 
jurisdiction is proper. 
 
Having established jurisdiction, we turn to whether the trial 
court departed from the essential requirements of law. Relief is 
reserved for a violation of a clearly established principle of law, 
Saints 120, LLC v. Moore, 292 So. 3d 1209, 1212 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2020), which can derive from a variety of sources, including “recent 
controlling case law, rules of court, statutes, and constitutional 
law.” Allstate Ins. Co. v. Kaklamanos, 843 So. 2d 885, 890 (Fla. 
2003).  This court has previously found “a departure from the 
essential requirements of law where, despite the assertion of a 
trade secret privilege, the trial court ordered production of 
5 documents without first conducting an examination of the 
documents.” Messer v. E.G. Pump Controls, Inc., 667 So. 2d 321, 
322 (Fla. 1st DCA 1995) ; see also  Becker Metals Corp. v. W. Fla. 
Scrap Metals, 407 So. 2d 380, 382 (Fla. 1st DCA 1981)  (“Without 
examination of the items claimed to be a trade secret, how can a determination be reached?”).  That determination usually requires 
an in camera review, though the court may instead hold an 
evidentiary hearing. Lewis Tree Serv., Inc. v. Asplundh Tree 
Expert, LLC, 311 So. 3d 206, 210 –11 (Fla. 2d DCA 2020); Sea Coast 
Fire, Inc. v. Triangle Fire, Inc., 170 So. 3d 804, 808 (Fla. 3d DCA 
2014).  
 
Moreover, where a timely action is filed, section 624.4213(2), 
Florida Statutes, bars release of records containing claimed trade 
secrets until a circuit court rules on their trade-secret status. The 
trial court did not follow that sequence. It made no exemption determination, yet ordered the sealed records produced to the 
requestor -intervenors and permitted their full participation and 
discovery. Respondents’ contention that the court had already 
conducted an in camera review misreads the record. The “initial 
review” made no trade-secret determination, and the order itself 
states that the court “will not conduct the hearing in camera.” 
Resolving the exemption at a hearing rather than through in 
camera review would have been permissible; ordering production 
and full participation of the requestor-intervenors before deciding 
exempt status is not. In other words, o rdering production before 
the trade -secret determination violates  the statutory safeguards  
and defeats the  declaratory actions’  purpose, giving the requestors 
access regardless of how the exemption is decided. Even if the 
records were found to be trade secrets, production would still 
require particularized findings of reasonable necessity that the 
trial court never made. KPMG LLP v. State, Dep’t of Ins., 833 So. 
2d 285, 286 (Fla. 1st DCA 2002); Laser Spine Inst., LLC v. Greer, 144 So. 3d 633, 633 –34 (Fla. 1st DCA 2014).  
 
The trade-secret exemption is not the only protection at stake. 
To the extent the records contain sensitive personal information of 
non-party insureds, that information is independently protected, 
both by statute and by constitutional right. See Thomas v. Smith, 
882 So. 2d 1037, 1043 –47 (Fla. 2d DCA 2004) (recognizing, under 
art. I, § 23, Fla. Const., a legitimate expectation of privacy in social 
6 security numbers); see also State, Dep’t of Fin. Servs. v. Danahy & 
Murray, P.A., 246 So. 3d 466, 468– 71 (Fla. 1st DCA 2018) 
(upholding, under art. I, § 24(c), Fla. Const., a statutory public-
records exemption protecting insureds ’ personal financial and 
health information).   
 
Furthermore, the trial court’s finding that the requestor-
intervenors “are in no sense competitors of the Insurers” does not 
save the order. The burden of proving trade-secret status rests on the party asserting it, and ordering production before that status 
is adjudicated deprives the petitioners of the opportunity to carry 
that burden. Managed Care of N. Am., Inc. v. Fla. Healthy Kids 
Corp., 268 So. 3d 856, 860 –61 (Fla. 1st DCA 2019). Whether the 
requestor -intervenors are competitors thus does not answer the 
dispositive question. What matters is whether the records are in 
fact exempt, a determination that must be made before they are 
ordered to be released. 
 
Therefore, we grant the consolidated petitions and quash the 
Order for Pre-Hearing Process. On remand, the trial court shall 
determine the exemption and trade-secret status of the disputed records before ordering any production or access.  That 
determination must be made through a confidentiality- preserving 
in camera inspection or evidentiary hearing that does not disclose the records to those seeking them. We take no position on whether 
the records are trade secrets or otherwise exempt.  
 Petitions 
GRANTED ; order on review QUASHED . 
 L
EWIS , WINOKUR , and N EFF, JJ., concur. 
 
_____________________________  
 Not final until disposition of any timely and 
authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or 
9.331.  
_____________________________  
  
M. Hope Keating and John K. Londot, Greenberg Traurig, P.A., 
Tallahassee; and Kathy J. Maus, William B. Collum, and Scott E. 
7 Damon, Butler Weihmuller Katz Craig LLP, Tampa , for Petitioner 
Heritage Property & Casualty Insurance Company.  
 
Fernando J. Valle and Matthew C. Scarfone, Colodny Fass, 
Sunrise, for Petitioners Florida Peninsula Insurance Company 
and Edison Insurance Company.  
 
Jeffrey A. Rapkin, Esq., Port Charlotte, for Respondents Jeffrey A. 
Rapkin and Virginia M. Rapkin.  
 
Francis A. Carbone , II, Jett L. Baumann, and Katie B. Privett, 
Office of the General Counsel, Florida Department of Financial 
Services,  Tallahassee, for Respondent Florida Department of 
Financial Services.  
 William F. Merlin, Jr., Shane S. Smith, and Yanet Cordova 
Quintero, Merlin Law Group, PLLC, Tampa, for Respondent 
Benjamin Mandell.  
 
Joshua R. Brownlee and John A. Tolley, II, JT Law Firm, P.A., 
Boca Raton; and Melissa A. Giasi, Giasi Law, P.A., Tampa, for 
Respondent Jordan  Lee.

items.summary:
An insurer (or any party) claiming a trade-secret or confidentiality exemption can obtain certiorari review before sealed records are handed to adversaries, because premature disclosure is unrecoverable harm that a confidentiality order may not cure, and the trial court must rule on exemption before compelling production; the requestors' non-competitor status does not excuse that sequencing.

Holding: Certiorari lies from a nonfinal order requiring material injury uncorrectable on postjudgment appeal plus a departure from the essential requirements of law; irreparable harm is a jurisdictional prerequisite and a prima facie showing suffices. Premature dissemination of claimed trade-secret material can cause irreparable "cat out of the bag" harm that a protective order may not prevent. Where a timely action is filed, section 624.4213, Florida Statutes, bars release of records containing claimed trade secrets until a circuit court rules on their trade-secret status, so a court commits a clear error by ordering production to records requestors and allowing their full participation and discovery before making that determination through in camera review or an evidentiary hearing that preserves confidentiality; the burden of proving the exemption rests on the party asserting it, and a finding that the requestors are non-competitors does not answer whether the records are exempt.

Disposition: Petitions granted; order quashed

items.summary:
Practical effect: a civil appellant who fails to provide a record or transcript of the underlying proceedings effectively forfeits the appeal, because the trial court's decision carries a presumption of correctness that the appellant cannot rebut without that record. Per curiam citation affirmance; opinion not final pending any timely rehearing motion.

Holding: Affirming a civil judgment against a pro se appellant, the court applies the general appellate principle that a trial court's decision is presumed correct and the appellant bears the burden of demonstrating error; absent a record of the trial proceedings, the appellate court cannot resolve the underlying factual issues or conclude that the judgment is unsupported by the evidence or by an alternative theory.

Disposition: Affirmed per curiam.
