Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
CROWN CASTLE SOUTH, LLC, et al ., 
Appellee.  
 
October 29, 2026  
 
GROSSHANS, J.  
Individuals can transfer land or establish  legal interests in it  
by executing deeds , contracts , and other documents .  Often, such 
instruments also impose continuing obligations.  Not surprisingly, 
these obligations are generally enforceable by and against the 
original parties as a matter of contract law.  But are those same 
contractual obligations  binding upon  subsequent parties who 
acquire an interest in the relevant land?  The answer depends, in 
part, on how closely the obligation is connected to the land itself.   
Where a sufficient connection exists and other requirements are 
 - 2 - satisfied, the obligation binds successors by operation of law and is 
said to “run with the land” —an ancient term of art.  
In this case,  the parties request that we answer a certified 
question from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, which asks whether a  prevailing -party attorney’s fee provision in an 
easement agreement runs with the land  as a matter of Florida law .  
RJ’s Int’l Trading, LLC v. Crown Castle S., LLC, 98 F.4th 1330, 1343 (11th Cir. 2024).
1  Framed  differently, is a promise to pay attorney’s 
fees an obligation that binds successors to the land ?  We conclude 
that it is not.   In so holding, we decline to extend the reasoning of 
our recent decision in Hayslip v. U.S. Home Corp. , 336 So. 3d 207 
(Fla. 2022) , which addressed a materially different obligation.  
I 
More than three  decades ago, Hidden Valley Corporation 
bought two neighboring properties  in Miami.  Hidden Valley leased 
one of them to BellSouth Mobility, later giving BellSouth (and its successors) permission to use for telecommunication purposes a 
portion of  the adjacent  property  (which Hidden Valley retained) .  In 
 
1.  We have jurisdiction.  See art. V, § 3(b)(6), Fla. Const.  
 - 3 - the easement agreement creating this nonpossessory interest , there 
is a section entitled “ Remedies  for Breach ,” which includes an 
attorney’s fee provision.  It states:  
In the event that it is necessary for either party hereto to 
file suit in order to enforce the terms hereof, then the prevailing party in such suit shall be entitled to receive 
reasonable attorney’s fees and court costs in addition to 
any other award that the court might make, from the non-prevailing party.  
 
Following creation of the easement, multiple transfers of both 
properties occurred.  At the time of the lawsuit in this case, RJ’s 
International Trading, LLC ( RJI) owned one of the properties  subject 
to the easement .  Crown Castle  South, LLC subleased the 
neighboring property from BellSouth  and had the right to use a 
portion of RJI’s property  by virtue of the easement . 
Conflict arose in 2020 when Cro wn Castle excavated portions 
of RJI’s land beyond  the easement and installed fiber optic cables  
underground.  Based on the unauthorized excavation and 
installation, RJI sued Crown Castle in federal court.  RJI asserted 
five claims, alleg ing trespass and  breach of the easement agreement  
as two of the theories of liability . 
 - 4 - The district court granted partial summary judgment for RJI, 
finding Crown Castle liab le on the trespass and breach -of-easement 
claims.  In doing so, the court ruled that a valid and enforceable 
easement existed.  It further ruled that Crown Castle’s excavation and installation activities exceeded  the easement’s boundaries and 
constituted a trespass.  The court made no determination as to damages.  
Ultimately, following a six -day trial, the jury awarded RJI $1 
for Crown Castle’s breach of the easement agreement and $40,000 for its trespass.
2  The district court entered a final judgment (later 
amended), which reflected the jury’s assigned damages for the breach -of-easement and trespass claims.
3  Crown Castle did not 
seek appellate review . 
After entry of the  updated judgment, RJI asked the district 
court for an award of attorney’s fees based on the prevailing -party 
provision in the easement agreement.  Relying on property -law 
 
2.  The jury declined  to award any punitive damages.  
3.  The jury awarded RJI a small amount of damages for its 
last remaining claim, but RJI dismissed that claim  prior to entry of 
the final judgment.  
 - 5 - principles, RJI reasoned that the fee provision was a “ real covenant ” 
that bound not only the original contracting parties  (Hidden Valley 
and BellSouth) but also those who succeeded them in interest 
(including RJI and Crown Castle) .  Recognizing what Florida law 
requires in this regard, RJI contended that the provision ran with  
the land.  
Crown Castle opposed RJI’s  motion  for fees , arguing that the 
fee provision  was too attenuated from the land to  “touch and 
concern ” it—one of the requirements for a provision to run with the 
land.  Instead, according to Crown Castle, the fee provision was 
merely a personal covenant that bound only the original parties  to 
the easement agreement : Hidden Valley and BellSouth . 
Siding with Crown Castle, the court denied RJI’s motion for 
attorney’s fees.  It  ruled that the promise to pay attorney’s fees did 
not touch and concern land and, thus, did not run with the land.  
In reaching this conclusion, the court noted  out-of-state cases , 
found support in Caulk v. Orange County, 661 So. 2d 932 (Fla. 5th 
DCA 1995), and distinguished our decision in Hayslip . 
 RJI appealed.  T he Eleventh Circuit first considered and 
rejected RJI’s argument that it was a “part[y] hereto ” as that term is 
 - 6 - used in the easement agreement.  RJ’s Int’l Trading , 98 F.4th at  
1339.  That interpretive issue is not before us.  
Having resolved this issue against RJI, the court next assessed  
whether the prevailing -party fee provision could be enforced as a 
covenant  running with the land.  Id. at 1339- 43.  It discussed  
Florida law  on this topic , including Caulk  and Hayslip .  In Caulk , 
the Fifth District Court of Appeal held that the  reservation of 
eminent -domain proceeds did not run with the land.  661 So. 2d at 
934.  Hayslip , on the other hand, involved an arbitration provision, 
which we found to touch and concern the land.  336 So. 3d at 210.  
In the Eleventh Circuit’s view, Hayslip  appeared to come closer  to 
answering the question  in this case.  RJ’s Int’l Trading, 98 F.4th at 
1342.  Yet , due to factual distinctions, the court was reluctant to 
treat Hayslip as controlling .  Id. at 1341 -42. 
 Based on this uncertainty  and other considerations, the 
Eleventh Circuit certified the following question to us: “Under Florida law, when an easement agreement contains a prevailing -
party attorney ’s fee provision, is the fee provision a real covenant 
such that it runs with the land?”  Id.  at 1343.  We accepted review.  
 - 7 - II 
A covenant or obligation  that “runs with the land” binds 
successor s who “become liable as promisors upon the promise 
made by their predecessor”  by virtue of their acquiring  an interest 
in the land.  Restatement (First) of Prop . § 530 cmt . a (A.L.I. 1944 ).  
Note that  this liability is not based on any promise or covenant that 
the successor  to the land  personally  made .  Id.; see also Huck v. 
Kenmare Commons Homes Ass’n , 382 So. 3d 759, 766 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2023) .  Invoking this doctrine , RJI maintains  that the attorney’s fee 
provision here runs with the land and is  binding  on Crown Castle 
as a matter of Florida law , even though Crown Castle did not 
personally promise to pay RJI’s attorney’s fees.  Based on our 
assessment of the law , we disagree.  
For a covenant to run with the land, three requirements must 
be satisfied .  First, the original contracting parties must intend for 
successors in interest to be bound by the covenant.  Hayslip, 336 So. 3d at 209.  Second, successors in interest must have notice of the covenant.  Id.   And third, the covenant must touch and concern 
the land.  Id.   Our focus is on the final requirement, which is  
dispositive in answering the certified question . 
 - 8 - A 
Many ju rists trace the touch  and concern requirement back to 
a 1583 English decision, known as Spencer’s Case, 5 Co. Rep. 16a, 
77 Eng. Rep. 72 (Q.B. 1583).4  In that decision, which arose in the 
landlord- tenant context, an  English court distinguished between 
covenants that touched and  concerned the land and those that were 
merely collateral to it.  Spencer’s Case, 5 Co. Rep. at 16b, 77 Eng. Rep. at 74.  The former could be enforceable against  an assignee; 
the latter could not.  To illustrate the distinction, the court identified several  collateral covenants that would not bind an  
assignee including : (1) a lessee’s promise to build a house for the 
lessor on land that was not the subject of the leas e and (2) a 
lessee’s promise to pay “any collateral sum” to the lessor.  Id.  
Two centuries later, that same English court explained that to 
touch and concern
5 the land, the covenant must “directly affect[] 
the nature, quality, or value of the thing demised, [or] the mode of 
 
4.  E.g. , A. Dan Tarlock, Touch and Concern Is Dead, Long Live 
the Doctrine , 77 Neb. L. Rev. 804, 814 (1998);  Gallagher v. Bell , 516 
A.2d 1028, 1032 (Md. Ct. Spec. App. 1986).  
5.  Since its earliest references, courts have used “touch or  
concern” and “touch and  concern” interchangeably.  
 - 9 - occupying it.”  Mayor of Congleton v. Pattison , 10 East, 130, 136, 
103 Eng. Rep. 725, 727 (K.B.  1808).  
In America, s tates accepted this  common  law concept as a 
limitation on the enforceability of covenants by or against 
successors.   See Regency Homes Ass’n v. Egermayer , 498 N.W.2d 
783, 789 -91 (Neb. 1993) (canvassing cases on this concept from a 
multitude of jurisdictions); Flying Diamond Oil Corp. v. Newton Sheep Co. , 776 P.2d 618, 623 (Utah 1989) (noting effect of the touch  
and concern requirement).  As for Florida, the first reported 
decision applying this requirement appears to be Dunn v. Barton, 16 
Fla. 765 (1878).  There, while not using the specific phrase “touch  
and concern,” we found that a restrictive covenant ran with the 
land because it affected  “the mode of enjoyment of the premises.”  
Id. at 771.  
 Since then, Florida courts have considered whether certain 
covenants or obligations  meet the touch  and concern requirement.  
Caulk , 661 So. 2d at  933 (reservation of right to proceeds f rom an 
eminent -domain proceeding); Maule Indus., Inc. v. Sheffield Steel 
Prods. , Inc., 105 So. 2d 798, 799 (Fla. 3d DCA 1958) (covenant 
requir ing maintenance of railroad facilities); Hagan v. Sabal Palms, 
 - 10 - Inc., 186 So. 2d 302, 304 (Fla. 2d DCA 1966) (covenant restrict ing 
what buildings could be constructed); Huck , 382 So. 3d at  766 
(prohibition on street parking); Keyes Co. v. Frazier , 213 So. 2d 276, 
277 (Fla. 3d DCA 1968) (promise to pay real estate commission); 
Winn -Dixie Stores, Inc. v. Dolgencorp, Inc., 964 So. 2d 261, 262 (Fla. 
4th DCA 2007) (restricting commercial use of certain property).  
In some cases, courts spoke in terms of the obligation  
enhancing the value of the land.  E.g. , Maule Indus. , 105 So. 2d at  
801.  But in those same cases and others, courts focused on whether the covenant affected the use, occupation, or enjoyment of the land.  Dunn, 16 Fla. at 771 ; Maule Indus. , 105 So. 2d at  801; 
Winn -Dixie Stores , 964 So. 2d at  265; Huck , 382 So. 3d at  765.  We 
think that this latter formulation is doctrinally sound and 
consistent with the concept’s history.  Accordingly,  when deciding if 
the touch  and concern requirement is met, courts should consider  
whether  the obligation  is sufficiently connected to  how the land is  
used, occup ied, or enjoy ed. 
B 
Florida  courts have not previously considered  the particular 
obligation at issue here.   That being said, we believe that Caulk —a 
 - 11 - case we cited with approval in Hayslip —provides helpful insight .  
The covenant at issue in Caulk  reserved to the original grantor 
proceeds from any eminent -domain proceeding  involving the land 
conveyed .  661 So. 2d at 933.  The Fifth District held that this 
covenant did not run with the land, stressing that “[a]lthough the 
covenant ‘concern[ed]’ the land” in some sense, it did so “only tangentially. ”  Id. at 934.  That is , the covenant did not directly 
impact  the property .  Id. 
Like the covenant in Caulk , the fee provision in question is 
simply too attenuated from the use, enjoyment, or occupation of the land to touch and concern it .  The obligation  does not restrict or 
proscribe  how the land RJI owns can be used.  Nor does it govern  
who can enjoy or make use of it .  Put simply , the fee provision itself  
does not meaningfully bear  on the  use of the land or  otherwise  
enhance the day -to-day enjoyment of it or  impact  its mode of 
occupation.   Although the fee provision may provide a financial 
benefit to the prevailing party  in a dispute , it does not alter the 
parties’ rights or remedies with respect to the property itself.  And, 
it only becomes relevant after the parties have exhausted all legal and equitable remedies in court.  
 - 12 - In light of this, we find that the fee provision  is, at best, only 
tangentially related  to the land .  See id. ; Huck , 382 So. 3d at 7 65-
66.  Thus, the attenuated connection between the fee provision and 
the land renders the provision incapable of running with the land 
so as to bind successors to the property , such as Crown Castle . 
We note that our holding aligns with the majority of courts 
outside of Florida that have addressed the precise issue of whether a fee provision touch es and concern s the land.  See Est. of Ogumoro 
v. Han Yoon Ko, No. CV -06-0015- GA, 2011 WL 5223117, at *14 (N. 
Mar. I. Oct. 20, 2011) (fee provision does  not run); Fusco v. 
Matsumoto , No. 2009 -SCC-0030 -CIV, 2011 WL 12673474, at *14 
(N. Mar. I. Dec. 30, 2011) (same); Keogh v. Peck, 259 Ill. App. 503, 518 (1931) (same); Paloma Inv. Ltd. P’ship v. Jenkins, 978 P.2d 110, 
116 (Ariz. Ct. App. 1998) (same); Lundeberg v. Dastrup, 497 P.2d 
648, 650 ( Utah 1972) (same).  To our knowledge,  only two courts 
have reached the opposite conclusion.  Jack Mathis Gen. 
Contractors, Inc. v. Murphy , 472 P.2d 820, 823 ( Or. 1970) (fee 
provision runs); Solky v. Smith , 129 Nev. 1152 n.4 (2013) 
(unpublished) (same).  
 - 13 - C 
This brings us to RJI’s most forceful  argument.  RJI contends 
that our recent decision in Hayslip  compels us to  hold that the fee 
provision  here touches and concerns the land.  W e see things 
differently. 
In Hayslip , we held that  an arbitration provision in a deed ran 
with the land.  336 So. 3d at 209- 10.  We reasoned  that the 
challenged provision touched and concerned the land as it 
established the means for resolving defects to the home and that the outcome of any arbitration proceeding necessarily affect ed both 
the home and homeowner.  Id.   
The fee provision here is different.  It is, as the Eleventh 
Circuit noted, further removed from the land than the arbitration provision in Hayslip .  Specifically, the Eleventh Circuit said:  
In Hayslip , arbitration was the means of resolving alleged 
defects in the property.  Hayslip had to arbitrate with the 
developer to force the developer to fix defective stucco —
part of the property.  The arbitration was thus one step 
removed from the property itself.   
By contrast, the fee provision here is two steps 
removed.  The parties have already litigated their dispute over Crown Castle ’s trespass and breach of the easement.  
And through that litigation, RJI has already been awarded both equitable and legal remedies.  
 
 - 14 - RJ’s Int’l Trading , 98 F.4th at 1342. 
 We underscore the nature of the obligation in Hayslip .  The 
defects subject to arbitration were construction -related, meaning 
that they were physical, built into the house, and in a real sense 
tied to the land.  See Hayslip , 336 So. 3d at 210 (characterizing the 
defects as being “in the home”).   And as alluded to above, w e also 
stressed that the outcome of the arbitration proceeding impacted the property, because it was the means by which the homeowners 
could seek recourse from the builder  for improvements or repairs to 
the property .  Id. 
By contrast, a prevailing -party fee provision does not govern 
the resolution of property -related disputes.  It comes into play only 
after the dispute has been finally resolved on the merits and serves 
solely to allocate litigation costs between the parties.  It is wholly 
unconnected to the use, enjoyment, or occupation of the property 
itself or any interest therein.   Accordingly, we find that Hayslip is 
distinguishable  and does not have controlling significance.  
We add one other point.  It is undisputed that the  touch  and 
concern requirement has not remained static since  the late 1500s.  
Decisions have, over time,  relaxed the rule to some extent and 
 - 15 - found covenants enforceable that would not have run with the land 
under the traditional common law.   See e.g. , Neponsit Prop. Owners ’ 
Ass’n v. Emigrant Indus. Sav. Bank , 15 N.E.2d 793, 796 -97 (N.Y. 
1938)  (promise to pay annual assessments to homeowners 
association  enforceable) ; Egermayer , 498 N.W.2d at  793 (similar ).  
Various  reasons have been offered  for this shift, including freedom 
of contract and the availability of recorded deeds that did not exist 
at common law.  See Richard A. Epstein, Notice and Freedom of 
Contract in the Law of Servitudes , 55 S. Cal. L. Rev. 1353, 1358 
(1982).  Hayslip, though not expressly relying on either rationale, is arguably consistent with that trend .
6  However, RJI has not 
convinced us to extend  Hayslip ’s reach  under the facts  presented 
here. 
 
6.  Neither party has argued that Hayslip is clearly erroneous 
or asked us to revisit  that decision in any respect .  Moreover, 
whether Hayslip was correctly decided and how these principles 
might apply beyond the circumstances presented here are beyond 
the scope of the question certified to us by the Eleventh Circuit.  See art. V, § 3(b)(6), Fla. Const. (providing that we “ [m]ay review a 
question of law certified by the Supreme Court of the United States or a United States Court of Appeals which is determinative of the cause and for which there is no controlling precedent of the supreme court of Florida”) . 
 - 16 - III 
 Based on the analysis above, we answer the Eleventh Circuit’s 
certified question in the negative and return this case to it  for 
further proceedings . 
It is so ordered.  
COURIEL, C.J., and LABARGA, MUÑIZ, and FRANCIS, JJ., concur.  
BARRIOS, J., concurs in result only with an opinion, in which 
TANENBAUM, J., concurs.  
TANENBAUM, J., concurs in result only with an opinion, in which BARRIOS, J., concurs.  
 NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE REHEARING MOTION AND, IF FILED, DETERMINED.  
 BARRIOS, J., concurring in result only.  
In response to the certified question, the majority articulates 
the test for whether a covenant touches and concerns the land in 
this way: “whether the obligation is sufficiently connected to how the land is used, occupied, or enjoyed.”  Applying this rule , the 
majority concludes that the attorney fee provision here does not touch and concern the land and consequently does not run with the land.  While I agree with the result reached, I do so for a different reason.  In my view, a covenant must be evaluated  using a complete 
understanding of the “used, occupied, or enjoyed” rule, which 
 - 17 - carries with it a requirement that the subject matter of the covenant 
have a direct effect on the physical use of the property.  I cannot square my understanding of the complete common -law rule with 
Hayslip v. U.S. Home Corp., 336 So. 3d 207 (Fla. 2022).  For those reasons, I concur in result only.  
The touch and concern test articulated by the majority has its 
roots in Dunn v. Barton, 16 Fla. 765, 772 (1878), where we said a covenant runs with the land when “it affects the mode of enjoyment of the premises.”  We applied that rule and concluded that an 
agreement limiting leased premises to be used in a way that would 
compete with an ad jacent bar -room business was a covenant 
running with the land.  Following Dunn , we continued to apply that 
rule, limiting the touch and concern test to covenants that directly 
impacted the physical use of the land.  See, e.g. , Armstrong v. 
Seaboard Air Line Ry. Co. , 95 So. 506, 510 (Fla. 1922) (covenant to 
maintain freight schedule and depot name did not touch and concern the land because it did not relate to a thing physically connected to or annexed to the property); Osius v. Barton , 147 So. 
862, 867 -68 (Fla. 1933) (covenant prohibiting commercial uses 
within a subdivision was one running with the land); Frumkes v. 
 - 18 - Boyer , 101 So. 2d 387, 389- 90 (Fla. 1958) (provision of deed 
dedicating portion of land for use as public road was a covenant 
running with the land).  
Both the rule and application deployed in Dunn were 
consistent with an understanding of the touch and concern requirement as an inquiry into the relationship between the covenant’s subject matter and the physical land itself.  This 
understanding was synthesized in the First Restatement of 
Property.  Restatement (First) of Prop . § 537 cmt.f (A.L.I. 1944) (“It 
must in some way make the use or enjoyment more satisfactory to his physical senses.”).  The restatement explains that “it is not 
enough that the performance of the promise operates to benefit 
either the promisor or the beneficiary of the promise in the use of 
his land but it must operate to benefit him in the physical use of his land.”  Id.  In other words, a promise cannot run with the land 
unless it relates to “the way in which [ their] land [] is used.”  Huck v. 
Kenmare Commons Homes Ass’n , 382 So. 3d 759, 765 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2023) (alterations in original) (“For the burden of a promise to run 
the promise must be one respecting the use of the land of the promisor.” (citing Restatement (First) of Prop. § 537 cmt. b)).  That 
 - 19 - qualifier —that the enjoyment or use be related to the physical use 
of the land —is critical for any coherent and principled application of 
the rule. 
More modern applications of the rule began uncoupling the 
use and enjoyment aspect of the rule from the physical use of the 
land.   For example,  in Palm Beach County v. Cove Club Investors, 
Ltd., 734 So. 2d 379 (Fla. 1999),  this Court considered whether a 
covenant requiring individual lot owners in a mobile home 
community to pay monthly recreation fees to an adjoining country 
club constituted a compensable property right when the 
government condemned one of the lots.  Over dissent, a majority of 
this Court held that the covenant was a covenant running with the 
land and that the country club’s right to receive the monthly fees 
was a compensable property interest upon condemnation.  Id. at 
390.  Then in Hayslip , a builder’s warranty deed contained a 
provision requiring that any dispute arising from a construction 
defect be resolved through binding arbitration.  We reasoned that the arbitration covenant touched and concerned the property itself because it affected the mode of enjoyment of the premises —
referencing  Dunn—and that the thing required to be done (arbitrate 
 - 20 - the dispute) touched the enjoyment of the land because the 
homeowners benefit from the defective stucco being resolved.  Hayslip , 336 So. 3d at 210.  
My best reading of both Hayslip  and Cove Club is that the 
results of those cases are based on a misapplication of the touch and concern test rather than an effort to move away from the established common -law rule.  My conclusion in this regard is 
supported by both the majority’s reliance on and the Hayslip 
Court’s “favorable citation” to Caulk v. Orange County, 661 So. 2d 
932 (Fla. 5th DCA 1995).  There, the Fifth District held that a 
covenant did not run with the land, stressing that “[a]lthough the 
covenant ‘concern[ed]’ the land” in some sense, it did so “only 
tangentially.”  Id.  at 934.  In describing what it meant by 
“tangentially,” the Fifth District explained that  
[u]nlike covenants respecting mineral rights and crops, 
for example, which directly impact the use of the land, 
the covenant . . . [had] no effect whatever on the land.  
The only thing the covenant in the instant case really “touches” and “concerns” is the intangible personal 
property, namely cash, that may be paid by a condemnor.  
Id. 
 - 21 - Viewed through this lens, I agree that, as the majority says, 
“[l]ike the covenant in Caulk , the fee provision in question is simply 
too attenuated from the use, enjoyment, or occupation of the land 
to touch and concern it.”  It is important to explain why though, and in my view, the attorney fee provision is too attenuated because it does not r elate to the physical use of the land.   I agree with the 
majority that Hayslip  is distinguishable and does not have 
controlling significance.  But it is difficult to discern the logical 
difference between an arbitration provision and a prevailing party 
attorney fee provision applicable to litigation over an easement.  So, I’d call Hayslip what it is —an outlier.  This distinction is worth 
articulating now, so when the next issue arises, whether it is a jury trial waiver or something else, parties are not left to guess how 
“tangential” the issue is and instead can order their affairs around a 
clear statement of th e applicable common -law rule.  
TANENBAUM, J., concurs.  
TANENBAUM, J., concurring in result only.  
 At the outset, I join  Justice Barrios’s concurrence in full.  I 
still want separately to expand on why a prevailing party attorney 
fee provision cannot ever be a real covenant.  
 - 22 - The Eleventh Circuit asks us whether a prevailing party fee 
provision in a contract granting an easement constitutes a covenant 
running with the land.  Both an easement and real covenant address restrictions and duties pertaining to the use of land but in a non- mutual way, as I will briefly explain.  By their very nature, 
then, neither of these could include within their definition a bilateral contract imposing mutuality of obligation.  In turn, a prevailing party attorney fee provision, including the one t he 
Eleventh Circuit asks us about here, could not —as a matter of 
law—run with the land.  
First consider an easement.  When an easement is created, “it 
modifies what would otherwise be the normal right of [a] possessor” of land.  2 A
MERICAN LAW OF PROPERTY : A TREATISE ON THE LAW OF 
PROPERTY IN THE UNITED STATES  § 8.4 at 231 (A. James Casner ed., 
1952).  A possessor “subject to the burden of the easement” has 
fewer possessory rights “as against the owner of the easement than 
they otherwise would be.”  Id.; see also id.  § 8.5 at 232 (“An 
easement consists in a privilege on the part of the person entitled to it to make some use of land subject to it.”).  
 - 23 - The grant of an easement is asymmetric; there is no mutuality 
of obligation in an easement.  Rather, an easement can entitle its 
owner to “positive action within or upon the land subject to it” or “to compel the owner of the land subject to [the easement] to refrain from action he could take were his land free from the easement.”  
Id. § 8.5 at 232.  In this respect, under an easement, there is a 
dominant estate (which owns the privilege to act or compel) and a 
servient estate (which is subject to the easement’s restrictions or 
requirements).  
A real covenant is similar, though it creates a contractual 
obligation and does not necessarily vest the property interest that 
an easement does.  Still, for a covenant to bind the assignee of a promisor or be enforceable by that of a promisee (absent an 
assumption contract), the covenant must either diminish the 
covenantor’s legal rights or increase the covenantee’s rights with 
respect to some physical use or enjoyment of the land.  See id. § 9.4 
at 342 –43.  Putting it a different way, there are two sides to the 
covenant, and the question about its running—whether it “touches and concerns” land —must be separately considered for each side.  
Id. § 9.13 at 374.  
 - 24 - On the one hand, “the covenant must always be capable of 
running with the land of the” covenantee, “in order to be able to run 
with the retained land of the” covenantor.  Id.  As to the benefit to 
the covenantee, it must be as to the physical use of the land, meaning that the benefit to the covenantee must at least be “by reason of [the covenantee’s] ownership” and “physical use” of his or 
her land.  Id. at 379 & n.40; see Dunn v. Barton , 16 Fla. 765, 771 
(1878) (“Such a covenant as existed between Mrs. Barton and Dunn 
would run with the land, affecting, as it does, the mode of 
enjoyment of the premises.”).  
By contrast, the most that can be said about the prevailing 
party fee provision at issue here is that it is a bilateral agreement pertaining to litigation involving the easement contract.   Cf. Levy v. 
Levy, 326 So. 3d 678, 681 (Fla. 2021) (noting that a one -way 
attorney -fee provision is “unilateral” and section 57.105(7), Florida 
Statutes, transforms such a “one- sided provision into a reciprocal 
provision”); D.L. Peoples Grp., Inc. v. Hawley, 804 So. 2d 561, 563 
(Fla. 1st DCA 2002) (defining “a bilateral contract” in terms of “mutuality of obligation”).  We cannot assess whether one party’s 
burden or the other’s benefit runs with the land under the provision 
 - 25 - because it simply is not that kind of agreement.  Rather, it is an 
agreement with a mutuality of obligation that is, at best, merely “collateral to the land” rather than “touch[ing] and concern[ing]” it.  A
MERICAN LAW OF PROPERTY , § 9.4 at 341.  Simply put, a prevailing 
party fee provision does not obligate one party to act or not act in a 
way that benefits the other party’s land.  Such a provision can have 
no connection to the land “over and above the fact that [it has] been placed in the” contract.  Id.   
So it is regarding the fee provision in the easement agreement.  
The prevailing party fee provision contained in the easement agreement has nothing to do with the easement itself or the servient property.  The premise underlying the Eleventh Circuit’s question, then, is flawed.  In this respect, so is the premise underlying Hayslip.  Regardless of whether a fee provision appears in an easement agreement or anywhere else, it is not the type of contractual obligation that ever could run with the land.  The answer to the certified question is no.  
BARRIOS, J., concurs.

for the Eleventh Circuit –  Case No. 22 -11977

items.summary:
Prevailing-party attorney's fee clauses placed in easements and similar land instruments will not bind successors in interest as real covenants, so they cannot be enforced by or against later landowners through the running-covenant doctrine, though they remain enforceable in contract against the original parties. The Court distinguishes Hayslip (a deed arbitration provision that did touch and concern the land) and does not revisit whether Hayslip was correctly decided. Issued October 29, 2026, within the October 26-November 8, 2026 window.

Holding: Answering a certified question from the Eleventh Circuit, the Court held that under Florida law a prevailing-party attorney's fee provision in an easement agreement is not a real covenant and does not run with the land. For a covenant to run, the original parties must intend to bind successors, successors must have notice, and the covenant must touch and concern the land; the touch-and-concern requirement asks whether the obligation is sufficiently connected to how the land is used, occupied, or enjoyed. A prevailing-party fee provision is too attenuated from the land's use, occupation, or enjoyment to satisfy that requirement: it does not restrict or govern use of the land, does not alter the parties' rights or remedies as to the property, and operates only to allocate litigation costs after the merits have been resolved, so it does not bind successors. The Court distinguished Hayslip v. U.S. Home Corp. (deed arbitration provision that touched and concerned the land) and declined to extend it, and did not address Hayslip's underlying correctness as beyond the certified question.

Disposition: Court answered the certified question in the negative and returned the cause to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit for further proceedings. The status metadata separately records "affirmed," which does not fit a certified-question answer; preserved without deciding. The opinion carries a notice that it is not final until the time to file a rehearing motion expires and, if filed, determined.

Author: Justice Grosshans

citations.quote: Pursuant to section 68.093(4), SAMUEL L. MCCRAY, JR., is prohibited from commencing, pro se, any new action in the Fourteenth Judicial Circuit without first obtaining leave of the Court. Disobedience of this Order may be punishable as contempt of court. Leave of court shall be granted by the Court only upon a showing that the proposed action is meritorious and is not being filed for the purpose of delay or harassment. The Court may condition the filing of the proposed action upon the furnishing of security as provided in section 68.093(3).

items.summary: The October 27, 2026 order adopts the magistrate's October 23 recommendation declaring Samuel L. McCray, Jr. a vexatious litigant. New pro se actions in the Fourteenth Judicial Circuit require court permission based on merit and absence of delay or harassment; permission may require security. Filings in the pending case must be signed by a Florida Bar member in good standing who certifies good faith and factual and legal support. For an unauthorized new action, the adopted order provides a notice-based stay and dismissal procedure, with an opportunity to move for leave. The court directs inclusion on the Supreme Court registry.

 Troutman Pepper Locke LLP, and Dorrella L. Gallaway (Atlanta, GA) ,

Before  FERNANDEZ, LINDSEY and BOKOR , JJ.

 2  Affirmed.  See Wittock v. Ramponi , 446 So. 2d 271 , 271  (Fla. 4th DCA 
1984)  (“The law is clear that the creation of a joint tenancy with a right of 
survivorship can be terminated by the conveyance of an interest of any joint 
tenant to a stranger. ”); see also  Andresix Corp. v. Peoples Downtown Nat ’l

items.summary:
Practically, a stranger who buys into property already under foreclosure with a recorded lis pendens gains no right to join the pending foreclosure action, and a co-owner who transfers that share ends the right of survivorship, so later changes in title do not disturb the mortgagee's foreclosure.

Holding: One joint tenant's conveyance of that tenant's interest to a third party severs a joint tenancy with a right of survivorship; and a purchaser of property that is already the subject of a pending mortgage-foreclosure action and accompanying lis pendens is not entitled to intervene in that action.

Disposition: Affirmed

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed  November 4, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________ 
 
No. 3D26 -0402  
Lower Tribunal No. 25-CA -965-M 
________________ 
 
 
John L. Criswell , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Heaven Bound Construction, LLC, etc., et al. , 
Appellee s. 
 
 
  An Appeal from a non -final order from the Circuit Court for Monroe  
County, Mark H. Jones , Judge.  
 
 Russo Lima Appellate Firm, P.A. , and Elizabeth Koebel Russo for 
appellant.  
 
 Jones Walker, LLP , and Matthew Maranges, and Lauren S. Rose , for 
appellees . 
 Before  FERNANDEZ, GORDO and BOKOR , JJ.  
  GORDO, J.  
 2 John Criswell appeals  an order granting Heaven Bound’s motion to 
stay pending arbitration.   We have jurisdiction.  See Fla. R. App. P . 
9.130(a)(3)( I).1  Because competent, substantial evidence supports the trial 
court’s finding that Heaven Bound did not act inconsistently with its 
arbitration right , we affirm.  
We review orders granting a motion to compel de novo but review a 
trial court’s waiver determination for competent, substantial evidence. See 
Concierge Auctions, LLC v. Coldwell Banker Residential Real Est., LLC , 394 
So. 3d 119, 124 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024) .  “Courts resolve all doubts regarding 
waiver in favor of arbitration rather than against it, and the party seeking to avoid arbitration bears the heavy burden of proving waiver. ” Id. at 124 n.2 
(citation modified) .  “It is well -established that Florida law and public policy 
strongly favors arbitration [.]” MV Ins. Consultants v. NAFH Nat ’l Bank , 87 So. 
3d 96, 98 (Fla. 3d DCA 2012) .  
“The right to arbitrate is based on contract and may be waived.” 
Metronet Techs., LLC v. United Fiber Works, LLC , 432 So. 3d 677, 680 (Fla. 
5th DCA 2026).   Whether a party has waived its right to arbitration is a fact -
intensive inquiry determined under the totality of the circumstances.  See 
 
1 Fla. R. App. P. 9.130(a)(3)( I) allows for review of non -final orders that 
determine a party’s  entitlement to arbitration.  
 3 Raymond James Fin. Servs. , Inc. v. Saldukas , 896 So. 2d 707, 711 (Fla. 
2005)  (defining waiver in the context of the right to arbitrate as “the voluntary 
and intentional relinquishment of a known right or conduct which implies the 
voluntary and intentional relinquishment of a known right ”).  Accordingly, the  
inquiry turns  on whether a party’s conduct, considered as a whole, 
demonstrates an intent to relinquish its contractual right to arbitration. See  
Truly Nolen of Am., Inc. v. King Cole Condo. Ass'n, Inc. , 143 So. 3d 1015, 
1017 (Fla. 3d DCA 2014)  (finding that waiver occurs by actions “inconsistent 
with the right to compel arbitration ” and “the essential question is whether, 
under the totality of the circumstances, the defaulting party has acted 
inconsistently with the arbitration right ”).  
This dispute arises in the context of construction lien law.  Critically, 
the parties’ contract expressly contemplated that judicial proceedings may 
serve to preserve lien rights notwithstanding an agreement to arbitrate , 
providing in relevant part:  
XI. Mediation and Arbitration of Disputes:  
 
(a) Generally. Any dispute, claim or controversy arising out of or 
relating to this Agreement or the breach, termination, 
enforcement, interpretation or validity thereof, including the 
determination of the scope or applicability of this agreement to 
arbitrate , shall, after the Parties first seek to mediate the dispute 
pursuant to Section XI(d) of this Agreement, be determined by 
arbitration  . . . . 
 
 4 (b) An action before a court of competent jurisdiction for 
injunctive or other equitable relief, rather than before AAA, where 
permitted under Section XI(a) of this Agreement, does not waive any right to arbitrate  . . . . 
 Consistent with that agreement  and after Criswell terminated the 
parties’ contract , Heaven Bound informed Criswell of its intent to pursue 
arbitration  and filed suit to protect its construction lien claim .  Immediately 
thereafter and prior to litigating the merits of its claim, Heaven Bound moved 
to stay after service was perfected while promptly demanding  arbitration  with 
the American Arbitration Association .  Under the totality of circumstances, 
that conduct supports the trial court’s finding that Heaven Bound  did not 
voluntarily and intentionally relinquish its arbitration  right. See MV Ins. 
Consultants , 87 So. 3d at 99 (“ [T]he determination of whether a particular 
dispute is subject to an arbitration provision necessarily rests on the intent of 
the parties. ” (citation modified )).  That finding is supported by competent, 
substantial evidence.  See Concierge Auctions, LLC , 394 So. 3d at  124. 
Affirmed.

items.summary:
Practically, a contractor bound by an arbitration clause does not forfeit that right by first suing to preserve a construction lien—especially where the contract permits court action to protect lien rights—so long as it promptly demands arbitration before litigating the merits; the party opposing a stay must show clear, intentional relinquishment to defeat arbitration.

Holding: Whether a party waived its contractual right to arbitrate is a fact-intensive totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry reviewed for competent, substantial evidence (the underlying entitlement being reviewed de novo); doubts are resolved in favor of arbitration and the party resisting arbitration bears the heavy burden of proving waiver through voluntary and intentional relinquishment or conduct inconsistent with the arbitration right; and where the contract permits court proceedings to preserve construction lien rights without waiving arbitration, filing suit to protect that lien claim while promptly demanding arbitration is not a waiver.

Disposition: Affirmed

Author: Judge Gordo

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed  October 29 , 2026.  
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________ 
 
No. 3D25 -1573  
Lower Tribunal No. 21-15580 -CA-01 
________________ 
 
 
People's Trust Insurance Company , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Yamirka Castro Almora, et al. , 
Appellee s. 
 
  An Appeal from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, Reemberto 
Diaz, Judge.  
  Cole, Scott & Kissane, P.A., and Brandon J. Tyler  and David C. 
Borucke (Tampa) , for appellant.  
  Kula & Associates, P.A., and Elliot B. Kula, William D. Mueller  and 
Elaine D. Walter , for appellees . 
  Before  FERNANDEZ, LOGUE and MILLER , JJ.  
 
 PER CURIAM.  
 2  Affirmed.  See Miami -Dade Cnty. v. Guyton , 388 So. 3d 50, 51 -52 (Fla. 
3d DCA 2023)  (“While we apply de novo review to these rulings, in reviewing 
the trial court's denial of the County's motion for directed verdict (and motion 
for judgment in accordance with its earlier motion for directed verdict) ‘[a]n 
appellate court must evaluate the evidence in the light most favorable to the 
non-moving party, drawing every reasonable inference flowing from the 
evidence in the nonmoving party ’s favor,’ and ‘[i]f there is conflicting evidence 
or if different reasonable inferences may be drawn from the evidence, then 
the issue is factual and should be submitted to the jury for resolution. ’” 
(citations modified) ); L.D.G. v. State , 960 So. 2d 767 , 767 -68 (Fla. 4th DCA 
2007) ( holding that testimony about money actually paid constitutes 
competent substantial evidence) ; Weitzer Oak Park Est., Ltd. v. Petto , 573 
So. 2d 990, 991 (Fla. 3d DCA 1991)  (holding that o wner testimony regarding 
expenditures related to property constitutes competent evidence sufficient to support a verdict without documentary corroboration); Greenaker v. 
Universal Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co., 434 So. 3d 526, 536 (Fla. 2d DCA 2026) 
(emphasis in original)  (“[T]he term [replacement cost value] is used to 
communicate the objective of replacing  what the insured once had— the full 
value of the insured’s loss as a result of the destructive event as opposed to a reduced value that accounts for depreciation.” ); § 627.7011(3)(a), Fla. Stat. 
 3 (2020)  (“[T]he insurer must initially pay at least the actual cash val ue of the 
insured loss  . . . . The insurer shall pay  any remaining amounts necessary to 
perform such repairs as work is performed and expenses are incurred.” ); 
Argonaut Ins. Co. v. May Plumbing Co. , 474 So. 2d 212, 214-15 (Fla. 1985)  
(holding that Florida follows the “loss theory” of prejudgment interest, where 
prejudgment interest is calculated to make the plaintiff whole from the date 
of loss, not to punish the defendant or adjust for inflation ); Capitol Env ’t 
Servs.,  Inc. v. Earth Tech, Inc. , 25 So. 3d 593, 597 (Fla. 1st DCA 2009)  
(“Damages can become fixed on different dates for purposes of an award of 
prejudgment interest.” ); Whitman v. Castlewood, Int’l Corp., 383 So. 2d 618, 
619 (Fla. 1980) (holding that “ where there is no proper objection to the use 
of a general verdict, reversal is improper  where no error is found as to one 
of two issues submitted to the jury on the basis that the appellant is unable 
to establish that he has been prejudiced ”); Papcun v. Piggy Bag Disc. 
Souvenirs, Food & Gas Corp. , 472 So. 2d 880, 881 (Fla. 5th DCA 1985) 
(holding that “a failure to object to a verdict form regarding defects not of a 
constitutional or fundamental character constitutes a waiver of such 
defects”).

items.summary:
Practical effect: the insurer's challenges to a first-party coverage judgment fail. Insured/owner testimony alone can sustain the damages award without documentary proof; replacement cost value is measured without depreciation subject to the statutory actual-cash-value-then-progress-payments scheme; prejudgment interest runs on the loss theory from the date of loss; and unobjected-to general-verdict and non-fundamental verdict-form defects are waived. Per curiam citation affirmance; opinion not final pending any timely rehearing motion.

Holding: Affirming a first-party insurance judgment, the court restates governing principles: denial of a directed verdict/judgment notwithstanding the verdict is reviewed de novo, but the evidence is viewed in the light most favorable to the non-moving party and conflicting evidence or competing reasonable inferences must go to the jury; testimony about amounts actually paid, and an owner's testimony about property expenditures, is competent substantial evidence even without documentary corroboration; replacement cost value means the full objective cost to replace the insured's loss rather than a depreciated value, and section 627.7011(3)(a) requires the insurer to pay at least actual cash value initially and the remaining amounts as work is performed and expenses are incurred; prejudgment interest follows the loss theory (to make the plaintiff whole from the date of loss), and damages may become fixed on different dates for that computation; and absent a proper objection, a general verdict stands if no error is found as to at least one submitted issue, while failure to object to non-constitutional or non-fundamental verdict-form defects waives them.

Disposition: Affirmed per curiam.

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 28, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D26 -1540  
Lower Tribunal No. 24-18418 -FC-04 
________________  
 
 
Kristen Martinez , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Omar Guardia , 
Appellee.  
 
 
 
 An Appeal from  a non -final order from  the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Charles Kenneth Johnson , Judge.  
 
 Maria del Carmen Calzon,  for appellant.  
 
  Perez -Abreu & Martin -Lavielle, P.A., and Javier Perez -Abreu  and 
Andy W. Acosta, for appellee.  
 
 
Before  MILLER, GOODEN, and REBULL,  JJ.  
 
 MILLER, J . 
 2 This is a nonfinal appeal from  an order denying the disqualification of 
counsel in  a high -conflict dissolution proceeding.  Appellant, Kristen 
Martinez, challenges an order denying her motion to disqualify trial court 
counsel for  appellee, Omar Guardia .  On appeal, she contends that by 
securing payment of their fees with a mortgage on disputed property, counsel 
ran afoul of rule 4 -1.8 of the Rules Regulating The Florida Bar.  We need not 
decide this issue because the trial court’s finding that the motio n was 
untimely is well supported.  
I 
A 
Martinez and Guardia were once romantically involved.  Since  2023, 
they have been embroiled  in a series of legal disputes , including  dissolution, 
ejectment, domestic violence, and partition proceedings.  The case before 
us involves  the dissolution action.  Martinez has claim ed that she  and 
Guardia entered into a common law marriage in Colorado.  Guardia has 
denie d they were ever married  and counter -petitioned  to establish the 
paternity of Martinez’s minor child . 
Two properties are relevant to this appeal .  The first is titled  solely in 
Guardia ’s name .  The second is owned jointly by the parties.  In 2023, 
Guardia sued to partition the jointly owned property, which is also subject to 
 3 foreclosure proceedings  because a secured loan held by PennyMac went 
unpaid.  The partition action remains  pending .   
That same year, Guardia filed an ejectment action , seeking to oust 
Martinez from the property titled in his name.  Months later, Martinez 
obtained  a final injunction against domestic violence  that awarded her  sole 
possession of that very property .  Guardia  successfully moved to have the  
injunction modified to restore his exclusive possession .  That  injunction is the 
subject of a separate, pending appeal . 
Now come the facts on which this appeal turns.  In June 2025, Guardia 
granted  his lawyers, Javier Perez -Abreu and Perez -Abreu & Martin -Lavielle, 
P.A. (collectively “Perez -Abreu”)  mortgages  on both properties to secure his 
unpaid legal fees and costs .  The mortgages  were recorded  the same month  
in the  public records of Miami -Dade County . 
Martinez discovered the mortgages.  On December 9,  2025 , she  filed 
a quiet title action seeking to invalidate both mortgages , and that action 
remains pending.  Later the same month, the  parties proceeded to trial on 
the ejectment case.  Final judgment of ejectment was entered against 
Martinez on  January 20, 2026 .  That  judgment is on appeal, as well .   
On May 18, 2026 , eleven months after the mortgages were recorded 
and five months after she moved to invalidate them, and four months after 
 4 she lost the ejectment trial, Martinez moved to  disqualify Perez -Abreu in all 
seven cases .  She claimed that counsel had improperly “obtain [ed] a 
financial interest  in the properties through mortgages and notes issued by 
Guardia . . . without the knowledge of Martinez,” and that Perez -Abreu would 
have to testify as material witnesses about their own financial stake .  
Martinez maintains that the conduct underlying each motion differs from 
“case to case.”  It does not.  The seven motions are virtually identical.  
Guardia filed an omnibus response, arguing , among other things , that 
the disqualification motion was untimely .  At a multi -day hearing, Martinez 
first told the court that no evidentiary hearing was needed because the 
outcome hinged  on legal argument.  On the second day, she reversed 
cours e.  The trial court declined to take evidence, as no one disputed that 
the security interests existed .  See First Fid. Tr. Servs., Inc. v. Shelter Cove 
Condo. Ass’n, Inc. , 329 So. 3d 222, 228 (Fla. 1st DCA 2021) (“It is true that 
‘where material facts are in dispute, an evidentiary hearing is required[;] ’ 
[h]owever, an evidentiary hearing is not required for a motion to disqualify 
counsel where the factual allegations warranting disqualification are not in 
dispute.” (citations omitted) ).  The court denied the motion as untimely and 
legally insufficient under Lee v. Gadasa Corp. , 714 So. 2d 610 (Fla. 1st DCA 
1998) . This appeal followed.  
 5 II 
A 
We review an order on a motion seeking the disqualification of counsel 
for abuse of discretion.  See Young v. Achenbauch , 136 So. 3d 575, 580 –81 
(Fla. 2014 ); Schneider v. Tirikian , 410 So. 3d 79, 80 (Fla. 3d DCA 2025).  
B 
Martinez contends, as she did below,  that the security interest in  the 
property confers a stake in the litigation that requires  disqualification  and 
violates  rule 4-1.8(i) of the Rules Regulating The Florida Bar.   Perez -Abreu 
counters that  Martinez waived disqualification by failing to act with 
“reasonable promptness ,” Lee, 714 So. 2d at 612  (quoting Transmark, 
U.S.A. v. State, Dep’t of Ins. , 631 So. 2d 1112 , 1116  (Fla. 1st DCA 1994)) , 
and alternatively argues that Martinez lacks standing, the security interest is 
consistent with rule 4 -1.8(i), and Guardia could only encumber his own 
interest in the property, so Martinez’s interest remains  unaffected.  Because 
it is dispositive  on these facts , we write only to address timeliness.  
C 
It is long established that d isqualification of a party’s chosen counsel 
is “an extraordinary remedy —one that should be rare.”  Phinney v. Phinney , 
427 So. 3d 1041, 1042 (Fla. 3d DCA 2025).   Courts view motions to 
 6 disqualify with disfavor and skepticism , and for good reason.  Such motions  
interfere with a party ’s right to the lawyer of his choice  and may be misused 
to frustrate and delay the proceedings.   See Alexander v. Tandem Staffing 
Sols., Inc. , 881 So. 2d 607, 608 –09 (Fla. 4th DCA 2004).   The movant bears 
the burden of establishing that disqualification is obligatory .  See State v. De 
La Osa , 28 So. 3d 201, 203 (Fla. 4th DCA 2010).  
The motion must be timely.  “A motion to disqualify should be made 
with reasonable promptness after the party discovers the facts which lead to 
the motion.”  Lee, 714 So. 2d at 612 (quoting Transmark , 631 So. 2d at 
1116) .  We acknowledge  that “[t]here is no bright -line rule governing the 
amount of time within which a party can be found to be reasonably prompt .”  
See Glob. Lab Partners, LLC v.  Patroni Enters., LLC , 327 So. 3d 453, 457 
(Fla. 1st DCA 2021) .  The inquiry  instead turns on the facts .   
The purpose of requiring “reasonable promptness” is evident.  Undue 
delay suggests a strategic motive, and disqualification is not a means for a 
litigant “to deprive his opponent of counsel of his choice after completing 
substantial preparation of the case.”   Transmark , 631 So. 2d at 1116 .   
In evaluating whether a disqualification motion is timely, courts 
consider (1) when the movant learned of the grounds for disqualification; (2) 
whether the movant kept litigating rather than moving  for disqualification; and 
 7 (3) whether the nonmovant would suffer prejudice.   See Zayas -Bazan v. 
Marcelin , 40 So. 3d 870, 87 2–73 (Fla. 3d DCA 2010) ( “A party can waive his 
right to seek disqualification of the opposing party ’s counsel by failing to 
promptly move for disqualification upon learning of the facts leading to the 
alleged conflict.” ); Glob. Lab Partners , 327 So. 3d at 457 (holding the 
circumstances did not support a finding of waiver where the motion to 
disqualify was filed “between pleadings and discovery, a natural demarcation 
in the proceedings, and the motion was not preceded by a great deal of work 
done by either side ’s counsel”) ; Case v. City of Miami , 756 So. 2d 259, 261 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2000) (“Under the circumstances in this case, the 
disqualification of retirees ’ counsel would result in a serious injustice to their 
case.”).    
D 
Here,  the factors support  the trial court’s decision.  Martinez  had 
constructive knowledge of the purported conflict as soon as  the mortgages 
were recorded in June 2025 , eleven months before she filed her motions to 
disqualify.   This knowledge is imputed  by Florida’s recording statute.   See 
Fla. Stat. § 695.11  (entitled  “Instruments deemed to be recorded from time 
of filing”) ; see also  Tikhomirov v. Bank of N.Y. Mellon , 223 So. 3d 1112, 111 4 
n.2 (Fla. 3d DCA 2017) (quoting Whitburn, LLC v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. , 
 8 190 So.  3d 1087, 1091 (Fla. 2d DCA 2015)  (“The act of recording an 
instrument in accordance with [Florida's recording] statute constitutes 
constructive notice of a prior encumbrance on the property which is the 
subject of the instrument.” ) (citing Fla. Stat. § 695.11 )).  But we need not rely 
on constructive knowledge alone, since Martinez’s own quiet title complaint 
established that she had actual knowledge no later than December 2025, six 
months before she filed her disqualification motions.   
Despite this knowledge, Martinez continued  litigating on multiple fronts.  
She tried the ejectment case to verdict ; and it was on ly after losing that case 
and the  injunction modification that she  finally  moved for disqualification .  
This course of action supports a finding of waiver .  See Transmark , 631 So. 
2d a t 1116 (holding a ten -month delay sufficient to waive right to seek 
disqualification of opposing counsel); L.E.B. v. D.D.C. , 304 So. 3d 54, 58 
(Fla. 2d DCA 2020) (holding a fourteen -month  delay sufficient to  waive a 
motion for disqualification) . 
The record further  supports an inference of prejudice to Guardia, the 
nonmovant.  The dissolution docket contains  215 entries ; 198 predate the  
disqualification motion s.  Of those,  121 entries appear between the recording 
of the mortgages and the filing of the motions .  In that period, the parties 
conducted substantial discovery, agreed to timesharing orders, attended 
 9 mediation, filed numerous motions, and noticed depositions.  This  is the 
“great deal of work” by counsel that weighs in favor of a finding of prejudice 
and against disqualification .  Glob. Lab Partners , 327 So. 3d at 457.    We 
therefore  find ample support for the conclusion that the motion was a thinly 
veiled attempt to obtain a strategic advantage , and we  affirm the order under 
review.  
Affirmed.

items.summary:
Practical effect: a party who sits on a disqualification issue and keeps litigating-including taking a related case to verdict-waives the motion, because disqualification of opposing counsel is an extraordinary remedy that must be sought with reasonable promptness, and delay plus the opponent's substantial preparation weigh against it. The court rested solely on timeliness/waiver and did not reach whether a lawyer's fee security interest (a mortgage on disputed property) violates Bar rule 4-1.8(i). Nonfinal appeal; opinion not final pending any timely rehearing motion.

Holding: Orders on motions to disqualify counsel are reviewed for abuse of discretion. A motion to disqualify must be made with reasonable promptness after the movant discovers the grounds; there is no bright-line period, and timeliness turns on (1) when the movant learned the grounds, (2) whether the movant continued litigating instead of moving, and (3) prejudice to the nonmovant. Recording an instrument gives constructive notice under section 695.11. Delay of about eleven months from recordation (and about six months from actual knowledge), continuing through trial of a related action, together with substantial discovery, mediation and depositions by the nonmovant's counsel, supports waiver as a strategic delay, so disqualification is not obligatory. A court may resolve timeliness without deciding the underlying conflict or the propriety of a lawyer's security interest.

Disposition: Nonfinal order denying the motion to disqualify opposing counsel affirmed.

Author: Judge Miller

Respondent s. 
_____________________________  
 
Petition for Writ of Certiorari to the Circuit Court for Orange County.  
Kevin B. Weiss , Judge.  
 
October 30, 2026  
 
GANNAM , J. 
  Petitioner seeks certiorari review of a  contempt order imposing monetary and 
other sanctions for violation of an order prohibiting pro se filings . To be sure, t he 
trial court had both authority and good reason to bar pro se filings by Petitioner. See 
State v. Spencer , 751 So. 2d 47 (Fla. 1999). The court ’s Spencer order, however, 
only prohibits Petitioner ’s pro se filing of “ further pleadings and motions ,” and 
“pleadings and motions ” have precise meanings under the so- named Florida Rule of 
2 Civil Procedure 1.100. The filings for which Petitioner was held in contempt of the 
Spencer order did not include any complaint, petition, answer, or reply, see Fla. R. 
Civ. P. 1.100(a) ( “No other pleadings will be allowed. ”), or any “ application to the 
court for an order [which] must be by motion, ” Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.100(b).1 While the 
trial court may have intended its Spencer  order to bar all pro se filings, the court 
“cannot base contempt upon noncompliance with something an order does not say. ” 
Prieto v. Rossi , 385 So. 3d 144, 148 (Fla. 4th DCA 2024) (quoting Kovic v. Kovic, 
336 So. 3d 22, 26 (Fla. 4th DCA 2022)). Nevertheless, even if we were to conclude 
that the contempt order departed from the essential requirements of the law,  we do 
not have certiorari jurisdiction to review it because any such error is correctable on 
post-judgment appeal . See State v. Lobato, 394 So. 3d 1219, 1221–22 (Fla. 6th DCA 
2024). But the trial court “retains inherent authority to reconsider and, if deemed 
appropriate, alter or retract any of its nonfinal rulings prior to entry of the final 
judgment or order terminating an action. ” Silvestrone v. Edell , 721 So. 2d 1173, 1175 
(Fla. 1998).  
PETITION DISMISSED.  
STARGEL and KAMOUTSAS , JJ., concur.  
 
 
Kristen Cox, Lakeland, pro se.  
 
 
1 Petitioner did file a copy of a discovery motion of Respondents in which 
they applied for an order from the trial court , but she filed no motion of her own.  
3 No Appearance for Respondents.  
 
 
NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE MOTION FOR REHEARING 
AND DISPOSITION THEREOF IF TIMELY FILED

items.summary:
A contempt sanction for violating a bar on pro se filings cannot rest on conduct outside the bar's actual terms, but a contempt order entered in an ongoing civil case generally stays reviewable on post-judgment appeal rather than by certiorari, so the petitioner's recourse lay with the trial court's power to revisit its own interim rulings.

Holding: Contempt cannot be based on noncompliance with something an order does not say, so a sanctions order barring a pro se litigant's "pleadings and motions" reaches only those filings as defined by Rule 1.100 (complaint, petition, answer, reply, or a motion seeking a court order) and not other filings, even if the court intended a broader bar. A court nonetheless lacks certiorari jurisdiction to review such a contempt order because any error is correctable on post-judgment appeal; the trial court retains inherent authority to reconsider, alter, or retract its nonfinal rulings before entry of the final judgment or an order terminating the action.

Disposition: Petition dismissed

Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
The Collection LLC ,

 An Appeal from a non -final order from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Lisa S. Walsh , Judge.  
 
 Dentons US LLP, and Trumon J. Phillip ; DLA Piper LLP, and Janelly 
Crespo , for appellant.  
 
 Kula & Associates, P.A., and Elliot B. Kula and William D. Mueller ; 
Burstyn Law PLLC, and Sean A. Burstyn , for appellee.  
 
 
Before LINDSEY, MILLER and REBULL, JJ.  
 
 PER CURIAM.  
 
 2  Affirmed.  See Ford Motor Co. v. Mont. Eighth Jud. Dist. Ct. , 592 U.S. 
351, 352 (2021) ( “To be subject to . . . [specific]  jurisdiction, the defendant 
must take ‘some act by which [it] purposefully avails itself of the privilege of 
conducting activities within the forum State. ’ And the plaintiff's claims ‘must 
arise out of or relate to the defendant 's contacts ’ with the forum. ” (citations 
omitted )); Mazda Motor Corp. v. Triche , 365 So. 3d 403, 411 (Fla. 3d DCA 
2023) (affirming exercise of specific jurisdiction over a Japanese foreign 
automobile manufacturer, Mazda Japan, finding it targeted Florida by   
“designing vehicles for, shipping vehicles to,” and ordering recalls for it s 
vehicles owned in Florida:  “If not Florida, what market were these actions of 
Mazda Japan intended to reach?”); see also  Machtinger v. Inertial Airline 
Servs., Inc. , 937 So. 2d 730, 73 6 (Fla. 3d DCA 2006) (“Directing a conspiracy 
toward Florida establishes sufficient minimum contacts to satisfy due 
process.”); Mazda  Motor Corp. , 365 So. 3d at 414 (holding the exercise of 
specific jurisdiction over Mazda Japan comported with traditional notions of 
fair play and substantial justice, reasoning : “[O]nce  it is established that the 
non-resident defendant purposefully availed itself of the market (and 
therefore the laws) of a State, the interest of the State to oversee the safety 
of its residents within the State is obvious and compelling”).  
 LINDSEY and MILLER, JJ., concur.  
 
 3 Dr.-Ing. H.C.F. Porsche v. The Collection LLC  
3D2025 -2148  
 
Rebull, J., concurring.  
 I unreservedly join the affirmance of the learned trial judge’s decision 
to deny Porsche AG’s motion(s) to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. I 
write separately to briefly address its contention that the trial court erred in 
failing to hold an evid entiary hearing.  
 This is what Porsche AG wrote in a footnote in its reply in support of its 
motion to dismiss the second amended complaint for lack of personal juris-
diction:  
Even if The Collection had found some evidence to cite, that 
would not create personal jurisdiction: At most, it would warrant 
an evidentiary hearing so that the Court could resolve the com-
peting evidence. See Estes v. Rodin , 259 So. 3d 183, 198 (Fla. 
3d DCA 2018) ("If the material facts alleged in the opposing affi-
davits conflict with one another, the trial court is required to hold 
an evidentiary hearing to resolve the jurisdictional issue."). For-
tunately, the Court need not waste its time with such a hearing 
given The Collection’s failure of proof.  Id. at 190 (where affidavits 
"can be harmonized," no evidentiary hearing is needed).  
 
(emphasis added).  
 There is no reasonable contextual reading of this as anything other 
than a waiver by Porsche AG of its right to an evidentiary hearing. It rolled 
the dice and decided that it could win “on the papers,” and that no evidentiary 
hearing was necessary. Moreov er, an argument only made in a footnote is 
 
 4 legally insufficient. Cf. Dixon v. Brown , 423 So. 3d 963, 970 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2025); Shobola v. Shobola , 355 So. 3d 458, 462 (Fla. 2d DCA 2022). “Proper 
preservation requires the following three steps from a party: (1) a timely, con-
temporaneous objection; (2) a legal ground for the objection and; (3) in order 
for an argument to be cognizable on appeal, it m ust be the specific conten-
tion asserted as legal ground for the objection, exception, or motion  below.” 
State v. Johnson , 295 So. 3d 710, 714 (Fla. 2020) (emphasis added) (internal 
quotations and citations omitted). Beyond the footnote in the motion, the ne-
cessity of an evidentiary hearing before the trial court made any factual find-
ings adverse to Porsche AG did not come u p at all in the transcript of the 
hearing held on the motion on September 8, 2025.  
 Had Porsche AG wished to put The Collection to its proof and require 
it to prove its jurisdictional facts with admissible evidence, it should have ex-
pressly and clearly argued that to the trial court. At an evidentiary hearing, a 
plaintiff must prove juris diction by a preponderance of the evidence. See 
Stonepeak Partners, LP v. Tall Tower Capital, LLC , 231 So. 3d 548, 552 (Fla. 
2d DCA 2017); see also  AcryliCon USA, LLC v. Silikal GmbH , 985 F.3d 1350, 
 
 5 1364 (11th Cir. 2021).1 Porsche AG did not elect to do that in this case. For 
this additional reason, I concur that the decision below is properly affirmed.  
 
1 In the Federal system, trial courts are permitted to defer resolving the 
factual dispute where the jurisdictional facts are “intertwined” or “overlap” 
with the merits of the dispute. See Grayson v. Anderson , 816 F.3d 262, 268 
(4th Cir. 2016) (citing  Adams v. Bain , 697 F.2d 1213, 1219 (4th Cir.1982) 
(noting that, “where the jurisdictional facts are intertwined with the facts 
central to the merits of the dispute,” deferring resolution of that factual 
dispute to a proceeding on the merits “is the better view”); see also  Welt 
Indus., Inc. v. Weingart, Inc. , 660 F. Supp. 424, 425 (N.D. Ga. 1987). While 
the Florida rules of civil procedure are patterned after the Federal rules (and 
more so now than ever), it does not appear that this deferral is an option for 
trial judges under the Venetian Salami  framework. Although understandably 
less desirable, a defendant does have an option, however, to raise “lack of 
jurisdiction over the person’ as an affirmative defense in a responsive 
pleading – and not by motion – and save the issue for trial or summary 
judgment. See Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.140(b) (noting that at the pleader’s option 
lack of personal jurisdiction may be asserted by motion or in the responsive 
pleading).

items.summary:
The court affirmed—by per curiam citation—the denial of a foreign manufacturer's motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction under the specific-jurisdiction framework. A concurring judge would also affirm because the movant waived any right to a jurisdictional evidentiary hearing (its request appeared only in a reply footnote that conceded one was unnecessary) and footnote-only arguments are legally insufficient; where preserved, jurisdiction is proved by a preponderance.

Holding: Specific personal jurisdiction requires that the nonresident defendant purposefully availed itself of the privilege of conducting activities in the forum and that the plaintiff's claims arise out of or relate to those forum contacts; directing a conspiracy or other conduct toward the forum establishes sufficient minimum contacts, and designing vehicles for, shipping vehicles to, and issuing recalls for the Florida market supports specific jurisdiction over a foreign manufacturer consistent with fair play and substantial justice.

Disposition: Affirmed.
