FIRST DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
No. 1D2026 -1153  
_____________________________  
 
HERITAGE PROPERTY & 
CASUALTY INSURANCE COMPANY , 
 
Petitioner,  
 
v. 
 
JEFFREY A. RAPKIN , VIRGINIA M. 
RAPKIN , FLORIDA DEPARTMENT 
OF FINANCIAL SERVICES , 
FLORIDA PENINSULA INSURANCE 
COMPANY , EDISON INSURANCE 
COMPANY , BENJAMIN MANDELL , 
and J ORDAN LEE, 
 
Respondents.  
_____________________________  
 
No. 1D2026 -1171  
_____________________________  
 
FLORIDA PENINSULA INSURANCE 
COMPANY  and E DISON 
INSURANCE COMPANY , 
 
Petitioners,  
 
v. 
 
FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF 
FINANCIAL SERVICES , HERITAGE 
PROPERTY & CASUALTY 
INSURANCE COMPANY , JEFFREY 
2 A. RAPKIN , VIRGINIA M. RAPKIN , 
BENJAMIN MANDELL , and 
JORDAN LEE, 
 
Respondents.  
_____________________________  
 
 
Petition s for Writ of Certiorari—Original Jurisdiction.  
  
November 4, 2026  
  
P
ER CURIAM . 
 
Heritage Property & Casualty Insurance Company, Florida 
Peninsula Insurance Company, and Edison Insurance Company 
seek certiorari review of an Order for Pre-Hearing Process that 
compels them to disclose sealed records to two public-records 
requestors before the trial court determines whether the records 
are exempt. Because that ruling causes irreparable harm and 
departs from the essential requirements of law, we grant the 
petitions and quash the order.  
 
This consolidated certiorari matter arises from public-records 
requests tied to a Florida Department of Financial Services investigation into insurers’ claim-handling practices. Three suits 
followed: the insurers sought declaratory and injunctive relief to 
prevent disclosure of records concerning claimed  trade secrets, 
Florida Peninsula and Edison in one action and Heritage in another, while Jeffrey and Virginia Rapkin petitioned for a writ of 
mandamus to compel disclosure.  The court consolidated all three 
and abated the Rapkins’ mandamus suit pending resolution of the 
insurers’ claims that the records are exempt. Benjamin Mandell and Jordan Lee, the requestor-intervenors, filed public- records 
requests of their own and were granted intervention in the lower 
proceeding.  
 
Under a joint litigation plan the court adopted, the 
Department was to submit redacted and unredacted records to the 
3 court under seal, after which the court would conduct an in camera  
review and hold an evidentiary hearing on trade-secret status. The 
Department submitted the records under seal, but the court then 
conducted a mere “initial review,” which did no more than identify 
which of the 878 sealed pages carried a claimed exemption.  
 
On March 26, 2026, the court entered the Order for Pre-
Hearing Process , which states that the court “will not conduct the 
hearing in camera.” Instead, it directs that the sealed records be 
provided to the requestor-intervenors, who may “participate fully” 
in the evidentiary hearing and engage in discovery, subject to a 
confidentiality order. The day after the order was entered, Lee, 
who is also engaged in separate litigation against Heritage, served discovery requests on Florida Peninsula and Edison, and later 
noticed the deposition of Heritage’s corporate representative. The 
insurers moved for reconsideration, a protective order, and a 
temporary stay; on April 16, 2026, the court only granted a 
temporary stay. These petitions followed. 
 
To obtain certiorari relief from a nonfinal order, a petitioner 
must establish “(1) a departure from the essential requirements of 
the law, (2) resulting in material injury for the remainder of the 
case (3) that cannot be corrected on postjudgment appeal.”  
Lacaretta Rest. v. Zepeda, 115 So. 3d 1091, 1092 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2013). The latter two elements constitute irreparable harm, a 
jurisdictional condition precedent evaluated first. Id.  
 
Certain information may reasonably cause material injury of 
an irreparable nature, such as “cat out of the bag” material that could be used by an unscrupulous litigant to injure another person or party outside the litigation. Martin-Johnson, Inc. v. Savage, 509 
So. 2d 1097, 1100 (Fla. 1987) , superseded by statute on other 
grounds, § 768.72, Fla. Stat. The petitioners have made that 
showing: the sealed records are claimed to hold such material. And, although irreparable harm generally cannot be speculative, 
an exception applies to the premature dissemination of such 
information because “once the documents are disseminated, a 
privacy or trade secret interest has been invaded which cannot be 
remedied on direct appeal.” Wal-Mart Stores E., L.P. v. Endicott, 
81 So. 3d 486, 49 0–91 (Fla. 1st DCA 2011); see also Allstate Ins. 
Co. v. Langston, 655 So. 2d 91, 94 (Fla. 1995). The Order for Pre-
4 Hearing Process threatens this harm by requiring the sealed 
records to be produced to the requestor-intervenors.  
 
The confidentiality order the trial court contemplated does not 
avoid that result. A protective order permitting trade- secret or 
confidential material to be shared is not always sufficient to 
prevent harm . See Endicott, 81 So. 3d at 491; Am. Express Travel 
Related Servs., Inc. v. Cruz, 761 So. 2d 1206, 1209 (Fla. 4th DCA 
2000). “[O]nce the information becomes public, its confidentiality is lost forever.” Shands Teaching Hosp. & Clinics, Inc. v. Beylotte, 
357 So. 3d 307, 309 (Fla. 1st DCA 2023). The risk here is not 
hypothetical.  Lee served discovery the day after the order 
permitting his participation, confirming that the requestor-
intervenors are positioned to obtain and use the claimed-exempt 
materials outside the context of the litigation. Ordering production 
before a trade-secret determination forecloses  the exemption 
question  and inflicts injury that cannot be remedied on appeal. See 
Coventry First, LLC v. State, Off. of Ins. Regul., 30 So. 3d 552, 558–
61 (Fla. 1st DCA 2010)  (recognizing a vested property right in “the 
continuing confidentiality and exemption of [a provider’s] trade 
secrets and other work papers already submitted to the OIR,” and that disclosure of such records causes “legal and financial 
detriment”).  
 In any event, at this stage the petitioners need not establish 
that the records are, in fact, trade secrets. A prima facie showing 
of irreparable harm is enough to invoke certiorari review. 
Commonwealth Land Title Ins. Co. v. Higgins, 975 So. 2d 1169, 
1176 (Fla. 1st DCA 2008). That threshold is met, and certiorari 
jurisdiction is proper. 
 
Having established jurisdiction, we turn to whether the trial 
court departed from the essential requirements of law. Relief is 
reserved for a violation of a clearly established principle of law, 
Saints 120, LLC v. Moore, 292 So. 3d 1209, 1212 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2020), which can derive from a variety of sources, including “recent 
controlling case law, rules of court, statutes, and constitutional 
law.” Allstate Ins. Co. v. Kaklamanos, 843 So. 2d 885, 890 (Fla. 
2003).  This court has previously found “a departure from the 
essential requirements of law where, despite the assertion of a 
trade secret privilege, the trial court ordered production of 
5 documents without first conducting an examination of the 
documents.” Messer v. E.G. Pump Controls, Inc., 667 So. 2d 321, 
322 (Fla. 1st DCA 1995) ; see also  Becker Metals Corp. v. W. Fla. 
Scrap Metals, 407 So. 2d 380, 382 (Fla. 1st DCA 1981)  (“Without 
examination of the items claimed to be a trade secret, how can a determination be reached?”).  That determination usually requires 
an in camera review, though the court may instead hold an 
evidentiary hearing. Lewis Tree Serv., Inc. v. Asplundh Tree 
Expert, LLC, 311 So. 3d 206, 210 –11 (Fla. 2d DCA 2020); Sea Coast 
Fire, Inc. v. Triangle Fire, Inc., 170 So. 3d 804, 808 (Fla. 3d DCA 
2014).  
 
Moreover, where a timely action is filed, section 624.4213(2), 
Florida Statutes, bars release of records containing claimed trade 
secrets until a circuit court rules on their trade-secret status. The 
trial court did not follow that sequence. It made no exemption determination, yet ordered the sealed records produced to the 
requestor -intervenors and permitted their full participation and 
discovery. Respondents’ contention that the court had already 
conducted an in camera review misreads the record. The “initial 
review” made no trade-secret determination, and the order itself 
states that the court “will not conduct the hearing in camera.” 
Resolving the exemption at a hearing rather than through in 
camera review would have been permissible; ordering production 
and full participation of the requestor-intervenors before deciding 
exempt status is not. In other words, o rdering production before 
the trade -secret determination violates  the statutory safeguards  
and defeats the  declaratory actions’  purpose, giving the requestors 
access regardless of how the exemption is decided. Even if the 
records were found to be trade secrets, production would still 
require particularized findings of reasonable necessity that the 
trial court never made. KPMG LLP v. State, Dep’t of Ins., 833 So. 
2d 285, 286 (Fla. 1st DCA 2002); Laser Spine Inst., LLC v. Greer, 144 So. 3d 633, 633 –34 (Fla. 1st DCA 2014).  
 
The trade-secret exemption is not the only protection at stake. 
To the extent the records contain sensitive personal information of 
non-party insureds, that information is independently protected, 
both by statute and by constitutional right. See Thomas v. Smith, 
882 So. 2d 1037, 1043 –47 (Fla. 2d DCA 2004) (recognizing, under 
art. I, § 23, Fla. Const., a legitimate expectation of privacy in social 
6 security numbers); see also State, Dep’t of Fin. Servs. v. Danahy & 
Murray, P.A., 246 So. 3d 466, 468– 71 (Fla. 1st DCA 2018) 
(upholding, under art. I, § 24(c), Fla. Const., a statutory public-
records exemption protecting insureds ’ personal financial and 
health information).   
 
Furthermore, the trial court’s finding that the requestor-
intervenors “are in no sense competitors of the Insurers” does not 
save the order. The burden of proving trade-secret status rests on the party asserting it, and ordering production before that status 
is adjudicated deprives the petitioners of the opportunity to carry 
that burden. Managed Care of N. Am., Inc. v. Fla. Healthy Kids 
Corp., 268 So. 3d 856, 860 –61 (Fla. 1st DCA 2019). Whether the 
requestor -intervenors are competitors thus does not answer the 
dispositive question. What matters is whether the records are in 
fact exempt, a determination that must be made before they are 
ordered to be released. 
 
Therefore, we grant the consolidated petitions and quash the 
Order for Pre-Hearing Process. On remand, the trial court shall 
determine the exemption and trade-secret status of the disputed records before ordering any production or access.  That 
determination must be made through a confidentiality- preserving 
in camera inspection or evidentiary hearing that does not disclose the records to those seeking them. We take no position on whether 
the records are trade secrets or otherwise exempt.  
 Petitions 
GRANTED ; order on review QUASHED . 
 L
EWIS , WINOKUR , and N EFF, JJ., concur. 
 
_____________________________  
 Not final until disposition of any timely and 
authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or 
9.331.  
_____________________________  
  
M. Hope Keating and John K. Londot, Greenberg Traurig, P.A., 
Tallahassee; and Kathy J. Maus, William B. Collum, and Scott E. 
7 Damon, Butler Weihmuller Katz Craig LLP, Tampa , for Petitioner 
Heritage Property & Casualty Insurance Company.  
 
Fernando J. Valle and Matthew C. Scarfone, Colodny Fass, 
Sunrise, for Petitioners Florida Peninsula Insurance Company 
and Edison Insurance Company.  
 
Jeffrey A. Rapkin, Esq., Port Charlotte, for Respondents Jeffrey A. 
Rapkin and Virginia M. Rapkin.  
 
Francis A. Carbone , II, Jett L. Baumann, and Katie B. Privett, 
Office of the General Counsel, Florida Department of Financial 
Services,  Tallahassee, for Respondent Florida Department of 
Financial Services.  
 William F. Merlin, Jr., Shane S. Smith, and Yanet Cordova 
Quintero, Merlin Law Group, PLLC, Tampa, for Respondent 
Benjamin Mandell.  
 
Joshua R. Brownlee and John A. Tolley, II, JT Law Firm, P.A., 
Boca Raton; and Melissa A. Giasi, Giasi Law, P.A., Tampa, for 
Respondent Jordan  Lee.

items.summary:
An insurer (or any party) claiming a trade-secret or confidentiality exemption can obtain certiorari review before sealed records are handed to adversaries, because premature disclosure is unrecoverable harm that a confidentiality order may not cure, and the trial court must rule on exemption before compelling production; the requestors' non-competitor status does not excuse that sequencing.

Holding: Certiorari lies from a nonfinal order requiring material injury uncorrectable on postjudgment appeal plus a departure from the essential requirements of law; irreparable harm is a jurisdictional prerequisite and a prima facie showing suffices. Premature dissemination of claimed trade-secret material can cause irreparable "cat out of the bag" harm that a protective order may not prevent. Where a timely action is filed, section 624.4213, Florida Statutes, bars release of records containing claimed trade secrets until a circuit court rules on their trade-secret status, so a court commits a clear error by ordering production to records requestors and allowing their full participation and discovery before making that determination through in camera review or an evidentiary hearing that preserves confidentiality; the burden of proving the exemption rests on the party asserting it, and a finding that the requestors are non-competitors does not answer whether the records are exempt.

Disposition: Petitions granted; order quashed

items.summary:
Practically, an appellant cannot obtain appellate review by failing to raise the specific ground below or by not providing a transcript; the burdens of preserving issues and building the record rest on the appealing party.

Holding: An issue is preserved for further review only if the specific legal argument or ground to be raised on appeal was presented to the lower court; and absent a transcript, an appellate court cannot reasonably conclude that the trial judge misconceived the law or that the judgment is unsupported by the evidence, so reversal is not warranted.

Disposition: Affirmed

FOURTH DISTRICT  
 
MOREY WRIGHT, JR., 
Appellant,

[October 28, 2026] 
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit, 
Broward County; Michael A. Robinson, Judge; L.T. Case No. 
062026CA014602AXXXCE.   
 
Joseph S. Geller of Greenspoon Marder LLP, Fort Lauderdale, and 
Benedict P. Kuehne, Michael T. Davis, and Johan Dos Santos of Kuehne 
Davis Law, P.A., Miami, for appellant. 
 
Dedrick D. Straghn of Straghn Law, PLLC, Delray Beach, for appellee  
Mike Gelin. 
 
PER CURIAM . 
 
Morey Wright, Jr., appeals from an October 14, 2026 final judgment 
disqualifying him as an incumbent candidate for City of Tamarac 
Commissioner, District 2.  We affirm because the trial court correctly 
determined that Wright failed to comply with basic qualification requirements. 
 
Background 
 
Wright sought candidacy for City of Tamarac Commissioner, District 2.  
On October 2, 2025, Wright filed Department of State, Division of Elections 
Form DS-DE 9 to designate his campaign treasurer and a depository with the City Clerk (the “2025 Form”).  Wright listed Wells Fargo bank in item 
19 and filled out the bank’s address in items 20 to 24.  He did not, however,  
2 
 complete item 18, which required him to specify whether he was 
designating the bank as a primary or secondary depository. 
 On June 12, 2026, the last day of the qualifying period, Wright filed 
another Form DS-DE 9, and personally signed a check paying the 
qualifying fee from a Wells Fargo account named: “Morey Wright Campaign.”  Wright’s 2026 form did not complete item 1, which required 
him to indicate whether this was an initial filing of the form or a refiling to 
change a prior designation.  Item 10, which required Wright to specify 
whether he was appointing a campaign treasurer or deputy treasurer, was 
likewise incomplete.  Additionally, items 18 through 24 were left entirely 
blank.  These items required Wright to designate a bank as a primary or 
secondary depository and to provide the name and address of the bank.  
Wright signed the form in item 27, which required him to print the name 
of the person accepting the appointment.  He checked the box within this 
item accepting appointment as “deputy treasurer.”  But he did not sign in item 29, which required the signature of the campaign treasurer or deputy 
treasurer accepting the appointment.  Instead, item 29 was left blank. 
 
The City Clerk accepted Wright’s qualifying papers and payment and 
deemed him qualified as a candidate for the District 2 commissioner seat.  
 On September 9, 2026, Wright’s only opponent, appellee Mike Gelin, 
filed a complaint seeking declaratory and injunctive relief.  Gelin alleged 
that Wright had failed to comply with statutory qualification requirements.  
Gelin requested the court disqualify Wright as a candidate.   Wright filed a 
response. 
 
After an October 9, 2026, non-jury trial, at which the trial court heard 
testimony and reviewed documentary evidence, the trial court rendered 
the final judgment at issue.  The trial court found that Wright had failed 
to comply with basic statutory election qualification requirements, and 
disqualified Wright from appearing on the ballot. 
 Wright appeals, arguing that he had substantially complied with the 
statutory requirements, and the trial court erred in concluding that he had 
not properly designated himself as deputy treasurer before signing the 
check paying the fee from his campaign account. 
 
3 
 Discussion 
 
We review the trial court’s purely legal determination and interpretation 
of the statute de novo.  Wright v. City of Miami Gardens, 200 So. 3d 765, 
770 (Fla. 2016). 
 
Section 99.061(7)(a), Florida Statutes (2026), provides, in relevant part: 
 
In order for a candidate to be qualified, the following items 
must be received by the filing officer by the end of the qualifying period: 
 
1. A properly executed check drawn upon the candidate’s 
campaign account payable to the person or entity as 
prescribed by the filing officer in an amount not less than the 
fee required by s.  99.092, unless the candidate obtained the 
required number of signatures on petitions pursuant to s. 99.095.  The filing fee for a special district candidate is not 
required to be drawn upon the candidate’s campaign account.  
If a candidate’s check is returned by the bank for any reason, the filing officer shall immediately notify the candidate and the candidate shall have until the end of qualifying to pay the fee 
with a cashier’s check purchased from funds of the campaign 
account.  Failure to pay the fee as provided in this 
subparagraph shall disqualify the candidate.  2. The candidate’s oath required by s. 99.021, which must 
contain the name of the candidate as it is to appear on the ballot; the office sought, including the district or group 
number if applicable; and the signature of the candidate, which must be verified under oath or affirmation pursuant to s. 92.525(1)(a). 
 
….  
5. The completed form for the appointment of campaign 
treasurer and designation of campaign depository, as required by s. 106.021. 
 …. 
 
7. An oath or affirmation in writing that states whether the 
candidate is a citizen of another country in addition to being 
4 
 a citizen of the United States and, if so, discloses any other 
country of which the candidate is also a citizen. 
       
§ 99.061(7)(a), Fla. Stat. (2026). 
 
Payment of the fee with “[a] properly executed check drawn upon the 
candidate’s campaign account,” as section 99.061(7)(a)1. requires, is a 
basic qualification requirement and must be strictly followed.  Wright, 200 
So. 3d at 772.  Section 99.061(7)(a)1. creates a “true bright line” rule.  Id.1  
Courts must strictly enforce this statute, which plainly states that 
“[f]ailure to pay the fee as provided in this subparagraph shall disqualify 
the candidate.”  § 99.061(7)(a)1., Fla. Stat. (2026); see, e.g., Spiritis v. Botel, 
384 So. 3d 260, 263 (Fla. 4th DCA 2024) (applying Wright and concluding 
that payment by cashier’s check was not sufficient); Boatman v. Hardee, 
254 So. 3d 604, 609 –10 (Fla. 1st DCA 2018) (same); Thompson v. N. Bay 
Vill., 51 Fla. L. Weekly D1727 (Fla. 3d DCA Aug. 21, 2026) (same). 
 
The Florida Supreme Court’s recent decision in Amador v. Secretary, 
Florida Department of State, No. SC2026-1039, 2026 WL 2323248 (Fla. 
Aug. 11, 2026), is instructive.   There, the Department of State had deemed 
a candidate’s submission for election “incomplete,” on the ground that the 
check used to pay the candidate’s qualifying fee had not been drawn upon 
the candidate’s “campaign account,” as section 99.061(7)(a)1. 
requires.  Instead, the candidate’s qualifying fee had been  paid from a 
bank that was named as a “secondary depository.”  2026 WL 2323248 at 
1-2.  The Supreme Court denied the candidate’s mandamus petition,  
clarifying that the “candidate’s campaign account,” as referenced in 
section 99.061(7)(a)1., means the “primary campaign depository” which  
the candidate must designate under section 106.021(1)(b), Florida 
Statutes.  Id. 
 Here, the trial court similarly and properly concluded that Wright had 
failed to meet section 106.021’s requirement to designate a primary 
campaign depository .  Wright’s October 2025 form designated a treasurer 
(Michelle Webb) and named Wells Fargo bank.  But, item 18 of the form 
was incomplete and did not designate the bank as either a primary or a 
secondary depository.  The form which Wright later filed on the qualifying 
period’s last day in September 2026 also was incomplete and did not name 
 
1 The Supreme Court in Wright recognized a constitutional exception , because 
the candidate’s fee was rejected by bank error outside the candidate’s control.  
200 So. 3d at 774 -78.  No such error or exception applies here.  
 
5 
 any bank at all, let alone designate one as a primary or secondary 
depository.  
 
Wright’s 2026 form also failed to designate him as treasurer or deputy 
treasurer.  Importantly, Wright did not complete item 10 of the form, which 
required him to specify whether he was appointing a treasurer or deputy treasurer.  Additionally, he did not sign in item 29 as required.  He only 
signed within item 27, where the appointee’s name must be printed.  He 
checked the box within this item, however, indicating he was accepting 
appointment as “deputy treasurer.” 
 
Because Wright had never designated a primary campaign depository, 
and because he did not properly appoint himself as deputy treasurer, the 
fee was not paid by a check properly drawn on the primary campaign account.  Section 106.11(1)(a), Florida Statutes (2026), provides that 
expenditures from the primary campaign depository may be made “only by means of a bank check drawn upon the campaign account,” and section 
106.11(1)(b)4., Florida Statutes (2026), requires that the check contain 
“[t]he signature of the campaign treasurer or deputy treasurer.”  Wright’s 
check was not signed by either. 
 Wright argues that he “substantially complied” with section 
99.061(7)(a)1.’s technical requirements, as State ex rel. Siegendorf v. Stone, 
266 So. 2d 345, 346 (Fla. 1972), permitted.  But the “substantial 
compliance” doctrine does not apply to basic qualification requirements, 
like proper payment of the fee.  Id. at 347 n.3 (recognizing that substantial compliance does not apply to basic requirements, “i.e., paying a proper fee, 
the filing of necessary qualifying papers and registering to vote”); Wright, 
200 So. 3d 765, 772 n.3 (“We also note that our precedent concerning the doctrine known as substantial compliance has no place in our analysis 
because the statute at issue is not ambiguous and directly addresses the 
facts presented.”).  
 In Pedraza v. City of Miramar, 401 So. 3d 1195 (Fla. 4th DCA 2025), we 
extended the basic-requirement principle beyond payment of the fee “to 
substantive statements in election qualifying papers.”  Id. at 1199.  There, 
the candidate had mistakenly checked boxes on two different forms, opting 
to run as a write-in candidate.  Id. at 1196.  We rejected the argument that 
substantial compliance cured the candidate’s own errors on the forms.  Id. at 1199 (holding that a trial court may not “re-write a candidate’s 
substantive statements and selections on the qualifying forms”).  
 
Likewise, a “completed” form appointing a campaign treasurer and 
designating a campaign depository is a mandatory basic qualification 
6 
 requirement.  § 99.061(7)(a)5., Fla. Stat. (2026).  Section 99.061(7)(a)5. is 
unambiguous and must be enforced as written.  Siegendorf itself 
recognizes that “the filing of necessary qualifying papers” is a basic 
requirement that must be strictly followed.  266 So. 2d at 347, n.3.  
 
To the extent Wright argues that the Clerk’s acceptance of his 
documents excuses his incomplete filing, or converts the filing into a 
compliant qualification, we are not persuaded.  In Pedraza, we explained:  
Section 99.061(7)(c), Florida Statutes (2024), 
unambiguously states:  
The filing officer performs a ministerial function in 
reviewing qualifying papers.  In determining whether a 
candidate is qualified, the filing officer shall review the 
qualifying papers to determine whether all items 
required by paragraph (a) have been properly filed and 
whether each item is complete on its face, including 
whether items that must be verified have been properly 
verified pursuant to s. 92.525(1)(a).  The filing officer 
may not determine whether the contents of the 
qualifying papers are accurate. 
 401 So. 3d at 1199–200 (emphasis in original). 
 
Furthermore, the Legislature imposed a duty on the filing officer 
receiving qualifying papers to “make a reasonable effort to notify the candidate of the missing or incomplete items” only if the filing officer 
receives those qualifying papers “prior to the last day of qualifying.”  § 99.061(7)(b), Fla. Stat. (2026) (emphasis added).  Here, Wright’s 2026 form 
was filed on the last day of qualifying.  The City Clerk accepted the Form DS-DE 9 which Wright had provided, but this does not excuse Wright’s 
failure to properly complete the form.  The filing officer did not have to 
make a reasonable effort to notify the candidate regarding any missing or incomplete items, nor did the filing officer have a duty to ensure whether 
each item contained in the form was correctly completed.      
 Accordingly, we find no error in the trial court’s conclusion that Wright 
failed to satisfy the mandatory qualification requirements of sections 99.061(7)(a)1. and 99.061(7)(a)5.
2   
 
2 Having found Wright failed to comply with these two subsections and thus did 
not lawfully qualify as a candidate, we decline to address whether Wright 
complied with section 99.061(7)(a)7.  
7 
  
The above cases, including the Supreme Court’s recent decision in 
Amador, support the trial court’s conclusion that compliance with these basic requirements is required.  Wright’s completion of some sections of 
his Form DS-DE 9 did not suffice to meet the qualification requirements.  
Disqualification may be a harsh result, but we must enforce the law as 
written.  See Spiritis, 384 So. 3d at 264 (“[S]ection 99.061(7) is clear, and 
it is not for us to rewrite a statute to save a party in such a situation.  We 
must enforce the law as written.”).   
 
Affirmed. 
M
AY, SHEPHERD  and SHAW, JJ., concur. 
 
*            *            * 
 
Due to the election’s timing, no motions for rehearing are permitted.  
The mandate shall issue immediately.

items.summary:
An incumbent city-commissioner candidate who never designated a primary campaign depository, never properly appointed himself deputy treasurer, and paid the qualifying fee by a check not properly drawn on the primary campaign account was disqualified from the ballot. Because qualifying requirements such as proper fee payment and a completed treasurer/depository form are basic bright-line mandates, substantial compliance could not cure the omissions, the Clerk's ministerial acceptance of the papers did not excuse them, and disqualification stands even though harsh.

Holding: Unambiguous candidate-qualification requirements under section 99.061(7)(a)—such as payment of the qualifying fee by a check properly drawn on the candidate's primary campaign account and a completed campaign-treasurer/designated-depository form—are basic mandatory requirements that must be strictly enforced as written; the substantial-compliance doctrine does not apply to such basic requirements; a filing officer performs only a ministerial review, so acceptance of the papers does not cure a noncompliant filing; and a candidate's 'campaign account' means the primary campaign depository designated under section 106.021.

Disposition: Affirmed.

Supreme Court of Florida  
 
____________ 
 
No. SC2024 -0922 
____________ 
 
THE FLORIDA BAR,  
Complainant , 
 
vs. 
 
OMAR MEDINA, JR. , 
Respondent.  
 
October 29, 2026  
 
PER CURIAM.  
We have for review a report of referee recommending that 
Respondent, Omar Medina, Jr., be found not guilty of misconduct.1  
We approve the referee’s findings of fact  and recommendations as to 
Respondent’s guilt. 
BACKGROUND  
 On June 20, 2024, The Florida Bar filed a formal complaint 
against Respondent.  T he Bar  alleged that Respondent failed to 
appear at a case management conference, ordered by the U.S. 
 
 1.  We have jurisdiction.   See art. V, § 15, Fla. Const.   
 - 2 - District Court for the Middle District of Florida, resulting in his 
client’s suit being dismissed .  Respondent  then filed a motion to 
vacate the dismissal  and attached a signed affidavit.  The Bar 
alleged that the motion and affidavit included statements that were knowingly false.  The Bar argued  that this conduct violated Rules 
Regulating The Florida Bar 3 -4.3 (Misconduct and Minor 
Misconduct), 4 -3.3(a)(1) (Candor Toward the Tribunal; lawyer shall 
not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously 
made to the tribunal by the lawyer), and 4 -8.4(a) (Misconduct; 
lawyer shall not violate or attempt to violate the Rules of 
Professional Conduct).   
 After conducting a hearing on guilt, the assigned referee found 
that the Bar failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that 
Respondent knowingly made false statements to a tribunal and 
recommended that Respondent  be found not guilty of the charged 
rule violations.  The Bar now seeks  review of the referee’s report,  
asking us to find Respondent guilty of violating the relevant Bar 
rules  and to remand for a hearing  on sanctions .  Respondent asks 
 - 3 - us to approve the report of referee in its entirety.   We hereby 
approve the report.  
FINDINGS OF FACT  
The referee found that the disciplinary charges in this case 
center on  statements in the second paragraph of the  affidavit  
Respondent  attached with his motion to vacate:  
The undersigned affiant failed to meet in  the case 
management conference because I did not receive the 
appropriate notice of the hearing.  Moreover, there was no communication received regarding the hearing.  Counsel investigated why no notice was received and was able to determine that despite h aving notified the court 
and opposing counsel o[f] the appropriate email addresses inexplicably the clerk of this court sent notices to email addresses that do not exist and have not existed 
as part of the plaintiff’s counsel’s law firm for more than 
10 ye ars. 
Respondent made similar statements i n the sixth paragraph of his 
motion to vacate , writing : 
Additionally undersigned counsel had properly notified 
the court and counsel of the appropriate email addresses 
to use however inexplicably the clerk of this court sent notices to email addresses that do not exist and have not existed as part of the plaintiff’s counsel’s law firm for 
more than 10 years.  
The Bar alleged that several statements in these passages 
violated rule 4 -3.3(a)(1).  In particular, the Bar objected to 
 - 4 - Respondent asserting  that he did not receive appropriate notice of 
the conference,  that he had notified the court and opposing counsel 
of the appropriate email addresses, and that the clerk of court had 
“inexplicably” sent notice to email addresses that had not existed 
with Respondent’s firm for more than 10 years.   
Notably, Respondent also wrote: “The more significant 
importance is the fact that [Respondent] has had difficulty with the pacer system” (PACER being the federal court public records access and filing system) and learned after missing the conference that his 
PACER account had been deactivated for years.  Respondent 
suggested that this problem was “one of the possible reasons” he 
missed the conference, offering no other possible reasons.  
The referee found that Respondent had mismanaged his 
PACER account and did not understand how the federal court filing 
system worked under the relevant local rules.  Respondent  believed 
that designations he had made in state court would be used by the 
federal court upon removal of the case.  In accordance with the PACER handbook and local rules, t he local district court clerk sent 
notice of the case management conference to three email addresses that Respondent listed in his PACER account many years earlier : 
 - 5 - omedina@medinalawfirm.com; cgoldthwait@medinalawfirm.com; 
and imorfin@medinalawfirm.com .  The  referee found that the 
“omedina ” address was still in  use by Respondent  at the time he  
filed his motion to vacate, t hat the “cgoldthwait ” address had been 
inactive for more than 10  years, and  that it was unclear  from the 
evidence presented  how long the “ imorfin ” address had been 
inactive.  
The referee explained  that at the hearing on Respondent’s 
motion to vacate, the presiding district judge confronted 
Respondent about the fact that he was using one of the email 
addresses to which notice had been sent.  Respondent said  he never 
intended to blame the clerk of court and should have been clearer 
in his motion that while notice had been sent to the “ omedina ” 
address, neither he nor his staff ever saw any emails relating to the conference.  He posited that the notice might have made it to his 
server but not to his inbox.  He apologized and took the blame for 
mismanaging his emails and PACER account, saying he did not want to blame his staff because it was his responsibility.  
The referee found that Respondent’s testimony at the 
disciplinary hearing showed a lack of understanding as to the 
 - 6 - manner in which federal courts notice litigants and counsel.  The 
referee found  that Respondent made appropriate email designations 
in state court  and genuinely (though mistakenly) assumed  the clerk 
of court would update its e -filing with the pleadings made in the 
state court system —an assumption  that was inconsistent with the 
PACER handbook and local rules.   
The referee found that Respondent failed to update the clerk of 
court in a way that would ensure he received electronic filings and 
was negligent in maintaining his PACER account .  However, the 
referee also found th at Respondent’s negligence did not rise to the 
level of misconduct and his lack of comprehension of the federal 
filing system did not prove that he knowingly made false statements 
to the court. 
Notably, at one point during the disciplinary hearing, Bar 
counsel asked questions about when the “ imorfin ” address had last 
been used, and Respondent testified that Ms. Morfin may have 
worked for him as recently as 2022.  However, later  in the hearing, 
Respondent  stated that he believed the earlier line of questioning 
had been about a different assistant, Ms. Bland, who worked for him more recently.  Respondent  testified that he did not know the 
 - 7 - dates of Ms. Morfin’s employment.  The referee found that the most 
recent  active usage of the “ imorfin ” address had not been 
established.  
ANALYSIS  
In a Bar discipline case, a “referee’s findings of fact regarding 
guilt carry a presumption of correctness that should be upheld unless clearly erroneous or without support in the record.”  Fla. Bar v. Barrett, 897 So. 2d 1269, 1275 (Fla. 2005) (citation omitted).  If the referee’s findings are supported by competent, substantial 
evidence, this Court will not reweigh the evidence or substitute its 
own judgment for that of the referee.  Fla. Bar v. Schwartz , 284 So. 
3d 393, 396 (Fla. 2019).   
When reviewing a referee’s recommendations of  guilt, the 
referee’s factual findings must be sufficient under the applicable 
rules to support the recommendations.  Fla. Bar v. Shoureas, 913 
So. 2d 554, 557 -58 (Fla. 2005).   Ultimately, the party challenging a 
referee’s findings of fact or conclusions regarding  guilt has the 
burden of showing “that there is no evidence in the record to support those findings or that the record evidence clearly 
contradicts the conclusions.”  Fla. Bar v. Germain , 957 So. 2d 613, 
 - 8 - 620 (Fla. 2007).  A party cannot meet this high burden “simply by 
pointing to contradictory evidence” when there is also competent, substantial evidence that supports  the referee’s findings.  Fla. Bar v. 
Glick , 693 So. 2d 550, 552 (Fla. 1997).  
Here, the Bar argues that the evidence introduced  at the 
disciplinary hearing shows that Respondent violated rule 4 -3.3(a)(1) 
and therefore violated rules 3 -4.3 and 4- 8.4(a) , and it argues that 
the referee erred in finding otherwise.  W e find no clear error in the 
referee’s finding that the Bar failed to prove every element  of the 
charged rule violations, particularly the “knowingly” element, by clear and convincing evidence.  The Bar makes inferences of fact 
and points us to  contradictory evidence in the record , but the 
referee’s findings are supported by competent, substantial evidence 
and will not be reweighed . 
Notably, the referee identified only a single “ untrue ” statement  
in the motion and affidavit : Respondent’s assertion that the local 
federal clerk sent notice to email addresses (plural) that did not 
exist and had not existed as part of his  law firm for more than 10 
years.  From the evidence and testimony presented at the disciplinary hearing, the referee found that only the “ cgoldthwait ” 
 - 9 - address had been inactive for more than 10 years.  T he “imorfin ” 
address was found to have  been inactive for an unknown period of 
time, and the “ omedina ” address was still being used.  However, 
while Respondent’s statement was incorrect, the referee found that 
the Bar failed to prove that Respondent knew  he was making an 
untrue statement at the time.  We approve this findi ng. 
The Bar relies on Florida Bar v. Grieco, 389 So. 3d 1257, 1262 
(Fla. 2024), for the proposition that to prove the knowingly element, the Bar  need only  show that the lawyer deliberately engaged in the 
activity in question .  The Bar argues that Respondent ’s “activity ” 
was knowingly typing words into his motion  and affidavit  and then 
knowingly filing th ose documents .  The Bar contends that  it did not 
have to prove  that Respondent  knew his statements were false at 
the time he wrote  and filed the motion .   
The Bar’s interpretation of this  element is contrary to our case 
law.  In Florida  Bar v. Miller, 863 So. 2d 231, 234 (Fla. 2003) , we 
explained that the record evidence showed that “ Miller intentionally 
deceived the federal court ,” and we pointed to evidence in the record 
showing that Miller knew his statements were untrue at the time they were made.   
 - 10 - The Bar’s reliance on Grieco  is also misplaced , for in Grieco , we 
declared that “competent, substantial evidence in the record 
supports the referee’s finding that Grieco deliberately engaged in a pattern of dishonest conduct by making repeated false or misleading statements.”  389 So. 3d at 1264.  We emphasized that 
our holding was based on the referee’s findings about Grieco’s 
“shifting narrative” and  efforts to deliberately mislead, particularly 
the referee’s finding that “on more than one occasion, Grieco 
intentionally deceived or misled the public.”  Id.    
Here, the referee found the opposite, finding that Respondent 
never intended to mislead the federal court.  And we reiterate —the  
Bar must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the charged 
lawyer knew he or she was making false statements at the time the 
statements were made.  
However,  even if the Bar w ere operating under the correct 
standard, we must still assess whether the referee erred in finding 
that the Bar failed to prove that Respondent kne w he was making 
false statement s to the court.  The Bar claims  Respondent 
knowingly made a false statement by stating that the clerk “sent 
notices to email addresses that do not exist and have not existed as 
 - 11 - part of the plaintiff’s counsel’s law firm for more than 10 years.”  
The Bar argues that if only a single email address was inactive for more than 10 years, then Respondent’s statement about multiple inactive email addresses being noticed was a false statement.  T he 
Bar acknowledges that the “ cgoldthwait ” email address was  inactive 
for over 10 years, but it  argues that the “ omedina ” address was 
never inactive, and it  points to testimony elicited at  the disciplinary 
hearing in which Respondent suggested that the “ imorfin ” email 
address could  have been used by a former assistant , Ms. Morfin , 
within the past 10 years.   
As stated above, pointing to contradictory evidence will not  
establish clear error when there is also record e vidence in support  
of the  referee’s findings.   Here, Respondent testified that he thought  
Bar counsel’s questions about Ms. Morfin had been referring  to a 
different assistant who worked for him  more recently.  Bar counsel 
did not definitively pin  down  when the “imorfin ” address was last 
active, and , more importantly, Bar counsel failed to elicit that 
Respondent knew , at the time he filed his motion, that the “imorfin ” 
address had been  active more recently than he suggested in his 
motion and affidavit . 
 - 12 - The Bar’s next argument concerns Respondent’s remark about 
the clerk “inexplicably” sen ding notice to inactive email addresses.   
The Bar contends that this statement can only be interpreted as 
Respondent blaming the clerk of court  when he  knew that his own 
negligence was to blame for miss ing the  conference.  Notably, the 
referee wrestled with this issue, declaring  that he consider ed the 
“inexplicably” statement for three days before  ultimately  finding 
that it was just a statement.   
While the clerk’s actions were certainly  not “inexplicable” with  
an understanding of the PACER system  and local rules, given  
Respondent’s lack of understanding of the federal system  (as found 
by the referee) , Respondent  may well have been sincerely confused 
by the clerk’s actions given  the information he had at the time.  
Moreover, shortly after stating  that the clerk “inexplicably” 
sent notice to inactive email addresses, Respondent wrote “ [t]he 
more significant importance is the fact that [Respondent] has had difficulty with the pacer system” and  stated that he  learned after 
missing the conference that his PACER account had been deactivated for years.  Respondent suggested that this problem was 
“one of the possible reasons” he missed the conference, and h e 
 - 13 - offered no other possible reasons.  Thus, while the Bar insists that 
the only interpretation of Respondent’s “inexplicabl y” remark is that 
he was blaming the clerk of court for his  own failure to appear at 
the conference, Respondent immediately offered an explanation for 
his failure to attend, and that explanation assigned the blame to 
himself.  We therefore find no error in  the referee’s finding that the 
“inexplicably”  remark was just a statement —more specifically, an 
expression  that Respondent could not explain  at that time why 
outdated email addresse s had been used to notice the conference.  
Next, the Bar argues that in his  motion to vacate, Respondent 
accused opposing counsel of engaging in fraud on the court.  The 
Bar interprets this as Respondent falsely blaming opposing counsel 
for his own failure to attend the case management conference.  But  
Respondent ’s fraud on the court assertion was part of an argument 
made  early in his  motion on why he believed the case should not 
have been removed to federal court in the first place.  His “ fraud on 
the court”  statement was not even referring to  the missed case 
management conference, let alone blaming opposing counsel for his 
absence at that conference.  
 - 14 - The Bar’s next  argument is that Respondent knowingly made a 
false statement when he said  that he “properly notified the court 
and counsel of the appropriate email addresses to use.”  T he referee 
found that Respondent “did update the Clerk of Court of his 
address; just not in a way that would ensure he would receive 
electronic filings.”  Th is finding is supported by Respondent’s 
testimony at the disciplinary hearing.  When questioned about his 
statement on properly notifying the court of the appropriate email 
addresses, Respondent answered: “I did.  My understanding  is, as 
[opposing counsel]  testified, that the whole file was copied, 
including my email designations that were the active emails . . . .”  Thus, though Respondent had not  in fact “properly notified the 
court” of the correct email addresses, testimony in the record 
supports the referee’s finding that Respondent sincerely believed, at 
the time he filed his motion to vacate, that the designations he 
made in state court had been trans mitted with the case upon  
remov al to the federal system .  Therefore , we find no error in the 
referee ’s finding that the Bar failed to show that Respondent  
knowingly ma de a false statement when he  assert ed that he had 
properly notified the court of the correct email addresses.  
 - 15 - Finally, the Bar argues that the referee clearly erred in 
concluding that no competent, substantial evidence was presented 
showing that Respondent received any PACER filings.  Because the referee was referring to actual notice, we find no clear error in th e 
referee’s determination . 
CONCLUSION  
In conclusion, the referee’s findings of fact are supported by 
evidence in the record.  Because the referee’s findings of fact are 
supported by competent, substantial evidence, and because the 
referee’s legal conclusions and recommendations drawn from the 
findings of fact are not clearly contradicted by the record  evidence, 
we approve the report of referee  and find Respondent not guilty of 
violating rules 3 -4.3, 4 -3.3(a)(1), and 4- 8.4(a).  Judgment is hereby 
entered in favor o f Respondent, Omar Medina, Jr. 
It is so ordered.  
COURIEL, C.J., and LABARGA, MUÑIZ, GROSSHANS, FRANCIS, 
BARRIOS, and TANENBAUM, JJ., concur.  
 NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE REHEARING MOTION AND, IF FILED, DETERMINED.  
 Original Proceeding –  The Florida Bar  
 
 - 16 - Joshua E. Doyle, Executive Director, Patricia Ann Toro Savitz, Staff 
Counsel, and Mark Lugo Mason,  Bar Counsel, The Florida Bar, 
Tallahassee, Florida,  
  for Complainant  
 Donald A. Smith, Jr. of Smith, Tozian, Daniel & Davis, P.A. , Tampa, 
Florida ; and David M. Caldevilla of de la Parte, Gilbert, McNamara 
& Caldevilla, P.A. , Tampa, Florida,  
 
for Respondent

items.summary:
For lawyer discipline under rule 4-3.3(a)(1) (candor toward the tribunal), the Bar must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the lawyer knew the statement was false when made; deliberately drafting and filing the document, without more, does not establish the 'knowingly' element, so discipline turns on contemporaneous knowledge of falsity rather than mere negligence or a sincere but mistaken belief. The Court deferred to the referee's not-guilty findings supported by competent, substantial evidence. Issued October 29, 2026, within the October 26-November 8, 2026 window.

Holding: In reviewing a referee's recommendations on guilt in a Bar disciplinary case, the referee's findings of fact carry a presumption of correctness and are upheld if supported by competent, substantial evidence; the party challenging them must show that no record evidence supports them or that the record clearly contradicts the conclusions. To prove a knowing-false-statement violation of rule 4-3.3(a)(1), the Bar must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the lawyer knew the statement was false at the time it was made; the Bar's theory that deliberately typing and filing the documents alone satisfies the 'knowingly' element is contrary to case law (distinguishing Florida Bar v. Grieco; citing Florida Bar v. Miller). Negligence in maintaining an e-filing/PACER account or a sincere but mistaken belief that proper notice was given does not establish a knowing false statement.

Disposition: Court approved the referee's report and findings, found the respondent not guilty of violating rules 3-4.3, 4-3.3(a)(1), and 4-8.4(a), and entered judgment in favor of the respondent. The status metadata separately records "affirmed," which does not fit approval of a not-guilty finding (judgment for respondent); preserved without deciding. The opinion carries a notice that it is not final until the time to file a rehearing motion expires and, if filed, determined.

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 28, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D25 -1097  
Lower Tribunal No. 21-1806 -CA-01 
________________  
 
 
Citizens Property Insurance Corporation , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Mirna Rodriguez , 
Appellee.  
 
 
 
 An Appeal from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, Daryl E. 
Trawick , Judge.  
 
 Traub Lieberman Straus & Shrewsberry, LLP, and C. Ryan Jones, and 
David T. Burr  (St. Petersburg) ; Simms Goatache, P.A., and L esley Simms 
(Hollywood),  for appellant.  
 
 Robert J. Lee, P.A. , and Robert J. Lee, Steven C. Silverberg and  
Samuel Perez , for appellee.  
 
 
Before  FERNANDEZ, MILLER, and LOBREE, JJ.  
 
 MILLER, J.  
 
 2  Appellant, Citizens Property Insurance Corporation,  challenges a trial 
court order ratifying a general magistrate’s recommendation and awarding 
attorney’s fees to appellee, Mirna Rodriguez, under the fee shifting 
framework in section 627.428, Florida Statutes  (2021) .  The court awarded 
lead counsel his current  market billing rate  rather than his historical one and 
then added prejudgment interest from the date of entitlem ent.  On appeal, 
Citizens contends  this approach compensates the same harm —a delay in 
payment —twice.  We agree with Citizens and, in so doing, we adopt the 
reasoning of  our sister court in Philip Morris USA, Inc. v. Brown , 313 So. 3d 
898 (Fla. 1st DCA 2021 ). 
I 
  The facts require little elaboration.  This is a first -party homeowners 
insurance dispute  arising out of a Tropical Storm Eta claim.  The parties 
settled on the eve of a 2022 trial and stipulated that the insured was entitled 
to fees .  They then spent the better part of two years litigating how much 
those fees should be .   
 After an evidentiary hearing, t he general magistrate recommended  
current market rates for lead counsel,  plus prejudgment interest from the 
date of entitlement.  Citizens filed exceptions, arguing  that this combination 
 
 3 produced an impermissible windfall .  The trial court overruled the exceptions 
and entered judgment.  This appeal followed . 
II 
A 
 The question presented in this appeal  is a pure issue of law: may a 
prevailing insured  recover both current market billing rates  for its counsel  
and prejudgment interest , where each is designed to compensate for the 
same harm —a delay in payment?  We thus conduct a de novo review.   See 
G4S Secure Sols . USA, Inc. v. Golzar , 208 So. 3d 204, 207 –08 (Fla. 3d DCA 
2016).  
B 
 In Florida, prejudgment interest is not a penalty.  It is “merely another 
element of  pecuniary damages .”  Argonaut Ins. Co. v. May Plumbing Co. , 
474 So. 2d 212, 214 –15 (Fla. 1985).   Once  a plaintiff establishes a liquidated 
loss, prejudgment interest ordinarily follows as a matter of course.   
 Attorney’s fees are no exception.  In Quality Engineered Installation, 
Inc. v. Higley South, Inc., 670 So. 2d 929 (Fla. 1996), the Florida Supreme 
Court held that prejudgment interest accrues from “the date the entitlement 
to attorney fees is fixed through agreement,  arbitration award, or court 
determination, even though the amount of the award has not yet been 
 
 4 determined.”   Id. at 93 0–31.  T he court’s reasoning was twofold.   Accrual 
from entitlement “ serves as a deterrent to delay by the party who owes the 
attorney fees and is appropriate in conjunction with our decision that attorney 
fees are not to be assessed for litigating the amount of an attorney -fee 
award.”  Id. at 931.  
 In a parallel line of authority, Florida courts have approved fee awards  
calculated at current rather than historic al billing rates in cases involving 
substantial delay.  See Fla. Dep’t  of Agric. & Consumer Servs. v. Bogorff , 
132 So. 3d 249, 257 (Fla. 4th DCA 2013) .  This practice is not limited to 
Florida.  A myriad of opinions from around the country  have authorized this 
practice.  See, e.g. , Vega v. Chi. Park Dist., 12 F.4th 696, 706 (7th Cir. 2021) ; 
L.H. v. Hamilton Cnty. Dep’t of Educ. , 356 F. Supp. 3d 713, 723 (E.D. Tenn. 
2019) ; Radtke v. Caschetta , 254 F. Supp. 3d 163, 182 (D.D.C. 2017) ; 
Parkinson v. Hyundai Motor Am ., 796 F. Supp. 2d 1160, 1174 (C.D. Cal. 
2010) ; JHC Indus . Servs., LLC v. Centurion Co s., 263 A.3d 1105, 1111  n.5 
(N.J. Super. Ct. App. Div. 2021) . 
 Consequently, each  remedy is lawful standing alone.  The difficulty 
arises only when one is stacked on top of another , which is exactly what 
happened here.  The First District confronted this approach in Brown  and 
resoundingly rejected it.  313 So. 3d at 900.  There , the trial court  awarded 
 
 5 current rates because “the litigation spanned the better part of a decade 
during which the billing rates for the attorneys increased.”  Id. at 899.  In 
approving that decision, t he Brown  court  relied on  Bogorff , which had itself  
relied on Perdue v. Kenny A. , 559 U.S. 542 (2010) , and Gray v. Bostic , 613 
F.3d 1035 (11th Cir. 2010 ).  Both decisions approved of current market rates 
where the prevailing party demonstrate s excepti onal, unanticipated d elay.  
Bogorff , 132 So. 3d at 257.  
 But Brown  refused to sanction an award of  prejudgment interest on  top 
of current market rates .  The court’s  reasoning was mathematical ; “[t]he 
current rate approach . . . tacitly includes an adjustment for the time value of 
money.”   Brown , 313 So. 3d at 900 .  That “approach —which will generally 
result in a higher fee award —already includes the time value of money that 
an award of prejudgment interest would partially replicate or possibly 
duplicate. ”  Id.   
 But the Brown  court candidly acknowledged that the methodology was 
not perfect, noting that the current market rate merely provides “an 
approximation of what the more analytically -intense [present value] 
approach would produce.”  Id.  But approximate or not, current rates 
compensate for the same harm prejudgment interest addresses.   Thus, 
 
 6 simultaneously awarding both “overcompensates the fee award by 
compounding the interest component of [the] award.”  Id. 
 The federal courts reached this conclusion long ago.  The Supreme 
Court has told us in no uncertain terms that “[i]nterest  and a delay factor 
share an identical function.  They are designed to compensate for the belated 
receipt of money.”  Libr. of Cong . v. Shaw , 478 U.S. 310 , 322  (1986).  Fee 
enhancements are  included  among acceptable delay factors.  See Missouri 
v. Jenkins , 491 U.S. 274 , 282  (1989).    
 Because both remedies compensate for the same harm, they function 
as substitutes rather than  supplements.  Judge  Richard  Posner , a leading 
economics expert,  cogently explained why a choice between the two  is 
economically sound:  
The judge refused to award the lawyers prejudgment interest.   
His reason was that he was using as the lodestar their 1988 
billing rates and thus automatically compensating them for the 
loss of the use of their money. The alternative . . . would have 
been to base the award on the rates the lawyers charged when 
they rendered the services to the class and to add interest on 
that amount to the present.  Both approaches have been deemed 
acceptable.  In many, perhaps most, cases the second is mor e 
straightforward.  The cost of delay in receiving money to which 
one is entitled is the loss of the time value of money, and interest 
is the standard form of compensation for that loss.  Changes in 
billing rates from year to year reflect at most only one component 
of an interest rate —the rate of inflation —and that component 
may be swamped by factors having nothing to do with the time  
value of money, such as the demand for and supply of the 
services of particular lawyers, firms, or specialties, or of the 
 
 7 profession as a whole.  Suppose that, because of the troubled 
state of the legal -services market today, the billing rates of the 
class counsel have actually fallen since the time when they 
rendered their services to the class. In that event, to award them 
a fee on the basis of the current rates would be in effect to award 
them negative interest.  Yet —to recur to the essential touchstone 
of analysis in these cases —if the lawyers had rendered the 
services to paying clients, their fees would have been computed  
and paid at the lawyers' then current billing rates, and the lawyers 
would have earned interest on those fees to the present.  A 
further consideration is that there may be better information 
about past than about current billing rates.  Past rates are rat es 
that were actually charged to paying clients; current rates may 
be mere estimates of rates to be charged to those clients.  
 
Matter of Cont’l Ill. Sec. Litig. , 962 F.2d 566 , 570–71 (7th Cir. 1992) (citations 
omitted) .  
  We rec ognize that neither method is perfect.  “ The use of current rates 
is, at best, an imperfect proxy for the loss to counsel from a delay in payment.  
It will undercompensate counsel when interest rates exceed the rate of 
inflation of attorney’s fees, just as it will overcompensate counsel when the 
inflation rate exceeds the interest rate.”  M.H.  v. N.Y.C. Dep’t of Educ. , 20-
cv-1923, 2021 WL 4804031, at *31 (S.D.N.Y. Oct. 13, 2021) .  But 
imperfection is a reason to carefully exercise a choice of remedies, not a 
license for double recovery.  A ttorneys are best situated to  assess the market 
 
 8 and elect the a venue that will most fully compensate  them  for delay  in a given 
case .1 
C 
 Armed with these principles, we turn to this case .  By awarding  lead 
counsel  both curre nt rates and prejudgment interest, the trial court effectively 
compensated him twice for the loss of use of his fee.  In our view, this created 
an unwarranted windfall.   The error, however, was confined, as it only 
infected the award to lead counsel.  All other  legal profession als were  
compensated at rates below their current market rates.  We therefore affirm 
the order under review in all respects,  save the prejudgment interest 
awarded on lead counsel’s fees.  
 Affirmed in part; reversed in part; remanded.  
 
1 Rodriguez’s reliance on United Auto. Ins. Co. v. Coastal Radiology, LLC , 
340 So. 3d  528 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022) , does not invalidate Brown .  The opinion 
is devoid of any facts or analysis bearing on this issue.  Nor does the 
argument that current rates reflect only market appreciation while interest 
compensates for loss of use  carry the day.

items.summary:
In a delayed section 627.428 first-party fee award, prevailing counsel must elect either current market billing rates or prejudgment interest to compensate delay in payment; recovering both is an impermissible windfall. Here the double recovery was confined to lead counsel, so the fee order is reversed only as to prejudgment interest on his fees and remanded, with the balance affirmed.

Holding: A prevailing insured may recover either current market billing rates or prejudgment interest for delay in paying section 627.428 attorney's fees, but not both, because the current-rate approach tacitly incorporates the time value of money, so stacking prejudgment interest compounds the same delay component and overcompensates; the two function as substitutes rather than supplements, and electing the remedy is generally the fee claimant's choice.

Disposition: Affirmed in part; reversed in part; remanded.

Author: Judge Miller

DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA  
SECOND  DISTRICT  
 
 
ADVANCED WOUND CARE, LLC , 
 
Appellant,  
 
v. 
 
CONTACT MEDICAL SUPPLY, LLC , 
 
Appellee.  
 
No. 2D 2026 -0764  
 
 
October 28 , 2026  
Appeal pursuant to Fla. R. App. P. 9.130 from the Circuit Court for 
Hillsborough County; Mark R. Wolfe, Judge.  
 
V. Stephen Cohen, Jacquelyn H. Konakovic, and Connor Kennedy of Bajo 
Cohen Agliano, P.A. , Tampa ; and Adam Hersh of Blue Chip Law, Tampa, 
for Appellant . 
 
Jonathan B. Harris of The Law Offices of Jonathan B. Harris, P.A., Coral 
Gables  (withdrew after briefing) ; Michael S. Hoffman of Lessne Hoffman, 
PLLC, Ft. Lauderdale, for Appellee.  
 
 
KHOUZAM, Judge . 
 Advanced Wound Care (plaintiff below) appeals the nonfinal order 
granting the motion to quash service of process and transfer venue filed 
by Contact Medical Supply (defendant below).  Contact Medical Supply 
has filed a confession of error, conceding that t he trial court erred in 
2 
 granting the motion  and requesting reversal.   We accept the confession of 
error and revers e.   
Contact Medical Supply  appropriately concedes that the trial 
court's ruling cannot be supported by good faith argument.  The trial 
court  quashed Advanced Wound Care 's substituted service upon Contact 
Medical Supply  in this action in Hillsborough County and transferred 
venue to  Miami -Dade County  where Contact Medical Supply  had filed its 
related action, in which Contact Medical Supply  had perfected personal 
service upon Advanced Wound Care .  The trial court's ruling was 
premised on its finding that Advanced Wound Care  had failed to effect 
substituted service by failing to strictly comply with the mailing 
requirement of section 48.161(3), Florida Statutes  (2025) .  But the record 
shows that Advanced Wound Care  did not have an address for Contact 
Medical Supply  due to Contact Medical Supply 's own evasiveness and 
gamesmanship.  Under these circumstances, t he doctrine of equitable 
estoppel preclude s Contact Medical Supply  from benefitting from its own 
deceptive  actions.  See, e.g. , Triad Discount Buying Servs ., Inc. v. Special 
Data Processing Corp. , 761 So. 2d 1181, 1182 (Fla. 4th DCA 2000)  
(applying equitable estoppel where appellee filed suit first only because of 
its own gamesmanship and deceit).  Accordingly, we  revers e and remand 
for th is case to proceed in Hillsborough County.  
Reversed and remanded with instructions.  
 
MORRIS  and GUARD, JJ., Concur.  
 
 
Opinion subject to revision prior to official publication.

items.summary:
Reinforces that equitable estoppel bars a litigant from benefiting from a process defect it engineered through concealment: where the non-moving defendant concealed its address, the plaintiff's substituted service should not be quashed for missing the statutory mailing, and the action proceeds in the plaintiff's chosen county. The disposition rests on the defendant's accepted confession of error. Opinion is marked subject to revision prior to official publication.

Holding: A party may not quash substituted service and secure a venue transfer by relying on its opponent's failure to strictly comply with the mailing requirement of section 48.161(3) when the party's own evasiveness and gamesmanship deprived the opponent of the address needed to comply; on this record equitable estoppel precluded that reliance, the movant's confession of error was accepted, and the order was reversed.

Disposition: Nonfinal order granting the motion to quash service and transfer venue reversed and remanded with instructions to proceed in the original county (confession of error accepted; appeal under Rule 9.130).

Author: Judge Khouzam

FIFTH  DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________ 
 
Case No. 5D2025-0813 
LT Case No.  2018 -CA-008373 
_____________________________ 
 
ADOLFO POSADAS SAN MARTIN , 
 
Appellant,  
 
v. 
 
ANA POSADAS , 
 
Appellee.  
_____________________________ 
 
 On appeal from the Circuit Court for Duval  County . 
Robert M. Dees, Judge.  
 
Jonathan Lucas and David H. Willis, of Willis- Lucas Law Group, 
P.A., Jacksonville , for Appellant.  
 Theresa C. Pontieri, of Lesak, Hamilton, Calhoun & Pontieri, 
PLLC, Jacksonville, for Appellee.  
 
October 30, 2026  
 
 
P
ER CURIAM .  
 
  Appellant, Aldolfo Posadas San Martin, appeals the trial 
court’s August 2024 order discharging a mechanic’s lien, which Appellant filed in an effort to secure payment for labor and 
materials he provided with regard to certain structures owned by 
Appellee, Ana Posada.  Appellant filed a motion for rehearing, 
which the trial court denied in an order entered several months 
2 later, following which, Appellant filed his notice of appeal.  
Generally, a petition for certiorari is the appropriate manner of 
seeking review of an order discharging a lien.  Dracon Constr., Inc. 
v. Facility Constr. Mgmt., Inc. , 828 So. 2d 1069, 1070 (Fla. 4th DCA 
2002).  The petition must be filed within thirty (30) days of 
rendition of that order.  Fla. R. App. P. 9.100(c)(1).  A motion for 
rehearing does not toll the time to seek review of a non- final order.  
See Lovelace v. Lovelace , 124 So. 3d 447, 447 (Fla. 1st DCA 2013).  
“As with an untimely notice of appeal, an untimely petition for writ 
of certiorari is ineffective to confer jurisdiction on the appellate 
court.”  Caldwell v. Wal- Mart Stores, Inc. , 980 So. 2d 1226, 1228 
(Fla. 1st DCA 2008).  Accordingly, Appellant’s effort to seek 
appellate review is untimely and hereby dismissed.   
 
 Appellant also appeals an order finding Appellee entitled to 
an award of attorney’s fees; however, no amount was set in that 
order and no order setting an amount is included in the record on 
appeal.  Accordingly, we dismiss that aspect of the appeal as 
premature.  See Allstate Ins. Co. v. Jenkins , 32 So. 3d 163, 165 (Fla. 
5th DCA 2010); Mills v. Martinez , 909 So. 2d 340, 342 (Fla. 5th 
DCA 2005).  This dismissal is without prejudice to timely seek 
appellate review of a final order once one is rendered.   See Libman 
v. Fla. Wellness & Rehab. Ctr., Inc. , 260 So. 3d 515, 518 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2018).  
 
 Although a copy of the trial court ’s order granting summary 
judgment was not attached to or referenced in his notice of appeal, 
a review of Appellant’s brief suggests that he appears to be 
attempting to appeal that order.  However, an order simply 
granting a motion for summary judgment is not a final appealable 
order; thus, we dismiss that aspect of the appeal as premature.  
Boyd v. Goff , 828 So. 2d  468, 469 (Fla. 5th DCA 2002).  This 
dismissal is also without prejudice to a timely appeal once a final 
order has been rendered.  
 
  
DISMISSED . 
 
LAMBERT , EDWARDS , and  KILBANE , JJ., concur . 
 
3 _____________________________ 
 
Not final until disposition of any timely and 
authorized motion under Fla. R. App. P. 9.330 or 
9.331.  
_____________________________

items.summary:
A party seeking review of an order discharging a mechanic's lien must file a certiorari petition within thirty days of rendition, and a motion for rehearing does not toll that deadline, so an untimely petition leaves the appellate court without jurisdiction; appeals of a fee order that sets no amount and of an order merely granting summary judgment are premature and dismissed without prejudice pending a final order.

Holding: Review of an order discharging a lien is ordinarily sought by petition for writ of certiorari filed within thirty days of rendition under Rule 9.100(c)(1); a motion for rehearing does not toll the time to seek review of a non-final order, and an untimely certiorari petition is ineffective to confer appellate jurisdiction. A fee order that sets no amount and an order simply granting summary judgment are not final appealable orders, so appeals of them are premature and dismissed without prejudice to a timely appeal once a final order is rendered.

Disposition: Dismissed

DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA  
SECOND  DISTRICT  
 
 
 ANDREW CALHOUN SAXON , 
 
Appellant , 
 
v. 
 
BAY RANCH MOBILE VILLAGE, LLP d/b/a  
BAY RANCH MOBILE HOME PARK , 
 
Appellee.  
 
 
No. 2D20 26-1143  
 
 
November 6, 2026 
 
Appeal pursuant to Fla. R. App. P. 9.130 from the County Court for  
Pinellas County; Susan Bedinghaus, Judge.  
 
Andrew Calhoun Saxon, pro se.  
 
Patrick M. Singer of Landlord Law, P.A., Tampa, for Appellee.  
 
 
MORRIS, Judge . 
In this mobile home lot eviction action, Andrew Calhoun Saxon 
appeals from a Judicial Default and Default Final Judgment for 
Possession .  We remand for the correction of a scrivener's error in the 
judgment .  We affirm the judgment in all other respects.  
In the Judicial Default and Default Final Judgment for Possessio n, 
the county court  found that  Mr. Saxon's failure  to deposit rent as 
 
2 
 ordered by the court was an absolute waiver of his defenses under 
section 723.063(2), Florida Statutes ( 2026 ), and that the mobile home 
park owner, Bay Ranch Mobile Village , was thus entitled to a default 
judgment  in its favor .  We find no error there.  See § 723.063(2) (" The 
failure of the mobile home owner to pay the rent, or portion thereof, into 
the registry of the court as required herein constitutes an absolute 
waiver of the mobile home owner's defenses other than payment, and the 
park owner is entitled to an immediat e default .").  However, although the 
judgment correctly states in paragraph three that "[a] Judicial Default is 
entered against Defendant, ANDREW CALHOUN SAXON ," as required by 
section 723.063(2), the judgment  then erroneously cites section 83.60(2) , 
Florida Statutes ( 2026 ).  Bay Ranch Mobile Village concedes in its 
answer brief that citing section 83.60(2) was error.   
Because the judgment correctly entered a judicial default against 
Mr. Saxon  as required by section 723.063(2) but cited the wrong statute, 
we affirm the judgment but remand for the trial court to correct this 
scrivener's error with an amended judgment  that cites  the operative  
statute .  See T.M. v. Dep't of Child. & Fams. , 298 So. 3d 146, 147 (Fla. 2d 
DCA 2020)  (affirming the judgment but remanding for correction of 
scrivener's errors when "the written judgment cite[d] the incorrect 
[statutory] subsections for three of the grounds") ; Tunstall v. Gonzalez -
Tunstall , 278 So. 3d 254 , 254  (Fla. 2d DCA  2019)  (affirming an order in 
all respects but remanding to correct a scrivener's error when the error 
"had no substantive effect " (citing Mitchell v. Mitchell , 841 So. 2d 564, 
568 (Fla. 2d DCA 2003) )). 
Affirmed and r emanded to correct scrivener's error . 
 
KHOUZAM and GUARD , JJ., Concur.  
 
3 
  
 
Opinion subject to revision prior to official publication.

items.summary:
In a mobile-home lot eviction, a lot owner who fails to deposit the court-ordered rent into the registry of the court loses the right to assert defenses (other than payment) and faces an immediate default judgment for possession; an otherwise correct default judgment that merely cites the wrong governing statute contains only a scrivener's error, which is fixed on remand with an amended judgment rather than reversed.

Holding: Under section 723.063(2), a mobile home owner's failure to pay rent, or the portion of it ordered, into the registry of the court constitutes an absolute waiver of the owner's defenses other than payment, entitling the park owner to an immediate default; and a judgment that correctly enters that default but erroneously cites a different statute contains only a scrivener's error, which is corrected by an amended judgment on remand without disturbing the affirmance where the mis-citation has no substantive effect.

Disposition: Affirmed and remanded to correct scrivener's error

Author: Judge Morris
