DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA  
SECOND DISTRICT  
 
THE BANK OF NEW YORK MELLON f/k/a THE BANK OF NEW 
YORK AS TRUSTEE FOR THE BENEFIT OF THE CERTIFICATE 
HOLDERS OF THE CWABS INC. ASSET -BACKED 
CERTIFICATES, SERIES 2007 -BC3, 
 
Appellant , 
v. 
MICHAEL  FERNANDEZ  and D IANNA  FERNANDEZ , 
Appellees.  
No. 2D2025 -1819  
 
November 4, 2026  
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for Hillsborough County; Jennifer X. 
Gabbard, Judge.  
 
Eric M. Levine and Adam G. Schwartz of Atlas | Solomon LLP, Stuart, for 
Appellant.  
 
Alan Borden of Debt Relief Legal Group, LLC, Tampa, for Appellees.  
 
 
GUARD , Judge . 
 The Bank of New York Mellon  (Bank)  appeals a n adverse  final 
judgment denying it s foreclosure of a mortgage  based on a failure  to 
prove a default .  Because the undisputed evidence at trial was that 
Michael and Diann a Fernandez had not made a payment since June  
2017  and no defense allowed them to stop paying their mortgage , we 
reverse.  
 
2 
 I. 
In 2007, the Fernandezes executed a $160,000 note  secured by a 
mortgage on their home .  In 2012, t he Fernandezes filed Chapter 13  
bankruptcy.  During  that bankruptcy, the Fernandezes entered a 
modification agreement  with the then servicer  of their loan , modifying the 
terms of their mortgage .  Then, on August  21, 2015, Bank of America, 
N.A. (Bank of America), who was the Bank 's servicer  at that time , 
reversed  four previous payments made in 2015.  While a Bank of 
America payment history shows those reversal s, the payment history 
contains no explanation of why those payments were reversed.  At trial, 
the Bank 's witness  was unable to testify regarding the reason for the 
reversals other than to speculate about w hat would normally cause such 
reversals.  At trial, Diann a Fernandez testified that she made the 
reversed payments and th at funds for those payments were never 
returned to her.   
The effect of t he reversal s was that it  placed the  Fernandezes ' loan 
in default  by four payments .  Despite that fact , from August 2015 
through April 2017, the Fernandezes continued to make  their monthly 
payments , and Bank  of America accepted those payments .  In May 2017, 
Bank of America returned the Fernandezes ' May 2017 payment because 
it was for less than the total amount owed  as it did not  includ e the four 
revers ed payments .  Approximately t wo times in or around May 2017, 
Diann a Fernandez went into a Bank of America branch and attempted to 
make a single mortgage payment.  Bank of America refused to take those 
payments.  That same year, Bank of America sued to foreclose on the 
loan but voluntarily dismissed its case  before trial.  
In January 2021, the Bank sought  again to foreclose on the 
Fernandezes ' home .  In its complaint, the Bank alleged  that "[t]here has 
 
3 
 been a default under the note and mortgage, as modified, held by 
Plaintiff in that the payment due January 1, 2017, and all subsequent 
payments have not been made. "  The January 1, 2017 , date in the 
complaint was only accurate if the four reversed payments should have 
been reversed.  At trial, evidence and testimony showed that the  last 
payment the Fernandezes  made  was in May 2017.  Though, Bank of 
America returned th at payment.   Diann a Fernandez admitted that their 
last accepted payment was made in April 2017 .  She also admitted that 
they did not have sufficient funds to bring the mortgage current  when 
the action was filed .  In their answer and affirmative defenses, the 
Fernandezes asserted one defense relevant to this appeal .  In their 
second affirmative defense, the Fernandezes alleged:  
II. UNCLEAN HANDS  
15. Defendants assert that the bad action of the Plaintiff 
has caused the loan to be in default.  
16. Plaintiff states the Defendants have not made a 
payment since January 1, 2017.  This is false, 
Defendants made all payments until Plaintiff stopped 
taking payments.  
17. Plaintiff 's own actions of not accepting payments 
caused any default and this bars Plaintiff from 
foreclosing on the property.  
After a bench trial , the trial court entered judgment against the 
Bank, concluding that it failed to prove a default.  The trial court made 
the following relevant findings:  
3. The Court finds that as of the Plaintiff 's alleged 
default date of January 1, 2017, the accounting showed 
that the Defendants made on time payments as required 
under the contract, but there were transactions 
reported which showed a reversal of four payments 
occurring on August 21, 2015.  The Plaintiff 's 
representative failed to provide any explanation as to 
the reason for the reversals or any explanation that 
would indicate the reversals were caused due to a 
 
4 
 contractual default by the Defendants. The Plaintiff 's 
witness couldn 't give competent testimony as to why 
those reversals occurred.  
4.  The Court finds that the Defendant, Mrs. 
Fernandez, was credible in her testimony as to the 
payments she made on a monthly basis in accordance 
with the Note and Mortgage contract from January 2015 
until April of 2017. Defendants ['] May 2017 payment 
was returned by the Plaintiff, and subsequent attempts 
to pay directly at the servicer, Bank of America, were 
not accepted after May 2017.  
The trial court did not cite any authority , and it is unclear  whether 
it relied  on the Fernandezes ' second affirmative defense in reaching its 
conclusion  or something else .  The Bank timely appealed.  
II. 
As explained below, we conclude that there was legally sufficient 
evidence that the Fernandezes defaulted on the note and mortgage after 
May 2017.  We also hold that, under these circumstances, the Bank 's 
failure to accept the May 2017 payment did not excuse the Fernandezes 
from their ongoing obligations under the note and mortgage.  A dispute 
over the proper  accounting of payments with a bank or servicer does not, 
without more, excuse a borrower 's obligation to make timely payments.   
On remand, the trial court should remove the principal amount of the 
four revers ed payments, interest before June 2017, and any fees claimed 
against the Fernandezes before July 2017.  Also, because the main issue 
litigated below concerned the four reversed payments, the trial court may 
reduce  any attorney 's fees awarded  by the  amounts spent litigating the 
four reversed payments.  
A.   
This case reaches us after a bench trial.  We have held that we 
review the legal conclusions  of a trial court after a bench trial de novo.  
Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v. Dias , 331 So. 3d 755,  760 (Fla. 2d DCA 2021) 
 
5 
 (quoting  Jasser v. Saadeh , 91 So. 3d 883, 884 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012)).  We 
also have stated that we review the legal sufficiency of the evidence in a 
civil, nonjury trial de novo.  Mace v. M&T Bank , 292 So. 3d 1215,  1219  
(Fla. 2d DCA 2020) (citing  Norman v. Padgett , 125 So. 3d 977, 978 (Fla. 
4th DCA 2013)).  We have explained that legally sufficient evidence is 
equal to competent substantial evidence.  Id.  We have further 
commented that the competent substantial evidence standard is met 
when there is properly  admitted  evidence  that has "a 'definite probative 
value. ' "  Id. (quoting Savage v. State , 120 So. 3d 619, 621 (Fla. 2d DCA 
2013)).  
B. 
To be entitled to foreclose a mortgage, a lender must prove  (1) an 
agreement, (2) a default, (3) a proper acceleration, and (4) the amount 
owed or due.  Ernest v. Carter , 368 So. 2d 428, 429 (Fla. 2d DCA 1979).  
The trial court found that the bank failed to prove the second element, a 
default.  Each  failed monthly payment is a separate default.  Bartram v. 
U.S. Bank Nat 'l. Ass 'n, 211 So. 3d 1009 , 1021 -22 (Fla. 2016) ( holding 
each new default is a separate cause of action for statute of limitations 
purposes ); Singleton v. Greymar Assocs ., 882 So. 2d 1004, 1006 -07 (Fla. 
2004) (concluding that a second foreclosure action founded on 
subsequent, different default was not barred by dismissal of a prior 
action ); U.S. Bank Home Mortg . v. Boivin , 403 So. 3d 421, 427 -28 (Fla. 2d 
DCA 2025) (discussing the interplay between  the separate, subsequent 
default concept and a laches defense); Grdic v. HSBC Bank USA, N.A.  as 
Tr. for Registered Holders of Ace Secs. Corp. , 267 So. 3d 473, 476 (Fla. 2d 
DCA 2019) (examining when statute of limitations runs in a foreclosure 
action  when subsequent defaults occur ).  Putting aside for the moment 
the four reversed payments, the Bank presented legally sufficient 
 
6 
 evidence that the Fernandezes failed to make payment and were in 
default from June 2017 onwards.  
In Lunn Woods v. Lowery , this court dealt with a foreclosure appeal  
not dissimilar to this a ppeal .  See 577 So. 2d 705, 706 (Fla. 2d DCA 
1991).  In that case, a plaintiff sought to foreclose a security interest 
under an agreement for deed.   Id.  In its complaint, t he plaintiff sought to 
foreclose based on both a failure to make payments and to timely pay 
real estate taxes.  Id.  At trial, the defendant proved that the plaintiff had 
misapplied payments and no payments were missed .  See id.   But the 
evidence showed that the  defendant failed to timely pay the taxes.  Id.  
The trial court denied the foreclosure .  Id.  We reversed.  Id.  In reversing, 
we stated that "despite the court having found an improper application of 
payments, it was error to deny foreclosure on that basis since there was 
uncontradicted evidence of [the defendant 's] breach of the covenant to 
pay real estate taxes and assessments. "  Id. at 707 (citing Heimer v. 
Albion Realty & Mortg.  Inc., 300 So. 2d 31 (Fla. 3d DCA 1974) ). 
Here, the Bank alleged a continuing default  from January 2017 
forward .  The dispute at trial centered over the four reversed payments 
from 2015, ignoring the missed payments from June 2017 onwards.  
While the trial court found —and the record supports —that the 
Fernandezes paid and did not have returned the four 2015 payments, 
that result does not change the failure to pay every month from June 
2017 forward.  Each of those missed payments was a separate default  
that entitled the Bank to a foreclosure , and the trial court 's conclusion to 
the contrary is erroneous.  
C. 
 That brings us to whether there was a basis, equitable or 
otherwise, for the trial court to deny the Bank 's right to foreclose.  The 
 
7 
 final judgment itself does not state any legal  basis  on which the trial 
court relied .  That is not surprising  given neither party argued  any such 
basis with precision at trial.  What we are left with in the final judgment 
is a finding  that "Defendants ['] May 2017 payment was returned by the 
Plaintiff, and subsequent attempts to pay directly at the servicer, Bank of 
America, were not accepted after May 2017. "  Those facts alone do not 
excuse the subsequent defaults by the Fernandezes.  It was only after the 
trial court entered final judgment that  various defenses and equitable 
principles were raised by the Bank in its motion for rehearing  to the trial 
court .  The trial court denied the Bank 's motion for rehearing without 
any analysis . 
 We have recognized that foreclosure can be refused by a trial court 
where (1) the mortgagee waives or is estopped from accelerating because 
of misconduct or unfulfilled conditions , (2) the mortgagor tenders 
payment after default but before acceleration, or (3) the mortgagor 's 
failure to make timely payments was stopped by a misunderstanding or 
excusable neglect coupled with some misconduct by the mortgagee which 
contributed to the default.  Lunn Woods , 577 So. 2d at 707 (citing 
Campbell v. Werner , 232 So. 2d 252 (Fla. 3d DCA 1970)) ; see also David 
v. Sun Fed. Sav. & Loan Ass 'n, 461 So. 2d 93, 9 6 (Fla. 1984) (refusing to 
prevent a foreclosure without one of those three "established principle s of 
equity " being proven) .  While not clearly  under either the Fernandezes ' 
second affirmative defense or the trial court 's findings, the second and 
third equitable principle s above  are close enough to both to cause us to 
analyze whether either was proven.  
1. 
 First, as to the second equitable principle from Lunn Woods , that 
defense  is a tender of payment defense.  See Delandro v. America 's Mortg. 
 
8 
 Servicing, Inc. , 674 So. 2d 184, 186 -87 (Fla. 3d DCA 1996).  Almost one 
hundred years ago, the Supreme Court of Florida stated:  
'Tender ' has a definite legal signification.  It imports not 
merely the readiness and ability to pay the money or to 
deliver the deed or other property, at the time and place 
mentioned in the contract, but also the actual 
production of the thing to be paid or delivered and an 
offer of it to the person  to whom the tender is to be 
made.  
Kreiss Potassium Phosphate Co. v. Knight , 124 So. 751, 754 (Fla. 1929)  
(citing Holmes v. Holmes , 12 Barb. 137, 144  (N.Y. Gen. Term  1851)) .  The 
court continued and specified that a  party asserting such a  defense had 
to deposit the money in the registry of the court for the defense to be 
successful.1  Id. at 755; see also Rissman ex rel. Rissman Inv. Co. v. 
Kilbourne , 643 So.  2d 1136, 1140 -41 (Fla. 1st DCA 1994) (requiring 
actual attempt to deliver money for a tender of payment to occur).   While 
we doubt  whether Knight 's requirement of  a deposit in the registry of the 
court is the only way to be successful on such a defense, the facts in this 
case are clear .  The Fernandezes neither offered to pay their unpaid 
mortgage payment s into the court 's registry nor did they have in their 
possession the amount due under the mortgage when th is suit  was 
initiated.   Accordingly, the defense of tender of payment fails and does 
not excuse the Fernandezes ' missed mortgage payments.    
 
1 The Bank claims that the Fernandezes waived t ender of payment 
as a defense.  The Fernandezes point to their second affirmative defense 
and counter that the Bank waived their failure to deposit monies by 
failing to plead an avoidance in their reply or otherwise timely raising it 
during trial.  The second affirmative defense was styled "UNCLEAN 
HANDS ," not "TENDER OF PAYMENT ."  But the second defense did 
mention a tender by the Fernandezes.  We decline to find either party 
waived or failed to preserve this issue and, instead, resolve the issue on 
the merits of the defense .  
 
9 
 2. 
 Second, as  to the third  equitable principle from Lunn Woods , that 
equitable principle resembles or is the defense of unclean hands.  See 
Proino Breakfast Club, II, Inc. v. OGI Cap. , Inc., 331 So. 3d 846, 848 (Fla. 
2d DCA 2021).  In Proino , we stated that the equitable defense of unclean 
hands is designed to prevent a party from engaging in misconduct "akin 
to fraud " and "its 'purpose is to discourage unlawful activity. ' "  Id. 
(quoting Cong. Park Off. Condos II, LLC v. First -Citizens Bank & Tr. Co. , 
105 So. 3d 602, 609 (Fla. 4th DCA 2013)).  To be a defense, we also 
stated that the party 's misconduct "must generally be connected with the 
matter in litigation and must affect the adverse party. "  Id. (quoting 
McCollem v. Chidnese , 832 So. 2d 194, 196 (Fla. 4th DCA 2002) ).   
Turning first to case law  from this district, i n Proino , we concluded 
that allegations regarding a breach of a promise to sell a restaurant and 
apply th ose sales proceeds to a loan  were legally sufficient to support an 
affirmative defense of unclean hands and defeat ed a motion for summary 
judgment.2  Id.  Similarly, i n Perry v. Turner , we concluded that unclean 
hands prevented an equitable cause of action.  365 So. 3d 1222, 1225 
(Fla. 2d DCA 2023).  In Perry , Perry fraudulent ly concealed his assets 
with his girlfriend for years to hinder his creditors and ex -wife from 
recover ing from him.  Id. at 122 3-24.  When the girlfriend and Perry 
broke up, Perry sought to recover his secreted assets from the girlfriend.  
 
2 In Proino , we cited with approval to the Fourth District 's case in 
Marin v. Seven of Five Ltd. , 921 So. 2d 699, 700 -01 (Fla. 4 th DCA 2006).  
Id.  Marin  involved a mortgage foreclosure based on a failure to make 
payments where the borrower alleged that the lender agreed to refinance 
the obligation and later reneged.  921 So. 2d at 700.   The Fourth District 
reversed summary judgment because it found those allegations  sufficient 
to state a defense of unclean hands and unre butted on summary 
judgment.  Id. at 700 -01. 
 
10 
 Id.  We affirmed a final judgment against Perry after a nonjury trial that 
concluded unclean hands denied Perry 's equitable cause of action.  Id. at 
1224 -25.  In affirming, we stated that unclean hands prevents someone 
from "profit[ing] from his own fraud or wrongdoing. "  Id. at 1224  (quoting 
Leila Corp. of St. Pete v. Ossi , 138 So. 3d 470, 473 (Fla. 2d DCA 2014)) . 
Turning next to mortgage foreclosure related case s, the First 
District reversed a final judgment for a borrower entered after a nonjury 
trial based on an unclean hands  defense .  U.S. Bank Nat 'l Ass 'n as Tr. for 
C-Bass Mortg . Loan Asset -Backed Certificates, Series 2006 -CB8 v. Qadir , 
342 So. 3d 855, 859 (Fla. 1st DCA 2022).  In reversing th at final 
judgment, the First District, in part, stated that there was no evidence 
that the bank had acted in a "sneaky, unscrupulous, or tricky " manner.  
Id.  As the court commented,  the defense only bars an equitable claim 
when "the plaintiff has engaged in some manner of unscrupulous 
conduct, overreaching, or trickery that would be 'condemned by honest 
and reasonable men. ' "  Id. (quotin g 21st Mortg. Corp. v. TSE Plantation, 
LLC, 301 So. 3d 1120, 1122 (Fla. 1st DCA 2020) ).  Similarly, i n Cong ress 
Park Off ice Condos II, LLC , the Fourth District affirmed a summary 
judgment of foreclosure  in favor of a lender .  105 So. 3d at 610.  As part 
of affirming that summary judgment, the Fourth District considered 
whether an unclean hands affirmative defense prevented foreclosure.  Id. 
at 609 -10.  In that case, the borrower had "intentional[ly] fail[ed] to 
comply with material terms of the mortgage and note. "  Id. at 610 
(alterations in original).  In rejecting the defense, the Fourth District 
stated , "A failure to comply with the material terms of a loan document 
may be a breach of contract, and it may not be nice, but it does not 
amount to  unclean  hands. "  Id. 
 
11 
 Here, the Fernandezes failed to present evidence of conduct 
amounting to fraud  or otherwise show that the Bank  (or its agents) acted 
in a "sneaky, unscrupulous, or tricky " manner.  See Qadir , 342 So. 3d at 
859.  Instead, the  Fernandezes  argue :  
[i]f the [Bank ] wanted to proceed with a working loan, 
they could have easily adjusted their accounting, 
modified the loan, adjusted the payments, negotiated to 
get some of the $20,000 the Fernandez 's [sic] had saved 
up and turned the loan right back into a performing 
loan.  The [Bank ] did nothing , but sit back for two more 
years and then bring the foreclosure at issue here.   
Those allegations do not even rise to the level of violating the loan  
documents, which is insufficient to state an unclean hands defense .  See 
Cong. Park Off. Condos II, LLC , 105 So. 3d at 610.   The Bank did not 
have a duty to reach out to the Fernandezes or offer to modify their loan.  
There is nothing in the record showing the Bank affirmatively doing 
anything but proceeding forward toward foreclosure based on their 
position on the four reversed payments.  We in no way condone how 
Bank of America  or the Bank prosecuted this action or  treated the 
Fernandezes .  We  do not believe that many of the decisions made here 
were particularly  wise or prudent .  But w e conclude that not being "nice" 
or doing what we consider to be  unwise or imprudent is insufficient to 
prove that the Bank acted with unclean hands . 
III. 
 While we reverse the trial court 's judgment and remand the case to 
the trial court to act consistent with this opinion, we are not 
unsympathetic to the situation that the Fernandezes find themselves in.  
The Fernandezes still have options to retain their home.  Under Florida 
law, the Ferna ndezes have the ability or possibility of redeeming the 
indebtedness.  See § 45.0315, Fla. Stat. (2026).  Alternatively, there may 
 
12 
 be options under federal law that would allow the Fernandezes to cure 
their indebtedness over time.   See, e.g. , 11 U.S.C. § 1301.   Both or any 
other possibilit ies exceed  this opinion and are ultimately up to the 
Fernandezes  to pursue .  
Reversed and remanded . 
 
SILBERMAN , J., Dissents with opinion . 
ATKINSON, J., Concurs in  result only.  
 
 
 
 
SILBERMAN, Judge, Dissenting . 
I would affirm the final judgment in the Fernandezes' favor because 
competent, substantial evidence supports the trial court's findings and 
conclusions.  As has long been established, "[i]t is not the function of the 
appellate court to substitute its judgm ent for that of the trial court 
through re -evaluation of the testimony and evidence from the record on 
appeal before it.  The test . . . is whether the judgment of the trial court 
is supported by competent evidence."  Shaw v. Shaw , 334 So. 2d 13, 16 
(Fla. 1976); see also  Kuhnsman v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. , 311 So. 3d 
980, 984 (Fla. 2d DCA 2020) (" [W]e review the trial court's findings of 
facts to determine if they are supported by competent substantial 
evidence ." (quoting Coconut Grove Acquisition, LLC v. S & C. Venture , 240 
So. 3d 92, 94 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018)) ).  Therefore, I respectfully dissent.  
The trial court made the following findings, all of which are 
supported by the record evidence:  
2. The Court finds that the Plaintiff failed to meet their 
burden to show that the Defendants breached the Note and 
Mortgage contract.  
 
 
13 
 3. The Court finds that as of the Plaintiff's alleged default date 
of January 1, 2017, the accounting showed that the 
Defendants made on time payments as required under the 
contract, but there were transactions reported which showed 
a reversal of four paym ents occurring on August 21, 2015. 
The Plaintiff's representative failed to provide any explanation 
as to the reason for the reversals or any explanation that 
would indicate the reversals were caused due to a contractual 
default by the Defendants. The Plai ntiff's witness couldn't give 
competent testimony as to why those reversals occurred.  
 
4. The Court finds that the Defendant, Mrs. Fernandez, was 
credible in her testimony as to the payments she made on a 
monthly basis in accordance with the Note and Mortgage 
contract from January 2015 until April of 2017.  Defendants  
[sic] May 2017 payment was returned by the Plaintiff, and 
subsequent attempts to pay directly at the servicer, Bank of 
America, were not accepted after May 2017.  
At trial, the evidence established that the Bank had reversed four 
payments that it had accepted and that were made by the Fernandezes 
from January through April 2015.  In August 2016, the Fernandezes 
received a letter from the then servicer, Bank of Ameri ca, indicating that 
they were in arrears by four payments, which apparently related back to 
the four payments that had been reversed.3 
Neither the Bank's witness nor its records explained the reason for 
the reversal of payments or whether the Bank had retained the funds 
represented by those payments.  But the evidence established that the 
Bank continued to accept and retain payments from the Fernandezes 
until they made the May 2017 payment.  After its acceptance of that 
payment, the Bank wrote a check and returned the funds from that 
payment and then rejected the Fernandezes' subsequent efforts to make 
monthly payments.  
 
3 Four different companies had serviced the loan during the time 
period giving rise to this dispute.  
 
14 
 In its complaint, the Bank asserted that the loan was in default 
because "the payment due January 1, 2017, and all subsequent 
payments have not been made."  Yet the evidence established that 
payments had been made through the May 2017 payment that the Bank  
initially accepted but then returned , and the Bank then refused further 
payments.    
As the majority notes, the Bank's witness could not explain why the 
early 2015 payments were reversed beyond offering unsubstantiated 
speculation.  The trial court rejected the witness's speculative testimony 
as well as his inability to establish that the reversals were due to any 
default by the Fernandezes.  Instead, the court found that Ms. 
Fernandez 's testimony was credible, including her testimony that all 
required payments had been made until the Bank returned the May 
2017 payment and then rejected the Ferdandezes' subsequent efforts to 
make payments.  
Although the Bank argues that the trial court erred in accepting 
the testimony of Ms. Fernandez, the law is clear that credibility 
determinations are the province of the trial court.  Shaw , 334 So. 2d at 
16.  The Bank properly recognizes that the burden of proof at trial in a 
civil case is the preponderance of the evidence standard.  See S. Fla. 
Water Mgmt. Dist. v. RLI Live Oak, LLC , 139 So. 3d 869, 872 (Fla. 2014).  
Yet the Bank challenges the trial court's findings and, in essence, argues 
that the evidence it offered should have been accepted over the 
Fernandezes' contrary evidence.  On that basis, it contends that the trial 
court erred in concluding that the Bank failed to carry its burden to 
establish that the Fernandezes breached their loan obligations.  
Foreclosure proceedings are equitable in nature, and "[a] court of 
equity may refuse to foreclose a mortgage when an acceleration of the 
 
15 
 due date of the debt would be an inequitable or unjust result and the 
circumstances would render the acceleration unconscionable."  Campbell 
v. Werner , 232 So. 2d 252, 256 (Fla. 3d DCA 1970) (quoting Althouse v. 
Kenney , 182 So. 2d 270, 272 (Fla. 2d DCA 1966) ); see also  Ivy Chase 
Apartment Prop., LLC v. Ivy Chase Apartments, Ltd. , 352 So. 3d 33, 43 
(Fla. 2d DCA 2022) (reiterating that foreclosure may be denied on 
equitable considerations such as unclean hands or unconscionability).   
Here, the Bank failed to establish the reason for its reversal of the 
early 2015 payments.  Although it claimed the account was in default 
when it filed suit, at trial it failed to establish that, in fact, a default 
existed through some fault of the Fernan dezes.  Based on the record 
evidence, the purported default appears to have been created based on 
the Bank's own conduct or actions taken by its loan servicers.  And to 
the extent the Bank claims a continuing default based on its rejection of 
the May 2017 payment and the Fernandezes' subsequent efforts to make 
payment, the record supports the view that it was the Bank's actions 
that put the loan into a default posture and kept the loan in that 
posture.  The majority misses the point when it holds that "the Bank's 
failure to accept the May 2017 payment did not excuse the Fernandezes 
from their ongoing obligations under the note and mortgage."  As 
explained above, it was the Bank 's conduct that created the ongoing 
purported default.   
Finally, as the majority opinion correctly points out, the Bank did 
not raise any issue with the trial court before or at trial regarding any 
obligation on the Fernandezes to tender funds into the court 's registry.    
Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.600 states as follows:  
In an action in which any part of the relief sought is a 
judgment for a sum of money or the disposition of a sum of 
money or the disposition of any other thing capable of 
 
16 
 delivery, a party may deposit all or any part of such sum or 
thing with the court upon notice to every other party and by 
leave of court.  
(Emphasis added .)4  See First States Invs . 3300, LLC v. Pheil , 52 So.  3d 
845, 848 (Fla. 2d DCA 2011) (concluding that rule 1.600 is voluntary in 
nature and noting that a hearing may be required to "resolve the issue of 
what monies were properly subject to being deposited into the court 
registry "); Morroni v. Fisher , 647 So. 2d 127, 129 (Fla. 2d DCA 1994) 
("Nothing in rule 1.600 authorizes a trial court to require a mortgagor to 
deposit mortgage payments into the court's registry."  (first citing Hughes 
v. First Fed . Sav. & Loan Ass'n , 621 So.  2d 557 (Fla. 4th DCA 1993); and 
then citing Law v. NCNB Nat 'l Bank of Fla. , 452 So.  2d 1119 (Fla. 4th 
DCA 1984) , superseded by statute on other grounds , § 697.07, Fla . Stat. 
(1989) , as recognized in  Williams v. First Union Nat 'l Bank of Fla ., 591 So. 
2d 1137 (Fla. 4th DCA 1992) )).  Under all the circumstances present in 
this case, the Bank's failure to timely raise this issue at or before trial 
precludes relief as to the issue.    
In sum, I find no fault with the trial court 's determination that the 
Bank failed to carry its burden that the Fernandezes defaulted on their 
loan obligations.  Accordingly, I would affirm the final judgment.  
 
 
Opinion subject to revision prior to official publication.  
 
4 The Florida Supreme Court adopted rule 1.600 in 1967, well after 
Kreiss Potassium Phosphate Co. v. Knight , 124 So. 751 (Fla. 1929) , was 
decided.

items.summary:
In a mortgage foreclosure, a borrower who has admittedly stopped making any accepted payment after a given month cannot defeat the lender's prima facie case merely by disputing an earlier, separate payment accounting or by pointing to the lender's later refusal to accept a payment; absent a recognized equitable defense—an actual tender of payment into the registry or lender misconduct akin to fraud—the lender is entitled to foreclosure, although on remand the judgment must be adjusted to exclude the disputed reversed payments and the related pre-default interest and fees.

Holding: A foreclosing lender must prove an agreement, a default, a proper acceleration, and the amount owed or due, and each missed monthly payment is a separate default. Where the undisputed evidence shows the borrowers made no accepted payment after a given month, legally sufficient (competent substantial) evidence of default exists even if an earlier disputed accounting for reversed payments is unresolved. A lender's refusal to accept a tendered payment does not excuse the borrower's continuing obligation to pay, and a court may deny foreclosure only on one of three established equitable principles: waiver or estoppel to accelerate based on the lender's misconduct or unfulfilled conditions; tender of payment made after default but before acceleration; or the borrower's failure to pay caused by a misunderstanding or excusable neglect coupled with mortgagee misconduct contributing to the default. A tender-of-payment defense requires actually producing and offering the funds (historically by deposit into the registry of the court), not mere readiness or ability to pay; and the unclean-hands defense requires misconduct akin to fraud—sneaky, unscrupulous, or tricky conduct generally connected with the matter in litigation—so a lender's breach of the loan terms, refusal to modify the loan, or merely unwise or unkind conduct is insufficient.

Disposition: Reversed and remanded

Author: Judge Guard

Supreme Court of Florida  
 
THURSDAY, OCTOBER 29, 2026  
 
Svyatoslav Mangushev,  
                    Petitioner(s)  
v. 
 
Alpha Team, LLC,  
                    Respondent(s)  
 SC2025 -1262  
Lower Tribunal No(s).:   
  4D2025 -2201;  
062017CA000351AXXXCE  
 
The “Petition for Writ of Certiorari ” is hereby treated as a 
petition to invoke all writs jurisdiction and is dismissed for lack of 
jurisdiction because Petitioner has failed to cite an independent basis that would allow the Court to exercise its all writs authority, 
and no such basis is apparent on the face of the petition.  See Williams v. State , 913 So. 2d 541, 543 -44 (Fla. 2005); St. Paul Title 
Ins. Corp. v. Davis, 392 So. 2d 1304, 1305 (Fla. 1980).  
No motion for rehearing will be considered by this Court.  
COURIEL,  C.J., and LABARGA, MUÑIZ, GROSSHANS, and 
FRANCIS,
 JJ., concur. 
BARRIOS, J., concurs in result.  
TANENBAUM, J., concurs in result with an opinion.  
 
TANENBAUM, J., concurring in result.  
 
The petitioner seeks review of a final order.  This court initially 
CASE NO.:  SC2025-1262 
Page Two 
 
   
 treated his petition for certiorari properly as a notice to invoke this 
court’s review jurisdiction.  We clearly do not have jurisdiction, and 
we could dismiss on that basis alone.  See Art. V, §  3(b), Fla. Const. 
(setting out various bases on which we can exercise discretionary 
review jurisdiction).  Simple and easy.  
So it is bewildering that the court would go through the 
academic exercise of then treating the petition as one invoking “all writs jurisdiction,” only to state that no basis for doing so appears on the face of the petition.  There are two problems with this  
approach.  
Most importantly, there is no such thing as “all writs 
jurisdiction” at all, and it makes no sense to re- characterize the 
petition as invoking such non -existent jurisdiction.  The Florida 
Constitution authorizes this court to issue, among other things, “al l 
writs necessary to the complete exercise of  its jurisdiction .”  Art. V, 
§ 3(b)(7), Fla. Const. (emphasis supplied).  This means that the 
court must first have a basis under section 3(b)(1) through (6) to exercise jurisdiction, and if it does, then it may issue one or more 
CASE NO.:  SC2025-1262 
Page Three 
 
   
 specified writs necessary to preserve that jurisdiction.  Again, 
nothing in section 3(b)(1) through (6) provides the necessary 
underlying authority to permit the review the petitioner is seeking 
here, so there is no jurisdiction to be preserved.  That should be the 
end of the matter.  
Additionally, there is no separate bag of remedies called “all 
writs” available for the asking.  Unless the petitioner is seeking one of the four prerogative writs listed in section 3(b) ( e.g., mandamus, 
prohibition, quo warranto, or habeas) —and he is not —it is 
incumbent on the petitioner to specify the one of over a hundred common -law writs historically available in England that he is 
seeking to preserve this court’s otherwise extant jurisdict ion.  See 
Antiquities of the Law , 1 A
LB. L.J. 247, 247 (1870) (listing and 
describing many such writs).  The petitioner here asks for certiorari review.  A writ of certiorari is one of those many ancient writs that we could issue under the proper circumstances ( viz.: when 
necessary to review a non -final order causing irreparable harm in a 
matter where we will have direct appellate jurisdiction over the 
CASE NO.:  SC2025-1262 
Page Four 
 
   
 
eventual final order).  Those circumstances, however, are not 
present in this case.  
Dismissal, of course, is the proper disposition.  The order 
dismissing this cause, however, does more work than is necessary —
in a constitutionally inaccurate way and in pursuit of no apparent meaningful end.  
A True Copy

items.summary:
A litigant cannot secure Florida Supreme Court review of a civil case by recasting a certiorari petition as invoking 'all writs' jurisdiction without an independent jurisdictional basis; the Court dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. Issued October 29, 2026, within the October 26-November 8, 2026 window.

Holding: The Court treated the 'Petition for Writ of Certiorari' as a petition to invoke all-writs jurisdiction and dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because the petitioner failed to cite, and the petition did not disclose on its face, an independent basis permitting the Court to exercise all-writs authority; the order states that no motion for rehearing will be considered. Concurring in result, Justice Tanenbaum reasoned that article V, section 3(b)(7) authorizes writs only as necessary to the complete exercise of existing jurisdiction, so an independent basis under article V, section 3(b)(1)-(6) must exist first and there is no freestanding 'all writs jurisdiction'; his reasoning is a concurrence in result, not the per curiam holding.

Disposition: Petition (treated as invoking all-writs jurisdiction) dismissed for lack of jurisdiction; the order states no motion for rehearing will be considered. The status metadata separately records "affirmed," which does not fit a jurisdictional dismissal of a petition; preserved without deciding.

DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA  
FOURTH DISTRICT  
 
LOUISE HADDAD, 
Appellant, 
 
v. 
 
LYFT FLORIDA, INC., et al., 
Appellees. 
 
No. 4D2025-0117 
 
[November 4, 2026] 
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit, 
Broward County; David Alan Haimes, Judge; L.T. Case No. 
062023CA007025AXXXCE. 
 
John S. Mills and Jonathan A. Martin of The Mills Firm, P.A., 
Jacksonville, for appellant. 
 
Andrew A. Harris of Harris Appeals, P.A., Palm Beach Gardens, David 
J. Sales of Barnes Trial Group, Tampa, and Blair M. Fazzio of Kanner & 
Pintaluga, Boca Raton, for Amicus Curiae Florida Justice Association, in 
support of appellant’s motion for rehearing, rehearing en banc, and 
certification. 
 
Brigid F. Cech Samole, James E. Gillenwater, and Bethany J. M. 
Pandher of Greenberg Traurig, P.A., Miami, for appellees. 
 
ON MOTION FOR REHEARING, REHEARING EN BANC, AND 
CERTIFICATION 
LOTT, J. 
 
We grant Appellant’s motion for rehearing, deny her motions for 
rehearing en banc and certification, withdraw our prior opinion in Haddad 
v. Lyft Florida, Inc., 51 Fla. L. Weekly D986 (Fla. 4th DCA May 13, 2026), and substitute this opinion in its place.  We also grant Florida Justice 
Association’s motion for leave to file an amicus brief in support of 
Appellant’s motion for rehearing, rehearing en banc, and certification, and 
accept its proposed amicus brief as filed. 
2 
 Louise Haddad claims she was assaulted by her Lyft driver.  She sued 
Lyft for negligent and fraudulent misrepresentation, alleging that 
statements on its website led her to believe that the ride would be safe, 
thus leading to the personal injuries she suffered at the hands of the 
driver. 
The merits of her claims are not before us .  Instead, Lyft argued that a 
relatively new statutory provision, section 627.748(18), Florida Statutes 
(2022) (“Subsection 18”), provides it with immunity against her claims.  The 
trial court agreed and dismissed the complaint.   
Haddad appealed, arguing that Subsection 18’s scope of immunity is 
not so broad as to cover her claims, which specifically allege that Lyft’s 
own negligence caused her injuries. 
With the benefit of oral argument, we affirm.  The scope of immunity 
provided by Subsection 18’s plain text is very broad.  It appears to sweep 
in practically any claim against Lyft (or a similar rideshare network 
operator) for injury that arises out of the use, operation, or possession of 
a motor vehicle operating as a rideshare, regardless of how Lyft may have 
directly caused or contributed to the injury—so long as Lyft otherwise 
complies with the requirements of the rideshare statute (Section 627.748) 
and does not engage in criminal conduct. 
Whether the legislators who voted on the text of the statute actually 
intended to confer such broad immunity is immaterial.1  Whether it is wise 
 
1 “Judges interpret laws rather than reconstruct legislators’ intentions.”  I.N.S. v. 
Cardoza -Fonseca , 480 U.S. 421, 452 –53 (1987) (Scalia, J., concurring); s ee also 
Advisory Op. to the Governor re Implementation of Amend . 4, The Voting 
Restoration Amend ., 288 So. 3d 1070, 1078 (Fla. 2020) (“[S ]uch extraneous 
considerations [i.e., legislative intent]  can result in the judicial imposition of 
meaning that the text cannot bear, either through expansion or contraction of 
the meaning carried by the text. ”); Antonin  Scalia & B ryan A. Garner, Reading 
Law: The Interpretation of Legal Texts  393 (2012) (“Each member voting for the 
bill has a slightly different reason for doing so.  There is no single set of intentions shared by all.  The state of the assembly’s collecting psychology is a hopeless 
stew of intentions  . . . [y] et the majority has undeniably agreed on the final 
language that passes into law.  That is all they have agreed on —and that is the 
sole means by which the assembly has authority to make law.” ).  
 
3 
 to confer such broad immunity is not a question for this branch to 
answer.2   
Rather, our job is to discern what the text says.3  And this text says 
that the immunity provided by Subsection 18 is considerably broad.   
I. Background 
A. Factual Allegations 
Haddad alleges that she took a Lyft ride on April 15, 2022.4  She claims 
that during her ride, the driver assaulted her, causing severe and 
permanent personal injuries. 
 
Lyft Florida, Inc. is a transportation network company (“TNC”) that uses 
a digital network to connect riders with drivers who provide prearranged transportation services. 
 
2 See, e.g., DeSantis v. Fla. Educ. Ass ’n, 306 So. 3d 1202, 1218 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2020) (“[T]he judiciary may not second guess the policy decisions of the political 
branches, no matter how appealing we may find contrary rationales.” (citation 
and quotations omitted )); Loper Bright Enters.  v. Raimondo , 603 U.S. 369, 403 
(2024) (“Courts interpret statutes, no matter the context, based on the traditional 
tools of statutory construction, not individual policy preferences.”) ; State v. 
Burris , 875 So.  2d 408, 414 n.2 (Fla. 2004)  (“If the legislature did not intend the 
results mandated by the statute’ s plain language, then the appropriate remedy 
is for it to amend the statute .” (quoting Overstreet v. State,  629 So. 2d  125, 126  
(Fla. 1993)) ). 
 
3 See, e.g., Lab. Corp. of Am. v. Davis , 339 So. 3d 318, 323 (Fla. 2022) (“In 
interpreting a statute, our task is to give effect to the words that the legislature 
has employed in the statutory text.”); Levy v. Levy , 326 So. 3d 678, 681 (Fla. 
2021) (“We strive to determine the text ’s objective meaning through the 
application of the text to given facts on the basis of how a reasonable reader, fully 
competent in the language, would have understood the text at the time it was 
issued.” (cleaned up) ); see also Homeowner ’s Choice Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. v. 
Oakes , 431 So.  3d 1005 , 1014 n.2  (Fla. 4th DCA 2026)  (“[I]t is emphatically the 
province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” (quoting 
Marbury v. Madison , 5 U.S. 137, 177 (1803)) ). 
 
4 “A motion to dismiss tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint and does not 
determine factual issues.   All allegations of the complaint must be taken as true 
and all reasonable inferences drawn therefrom must be construed in favor of the 
non-moving party.”  Doe v. Finkelman , 429 So. 3d 456, 469 (Fla. 4th DCA 2025)  
(citations and quotations  omitted).  
 
4 
  
Lyft advertises various rider-safety features, including “High safety 
standards” and “Proactive safety measures,” and represents that its 
drivers must pass background checks, undergo annual re-screening, be 
continuously monitored for criminal convictions, and complete a safety 
program.  Haddad alleges she reviewed Lyft’s website and relied on these 
representations in deciding to use Lyft’s services.   
 Haddad filed suit in 2022.  Haddad’s second amended complaint 
asserted three counts: negligence of the driver, and both negligent 
misrepresentation and fraudulent misrepresentation by Lyft.
5  The claims 
against Lyft alleged the company made false or misleading safety 
representations, Haddad relied on those representations in agreeing to the 
ride, and her injuries resulted from that reliance.   
Lyft moved to dismiss based on Subsection 18. 
B. Statutory Framework 
Section 627.748 was enacted in 2017 as part of a comprehensive 
framework governing transportation network companies.  In 2020, the legislature made several changes to the provision, including the addition 
of Subsection 18.  Section 627.748(18), Florida Statutes (2022), provides: 
Vicarious liability.— 
 
(a) A TNC is not liable under general law by reason of owning, 
operating, or maintaining the digital network accessed by a 
TNC driver or rider, or by being the TNC affiliated with a TNC 
driver, for harm to persons or property which results or arises 
out of the use, operation, or possession of a motor vehicle 
operating as a TNC vehicle while the driver is logged on to the 
digital network if: 
 
1. There is no negligence under this section or criminal 
wrongdoing under the federal or Florida criminal code on the 
part of the TNC; 
 
2. The TNC has fulfilled all of its obligations under this 
section with respect to the TNC driver; and 
 
 
5 The claims against the driver are not pertinent to this appeal.  
5 
 3. The TNC is not the owner or bailee of the motor vehicle 
that caused harm to persons or property. 
 
(b) This subsection does not alter or reduce the coverage or 
policy limits of the insurance requirements under subsection 
(7) or the liability of any person other than the vicarious 
liability of a TNC as described in paragraph (a). 
We note that this structure parallels the federal Graves Amendment, 
49 U.S.C. § 30106 ( 2022), enacted in 2005, which preempts state laws 
imposing vicarious liability on vehicle owners engaged in the business of 
renting or leasing motor vehicles.  Cf. Seagrave v. State, 802 So. 2d 281, 
290 (Fla. 2001) (“Florida’s well-settled rule of statutory construction [is] that the legislature is presumed to know the existing law when a statute 
is enacted . . . .”).  The Graves Amendment provides that such owners are 
not liable under state law solely by reason of ownership for harm arising 
from the use of the vehicle during the rental period, so long as the owner 
is not negligent or engaged in criminal wrongdoing. 
C. Procedural History  
Haddad opposed Lyft’s motion to dismiss, arguing that her claims were 
not barred because her claims were premised on Lyft’s own alleged 
misrepresentations rather than vicarious liability for the driver’s conduct.   
The trial court granted the motion, concluding the complaint failed to 
allege facts bringing the claims within any exception to Subsection 18’s 
default rule of nonliability.  This appeal followed. 
II. Analysis 
Haddad makes three arguments—two textual and one procedural—that 
her claims for negligent and fraudulent misrepresentation are not barred 
by Subsection 18.  We address and reject each.6 
 
6 The standard of review of an order granting a motion to dismiss is de novo.  
Aquarius Condo. Ass’n, Inc. v. Goldberg , 312 So. 3d 86, 87 (Fla. 4th DCA 2021).  
 
6 
 A. Subsection 18 immunity is broader than traditional vicarious 
liability. 
Haddad argues that Subsection 18 is not applicable to her claims 
because Subsection 18 only bars traditional “vicarious” liability by TNCs.7   
But that is simply not what Subsection 18 says. 
To be sure, Subsection 18 is titled “vicarious liability.”  But as Lyft 
correctly counters, “[t]he title of a statute and the heading of a section 
cannot limit the plain meaning of the text.”  Brooks v. Brooks, 164 So. 3d 
162, 164 (Fla. 2d DCA 2015) (citation omitted).  Instead, any title “must 
be read in conjunction with and does not override the text of the statute.”   
Id. (citing Fla. Dep’t of Revenue v. Piccadilly Cafeterias, Inc., 554 U.S. 33, 
47 (2008)). Courts should attempt to harmonize a header with the 
statutory text to the extent possible, but “[w]here statutory text and title 
are inconsistent, we go with the text.”  Kanapuram v. Dir., U.S. Citizenship 
& Immigr. Servs., 131 F.4th 1302, 1308 (11th Cir. 2025) (cleaned up) 
(quoting Bhd. of R.R. Trainmen v. Balt. & O. R. Co., 331 U.S. 519, 528–29 
(1947)).  “[A] title or heading should never be allowed to override the plain 
words of a text.”  Antonin Scalia & Bryan A. Garner, Reading Law: The 
Interpretation of Legal Texts 185 (2012).8 
Subsection 18’s plain text makes clear that the immunity conferred is 
much broader than traditional vicarious liability.  Breaking it down, 
Subsection 18’s operative provision provides that a TNC is:  
(1) not liable under general law;  
 
7 Cf., e.g ., Am. Home Assur. Co. v. Nat’l R.R. Passenger Corp. , 908 So. 2d 459, 467 
(Fla. 2005) (“The concept of vicarious liability can be described as follows: A 
person whose liability is imputed based on the tortious acts of another is liable 
for the entire share of comparative responsibility assigned to the other .” (citation  
omitted) ). 
8 Haddad argues that Subsection 18(b) affirms a traditional understanding of 
vicarious liability.   Subsection 18(b)  provides that “ [t]his subsection does not alter 
or reduce the coverage or policy limits of the insurance requirements under subsection (7) or the liability of any person other than the vicarious liability of a 
TNC as described in paragraph (a).”  But the mere  reference to “the vicarious 
liability of a TNC as described in paragraph (a)” does no more work than Subsection 18’s title. 
7 
 (2) by reason of owning, operating, or maintaining the digital 
network accessed by a TNC driver or rider, or by being the 
TNC affiliated with a TNC driver;  
(3) for harm to persons or property which results or arises 
out of the use, operation, or possession of a motor vehicle 
operating as a TNC vehicle while the driver is logged onto the 
digital network . . . 
In other words, this immunity is broad, applying to all claims “under 
general law.”   
And this broad immunity extends to any claim based upon (“by reason 
of”) Lyft “owning, operating, or maintaining” its network, or “being” 
affiliated with the driver.  That language is far broader than traditional 
vicarious liability, and applies to cases in which Lyft’s network affiliation 
with the driver is a but-for causal element of Lyft’s alleged liability.  See, 
e.g., Burrage v. United States, 571 U.S. 204, 213 (2014) (collecting 
authority wherein “the phrase, ‘by reason of,’ requires at least a showing 
of ‘but for’ causation” (citation omitted)). 
And Subsection 18 immunity extends to any claim for harm which 
“results or arises out of the use, operation, or possession of a motor 
vehicle” while the driver is logged into the platform.  Appellant did not 
argue in her initial brief (or reply brief)  that the trial court erred in holding 
that the injuries that she alleges were “harm to persons or property which 
results or arises out of the use, operation, or possession of a motor vehicle 
acting as a TNC vehicle while the driver was logged on the network.”  She 
has thus waived any argument to the contrary.  E.g., Hammond v. State, 
34 So. 3d 58, 59 (Fla. 4th DCA 2010) (“Claims for which an appellant has 
not presented any argument, or for which he provides only conclusory 
argument, are insufficiently presented for review and are waived.”). 
We accordingly assume, for the purposes of this case,  that her alleged 
injuries did arise out of the use, operation, or possession of a motor 
vehicle.  But to be clear, we are not passing on the question of whether her 
alleged injuries “ar[ose] out of the use, possession, or operation of a motor 
vehicle.”  We did not have the benefit of adversary briefing on that question, and accordingly, we leave that question for another day. 
Haddad brings negligent and fraudulent misrepresentation claims 
against Lyft for advertising misrepresentations that she claims caused her 
to take a Lyft ride and suffer harm when the driver assaulted her.   
8 
 These claims: (1) arise under “general law”; (2) causally relate Lyft’s 
alleged negligence (i.e., false representations regarding safety) to the harm 
suffered (i.e., personal injuries from the driver’s assault) via Lyft “owning, 
operating, or maintaining” the TNC network which the driver was logged 
into at the time; and (3) seek redress for injuries that arose out of the use, 
operation, or possession of the vehicle operating as a TNC vehicle while 
the driver was logged on to the network (or at least, we so assume). 
Accordingly, the claims fall within Subsection 18’s scope.  It does not 
matter that the complaint purports to plead negligence by Lyft rather than a traditional vicarious liability theory.  The statute is written to encompass 
her claims.
9   
B. The complaint does not allege “negligence under this 
section.” 
Haddad next argues that Subsection 18 immunity does not apply 
because she alleges “negligence under this section,” and the statute only 
affords immunity “if . . . [t]here is no negligence under this section.”  
§ 627.748(18)(a)1., Fla. Stat. (2022). 
Haddad argues that the phrase “negligence under this section,” as used 
in Subsection 18(a)1 ., means “related to Lyft’s operation of the digital TNC 
network,” because Section 627.748 generally concerns digital TNC 
networks.   
We disagree.   
Rather, the phrase “ negligence under this section” means “negligence 
under Section 627.748, Florida Statutes,” which plainly means a negligent 
failure to meet the statute’s requirements.  Section 627.748 provides a 
comprehensive set of requirements with which rideshare companies must 
comply.  Subsection 18 provides an immunity from certain liability so long 
as a TNC complies  with those requirements (and refrains from criminal 
wrongdoing).  Thus, “[a] TNC is not liable under general law . . . if . . . 
[t]here is no negligence under this section.” 
 
9 And in any event, Lyft’s alleged liability for the harm suffered at the hands of 
the driver is “indirect.”  Cf. Vicarious,  Black’s Law Dictionary (2026) (“Performed 
or suffered by one person as substitute for another; indirect; surrogate.”).  
 
9 
 We note also that the phrase “under this section,” does not appear in 
the Graves Amendment on which Subsection 18 was based, indicating a 
departure from the Graves Amendment’s meaning.  The Graves 
Amendment provides an exception to the general rule of non-liability 
“if . . . there is no negligence or criminal wrongdoing . . . .”  49 U.S.C. 
§ 30106(a)(2) (2022).  The Graves Amendment thus exempts from its 
operative non-liability provision any negligence, rather than only 
“negligence under this section.” 
Haddad argues that giving the phrase this meaning (as compared to 
her proposed meaning) would render Subsection 18(a)2.—which provides 
no liability if “[t]he TNC has fulfilled all of its obligations under this section 
with respect to the TNC driver”—superfluous.   
However, each canon of statutory construction is only one permissible 
indicator of meaning.  Sometimes different canons will cut different ways.  The fact that Subsection 18 is drafted in such a way that makes it 
impossible to cleanly apply every canon is a challenge that courts must 
confront, rather than an invitation to abdicate our interpretive role.
10  
Though Haddad argues that our interpretation would render 
Subsection 18(a)2. mostly superfluous,11 we note that her  interpretation  
(negligence “related to Lyft’s operation of the digital TNC network”) would 
also render the words “under this section” superfluous relative to the 
single word “negligence” in the Graves Amendment.  How else would a TNC 
network operator be negligent other than through its operation of a TNC 
network?   
Our goal in this exercise “is to arrive at a fair reading of the text by 
determining the application of the text to given facts on the basis of how a reasonable reader, fully competent in the language, would have understood the text at the time it was issued.”  Davis, 339 So. 3d at 323–
24 (cleaned up).   
 
10 See, e.g., Conage v. United States, 346 So. 3d 594, 598 (Fla. 2022) (“Viewed 
properly as rules of thumb or guides to interpretation, rather than as inflexible 
rules, the traditional canons of statutory interpretation can aid the interpretive 
process from beginning to end.”).  
  
11 Cf. Scalia & Garner,  Reading Law  at 176 –77 (“Put to a choice, however, a court 
may well prefer ordinary meaning to an unusual meaning that will avoid 
surplusage. . . . Sometimes drafts  do repeat themselves and  do include words 
that add nothing of substance . . . . ”). 
10 
 So, does “negligence under the section ,” as used in Subsection 18, 
mean “negligence with respect to the requirements of the section” or 
“negligence broadly related to the subject matter of this section”?   
Weighing all the indicia of meaning and giving effect to all the words in 
context, the former is the better reading. 
Thus, Haddad does not allege any “negligence under this section.” 
C. The trial court properly tested Subsection 18 immunity at 
the motion to dismiss stage. 
Haddad argues the trial court improperly applied the Subsection 18 
affirmative defense at the motion to dismiss stage.  As she argues, “[a]n 
affirmative defense is any matter that avoids the action and that, under 
applicable law, the plaintiff is not bound to prove initially but the 
defendant must affirmatively establish.”  Langford v. McCormick, 552 So. 
2d 964, 967 (Fla. 1st DCA 1989) (citation omitted).  And affirmative 
defenses “need not be negatived in the complaint.”  Avila S. Condo. Ass’n, 
Inc. v. Kappa Corp., 347 So. 2d 599, 604 (Fla. 1977).   
We address this argument last so the reader has a more fulsome 
understanding, given our previous discussion, of how Subsection 18 
operates.  With that understanding in mind, Subsection 18 immunity is 
not a traditional affirmative defense, but a broader immunity cutting to the core of a cause of action against a TNC. 
We see this from the emphatic opening language of the statute—“There 
is no liability . . . .”  This simply does not sound like an affirmative defense 
that the defendant is required to prove.  Cf. Custer Med. Ctr. v. United Auto. 
Ins. Co., 62 So. 3d 1086, 1096 (Fla. 2010) (“An affirmative defense is an assertion of facts or law by the defendant that, if true, would avoid the action and the plaintiff is not bound to prove that the affirmative defense 
does not exist.”); Katz v. Riemer, 305 So. 3d 663, 667 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020) 
(“[A]n affirmative defense is any matter that avoids the action and that the defendant must affirmatively establish.” (citation omitted)). 
11 
 And the legislature has not used the language, “there is no liability,” in 
the context of affirmative defenses.  Rather, it has used that language in 
the context of broader immunities.12   
While we recognize some precedent suggests that some immunities are 
affirmative defenses,13 we have not found any precedent recognizing an 
immunity with this statutory language—“There is no liability”—as an 
affirmative defense.  Based on Subsection 18’s plain language, the rule is 
immunity, and the inquiry otherwise stops if the operative conditions for 
immunity are satisfied.  The complaint needs to plead facts to overcome 
the immunity and background state of “no liability,” unlike the case with 
a traditional affirmative defense. 
Here, Subsection 18 is structured to establish a broad default rule of 
immunity, and Subsections (18)(a)1.–3. are exceptions to that general rule 
of immunity.  Subsection 18 begins with the broad statement that “[a] TNC 
 
12 See, e.g., § 408.910 (11)(e) , Fla. Stat. (2022) (“There is no liability on the part 
of, and no cause of action shall arise against, any member of the board or its 
employees or agents for any action taken . . . in the performance of their powers 
and duties under this section.”); § 847 .013(4)(d) , Fla. Stat. (2022) (“[T]here is no 
liability on the part of the state or the relator state attorney for costs or damages sustained by reason of such restraining order . . . .”); § 556.106 (1), Fla. Stat. 
(2022) (“There is no liability on the part of, and no cause of action of any nature 
shall arise against, the board members of the corporation . . . .”); § 631.918, Fla. 
Stat. (2022) (“There is no liability on the part of, and a cause of action  may not 
arise against, the corporation [and related actors] for any action taken . . . in the performance of their powers and duties under this section [.]”); § 111.09 (2)(c), (d) , 
Fla. Stat. (2022) (“There is no liability on the part of, and no cause of action of 
any nature may arise against, the first responder peer for disclosing information 
under this paragraph.”); § 651.034 (3), Fla. Stat. (2022) (“There is no liability on 
the part of, and a cause of action may not arise against, the commission, 
department, or office  . . . for any action they take . . . under this section.”); § 
627.351 (4)(c), Fla. Stat. (2022) (“There is no liability on the part of, and no cause 
of action shall arise against, [enumerated entities] for any action taken . . . in the 
performance of their powers and duties under this subsection.”).  
 
13 See, e.g. , Swope v. Krischer , 783 So. 2d 1164, 1166 n.1 (Fla. 4th DCA 2001)  
(“Although immunity is an affirmative defense  . . . .”); City of Delray Beach v. 
Sherman Williams Am. Legion, Post 188 , 358 So. 3d 440, 443 (Fla. 4th DCA 2023)  
(“[S]overeign immunity is generally an affirmative defense . . . .”); but see City of 
Miami v. Robinson , 364 So. 3d 1087, 1091 (Fla. 3d DCA 2023) (“ Much like subject 
matter jurisdiction, sovereign immunity isn ’t an affirmative defense, and it can 
be raised at any time. ”). 
 
12 
 is not liable under general law,” for certain types of claims (as discussed 
in Part II.A, above) “if” three conditions are met.  Indeed, t wo of these 
conditions are expressed in negative terms.14  The fact that these sub -
provisions are phrased as a positive conditional statement (“if”) followed 
by a negative condition (“not”), rather than a negative conditional 
statement (“unless”), does not convince us that these sub-provisions are 
not exceptions to the general rule of immunity which is clearly expressed 
at Subsection 18’s outset.  
This sort of construction is not unique.  Section 631.918 follows a 
similar pattern, providing that “there is no liability” for certain things 
“unless such action is found to be a violation of antitrust laws, was in bad 
faith, or was undertaken with malicious purpose or in a manner exhibiting 
wanton and willful disregard of human rights, safety, or property.”  
§ 631.918, Fla. Stat. (2022).  This language simply does not read like a  
traditional affirmative defense that survives a motion to dismiss even if the 
plaintiff does not plead an exception—a violation of antitrust laws, bad 
faith, etc.  And no court has suggested that such language is  an affirmative 
defense.  There, as here, the complaint must allege facts supporting an 
“exception” to overcome the general rule that “there is no liability.” 
In sum, Subsection 18’s plain language imposes a default rule of non -
liability unless certain exceptions are satisfied.  Other statutes using the 
same language do the same thing.  If Subsection 18’s operative conditions 
are satisfied,15 then in order to overcome the immunity in a suit against a 
TNC, plaintiffs must allege facts to satisfy an exception (in Subsection 
18(a)1.–3.) to the general “no liability” rule.  Haddad failed to do so here, 
even when given the explicit opportunity by the trial court.16 
 
14 See Subsection 18(a)1 . (“if . . . [t]here is no negligence under this section or 
criminal wrongdoing . . . .”); Subsection 18(a)3 . (“if . . . [t]he TNC is not the owner 
or bailee of the motor vehicle.”).   
 
15 That is, the claim is brought “under general law by reason of owning, operating, 
or maintaining the digital network accessed by a TNC driver or rider, or by being 
the TNC affiliated with a TNC driver, for harm to persons or property which 
results or arises out of the use, operation, or possession of a motor vehicle 
operating as a TNC vehicle while the driver is logged on to the digital network .”  
§ 627.748(18), Fla. Stat. (2022).  
 
16 The trial court’s  order on an interim motion to dismiss correctly held that the 
complaint “fail[ed] to include factual allegations supporting one or more of the 
enumerated exceptions to the default rule of non -liability under Subsection 
18(a),” and provided an opportunity to file an amended complaint.  
13 
 III. Conclusion 
Haddad’s claims for negligent and fraudulent misrepresentation are 
barred by section 627.748(18), Florida Statutes (2022).  The trial court 
correctly dismissed the claims with prejudice. 
Affirmed. 
KLINGENSMITH  and S HAW, JJ., concur. 
*            *            * 
 
Not final until disposition of timely-filed motion for rehearing.

items.summary:
Practically, a rideshare rider who sues the network company over safety statements on its website cannot escape the statutory non-liability bar just by pleading the platform's own misrepresentation rather than vicarious liability; unless the complaint pleads facts satisfying one of the statute's three exceptions, the claims are dismissed with prejudice at the pleading stage.

Holding: Section 627.748(18) grants a transportation network company a broad default statutory non-liability-broader than common-law vicarious liability and not controlled by the section's 'vicarious liability' title-for harm arising out of the use, operation, or possession of a logged-on rideshare vehicle, so long as the company complied with the statute (no 'negligence under this section,' meaning no negligent failure to meet the statute's own requirements rather than any negligence relating to the network) and engaged in no criminal wrongdoing; because the 'there is no liability' language creates a default rule rather than a traditional affirmative defense, the plaintiff must plead facts satisfying an exception in section 627.748(18)(a)1.-3. to survive a motion to dismiss.

Disposition: Affirmed
