DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA  
SECOND  DISTRICT  
 
 
 
META PLATFORMS, INC. , 
and INSTAGRAM, LLC,  
 
Petitioner s, 
 
v. 
 
OFFICE OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL,  
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS , 
 
Respondent.  
 
 
No. 2D2025 -3187  
 
 
November 4, 2026  
 
Petition for Writ of Certiorari to the Circuit Court  for Pasco County ; Alicia 
Polk, Judge.  
 
Laura K. Whitmore of Shook, Hardy & Bacon , LLP, Tampa; William P. 
Geraghty of Shook, Hardy & Bacon , LLP, Miami (withdrew after briefing); 
and Timothy C. Hester, Mark W. Mosier, and Stephen F. Petkis  of 
Covington & Burling, LLP, Washington, DC , for Petitioner s. 
 
James Uthmeier, Attorney General, and Karen E. Berger, Special 
Counsel, Assistant Attorney General, Fort Lauderdale; Donna Cecilia 
Valin , Special Counsel, Assistant Attorney General and Carol A. Field , 
Senior Assistant Attorney General, Orlando; Victoria Ann Butler , Director 
and Miles Walter Vaughn, Consumer Protection Division, Tampa, for 
Respondent.  
SMITH, Judge . 
2 
 Meta Platforms, Inc. , and Instagram, LLC (collectively Meta) , 
petition for  a writ of certiorari  quashing the trial court 's denial of its 
motion to dismiss the Attorney General 's complaint which alleged  
violations of Florida 's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act , chapter 
501, part II, Florida Statutes  (2024) (FDUTPA) , arguing a deprivation of 
both its statutory right of immunity under section 230 of the 
Communications Decency Act  (CDA) , 47 U.S.C. § 230, and its First 
Amendment1 rights .  Because Meta cannot establish the threshold 
jurisdictional showing of irreparable harm, w e dismiss the petition for 
the reasons outlined below.  
I. 
The Attorney General 's one-count  complaint for violations under 
FDUTPA generally allege d: 
Defendants ' Platforms cause serious harm to children, 
parents, and the community at large by deploying algorithms 
and other features designed to hijack the attention of its 
users, barrage them with advertisements, and relentlessly 
mine their interactions for monetiza ble data.   These features 
are designed to maximize user engagement and are 
particularly harmful to people under eighteen ( "Young 
Users "). 
In addition to seeking civil penalties  and other relief, the complaint also  
sought temporary and permanent injunction s to prevent Meta from 
future violations of FDUTPA.   
 
1 Meta argued violations of its First Amendment rights guaranteed 
by both the United States and the Florida Constitutions.  Because "[t]he 
scope of the protection accorded to freedom of expression in Florida 
under article I, section 4  [of the Florida Constitution] is the same as is 
required under the First Amendment " to the United States Constitution, 
Dep't of Educ. v. Lewis , 416 So. 2d 455, 461 (Fla. 1982) , we use the term 
"First Amendment " to describe the rights under both constitutional 
guarantees . 
3 
 Meta moved to dismiss the complaint, arguing , pertinent  here, that 
the action was barred by section 230 of the CDA and the First 
Amendment .  As for section 230 of the CDA, Meta argued that it enjoyed 
statutory immunity from both suit and liability, which protects a 
publisher of "information provided by another information content 
provider " and shields a publisher from liability for good  faith efforts to 
restrict access to objectionable material.2  47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1).  Meta 
also argued  that the "design features " identified by the Attorney General 
are directly related to the third -party content they provide and were thus 
protected  by the First Amendment .  Specifically, Meta raised three 
points: (1) it have the right to exercise editorial discretion over the third -
party content provided  on its platform s; (2) they have  the right to be free 
from government -compelled speech and cannot be forced to make certain 
representations or warnings to the public; and (3) its opinion and/or 
testimony before Congress is speech that is protected.    
The Attorney General responded to the motion to dismiss , arguing 
that its complaint did not reach Meta's editorial control of third -party 
content , which it concedes is protected under the First Amendment , but 
instead covers Meta 's own conduct —the design and use of "Addictive 
Features "—which  the Attorney General argued is deceptive and not 
protected speech.  Further, t he Attorney General argued that Meta is not 
immune where the complaint seeks to bar Meta's own deceptive practices 
in designing features to target young users in violation of FDUTPA , 
allegations which are  "entirely consistent " with the  purpose of section 
230 of the CDA. 
 
2 Meta does not challenge the trial court 's denial of its motion to 
dismiss on th e other basis raised  below—that the Attorney General failed 
to state a cause of action under FDUTPA . 
4 
 In a brief order , the trial court denied Meta 's motion to dismiss , 
finding that the complaint "sufficiently pleads the claims. " 
Meta now petitions for  a writ of certiorari quashing the denial  of its 
motion to dismiss , arguing that the order causes Meta irreparable harm 
by depriving it of its right to immunity from  both suit and liability as 
described in section 230 , as well as the right to free speech  under the 
First Amendment.   Meta also argue s that the order depart s from the 
essential requirements of the law, asserting that challenges to design 
features are barred by section 230 and that the First Amendment 
protects Meta 's statements of opinion and its editorial choices regarding  
the display of third -party speech.  
We find the jurisdictional issue of irreparable harm dispositive and 
do not reach the merits of the petition.    
II. 
We accept as true the "facts set forth in the complaint, as we 
must ," and construe all reasonable inferences in the light most favorable 
to the plaintiff , the Attorney General .  Clerk of Cir. Ct. & Comptroller of 
Collier Cnty . v. Doe , 292 So. 3d 1254, 1256 (Fla. 2d DCA 2020).    
A party aggrieved by a denial of immunity at the motion to dismiss 
stage may file for interlocutory review of the nonfinal order on direct 
appeal pursuant to Florida Rule of Appellate Procedure 9.130(a)(3) (F), if 
the motion   
(i) asserts entitlement to absolute or qualified immunity in 
a civil rights claim arising under federal law;  
(ii) asserts entitlement to immunity under section 
768.28(9), Florida Statutes ; 
(iii) asserts entitlement to sovereign immunity ;[3] or 
 
3 See In re Amends . to Fla . Rule App. P roc. 9.130 , 289 So. 3d 866, 
867 (Fla. 2020) ( amending Florida Rule of Appellate  Procedure 9.130 "to 
5 
 (iv) asserts entitlement to immunity under  section 776.032, 
Florida Statutes  . . . . 
As the immunity described in section 230 is not one of the 
enumerated immunities listed under rule  9.130(a)(3)(F), this petition 
proceeds under common law certiorari.   "[C]ertiorari is 'an extraordinary 
remedy and should not be used to circumvent the interlocutory appeal 
rule which authorizes appeal from only a few types of non -final orders. ' "  
Fish & Wildlife Conserv ation  Comm'n v. Jeffrey , 178 So. 3d 460,  464 (Fla. 
1st DCA 2015) (quoting Martin -Johnson, Inc. v. Savage , 509 So. 2d 1097, 
1098 (Fla. 1987), superseded by statute on other grounds , § 768.72, Fla. 
Stat. (2021)).   
[F]or a district court to "determine whether the 
circumstances " constitute "one of the rare cases . . . in which 
certiorari review is appropriate, " the district court must 
answer "yes" to these questions: Has there been : "(1) a 
departure from the essential requirements of the law, (2) 
resulting in material injury for the remainder of the case (3) 
that cannot be corrected on postjudgment appeal [?]."   
Univ. of Fla. Bd. of Trs. v. Carmody , 372 So. 3d 246 , 252  (Fla. 2023)  
(alteration in original) (citation omitted)  (quoting Williams v. Oken , 62 So. 
3d 1129, 1132 (Fla. 2011) ).  "The last two elements are jurisdictional and 
must be analyzed before the court may even consider the first element. "  
Williams , 62 So. 3d at 1132.   "In other words, before certiorari can be 
used to review non -final orders, the appellate court must focus on the 
threshold jurisdictional question: whether there is a material injury that 
cannot be corrected on appeal, otherwise termed as irreparable harm. "  
Citizens Prop. Ins. v. San Perdido  Ass'n, 104 So. 3d 344, 351 (Fla. 2012) ; 
cf. Fla. Power & Light Co. v. Rehab. Ctr . at Hollywood Hills, LLC , 285 So. 
 
expand  the availability of appellate review of nonfinal orders denying 
sovereign immunity "). 
6 
 3d 335 , 337 -38 (Fla. 4th DCA 2019) ( "When the Florida Supreme Court 
has amended Florida Rule of Appellate Procedure 9.130 to allow for 
immediate review of a nonfinal order determining that a party is not 
entitled to certain types of immunity from suit, it has done so only where 
the immunity c an be determined 'as a matter of law .' " (first quoting Fla. 
R. App. P. 9.130(a)(3)(C)(v); then citing Fla. R. App. P. 9.130(a)(3)(C)(vii); 
then citing Fla. R. App. 9.130(a)(3)(C)(x); and then citing Fla. R. App. P. 
9.130(a)(3)(C)(xi)) ).  And "while Florida courts 'have recognized exceptions ' 
to the general rule that 'certiorari review is an inappropriate means of 
challenging a trial court 's denial of a motion to dismiss, ' " Meta has not 
shown that this is one of them.  See Carmody , 372 So. 3d at 248 (quoting 
Univ. of Fla. Bd. of Trs. v. Carmody , 331 So. 3d 236, 237 (Fla. 1st DCA 
2021 )). 
The question presented , whether Meta will suffer irreparable harm , 
turns on whether section 230 confers an absolute  immunity , protecting 
Meta from being involved in a lawsuit of any nature.   In the context of 
certiorari, we review this case of first impression.   
III. 
Section 230  was enacted for the purpose s of provid ing service 
providers with protections from civil liability  for restricting objectionable 
online material and encouraging service providers to self-regulat e the 
distribution of offensive material , among other purposes .  Doe v. Am . 
Online, Inc. , 783 So. 2d 1010, 1014 (Fla. 2001) .  There are three key 
substantive components  of section 230 .  First are the safe harbor 
provisions of subsections  (c)(1) and (2):  
(c) Protection for "Good Samaritan " blocking and 
screening of offensive material  
(1) Treatment of publisher or speaker  
7 
 No provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be 
treated as the publisher or speaker of any information 
provided by another information content provider.  
(2) Civil liability  
No provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be 
held liable on account of -- 
(A) any action voluntarily taken in good faith to restrict access 
to or availability of material that the provider or user 
considers to be obscene, lewd, lascivious, filthy, excessively 
violent, harassing, or otherwise objectionable, whether or not 
such mater ial is constitutionally protected; or  
(B) any action taken to enable or make available to 
information content providers or others the technical means 
to restrict access to material described in [sub] paragraph [A].  
Second, section 230 sets forth "[o]bligations of interactive computer 
service " and requires providers of interactive computer service to notify 
customers of available parental control protections.  47 U.S.C. § 230(d).  
Third, the statute provides for its preemptive4 "[e]ffect on other laws, " 
including  
(3) State law  
Nothing in this section shall be construed to prevent any 
State from enforcing any State law that is consistent with this 
section.   No cause of action may be brought and no liability 
may be imposed under any State or local law that is 
inconsistent with this section.  
47 U.S.C. § 230(e)(3).   
 
4 Doe, 783 So. 2d at 1018 (referring to section 230 as a "preemptive 
law"); Gen. Steel Domestic Sales, L.L.C. v. Chumley , 840 F.3d 1178, 1182 
(10th Cir. 2016)  (stating that " 47 U.S.C. § 230(e)(3) is merely a 
preemption provision "); Kathleen R. v. City of Livermore , 87 Cal.  App. 4th 
684, 696 (Ca l. Ct. App. 2001)  (same) ; see also  Jordan v. AVCO Fin. Servs. 
of Ga., Inc. , 117 F.3d 1254, 1257 -58 (11th Cir. 1997)  (stating that a 
federal law which only clarified the boundaries of state and federal 
jurisdiction did not create an immunity from suit) .  
8 
 Meta meets the "interactive computer service " provider definition 
under the statute.  See 47 U.S.C. § 230(f)(2).   
Significantly, t he safe harbor provisions of subsections (c)(1) and (2) 
speak purely to immunity from "[c]ivil liability. "  See also  Simmons v. 
State , 886 So. 2d 399, 407 (Fla. 5th DCA 2004) (stating that section 230 
of the CDA "restricts civil liability  against providers or users of interactive 
computer services ").  The preemptive language in subsection (e)(3) clearly 
permits the enforcement of actions that are consistent with section 230, 
while at the same time disallowing actions under state or local law that 
are inconsistent with section 230.  See Doe, 783 So. 2d at 1016  (stating 
that if "the development of technologies, procedures and techniques by 
which objectionable material could be blocked or deleted either by the 
interactive computer service provider itself or by the families and schools 
receiving information via the Internet  . . . is frustrated by the imposition 
of distributor liability on Internet providers, then preemption is 
warranted " (quoting Zeran v. Am. Online, Inc. , 958 F. Supp. 1124, 1134 -
35 (E.D. Va. 1997) )). 
IV. 
Meta first equates the immunity conferred by section 230 to the 
absolute immunity afforded to public officials  and the like , arguing under 
Mills v. Kinnan , 411 So. 3d 501, 507 (Fla. 2d DCA 2025) , that they will 
suffer irreparable harm  as a result of "being forced to defend the suit[ , 
which] is itself a material injury ." 
To be sure, Florida courts have exercised certiorari jurisdiction in 
cases falling under the umbrella of absolute  immunity  by virtue of 
common law where a party is protected from being involved in a lawsuit 
of any nature and the irreparable harm is the evisceration of the 
immunity itself by requiring the party to  litigate .  Gay v. Jupiter Island 
9 
 Compound, LLC , 358 So. 3d 780 , 787  (Fla. 4th DCA 2023) ( "[Common law 
absolute immunity is] based chiefly upon a recognition of the necessity 
that certain persons, because of their special position or status , should 
be as free as possible from fear that their actions in that position might  
have an adverse effect upon their own personal interests. " (alteration in 
original) (quoting Fridovich v. Fridovich , 598 So. 2d 65, 68 (Fla. 1992) )).  
Overwhelmingly, those cases involve qualified immunity and appear in 
the realm of public  officials , judicial and quasi -judicial offices, and tribal 
sovereign immunity .  See, e.g. , Tucker v. Resha , 648 So. 2d 1187, 1189 
(Fla. 1994) ( "[T]he qualified immunity of public officials involves 
'immunity from suit  rather than a mere defense to liability ' " and as such 
"is effectively lost if a case is erroneously permitted to go to trial. " 
(quoting Mitchell v. Forsyth , 472 U.S. 511, 526 (1985))); Seminole Tribe of 
Fla. v. McCor , 903 So. 2d 353, 357  (Fla. 2d DCA 2005) ( "Certiorari 
jurisdiction exists in [the tribal sovereign immunity] context because the 
inappropriate exercise of jurisdiction by a trial court over a sovereignly -
immune tribe is an injury for which there is no adequate remedy on 
appeal. "); Stephens v. Geohegan , 702 So. 2d 517, 526 -27 (Fla. 2d DCA 
1997) (stating that police officers enjoyed absolute immunity from suit 
against them in their official capacities) ; Cent. Fla. Psych . Consults., Inc. 
v. Comas , 434 So. 3d 795, 802 (Fla. 5th DCA 2026) (holding that the 
litigation privilege protected a psychologist with absolute immunity); 
Harris v. Dazzo , 419 So. 3d 175 , 179  (Fla. 3d DCA 2025) (reaffirming that 
certiorari remains available for absolute immunity claims against 
arbitrators, similar to judges); Fla. State Univ. Bd. of Trs. v. Monk , 68 So. 
3d 316, 319 (Fla. 1st DCA 2011) (holding that an executive branch entity 
enjoys absolute immunity);  Fuller v. Truncale , 50 So. 3d 25, 27 -28 (Fla. 
10 
 1st DCA 2010) (holding that certiorari review was available to quash the 
denial of a motion to dismiss based on judicial immunity) . 
Meta's immunity claim under section 230 can hardly be reconciled 
with the se common law absolute and qualified immunity cases where 
Meta is a private company and holds no special status or position.  In 
fact, Meta sits in no better position than a governmental entity claiming 
limited statutory sovereign immunity, which the supreme court in San 
Perdido has held cannot overcome a showing of material injury beyond 
that of continuing to defend the litigation.  104 So. 3d at 355; see also 
Fla. R. App. P. 9.130(a)(3)(F)( iii) (providing for appeal of nonfinal orders 
that deny claims of  sovereign immunity ).  
Nevertheless, Meta insists that they enjoy complete immunity 
under section 230 , relying in part on Giordano v. Romeo , 76 So. 3d 1100, 
1102 (Fla. 3d DCA 2011) .  In Giordano , the Third District  affirmed the 
dismissal with prejudice of a defamation suit brought against interactive 
computer service provider Xcentric .  Id. at 1101.  The Giordano  court  
relied  on Doe, 783 So. 2d at 1018, and ultimately held that Xcentric 
"enjoye[d] complete immunity from any action brought against it as a 
result of the postings of third party  users of its website. "  Id. at 1102.  
Giordano misconstrued Doe in stating that the "Florida Supreme Court 
has held that the CDA provides absolute immunity to interactive 
computer services ."  76 So. 3d at 1101 .  This was not the holding in Doe.  
783 So. 2d at  1012.  Doe alleged, among other things , that AOL aided in 
the "sale and distribution of child pornography, including obscene 
images of John Doe."  Id.  The court in Doe approved the district court 's 
decision affirming the trial court 's dismissal of the complaint with 
prejudice based upon section 230 's preemption and addressed the 
following certified questions:   
11 
 [1] Whether  section 230  of the Communications Decency Act 
[CDA ] applies to complaints filed after its effective date where 
the complaint alleges a cause of action based upon acts 
occurring prior to its effective date?  
[2] If the answer [to question 1] is in the affirmative, whether  
section 230  of the Communications Decency Act preempts 
Florida law?  
[3] Whether a computer service provider with notice of a 
defamatory third party posting is entitled to immunity under  
section 230  of the Communications Decency Act?  
Id. at 10 11 (alterations in original) (quoting Doe v. Am. Online, Inc.,  718 
So. 2d 385, 390 (Fla. 4th DCA 1998)).  Significantly, Doe rephrased the 
second and third certified questions, eliminating any reference to 
"immunity ": 
Whether  section 230  preempts  Florida law as to causes of 
action based in negligence against an Internet Service 
Provider (ISP) as a distributor of information allegedly in 
violation of Florida criminal statutes prohibiting the 
distribution of obscene literature and computer pornograp hy? 
Id. at 101 3 (emphasis added).  Doe characterized section 230 not in 
terms of absolute immunity but as a preemptive law: "We specifically 
concur [with the court in Zeran , 958 F. Supp. at 1135 -37,] that section 
230 expressly bars 'any actions ' and we are compelled to give the 
language of this preemptive law  its plain meaning. "  Doe, 783 So. 2d at 
1018 (emphasis added).  The "bars 'any actions ' " language is contained 
in the supreme court 's analysis of the first certified question regarding 
the statute 's effective date.  Id.  And so, Doe was referring to the fact that 
section 230 broadly applies to "all suits filed after its enactment, 
notwithstanding when the operative facts arose. "  Id.   
Accordingly, with the exception of the outlier Giordano , based upon 
this court 's canvass of the decisional law, no court has held that section 
230 confers absolute immunity.  Although several courts have referred to 
12 
 section 230 immunity in terms of "federal immunity, " "full immunity, " 
and "broad immunity, " each of these courts limited section 230 's 
immunity to the very action protected under the safe harbor protections 
of subsection s (c)(1) and (2).  See Doe v. MySpace, Inc. , 528 F.3d 413, 418 
(5th Cir. 2008) ( "Congress provided broad immunity under the CDA  to 
Web-based service providers for all claims stemming from their 
publication of information created by third parties ."); Carafano v. 
Metrosplash.com, Inc. , 339 F.3d 1119, 1124 (9th Cir. 2003) ( "[S]o long as 
a third party willingly provides the essential published content, the 
interactive service provider receives full immunity regardless of the 
specific editing or selection process ."); Zeran v. Am. Online, Inc. , 129 F.3d 
327, 330 (4th Cir. 1997) ( "By its plain language, § 230 creates a federal 
immunity to any cause of action that would make service providers liable 
for information originating with a third -party user of the service. "); Fleites 
v. MindGeek S.A.R.L. , 801 F. Supp. 3d 1045, 1065 (C.D. Cal. 2025) 
("While § 230 immunity is broad, however, it is not absolute. ").5   
 
5 Numerous  federal and state  courts have held that section 230 
grants only immunity from liability.  See, e.g., e-ventures Worldwide, LLC 
v. Google, Inc. , 188 F. Supp . 3d 1265 , 1272 (M.D. Fla. 2016) (holding that 
section 230 immunity is an affirmative defense); Chumley , 840 F.3d at 
1182 (holding that subsection 230(e)(3) "does not contain an explicit bar 
to suit "); California v. Meta Platforms, Inc. , 186 F.4th 663, 673-76 (9th 
Cir. 2026)  (holding  that the court lacked jurisdiction to review the district 
court 's ruling on an interlocutory basis where section 230 provided a 
defense to liability and not immunity from suit) .  But see Nemet 
Chevrolet, Ltd. v. Consumeraffairs.com, Inc. , 591 F.3d 250 , 260  (4th Cir. 
2009)  (affirming the grant of the motion to dismiss holding that section 
230 confers immunity from suit).  Nevertheless, these cases have no 
binding effect on our court.  See, e.g. , Bd. of Cnty. Comm 'rs of Lee Cnty. v. 
Dexterhouse, 348 So. 2d 916, 918 (Fla. 2d DCA 1977)  ("The only federal 
decisions binding upon the courts of our state are those of the United 
States Supreme Court. " (quoting State v. Dwyer , 332 So.  2d 333 (Fla.  
1976) )). 
13 
 When immunity is less than absolute, our supreme court  has 
historically rejected the opportunity to extend certiorari jurisdiction  and 
instea d commissioned the Florida Bar Appellate Court Rules Committee 
to submit narrow rule amendments  to allow for nonfinal appeals  based 
upon specific statutory immunity claims  involving individuals who se 
claims are comparable to qualified immunity claims shared by 
government officials.  See San Perdido , 104 So. 3d at 355 (explaining that 
certiorari is not available where the statute provides immunity only "for 
certain designated claims " and not "absolute immunity where a party is 
protected from being involved in a lawsuit of any nature ," where Citizens 
claimed  immunity grounded on its  status as a governmental entity ); Keck 
v. Eminisor , 104 So. 3d 359 , 365 -66 (Fla. 2012) (declining to ut ilize 
certiorari to review an order denying summary judgment based on a 
claim of state sovereign immunity under section 768.28(9)(a) and 
requesting the Florida Bar Appellate Court Rules Committee  to submit a 
narrow rule amendment allowing for  nonfinal appeal  of the denial of 
such claims ); Tucker , 648 So. 2d at 1189 -90 (requesting that the rules 
committee submit a  rule amendment allowing for the expansion of 
nonfinal appeals  to include those  involving an individual qualified 
immunity against federal claims  based upon policy reasons ); cf. Dep't of 
Educ. v. Roe , 679 So. 2d 756 , 758  (Fla. 1996)  (declining  to expand the 
category of appealable nonfinal orders  to include those  denying limited 
claims of sovereign immunity ).   
The most recent illustration of the supreme court 's rejection of 
certiorari relief as the proper vehicle to address the denial of nonabsolute 
immunity claims can be seen in  Vericker  v. Powell , 406 So. 3d 939 (Fla. 
2025) .  There , the supreme court again declined to utilize certiorari re lief 
14 
 to address free-speech  immunity under the Anti -SLAPP6 statute , holding 
that the harm was not sufficient to support certiorari relief .  Id. at 945.  
Vericker argued that the Anti -SLAPP statute created a de facto immunity 
from the speech -targeted lawsuit.   Id. at 944.  Recognizing the continued 
availability of certiorari review for true immunity -from-suit claims , the 
supreme court reviewed the language of the statute  and noted the 
absence of the word "immunity " or other similar words and the absence 
of "structural or textual clues that might support an absolute right to be 
free from litigation. "  Id. at 944 -45.   
Ultimately, the supreme court rested on the grounds that the 
statute required a judicial determination that the lawsuit was without 
merit, which may "not be possible at the outset of a case and may require 
the development of a factual record. "  Id. at 945.   In holding that the 
denial of Vericker 's claimed immunity under the Anti -SLAPP statute did 
not support certiorari review, the supreme court reasoned that the onl y 
hardships raised were those related to the ongoing litigation.  Id. ("[W]e 
have repeatedly held that this sort of burden [hardships typically 
associated with continued litigation] do es not constitute irreparable harm 
in the ordinary circumstances .").  But before concluding its analysis , the 
supreme court acknowledged the statute 's purpose in swiftly resolving 
suits targeting free speech and  exercised its constitutional authority "to 
ensure that Florida 's procedural rules of court manifest the substantive 
legal enactments of the Legislature " and amend ed rule 9.130(a)(3) under 
separate opinion  to allow for nonfinal appeals of orders denying Anti -
 
6 The Anti -SLAPP statute protects people  from lawsuits based upon 
the exercise of their First Amendment right of free speech regarding a 
public issue.  See § 768.295(1) .  
15 
 SLAPP claims.  Id. at 946 (quoting Carmody , 372 So. 3d at 255); In re 
Amends. to Fla. Rule of App. Proc. 9.130 , 406 So. 3d 937 , 938  (Fla. 2025 ). 
Comparable to the statute addressed in San Perdido , here the plain 
text of section 230 only narrowly shields providers from claims seeking to 
treat them as the publisher or speaker of third -party content or to hold 
them liable for actions related to their screening of objectionable content.  
See 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1) -(2).  This type of limited statutory immunity is 
not absolute immunity from involvement in any type of lawsuit, such 
that, here, Meta would suffer irreparable harm merely by litigating the 
matter.  See San Perdido , 104 So. 3d at 355.  
Further , as in Vericker , section 230 equally contains no words of 
"immunity " or other similar words or any "structural or textual clues that 
might support an absolute right to be free from litigation. "  406 So. 3d at 
944-45.  But perhaps more importantly, Meta, like Vericker, asserts 
nothing more than the hardships of continued litigation, which the 
supreme court has held insufficient to support certiorari review.  See i d.   
No matter how  section 230 is described, we see no distinction 
between the protections in section 230 and the type of limited statutory 
immunity claimed in San Perdido  and Vericker .  See Almeida v. 
Amazon.com, Inc. , 456 F.3d 1316, 1321 -22 (11th Cir. 2006) ( "The 
majority of federal circuits have interpreted the CDA  to establish broad 
'federal immunity to any cause of action that would make service 
providers liable for information  originating with a third -party user of the 
service .' . . .  [B]ut even this broad statutory immunity does not apply 
without limitation. " (citation omitted) (quoting Zeran , 129 F.3d at 330)).  
Our interpretation of section 230 's limited statutory immunity is in line 
with the majority of other federal courts.  See, e.g., Roca Labs, Inc. v. 
Consumer Op . Corp. , 140 F. Supp. 3d 1311, 1321 (M.D. Fla. 2015) 
16 
 (applying safe harbor provision in a FDUTPA suit against the website 
creator whose edits were lawful but acknowledging that immunity is lost 
"when the [provider] substantively alters third -party content or becomes 
directly involved in the alleged illegality "); Alvi Armani Med., Inc. v. 
Hennessey , 629 F. Supp. 2d 1302, 1307 (S.D. Fla. 2008) (holding that 
where complaint alleged defendant itself created and developed content, 
defendant may not be entitled to immunity under section 230 and 
dismissal on this ground was inappropriate) ; Est. of Bride v. Yolo Tech s., 
Inc., 112 F.4th 1168, 1176 (9th Cir. 2024) ( "[N]either [subsection 230(c)] 
nor any other declares a general immunity from liability deriving from 
third-party content ." (second alteration in original) (quoting Barnes v. 
Yahoo!, Inc. , 570 F.3d 1096, 110 0 (9th Cir. 2009))); Fair Hous. Council of 
San Fernando Valley v. Roommates.Com, LLC , 521 F.3d 1157, 1164 -66 
(9th Cir. 2008) (holding that section 230 immunity did not apply to those 
acts where Roommate s was sued for the predictable consequences of 
creating a website designed to solicit and enforce housing preferences in 
violation of the Fair Housing Act and state laws; "[CDA] was not meant to 
create a lawless no -man's-land on the Internet ").  
Accordingly, Meta, at this stage in the underlying proceedings, has 
failed to establish irreparable harm sufficient to support certiorari review 
by virtue of its status as an interactive  computer service provider named 
in a lawsuit .   
V. 
Meta next asserts  that the order denying the motion to dismiss 
deprives them of its First Amendment  rights  and subjects it to speech -
chilling litigation on a daily basis.  We do not  find any merit in these 
allegations . 
17 
 Violations of First Amendment rights are potentially appropriate 
grounds for certiorari relief.   Cf. 3299 N. Fed. Highway, Inc. v. Bd. of 
Cnty. Comm 'rs of Broward Cnty. , 646 So. 2d 215, 222 (Fla. 4th DCA 
1994) (stating that appellants had sufficiently identified First 
Amendment rights that could potentially be imperiled by  the challenged 
county code but failed to demonstrate that the code harmed those rights 
and therefore could not show irreparable harm) .  "[First Amendment ] 
protections extend to not only unconstitutional laws, but also to 
unnecessary litigation  that chills speech. "  Green v. Miss United States of 
Am., LLC, 52 F.4th 773, 800 ( 9th Cir. 2022).  
However, t he Attorney General correctly counters  that certiorari is 
an extraordinary relief granted only in those limited circumstance s to 
"halt a miscarriage of justice where no other remedy exists. "  Broward 
County  v. G.B. V. Int'l, Ltd. , 787 So. 2d 838, 842 (Fla. 2001).  The 
challenged order does not come close to infringing on Meta 's First 
Amendment rights .  The order did not alter the status quo —it did not 
place any new restriction s on Meta , it did not  grant the Attorney 
General 's request for temporary or permanent injunctive relief regarding 
Meta's operations , it did not limit Meta 's speech or expression in any 
way, nor did it compel Meta to do anything .  In fact, n one of Meta 's First 
Amendment rights have been altered.   Accordingly, we are unpersuaded 
by the authorities upon which Meta rests its First Amendment argument  
to support certiorari in th is case .  See Belair v. Drew , 770 So. 2d 1164, 
1167 (Fla. 2000) ( holding  that the district court erred in denying 
certiorari review of a trial court order that "temporarily granted [a] 
grandmother visitation rights [of her grandchild] and set the matter for a 
future hearing to determine permanent visitation rights, " a ruling which 
"[o]n its face . . . directly contravene[d] the petitioner 's right to privacy 
18 
 and decision -making in rearing her child "); Est. of McPherson ex rel. 
Liebrech v. Church of Scientology Flag Serv . Org., 815 So. 2d 678, 679 
(Fla. 2d DCA 2002)  (quashing a discover y order which required the estate 
to produce documents  pertaining to the source of the funding of the 
litigation, as  the order would "create a chilling effect on  receiving  future 
funding " that could not be remedied on appeal ); Joseph v. State , 642 So. 
2d 613, 614 -15 (Fla. 4th DCA 1994) (exercising certiorari jurisdiction 
and quashing a trial court order that prohibited the petitioner "from 
wearing a sweat shirt and jeans with ostensible religious pictures and 
names " at trial) ; Green , 52 F.4th at 800 (stating that dispositive First 
Amendment issues can be resolved in summary proceedings to avoid 
"unnecessary and protracted litigation ").  
For these reasons, Meta has  again failed to demonstrate irreparable 
harm sufficient to support certiorari review.  
V. 
Because section 230 confers a nonabsolute immunity , "such 
immunity is not lost merely  because review must wait until after a final 
judgment ."  San Perdido , 104 So. 3d at 347 (quoting Citizens Prop. Ins. v . 
San Perdido Ass'n,  46 So. 3d 1052 (Fla. 1st DCA 2010)) .  Accordingly,  
Meta cannot show irreparable harm from the denial of its limited  
immunity claim under section 230 .  It also ha ve not established an 
irreparable violation of its First Amendment rights .  Therefore, we lack 
certiorari jurisdiction  and dismiss the petition .7  See Jeffrey , 178 So. 3d 
460 (dismissing certiorari petition where agency 's statutory immunity 
 
7 Nothing herein shall be construed in any way to constitute a 
comment on the merits of the Attorney General 's FDUTPA complaint or 
Meta's claim of immunity from liability under section 230 or the First 
Amendment.  
19 
 under  section 768.28  was only limited immunity from liability and not 
the suit itself) . 
Dismissed . 
 
MORRIS  and LABRIT , JJ., Concur.  
 
 
Opinion subject to revision prior to official publication.

items.summary:
An interactive computer service provider cannot obtain common-law certiorari review of the denial of its motion to dismiss founded on section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (or the First Amendment), because section 230 supplies a defense to civil liability rather than immunity from suit, so being forced to continue litigating is not irreparable harm and review must await appeal after final judgment; the court expressly reserved the merits of the Attorney General's FDUTPA claims and the underlying immunity defense.

Holding: Common-law certiorari over a nonfinal order denying a motion to dismiss lies only where the petitioner first establishes the jurisdictional element of irreparable harm—a material injury for the remainder of the case that cannot be corrected on post-judgment appeal. Because section 230 of the Communications Decency Act confers only immunity from civil liability (a preemption/affirmative-defense provision), not absolute immunity from suit, an interactive computer service provider named in a lawsuit suffers no irreparable harm merely from litigating; such limited statutory immunity is unlike absolute or qualified immunity from suit and is comparable to the limited governmental immunity in the San Perdido line and to the Anti-SLAPP free-speech claim in Vericker, so certiorari does not lie to review its denial at the motion-to-dismiss stage (and such claims are not among the immunities appealable as of right under Rule 9.130(a)(3)(F)). A First Amendment basis for certiorari likewise fails absent an order that alters the status quo—restricting or compelling speech or granting injunctive relief—because the ordinary hardships of speech-related litigation, standing alone, are not irreparable harm.

Disposition: Petition dismissed

Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed November 4, 2026 . 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________  
 
No. 3D25 -2497  
Lower Tribunal No. 19-CA-175-K  
________________  
 
 
Monroe County , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Roy's Trailer Park, Inc., etc., et al. , 
Appellee s. 
 
 
 An Appeal from the Circuit Court for Monroe  County, Bonnie J. Helms , 
Judge.  
 
 Bob Shillinger, Monroe County Attorney and Jessica Pierce Quiggle, 
Assistant County Attorney , for appellant.  
 
 VDF Law PLLC, and Van D. Fischer ,  for appellee  Roy’s Trailer Park, 
Inc.; Hoffman, Larin & Agnetti, P.A., and John B. Agnetti, for residents of 
Roy’s Trailer Park, Inc.  
 
 
Before  LINDSEY,  BOKOR and GOODEN , JJ.  
 
 BOKOR, J . 
 2 Roy’s Trailer Park, Inc., filed suit for a declaratory judgment that mobile 
home park owners  cannot be responsible for tenant fire code violations under 
section 723.024, Florida Statutes. The Count y countersu ed, seeking a 
declaration that they can be, and added  a count for injunctive relief to enforce 
the fire code at Roy’ s Trailer Park . The trial court dismissed  the County’s 
counterclaims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, citing the County’s failure 
to exhaust  administrative remedies  adopted  by local ordinance. The County 
appeals the final order of dismissal . For the following reasons, we reverse .  
BACKGROUND  
In May 2015, a fire at Roy’s Trailer Park led to the discovery that 14 
people were living in one  single -wide trailer.  Monroe County obtained an 
inspection warrant, whereafter the Fire Marshal and local enforcement board 
identified numerous safety issues .  
In 2018, Roy’s Trailer Park filed suit against the County as well as two 
of its tenants in county court.  In Count I , Roy’s  Trailer Park  sought to evict 
the tenants for fire code violations that endangered the “health, safety and 
welfare” of others.  Count II sought a declaratory judgment that a trailer park 
can’t be the “responsible party” for a code violation under section 723.024, 
 3 Florida Statutes,1 which affirms the authority of local governments to cite 
violations at mobile home parks notwithstanding the State’s more general 
preemption of  mobile home p ark regulation in Chapter 723.2  
The County countersued seeking  the opposite declaration, that a trailer 
park can be responsible  for violations under 723.024, as well as for an 
injunction prohibiting occupancy of Roy’s Trailer Park until its many “serious 
fire and life safety issues” were cured , and to appoint a receiver . On Roy’s 
motion the case was transferred to circuit court, and Roy’s  Trailer Park  then 
moved to dismiss the counterclaims for failure to join eighty -six tenants of 
the trailer park. The County amended its countersuit to add them.  
In September 2021, Roy’s  Trailer Park  moved for partial summary 
judgment on the counter claims . Roy’s  Trailer Park argued that because the 
County had adopted a code  enforcement procedure by local ordinance,3 the 
 
1 “Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter  . . . [i]f a unit of local 
government finds that a violation of a local code or ordinance has occurred, 
the unit of local government shall cite the responsible party  for the violation 
. . . .” § 723.024 (1), Fla. Stat. (emphasis added).  
 
2 “There is hereby expressly preempted to the state all regulation and control 
of mobile home lot rents in mobile home parks and all those other matters 
and things relating to the landlord -tenant relationship treated by or falling 
within the purview of this  chapter.” § 723.004(2), Fla. Stat.  
 
3 “There is hereby created a department  . . . . responsible for the 
enforcement of  . . . ordinances concerning:  . . . fire . . . as well as any other 
ordinances of the county.” Monroe County Code § 8 -2 
 4 trial court had no subject matter jurisdiction to hear the County’s claims in 
the first instance  as the  County was first required to exhaust “its own 
administrative remedies .”  
The court rejected this argument at first, denying partial summary 
judgment. But on the first day scheduled for bench trial, the counter -
defendants (including Roy’s  Trailer Park ) again moved to dismiss the 
counte rclaims on these  same  grounds. The y argued that the County was 
required to use local administrative process to enforce the fire code  and 
could not do so by injunction, seek a declaration as to the meaning of 
723.024 (as Roy’s  Trailer Park  had), or appoint a receiver . The County 
argued that it had not surrendered any rights existing elsewhere in state law 
by adopting local administrative procedures.  
This time, th e court agreed with the counter -defendants . It concluded 
that the administrative exhaustion doctrine applies to any claim “cognizable 
in the first instance by an administrative agency” and that it was therefore 
without subject matter jurisd iction, dismissing the counterclaims . Roy’s 
Trailer Park then voluntarily dismissed its own original claim seeking a 
declaration as to the meaning of section 723.024. Consequently, the court 
dismissed the entire action. The County moved for rehearing, which motion 
was denied , and this appeal timely followed.  
 5 STANDARD OF REVIEW  
 “A trial court ’s order granting a motion to dismiss is reviewed de novo.” 
Grove Isle Ass’n, Inc. v. Grove Isle Assocs., LLLP , 137 So. 3d 1081, 1089 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2014).  
ANALYSIS  
“Although often couched in jurisdictional terms, ‘the doctrine requiring 
the exhaustion of administrative remedies is not jurisdictional.  . . . [It] is a 
court -created prudential doctrine  . . . a matter of policy, not of power.’” State 
Dep’t of Env’t Prot. v. PZ Const r. Co. , 633 So. 2d 76, 78 n.3 (Fla. 3d DCA 
1994) (quoting State, Dep’t of Rev enue  v. Brock , 576 So. 2d 848, 850 (Fla. 
1st DCA 1991)); accord  Henry v. Santana , 62 So. 3d 1122, 1127 (Fla. 201 1). 
Here, the question isn’t whether a circuit court possesses jurisdiction to hear 
these types of claims . It does. The question is whether the statute triggers 
an administrative exhaustion requirement before the County can pursue its 
claim in court . It does not.  
Administrative exhaustion “ applies where a claim is cognizable in the 
first instance by an administrative agency alone .” Flo-Sun, Inc. v. Kirk , 783 
So. 2d 1029, 103 7 n.5  (Fla. 2001)  (emphasis added) (quoting United States 
v. W. Pac. R.R. Co. , 352 U.S. 59, 63  (1956) ). The  County could have pursued 
its counterclaims under a local process adopted by Monroe County Code § 
 6 8-2. But state law explicitly  provides that such claims are cognizable 
elsewhere , too . Every county in Florida has the power to provide “fire 
protection, including the enforcement of the Florida Fire Prevention Code,” 
by Florida statute. § 125.01(1)(d), Fla. Stat.   
Chapter 162, Florida Statutes , establishes that  the local code 
enforcement procedures it authorizes , such as Monroe County Code § 8 -2, 
are intended as “an additional or supplemental  means of obtaining 
compliance  . . . . [and that] nothing  . . . shall prohibit a local governing body 
from enforcing its codes by any other means .” § 162.13, Fla. Stat. 
(emphasis added).  And a local ordinance “cannot forbid what the legislature 
has expressly licensed, authorized or required .” Rinzler v. Carson , 262 So. 
2d 661, 668 (Fla. 1972). The County repeats this understanding that the local 
procedure for code compliance is in addition to, and not in lieu of, any other 
remedy available. Specifically , Monroe County Code § 8-36, entitled “[c]ode 
compliance by other means ,” sets forth that “[n]othing in this chapter shall be 
construed to preempt o r prohibit  the county from enforcing its codes by any 
other lawfully available means.”   
This court  noted in a similar context that Chapter 162, Florida Statutes, 
“lends itself to a single, readily ascertainable construction. A local 
government is permitted to enforce its ordinances through means other than 
 7 code enforcement boards  . . . . For instance  . . . by way of civil action  . . . .” 
City of Miami Beach v. Nichols , 314 So. 3d 313, 317 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020) . 
Additionally, a c ircuit court ha s jurisdiction to enforce ordinances by 
injuncti on. See Sirgany Int’l, Inc. v. Miami -Dade C ounty , 887 So. 2d 381, 383 
(Fla. 3d DCA 2004) (“[T]he circuit courts have been assigned jurisdiction to 
issue all injunctions  . . . includ[ing]  those enforcing ordinances.”); Metro. 
Dade Cnty. v. O ’Brien , 660 So. 2d 364, 365 (Fla. 3d DCA 1995) (“[T]he 
O’Briens began a business without complying with the county code  . . . and 
continue to violate county ordinances. Under these extreme circumstances, 
the trial court abused its discretion because the government has a clear legal 
right. . . . [T]his matter is remanded for entry of a temporary injunction.”). It 
also has broad jurisdiction to “render declaratory judgments on the 
existence, or nonexistence  . . . [o]f any immunity, power, privilege, or right ” 
or any “ fact upon which the existence or nonexistence of such immunity, 
power, privilege, or right does or may depend.” § 86.011, Fla. Stat.  (emphasis 
added). A declaratory action must allege a bona fide dispute as to some 
“right, status, immunity, power or privilege, or  . . . fact . . . [and] a bona fide, 
actual, present need for the declaration.”  Romo v. Amedex Ins. Co. , 930 So. 
2d 643, 64 8 (Fla. 3rd DCA 2006)  (quotation omitted). That was the case 
 8 here, as the parties had filed two directly conflicting claim s for declaratory 
relief over the meaning of section 723.024 .  
The cases Roy’s Trailer Park relies on require administrative 
exhaustion when challenging executive action. But they don’t requir e the 
government to go through its own administrative scheme before exercising 
an otherwise available judicial remedy. And this makes sense  not only  
considering  the statutory scheme referenced above, but also the  purpose of 
the exhaustion  doctrine :  
[T]o assur e that an agency responsible for implementing a 
statutory scheme has a full opportunity  to reach a sensitive, 
mature, and considered decision  upon a complete record 
appropriate to the issue [,] . . . . allow[] the agency to employ its 
discretion  and expertise, and help [] preserve executive and 
administrative autonomy . 
 
PZ Const r. Co. , 633 So. 2d 76, 79 (Fla. 3d DCA 1994) (emphasis added) 
(quoting Brock , 576 So. 2d at 850). “Exhaustion of administrative remedies 
should be required only when it promotes the purposes of the doctrine,”  
which is  “often viewed as protecting the executive branch from unwarranted 
judicial interference.” Pretzer v. Swearingen , 394 So. 3d 175, 186, 188 (Fla. 
1st DCA 2024).  
The court below cited Palm Lake Partners II, LLC. v. C  & C Powerline, 
Inc., 38 So. 3d 844, 853 (Fla. 1st DCA 2010), for the principle that exhaustion 
“applies to municipal governmental agencies.” But  the full quote is that 
 9 exhaustion “a pplies to municipal governmental agencies no less than it 
applies to state administrative agencies subject to the Administrative 
Procedure Act. ” Id. This doesn’t mean that a municipal agency must submit 
to and exhaust its own administrative procedures ; it means that 
administrative exhaustion applies to claims against municipal agencies “no 
less than ” it would against state agencies. So the First District applied the 
doctrine to the claim s of private individuals whose zoning questions  it held  
“should first be addressed to the City” (i.e., the “municipal governmental 
agenc[y]” to which it referred ). Id. at 852 –53.  
None of the other cases relied on support the proposition that 
administrative exhaustion means that the government gives up its right to 
enforce a violation through  alternative,  lawful means . See, e.g., DeCarlo v. 
Town of W est Miami , 49 So. 2d 596 (Fla. 1950) ( requiring administrative 
exhaustion in the context of a private claim against city); Cmtys. Fin. Corp. 
v. Fla. Dep’t of Env’t Reg ul., 416 So. 2d 813 (Fla. 1st DCA 1982) ( requiring 
administrative exhaustion in the context of a corporate claim against state 
agency); Browne v. City of Miami , 948 So. 2d 792 (Fla. 3d DCA 2006) 
(requiring administrative exhaustion in the context of a whistleblower against 
city, but estopping the city from raising the defense ); City of DeLand v. Lowe , 
 10 544 So. 2d 1165 (Fla. 5th DCA 1989) ( requiring administrative exhaustion in 
the context of a private claim against city) .  
CONCLUSION  
Because  the trial court  erred in  conclu ding that it lacked jurisdiction  
over the counterclaims  and that the County was required to exhaust 
administrative remedies before seeking relief in court, we reverse and 
remand for proceedings consistent with this opinion .  
Reversed  and remanded .

items.summary:
Practically, a local government that chooses to enforce a fire or building code in court—rather than before its own code board—does not forfeit or postpone that power, because adopting a local administrative scheme is optional and cumulative; the circuit court keeps subject-matter jurisdiction over the county's declaratory and injunction counterclaims, so the case must be heard on the merits instead of dismissed for a supposed failure to exhaust.

Holding: The exhaustion of administrative remedies is a court-created prudential doctrine, not a jurisdictional limit, and applies only where a claim is cognizable in the first instance by an administrative agency alone; because chapter 162 makes local code-enforcement procedures supplemental to other lawful means and sections 125.01(1)(d) and 86.011 independently authorize a county to pursue circuit court injunction and declaratory relief, a government need not exhaust its own local administrative process before seeking those judicial remedies, and dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction was error.

Disposition: Reversed and remanded

SIXTH DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________ 
 
Case No. 6D2025-0018 
Lower Tribunal No s. 2008- CA-003909 and 2015- CA-000309 
_____________________________ 
 
LITTLE BROWNIE PROPERTIES , INC., 
Appellant,  
v. 
ROP  HOLDING GROUP , INC., 
Appellee.  
_____________________________ 
 
Appeal from the Circuit Court for Orange  County.  
Jeffrey L. Ashton, Judge . 
 
November 6, 2026 
 
TRAVER , C.J. 
  Little Brownie Properties , Inc.  (“LBP”) appeals the trial court’s amended final 
order on proceedings supplementary .  We have jurisdiction.  See Fla. R. App. P. 
9.030(b)(1)(A).  Both LBP and ROP Holding Group, Inc. (“ROP”) purchased  
judgments from creditors of John Paul Brown and Peter Wood, who, at least at some 
point, were LBP shareholders .  We must determine who currently possesses the LBP 
shares originally owned by Brown and Wood.  And if Brown and Wood still own 
2 
 their LBP shares, we must decide whether the trial court erred when it awarded them 
unpaid LBP management fees because these were really “disguised dividends.”  
We reverse in part.  The trial court erred when it determined that Brown and 
Wood had not waived their rights to claim that they had never transferred shares to 
Banc of America Leasing & Capital, LLC (“BALC”), a judgment creditor.  Our 
conclusion’s result  is that Wood does not own any LBP shares , and that Brown owns 
only seventy  shares, instead of the 132.5 the trial court ruled that he owned.  So 
Wood is not entitled to any unpaid LBP management fees, and the trial court should 
determine what LBP owes Brown for these fees on remand.   
Finding that competent, substantial evidence supports the trial court’s other 
findings, we otherwise affirm.  This opinion involves a unique set of facts, likely 
restricting its holding to the parties involved in this appeal.  For clarity, and to 
summarize, this Court affirms that competent, substantial evidence supports the trial 
court’s ruling that neither Brown nor Wood legally transferred their shares, 
voluntarily or involuntarily, to BALC, and LBP’s management fees were disguised 
dividends.  We also find the trial court correctly concluded Brown did not involuntarily transfer his remaining seventy shares to LBP.  We comment no further 
on these issues, confining the remainder of this opinion’s scope to the specific circumstances by which Brown and Wood waived their right to contest the transfer of the 135 shares at issue to LBP.   
3 
 I. 
 
 Proceedings supplementary , equitable  in nature , are governed by statute.  See 
§ 56.29, Fla. Stat. (2024) .  They provide  a judgment creditor with means to 
investigate a judgment debtor’s assets that might be used to satisfy a judgment.  See 
id.; Sanchez v. Renda Broad.  Corp. , 127 So. 3d 627, 628 (Fla. 5th DCA 2013) ; 
Gamez v. First Union Nat ’l Bank of Fla. , 31 So. 3d 220, 223 (Fla. 4th DCA 2010) .  
In connection with proceedings supplementary, a trial court may order any non -
exempt property owned by a judgment debtor to be applied towards satisfaction of 
that debtor’s debt.  See § 56.29(6)(a) .  The facts contained in this opinion come from  
a multi- day evidentiary hearing following ROP’s and LBP’s consolidated 
proceedings supplementary against Brown and Wood.   
II. 
 
 LBP is a family -operated real estate company.  Brown’s father started LBP 
more than forty years ago, and its main asset is a property worth over $20 million.  
In 1978, LBP issued 70 shares to Brown.  In 1996, it issued 10 shares to Wood, who 
is a close family friend and Brown’s business partner.   That same year, LBP’s 
shareholders, including Brown and Wood, entered into a shareholders’ agreement.  
A key  provision  requires shareholders to notify LBP if they might involuntarily 
transfer  or have involuntarily transferred their shares  to someone else.  In that 
situation, LBP would have a  sixty -day option to buy the shares.  
4 
 In 2009, BALC  obtained a consent judgment exceeding $500,000 against 
Brown and Wood.  That year, Brown’s father died, and Wood was appointed as co -
personal representative of the estate.  BALC diligently pursued collection efforts 
against Brown and Wood, renewing its lien in 2014.  That year, following a hearing, 
BALC  obtained a court order requiring Wood to turn over his 10 LBP shares to 
BALC.  Wood complied with this order, delivering the shares to BALC .   He never 
sought their return.  
In 2018, BALC commenced garnishment proceedings on Brown’s father’s 
estate.  Wood, acting in his capacity as co -personal representative, distributed 62.5 
LBP shares to himself and 62.5 LBP shares to Brown in connection with Brown’s 
father’s wishes.  Accordingly, LBP issued stock certificates in these amounts to both 
Brown and Wood.  To avoid estate garnishment proceedings  on these 12 5 shares , 
Brown and Wood  delivered the se stock certificates to BALC.  Brown explained that 
BALC was just “holding” the now-total-135 shares because Brown and Wood 
wanted to negotiate for their return.1    
BALC then notified LBP that it had Brown ’s and Wood’s shares and insisted 
that an involuntary transfer from them to it had occurred.  It thus demanded LBP 
invoke its option under  the LBP shareholders’ agreement to buy the 135 shares .  If 
LBP declined this offer, BALC demanded that LBP issue a stock certificate in its 
 
1 Wood did not testify at the evidentiary hearing.    
5 
 name.  BALC identified itself as an LBP shareholder , and it copied Brown and Wood 
on its demand letter .  About a month later, Brown and Wood sent a notice to LBP 
under the involuntary transfer provision of the LBP shareholder agreement.   While 
each expressed doubt that this provision applied, both confirmed that they had 
“voluntarily delivered” these 135 shares to BALC.   
In January 2019, BALC and LBP executed a settlement agreement.  In it, 
BALC sold the 135 shares to LBP and assigned its rights to its judgment against 
Brown and Wood for $435,000.  Following execution of this agreement, BALC 
notified Brown and Wood via a notice filed in the lawsuit that led to  BALC’s 
judgment  that it planned to deliver  the 135 shares to LBP and assign to LBP all right, 
title, and interest  it had in those shares.  It directed Brown and Wood to object to  the 
transfer within ten days.  BALC and LBP jointly moved the trial court to approve 
the transfer, and they served notice of this motion on Brown and Wood.  It then 
noticed a hearing on this motion, again informing Brown and Wood.   
In February 2019, t he trial court entered an order approving the transfer.  Each 
received notice, and neither objected at any point during this process .  Neither moved 
to intervene, moved for rehearing, or appealed the trial court’s ruling.2  Following 
 
2 See Fla. R. App. P. 9.130( a)(3)(C)(ii) (allowing for review of nonfinal orders 
involving “the right to immediate possession of property”) ; see also  J.B. Harris, P.A. 
v. Virage Cap. Mgmt. LP , 404 So. 3d 504, 505  (Fla. 3d DCA 2024)  (explaining that 
district court ha d jurisdiction to review  appeal of nonfinal order granting judgment 
creditor’s motion to turn over stock under rule 9.130(a)(3)(C)(ii)) .   
6 
 the order’s issuance, BALC assigned its judgment to LBP and delivered the 135  
share s to LBP , who canceled them.  Soon after , the judgment lien LBP bought  from 
BALC expired.  
Before this expiration , a second judgment creditor obtained a judgment 
against Brown and Wood exceeding $1 million.  In December 2019, ROP bought 
that judgment  and filed its own judgment lien, which had priority over LBP’s 
(assigned, but now expired) judgment lien.  ROP moved to intervene in the se 
proceedings supplementary that LBP initiated against Brown and Wood.  ROP  
identified property that the trial court could apply to satisfy its purchased judgment.  This included the 135 shares LBP bought  from BALC .   
Before and a t the evidentiary hearing, LBP argued that Brown and Wood 
waived their right to argue that they had not transferred their shares to BALC .  It 
highlighted their persistent failure, despite regular notification, to object to BALC’s 
transfer of the 135 shares to LBP.  Under these circumstances, it insisted  that Brown 
and Wood could not now claim that BALC had merely been holding those shares while they tried to negotiate  their return.  In the trial court’s initial order, it failed to 
rule on LBP’s waiver defense.  In its amended final order, it rejected the defense 
without explanation.  Based on the  evidentiary record, this was error.   
 
 
 
 
7 
 III. 
 
Waiver is “the voluntary and intentional relinquishment of a known right or 
conduct which implies the voluntary and intentional relinquishment of a known 
right.”  Raymond James Fin. Servs., Inc. v. Saldukas , 896 So. 2d 707, 711 (Fla. 2005)  
(citing Major League Baseball v. Morsani , 790 So. 2d 1071, 1077 n.12 (Fla. 2001) ).  
“The elements of waiver are: (1) the existence at the time of the waiver of a right, privilege, advantage, or benefit which may be waived; (2) the actual or constructive knowledge of the right; and (3) the intention to relinquish the right.”   Zurstrassen v. 
Stonier , 786 So. 2d 65, 70  (Fla. 4th DCA 2001)  (quoting Leonardo v. State Farm 
Fire & Cas. Co. , 675 So.  2d 176, 178 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996) ).  “Waiver may be 
express , or implied  from conduct or acts that lead a party to believe a right has been 
waived ,” and “[a] party may waive any rights to which he is legally entitled.”   Taylor 
v. Kenco Chem. & Mfg. Corp. , 465 So. 2d 581, 587 (Fla. 1st DCA 1985) ; Thomas 
N. Carlton Est . v. Keller , 52 So. 2d 13 1, 133  (Fla. 1951) .  The acts and circumstances 
surrounding an implied waiver “ must make out a clear case.” Kirschner v. Baldwin , 
988 So. 2d 1138, 1142 (Fla. 5th DCA 2008)  (citing Woodlands Civic Ass’n v. David 
W. Darrow, D.C., P.A., 765 So. 2d 874, 877 (Fla. 5th DCA 2000) ).  And t he time in 
which a party has declined to exercise a right matters to  this determination.  See 
Cnty. of Brevard v. Miorelli Eng’g, Inc. , 703 So. 2d 1049, 1052 n.4 (Fla. 1997)  
(Anstead, J., concurring in part and dissenting in part)  (“Waiver does not arise from 
8 
 forbearance for a reasonable time, but may be inferred from conduct or acts ‘ putting 
one off his guard and leading him to believe that a right has been waived. ’” (quoting 
Gilman v. Butzloff, 22 So. 2d 263, 265 (Fla. 1945) )); Zurstrassen , 786 So. 2d at 70 
(“[W] hile forbearance for a reasonable time alone cannot constitute  waiver, . . 
. conduct leading one to believe that a right has been waived may imply such 
a waiver. ”).  In Kirschner , the Fifth District found no waiver when there was no 
objection for a few weeks to Baldwin’s construction of a garage.  988 So. 2d at 1142–
43.  By contrast, Brown’s and Wood’ s silence lasted years.  
IV. 
 
 Under the unique factual circumstances in this case , Brown  and Wood waived 
their right to  contend that they did not transfer their combined 135 shares to BALC, 
who then assigned those shares to LBP.  While much of Brown’s  and Wood’s waiver 
arises from the ir repeated  failure to object to this transfer, not all of it does.  Brown 
and Wood both sent  notices to LBP that the  voluntary delivery of their shares to 
BALC might  implicate the LBP shareholder agreement’s involuntary transfer 
provision.  While these notices were equivocal, Brown ’s and Wood’s subsequent 
conduct did nothing but affirm  their stated suspicion that an involuntary transfer had, 
in fact,  occurred .  Despite being notified at every critical stage of the process, both 
sat silent and raised no objection to BALC’s transfer of their shares to LBP .  This 
included a specific notice of an opportunity to object, a motion for the trial court to 
9 
 approve the transfer, a notice of hearing, and an order granting the motion.  LBP 
then canceled the certificates, again without even  a whisper from Brown and Wood.  
As it related to his shares, Wood’ s silence lasted  nearly  a decade.  And Brown and 
Wood only spoke up after they had arranged a separate deal to sell their  shares to 
satisfy ROP’s judgment against  them .  Under these circumstances, the trial court 
erred by ruling  that LBP’s waiver defense failed . 
V. 
  
We therefore conclude that because Brown and Wood waived any right to 
assert they had not transferred 135 LBP  shares in 2019, ROP cannot collect on its 
judgment by executing on this property.  ROP  can, however, execute on Brown’s 
remaining seventy LBP shares.  Wood is not entitled to management fees because 
he had no shares at the time LBP distributed what the trial court concluded were 
disguised dividends.  We remand for the trial court to recalculate Brown’s  dividends 
based on our decision .   
AFFIRMED in part; REVERSED in part; and REMANDED.  
 
WOZNIAK and WHITE , JJ., concur.  
  
Christopher V. Carlyle and John N. Bogdanoff, of The Carlyle Appellate Law Firm, 
Orlando,  and Eric S. M ashburn, of Law Office of Eric S. Mashburn, P.A., Winter 
Garden,  for Appel lant.  
  
 
10 
 Matthew D. Baylor and Jason M. Ellison, of Ellison | Lazenby, Saint Petersburg, for 
Appellee.  
  
NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE MOTION FOR REHEARING 
AND DISPOSITION THEREOF IF  TIMELY FILED

items.summary:
Practically, judgment debtors who stay silent for years, despite being notified at every step, while a creditor transfers their disputed stock to a buyer cannot later revive an ownership claim to defeat a second creditor's collection, because their inaction impliedly waived the claim; the court stressed the fact-specific nature of the ruling and otherwise left the trial court's findings intact that the shares were never lawfully transferred to the first creditor and that management fees were disguised dividends.

Holding: Waiver is the voluntary and intentional relinquishment of a known right, requiring (1) an existing waivable right, (2) actual or constructive knowledge of it, and (3) the intent to relinquish it; it may be express or implied from conduct or acts that lead a party to believe the right has been waived, and although forbearance for a reasonable time alone does not constitute waiver, prolonged silence-on these unique facts, years of failure to object despite notice at every stage of a judgment creditor's transfer of the debtors' corporate shares to a purchaser-can make out an implied waiver that, in section 56.29 proceedings supplementary, bars the debtors from later reasserting ownership of the transferred shares against a competing judgment creditor.

Disposition: Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded

Author: Chief Judge Traver
