Third District Court of Appeal  
State of Florida  
 
Opinion filed October 28, 2026.  
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing.  
 
________________ 
 
No. 3D26 -0312  
Lower Tribunal No. 23-29033 -CA-01 
________________ 
 
 
Reybel Hernandez , 
Appellant,  
 
vs. 
 
Barclays Mortgage Trust 2022- RPL1, Mortgage -Backed , 
Appellee.  
 
 
  An Appeal from a non -final order from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade 
County, Ariana Fajardo Orshan , Judge.  
 
 Reybel Hernandez, in proper person.   
 
 Atlas | Solomon LLP, and Eric M. Levine (Stuart) , for appellee.  
 
 Before  FERNANDEZ, LINDSEY and LOBREE , JJ.  
 
 LINDSEY, J . 
 2 Appellant Reybel Hernandez appeals the trial court ’s order denying his 
emergency motion to vacate a foreclosure sale and stay further proceedings, 
overruling his objection to the foreclosure sale, and directing the Clerk of 
Court to issue a certificate of title.1  Hernandez argues we should reverse 
the trial court ’s denial of his motion because: (1) appellee Barclays Mortgage 
Trust 2022 -RPL1 failed to file the original note and thus did not establish its 
standing to bring the foreclosure action; (2) Hernandez provided evidence of 
a broken chain of title and fraudule nt certification of the note, which the trial 
court did not address in denying his motion and objection; (3) the trial court 
erroneously applied section 702.036 even though Barclays was the 
purchaser of the property; and (4) the trial court erroneously fai led to grant a 
stay pending appeal.   The trial court did not err.  
We affirm because Hernandez failed to preserve any of his arguments 
for appellate review.  Even if Hernandez had preserved his arguments, we 
would still affirm because they do not establish reversible error.  
 
 
 
1 We have  jurisdiction.   See Fla. R. A pp. P. 9.030(b)(1)(A); U.S. Bank, N.A. 
v. Vogel , 137 So. 3d 491, 492 n.1 (Fla. 4th DCA 2014)  (citing Popescu v. 
Laguna Master Ass ’n, 126 So. 3d 449, 450 (Fla. 4th DCA 2013)  (explaining 
that an order denying a motion to vacate foreclosure sale is a discrete final 
order).  
 3 BACKGROUND  
Hernandez executed a promissory note and mortgage in favor of 
Countrywide Home Loans, Inc. in April 2005 and signed a modification in 
December 2014.  Barclays brought the underlying foreclosure action against 
Hernandez in December 2023, alleging that it was the holder of the original 
note and mortgage and that Hernandez had defaulted on the modified loan 
in November 2022.  
Barclays attached a “certification of possession”  and copy of the note 
to the complaint.  According to the certification of possession, Barclays was in possession of the note as of November 7, 2023.  The copy of the note 
reflected a blank indorsement.  Barclays filed the original note and mortgage 
with t he trial court in November 2024.  The original note reflected the same 
blank indorsement as the copy.  
In October 2025, the trial court entered a final judgment of foreclosure 
in Barclays ’ favor.  In the final judgment, the court explained that Barclays 
had established its standing via possession of the original note endorsed in blank.  Hernandez did not appeal the final judgment of foreclosure.   However, 
he filed  a motion to stay the foreclosure sale and vacate the final judgment.  
 4 The trial court rendered an order on Hernandez ’s motion on November 17, 
2025, but that order was not included in the appendix.2 
The property at issue was subsequently sold to Barclays at a 
foreclosure sale in January 2026.  Hernandez moved to vacate the 
foreclosure sale and stay further proceedings and filed an objection to the 
certificate of sale.  In his motion to vacate the fore closure sale, Hernandez 
argued that he had filed “emergency notices and motions ” informing the trial 
court of “pending federal proceedings involving the same parties and 
property ” and asked the trial court to stay the foreclosure sale prior to the 
foreclosure sale.  Hernandez argued that the foreclosure sale took place 
despite the lack of a ruling on these motions.  Hernandez asked the trial court to vacate the foreclosure sale and  enter a stay because “[v]acatur and a stay 
are necessary to preserve the status quo, avoid irreparable harm, and prevent conflicting rulings with the pending federal action. ”  
Hernandez ’s objection to the certificate of sale similarly argued that, at 
the time the certificate of sale issued, there were pending unresolved post -
judgment motions and jurisdictional issues.   Hernandez further argued that 
 
2 The appendix to the answer brief on appeal includes a summary of the trial 
court ’s docket, which reflects when  the trial court entered  its order on 
Hernandez ’s motion to vacate final summary judgment and stay the 
foreclosure sale.  
 5 there were contemporaneous proceedings pending in federal court.   
Hernandez argued issuance of the certificate of sale would cause irreparable 
harm by foreclosing judicial review of the unresolved issues.  The trial court 
denied Hernandez ’s motion and objection.  This appeal timely followed.  
ANALYSIS  
A. Standard of Review  
“We review a trial court ’s ruling on a motion to set aside a foreclosure 
sale for a gross abuse of discretion. ”  2275 NE 120 St., LLC v. Sanchez 
Struve Bus. Advisors, LLC , 336 So. 3d 757, 759 (Fla. 3d DCA 2021)  (citing 
Vogel , 137 So. 3d at 493).  The Florida Supreme Court first applied the gross 
abuse of discretion standard when reviewing trial court rulings on motions to 
vacate defaults.  See N. Shore Hosp., Inc. v. Barber , 143 So. 2d 849 , 852  
(Fla. 1962) ; Coggin v. Barfield, 8 So. 2d 9 , 11 (Fla. 1942) ; Benedict v. W.T. 
Hadlow Co. , 42 So. 239, 241  (Fla. 1906) ; Russ v. Gilbert , 19 Fla. 54, 57  
(1882) .  Application of this heightened level of deference in such cases 
furthers Florida ’s longstanding public policy of liberally granting motions to 
set aside defaults so that cases can be decided on their merits.  See M.W. 
v. SPCP Grp. V, LLC , 163 So. 3d 518 , 519-20  (Fla. 3d DCA  2015) ; Allstate 
Floridian Ins. Co. v. Ronco Inventions, LLC , 890 So. 2d 300 , 302  (Fla. 2d 
 6 DCA 2004)  (citing Lindell Motors, Inc. v. Morgan , 727 So.  2d 1112, 1113 
(Fla. 2d DCA 1999) ). 
Similarly, when reviewing rulings on motions to set aside foreclosure 
sales, appellate courts apply the gross abuse of discretion standard because 
bidders and buyers at such sales seek to make a profit, and establishing a 
precedent that encourages the easy  setting aside of foreclosure sales would 
“destroy the incentive which prompts bidding at [a] sale and thereby work a 
hardship on both debtors and creditors. ”  Long Beach Mortg. Corp. v. Bebble , 
985 So. 2d 611 , 613  (Fla. 4th DCA 2008)  (quoting City of Sanford v. Ashton , 
179 So. 765, 767 ( Fla. 1938) ).  Application of the gross abuse of discretion 
standard “ensure[s] a competitive market in the foreclosure sale process. ”  
Id.  
There is no definition of what  constitutes a gross abuse of discretion or 
how it differs from an abuse of discretion, though it is , on its face, more 
egregious than the garden  variety abuse of discretion  standard .  See Allstate 
Floridian Ins. Co. , 890 So. 2d at 302.  A typical abuse of discretion occurs 
when no reasonable person could take the view adopted by the trial court.  
Id. (quoting Canakaris v. Canakaris , 382 So.  2d 1197, 1203 (Fla. 1980) ).  
Thus, it follows that the  gross abuse of discretion standard requires an 
appellate court to be as deferential to a trial judge’s decision as possible, 
 7 “upsetting it very rarely and only with undeniable provocation. ”  Bethesda 
Mem ’l Hosp., Inc. v. Laska , 977 So. 2d 804, 806 (Fla. 4th DCA  2008) .  The 
burden this standard imposes on a litigant seeking appellate review is 
“almost insurmountable. ”  M.W. , 163 So. 3d at 519.  
B. Preservation  
As a preliminary matter, Hernandez failed to preserve any of the 
arguments he now raises for appellate review.  “[T]o be preserved for further 
review by a higher court, an issue must be presented to the lower court and the specific legal argument or ground to be argued on appeal or review 
must be part of that presentation if it is to be considered preserved .”  
Homeowner ’s Choice Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. v. Oakes, 431 So. 3d 1005 , 1013  
(Fla. 4th DCA 2026)  (emphasis added)  (quoting Sunset Harbour Condo. 
Ass’n v. Robbins , 914 So. 2d 925, 928 (Fla. 2005) ).  Arguments that are not 
preserved are waived.  Id. (quoting State v. Clark , 373 So. 3d 1128, 1131 
(Fla. 2023) ). 
In the proceedings below, Hernandez argued that the foreclosure sale 
should be vacated and the trial court proceedings stayed because there were 
pending federal proceedings involving the same parties and property and it 
was necessary  to preserve the status quo, avoid irreparable harm, and 
prevent conflicting rulings with the federal court.  In contrast, Hernandez ’s 
 8 arguments on appeal are that the trial court erred by denying his motion 
because: (1) Barclays did not establish its standing to foreclose because it 
failed to file the original note; (2) Hernandez provided evidence of a broken 
chain of title3; (3) Barclays was the purchaser of the property, and thus 
section 702.036, Florida Statutes, did not apply; and (4) the trial court should 
have granted Hernandez ’s request for a stay in light of the lack of original 
note, broken chain of title, and inapplicability of section 702.036.  Because 
Hernandez did not raise these specific arguments in his motion or objection 
below, they were not preserved for appeal and are waived.  See Oakes , 431 
So. 3d at 1013  (quoting Robbins , 914 So. 2d at 928). 
C. Merits  
Even if Hernandez had preserved these arguments for appeal, we 
would still affirm because the arguments raised do not establish a gross 
abuse of discretion on the part of the trial court.  First, Hernandez ’s claim 
that Barclays failed to provide the original note in the proceedings below is 
 
3 Hernandez also argues  he provided evidence that Barclays ’ certification of 
the note was fraudulent or misleading.  Beyond making this conclusory 
assertion, Hernandez offers no argument as to why the certification was 
fraudulent.   “Claims for which an appellant has not presented any argument, 
or for which he provides only conclusory argument, are insufficiently 
presented for review and are waived. ”  Hammond v. State, 34 So. 3d 58, 59 
(Fla. 4th DCA 2010) (first citing Doorbal v. State , 983 So. 2d 464, 482 -83 
(Fla. 2008); and then citing Shere v. State , 742 So. 2d 215, 217 n.6 (Fla. 
1999)).  
 9 refuted by the appendix, which reflects that Barclays filed the original note in 
November 2024.   By attaching a certification and copy of the note to the 
complaint and filing the original note prior to the entry of the judgment of foreclosure, Barclays satisfied the requirements of Florida law.  See Fla. R. 
Civ. P. 1.115(c) ( “If the claimant is in possession of the original promissory 
note, the claimant must file under penalty of perjury a certification contemporaneously with the filing of the claim for relief for foreclosure that 
the claimant is in possession of the original promissory note.  . . .  The original 
note and the allonges must be filed with the court before the entry of any 
judgment of foreclosure or judgment on the note. ”).  
Second, as to Hernandez ’s argument that he presented evidence of a 
broken chain of title, Florida law states that a litigant does not need to be the note holder and the note owner to have standing to bring a foreclosure 
action.  Aquasol Condo. Ass ’n, Inc. v. HSBC Bank USA, Nat ’l Ass ’n, 312 So. 
3d 105 , 110  (Fla. 3d DCA 2018) .  “[S]tanding may be established from a 
plaintiff ’s status as the note holder, regardless of any recorded 
assignments. ”  Roif v. JP Morgan Chase Bank , 283 So. 3d 383 , 385  (Fla. 
3d DCA 2019)  (emphasis added) (quoting McLean v. JP Morgan Chase 
Bank Nat ’l Ass ’n, 79 So. 3d 170, 173 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012) ).  Assuming 
Hernandez is correct that he presented evidence that the chain of title was 
 10 broken, such evidence is immaterial because Barclays established its 
standing to foreclose based on its status as the holder of the note, which 
bore a blank indorsement.  
Third, Hernandez argues the trial court erroneously treated the sale to 
Barclays as a protected sale under section 702.036, Florida Statutes  (2025) .  
However, the trial court made no reference to section 702.036 in its order 
denying Hernandez ’s motion, nor does there appear to be any other 
reference to section 702.036 in the appendix.  Accordingly, Hernandez has 
failed to establish reversible error on this point.  
Finally, Hernandez argues the trial court erred by denying his request 
for a stay pending appeal because the lack of original note, the fraudulent or misleading certification, the broken chain of title, and the inapplicability of 
section 702.036 establishe d his likelihood of success on the merits; he would 
suffer irreparable harm if he was displaced from his home; and public interest 
favored the entry of a stay.   Because we affirm as to Hernandez ’s other 
arguments, we also  affirm the trial court ’s denial of Hernandez ’s request for 
a stay because Hernandez has no likelihood of success on the merits.  See 
Dunn v. Flores , 426 So. 3d 576 , 577  (Fla. 3d DCA 2025)  (“Among the factors 
relevant in considering whether to issue a stay are ‘ the moving party ’s 
likelihood of success on the merits, and the likelihood of harm should a stay 
 11 not be granted. ’” (quoting Perez v. Perez , 769 So. 2d 389, 391 n.4 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 1999) )). 
CONCLUSION  
We affirm the trial court ’s order denying Hernandez ’s motion to vacate 
the foreclosure sale and overruling Hernandez ’s objection to the foreclosure 
sale.  Hernandez did not preserve the specific arguments he raises on 
appeal; and even if he had preserved them, they do not establish reversible 
error.  
Affirmed.

items.summary:
A borrower's challenge to a completed foreclosure sale fails when the on-appeal grounds were not presented below: claims about the missing original note, broken chain of title, inapplicability of section 702.036, and a stay are unraised (and partly conclusory) and so waived, and even on the merits the blank-endorsement note holder had standing and satisfied the note-filing rule, leaving no gross abuse of discretion and no likelihood of success to support a stay.

Holding: An order denying a motion to vacate a foreclosure sale is reviewed for gross abuse of discretion—heightened deference that upsets the sale only on undeniable provocation to preserve a competitive foreclosure-sale market; an issue is preserved only if the specific legal ground was presented below, and unraised or merely conclusory claims are waived; and a foreclosing plaintiff establishes standing through status as holder of a note endorsed in blank regardless of recorded assignments or chain-of-title challenges, having satisfied Rule 1.115(c) by filing a certification of possession with the complaint and the original note before judgment.

Disposition: Affirmed.

Author: Judge Lindsey

SIXTH DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL  
STATE OF FLORIDA  
_____________________________  
 
Case No. 6D2026- 1810  
Lower Tribunal No. 2025- CA-007690  
_____________________________  
 
HALIFAX HOSPITAL MEDICAL CENTER d/b/a  HALIFAX HEALTH  and MEDICAL 
CENTER OF DELTONA , INC., 
Petitioners  
v. 
UNITED HEALTHCARE OF FLORIDA , INC., 
Respondent . 
_____________________________  
 
Petition for Review of an Order Excluding Press and Public to the Circuit Court of Orange County.  
Patricia J. Strowbridge , Judge.  
 
November 6, 2026  
  
 NARDELLA, J.  
 
  This action was filed by Halifax Hospital Medical Center (“Halifax”) to 
confirm a final arbitration award.  During the proceeding, Halifax and the opposing 
party, UnitedHealthcare of Florida, Inc. (“United”), disagreed over whether the 
award should be file d under seal.  The trial court resolved the disagreement in 
United’s favor and, thus, sealed the entire award.    
Halifax now petitions this Court pursuant to Florida Rule of Appellate 
Procedure 9.100(d) for a writ quashing the order sealing the award.  A petition filed 
pursuant to rule 9.100(d) is reviewed under the same standard as a petition for writ 
2 
 of certiorari.  Miami Herald Media Co.  v. State , 218 So. 3d 460, 462 (Fla. 3d DCA 
2017) (applying certiorari standard when reviewing petition filed pursuant to rule 
9.100(d)); Lake v. State , 193 So. 3d 932, 932 n.1 (Fla. 4th DCA 2016) (same); Times 
Publ’g Co. v. State , 903 So. 2d 322, 324 (Fla. 2d DCA 2005) (same).   Under this 
standard, a petitioner must first demonstrate that the interlocutory order will cause 
them material injury for the remainder of the case that cannot be remedied on direct 
appeal.  State v. Garcia , 350 So. 3d 322, 325 (Fla. 2022).  Here, since Halifax is a 
party to the action and has complete access to the award  despite it being sealed , it 
has not shown that it will suffer a material injury that cannot be remedied on direct 
appeal.  Therefore, the petition is dismissed for want of jurisdiction.  
DISMISSED.  
 
STARGEL  and BROWNLEE , JJ., concur.  
 
 Samuel Alexander, of Alexander Appellate Law, P.A., Jacksonville, for Petitioners.  
 
Andrew R. Sperl and Sean S. Zabaneh, of Duane Morris LLP, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, Pro Hac Vice, for Petitioners .  
 
Eric Yesner and Daniel Alter, of GrayRobinson, P.A., Fort Lauderdale, and John A. 
Boudet, of GrayRobinson, P.A., Orlando, for Respondent.   
Eric Y. Choi and Scott J. Fisher, of Neal, Gerber & Eisenberg LLP, Chicago, Illinois, 
Pro Hac Vice, for Respondent.  
 
 
NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE MOTION FOR REHEARING 
AND DISPOSITION THEREOF IF TIMELY FILED

items.summary:
Practically, a party that wants its own sealed arbitration award unsealed cannot obtain rule 9.100(d) certiorari review, because as a party it already has full access to the document and therefore suffers no harm that a later direct appeal could not remedy; the unremediable-injury showing that certiorari demands belongs to the press, the public, or others actually denied access.

Holding: A petition under rule 9.100(d) to review an order excluding the press and public or sealing records is reviewed under the certiorari standard, which first requires the petitioner to demonstrate that the interlocutory order will cause material injury for the remainder of the case that cannot be remedied on direct appeal; because a party to the action retains complete access to the sealed record, it cannot show such unremediable material injury, and its petition to quash the sealing order is accordingly dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Disposition: Dismissed

If you need assistance you may call the Clerk's self-help center at 561-355-7048. Please see the below link for how to e-file or mail your documents to the Clerk.
Palm Beach County Clerk

The judicial assistant is not authorized to provide legal advice

The judicial assistant strives to substantively respond to all inquiries within one business day. If the judicial assistant is unable to substantively respond within one business day, your message will be responded to as soon as possible. Unauthorized ex-parte communications will not receive a response.

Court Schedule
County Civil trials are automatically scheduled on the day the case is filed. Parties shall consult the Uniform Differentiated Case Management Order and Order Setting Trial (DCMO), issued on the day the case is filed, for the calendar call and trial date. The Court maintains the trial schedule on Divisional Instructions.
Trial Docket Page

UMC
Uniform motion calendar (UMC) hearings are scheduled by the parties through
Online Scheduling
as follows:
Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays at 8:45 a.m.
UMC is strictly for
non-evidentiary
motions which can be heard in a total of 10 minutes (5 minutes per side).
Permitted at UMC
:
non-evidentiary motions, defaults/default final judgments, motions for summary disposition, and uncontested motions for summary judgment that can be heard in 10 minutes or less shall be set on the Uniform Motion Calendar.

contested

Matters will be heard in the order in which they appear on the docket or as otherwise determined by the Court for judicial efficiency.
Continuance Procedure
Motions for continuance are disfavored and will be granted only upon good cause shown. Successive continuances are highly disfavored. Lack of due diligence is not grounds for granting a continuance.
Motions to continue
trial
are strictly governed by
Rule 1.460
.
Motions for continuance must state with specificity: (1) the basis of the need for the continuance, including when the basis became known to the movant; (2) whether the motion is opposed; (3) the action and specific dates for the action that will enable the movant to be ready, including, but not limited to, confirming the specific date any required participants are available; and (4) the proposed date by which the case will be ready to proceed and whether that date is agreed by all parties. Except for good cause shown, the motion must be signed by the party requesting the continuance, as required by Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.545(e).

See above under UMC or Special Set Hearings

Landlord-Tenant cases
: Residential final hearings and rent determination hearings are heard on Thursday mornings with mediation. These cases are set by the Court when the Court deems appropriate upon review of the file. Mediators are available at no charge to the parties.

Scheduling Services Pilot Program
This division is participating in a pilot program designed to improve access to hearing time availability and expedite communication with the Court regarding scheduling hearings in the 15th Judicial Circuit's Online Scheduling (OLS) system. Available services include
text and email
notifications for newly published hearing dates; a
priority standby list
for earlier hearing opportunities resulting from cancellations; and
downloadable calendar appointments
for scheduled hearings. These services are available to registered OLS users and are intended to enhance communication and scheduling efficiency for parties and counsel.
Training resources are available through the
Circuit’s CourtHelp4U YouTube channel
. As this pilot program is subject to modification, parties should continue to review divisional instructions regularly for current procedures, requirements, and updates.
Details on these new services are below and on the Circuit's YouTube
CourtHelp4U

Text/Email Notifications
Registered OLS users may subscribe to receive text and/or email notifications when new special set hearing time slots become available or when new UMC dates are published. Standard messaging and data rates may apply to text notifications.
Priority Standby List for Available Hearing Times
Parties may request that the Court place an upcoming hearing on a priority standby list for earlier hearing dates that become available due to cancellations.
If approved, you will receive a text message and/or email notification when an earlier hearing slot becomes available.
The notification will include a one-time link allowing you to either schedule your hearing for the available time or decline the offer.
If you decline, your hearing will remain on the priority standby list and be considered for future openings.
Downloadable Calendar Appointments for Scheduled Hearings
Users may now download a calendar appointment for any hearing scheduled through OLS. Appointments are compatible with Microsoft Outlook, Gmail, and most standard calendar applications.
Downloaded appointments can be added to the user's calendar or forwarded for inclusion on another calendar.
Each appointment includes the case number and matter in the subject line, as well as the case style, hearing type, scheduling confirmation number, division, motions to be heard, and, when applicable, the Zoom meeting link.

Emergency and Other Urgent Matters
Requirements
If a party believes there is a factual basis for setting an emergency hearing, a detailed motion setting forth the following must be filed: (1) the issues to be resolved, (2) reasons why an emergency hearing is necessary, and (3) the amount of time needed for each party's presentation.
Scheduling
If the Court determines that an emergency exists, the judge shall decide whether an emergency exists, and if so, shall schedule a hearing, enter any ex parte order deemed necessary, or take any other appropriate action. All parties shall make themselves available for the emergency hearing, barring exigent circumstances. Otherwise, the Court will rule on the emergency motion on the papers.

Case Management Conference (CMC)

Court Schedule:
Trials
In Division AI, trials are conducted Monday through Thursday. Fridays are reserved for special set hearings.
Pursuant to the 15th Judicial Circuit's
Administrative Order 3.110
(as amended 12/24)
at the time of filing
cases that are not exempt under the administrative order will be automatically designated to one of three tracks. Cases will receive one of the three Uniform Differentiated Case Management Order and Order Setting Trial (DCM) orders below:
The General Track (DCMGJT) is for JURY TRIALS. Time to disposition is within 18 months.
The Streamlined Track (DCMSNT) is for NON-JURY TRIALS. Time to disposition is within 12 months.
The Expedited Track (DCMENT) is for FORECLOSURE TRIALS. Time to disposition is within 12 months.
The Complex Track. Cases will not be automatically designated as complex. A motion must be filed and set for hearing. The Court will determine if a case is eligible to be designated as complex. Time to disposition is within 30 months.
Cases will be reassigned tracks only under very limited circumstances. Re-designation is not for modifying deadlines or obtaining continuances. See Part 4 of
Administrative Order 3.110
.
THE DCM ORDER IS YOUR TRIAL ORDER. Notices for trial are not necessary.
Every DCMO contains a schedule with a calendar call date and pretrial deadlines. These are firm deadlines. Cases must be ready for trial by the calendar call date.

as long as the case remains on the same assigned trial docket

In-person appearance at calendar call is strongly preferred. If a party wishes to appear via Zoom because of extenuating circumstances, a motion and order is required.

An announcement will be posted on the Division AI website, and orders regarding calendar call will be issued in advance to all cases on the docket. An E-calendar call form will be attached to the order with instructions regarding its submission.
Cases are ordered to be ready for trial by the date of calendar call.
Ready for trial means that:
the parties have complied with all provisions of the case management order;
have completed mediation;
timely filed a joint pretrial stipulation with all exhibit and witness lists attached; and
all motions have been heard or are set for hearing.
Willful or grossly neglectful failure to appear ready for trial may result in dismissal or other sanctions (striking of witnesses, defenses, claims, jury trial, etc.).
At calendar call, counsel must be prepared to confirm whether the trial is jury or non-jury, to advise the Court of the number of days anticipated for trial, and the number of potential jurors requested for the venire.
Unless an enlarged panel has previously been ordered by the Court after motion and a hearing, the maximum is 42 jurors.
Advance approval of the Chief Judge and Jury Office is necessary for jury panels exceeding 42 jurors.
To ensure enough jurors are available, requests for enlarged jury panels must be resolved at least six (6) months before calendar call.
The requests must be made via motion and scheduled for hearing on the Court's UMC docket or as part of a case management conference.
Without an order granting a motion for enlarged panel, a venire of more than 42 potential jurors may not be accommodated. Per the DCMO, failure to timely request an enlarged panel may result in court-ordered sanctions, including a limitation on peremptory challenges.

prior
to calendar call to discuss which weeks of the trial docket that they, their clients, witnesses and experts will be available for trial. At calendar call, counsel will advise the Court of at least two (preferably three) weeks of the docket period that they will be available and ready for trial.
Conflicts recognized by the Court are limited to specially set trials and "Life before Law" personal attorney issues (i.e., pre-paid vacations, life events, medical issues). An appearing attorney must be prepared to advise the Court of all attorneys' availability for trial and future hearings as necessary, or those conflicts will not be recognized by the Court.
Any other lawyer conflicts, as well as witness and litigant conflicts, will be considered as preferences. Counsel shall be prepared to advise the Court of efforts made to preserve testimony, arrange for remote appearance, or otherwise resolve any witness or litigant appearance conflicts.
The trial docket will be posted on the website the week following calendar call (or E-calendar call if applicable). The number one case for each trial week will receive an order setting a trial date certain and a pretrial case management conference.

Uniform Motion Calendar (UMC)
UMC hearings are held Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday at 8:30 A.M. and are set on the

UMC hearings are set and cancelled by the parties.
Each party has the option to appear via Zoom or in the courtroom if they wish.
UMC is for non-evidentiary motions that can be heard in a total of 10 minutes (5 minutes per side).
Attorneys/pro se parties must first file a motion with the Clerk's office and give opposing side(s) at least five (5) business days' notice (unless the parties have agreed to short notice).
Attorneys should always attempt to clear a date chosen with opposing counsel.

CAD-DivisionAI@pbcgov.org
for permission to add the hearing. You will be provided with some options and directed to confer with the opposing parties for the date when all are available. File a notice of hearing and email a copy of the notice of hearing and motion to the Court at
CAD-DivisionAI@pbcgov.org
The judicial assistant will add the hearing to the UMC docket on the chosen date.
UMC hearings set through the judicial assistant as described in the paragraph above are not set or canceled using the online system.
If cancelling such a UMC hearing, please advise chambers as soon as possible by sending an email to the Court at
CAD-DivisionAI@pbcgov.org
, with all parties copied.
Motions for attorney's fees, summary judgment, and any evidentiary matters are NOT appropriate for UMC and should be specially set for hearing.

uncontested

Continuance Procedure:
Motions for continuance are disfavored and will be granted only upon good cause shown. Successive continuances are highly disfavored.
Lack of due diligence is not grounds for granting a continuance. Except for good cause shown, the motion must be signed by the party requesting the continuance, as required by Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.545(e).
Motions for continuance must comply with Rule 1.200 and Rule 1.460, Florida Rules of Civil Procedure and state with specificity:
the basis of the need for the continuance, including when the basis became known to the movant;
whether the motion is opposed;
the action and specific dates for the action that will enable the movant to be ready, including, but not limited to, confirming the specific date any required participants are available; and
the proposed date by which the case will be ready to proceed and whether that date is agreed by all parties.
Except for good cause shown, the motion must be signed by the party requesting the continuance, as required by Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.545(e).
Motions for continuance of trials, even if agreed, must be set for hearing on UMC. Written client consent must be included in the motion and a proposed order included with the motion setting forth the required modifications.

Pretrial Procedures and Conferences
Case Management Conference (CMC):
All parties may set a CMC when a case requires, and they are especially encouraged to do so when they are having ongoing difficulty scheduling matters. In cases where such difficulty exists, a case management conference may be set unilaterally with at least five business days’ notice. There are few excuses that the Court will accept should a party significantly delay setting a CMC to get hearing time. It is a 5-minute Zoom call…enough said.
The Court strongly encourages the early use of CMCs in more complex cases, multiple-party litigation, or any case that might benefit from court intervention.
The Court can set, or the parties can request, case management conferences as-needed or on an ongoing basis. The Court encourages this practice.
Unless excused by the court in advance, all CMCs are mandatory for attorneys and self-represented litigants. Parties represented by counsel are not required to appear at a CMC.
Scheduling
The Court can set a case management conference, or the parties can notice one. The notice must be "reasonable."
Case management conferences are set online at any available UMC date at 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday and are held via Zoom.
If noticed by a party, the notice "must identify the specific issues to be addressed during the case management conference AND must also provide a list of all pending motions."
Issues that may be addressed
The Court can address any issue during the conference that could impact the case.
On reasonable notice and if there is adequate time, the Court may require the parties to argue any pending motion on the list EXCEPT motions for summary judgment and anything needing an evidentiary hearing.
Preparation is required
Parties must be prepared to talk about any motion on the list, to make decisions about the conduct of the case, and have authority to make binding representations on motions, issues and scheduling. Counsel are advised to have their calendars handy. The parties (as opposed to counsel), are not required to attend case management conferences unless the Court specifically orders such.
The Notice of Hearing for Case Management Conference must comply with Rule 1.200. As such, it must identify the specific issues to be addressed during the Case Management Conference and must also provide a list of all pending motions, including any motions which were not able to be coordinated.
Failure of counsel or a self-represented party to attend a Case Management Conference may result in the Court dismissing the action, entering a default, striking the pleadings, limiting proof or witnesses, or taking any other appropriate action against the party failing to attend. Rule 1.200(j)(6).

Other Division Procedures
Motions Decided on Written Submissions
In an effort to conserve hearing time, a party in a civil action may choose to seek a ruling from the Court on a pretrial, non-evidentiary motion based on written submissions that do not necessitate a hearing before the Court.
A party is afforded due process on such matters when given an opportunity to present a legal memorandum, and then the Court may enter an order based upon written submissions without a noticed hearing and argument of counsel.
Motions that may be ruled on based on written submissions include but are not limited to:
Motions to Strike
Motions to Compel
Motions to Dismiss
Motions to Take Judicial Notice
Motions to Stay
Motions to Reschedule Mortgage Foreclosure Sale
Motions for Continuance
Motions for Disqualification
Please note: Motions for Summary Judgment
may not
be decided via the written submissions procedure.
Rollover Cases
If your case is not reached on the scheduled docket, the case will be reset as soon as practicable or the Court will set a CMC to discuss rescheduling as soon as practicable. Unless the Court enters an order or the parties agree in writing otherwise, no additional discovery, witnesses or exhibits are allowed.
The parties are required to be trial ready at the first docket.
Motion Practice
For non-evidentiary contested matters, the parties are encouraged to submit such motions to the Court to address without a hearing. The parties may do so by letter to the judicial assistant enclosing all necessary papers and proposed orders, and stating the parties’ agreement to allow the Court to rule on the papers without a hearing. This suggestion is made by the Court to allow hearing time to be used for those matters that need a hearing to be properly addressed by the Court. If a party files a motion, it is required diligently to set it for a hearing. Should a party fail to do so, the Court may
sua sponte
rule that the motion is abandoned.
Despite the Court’s best intentions, should the Court fail to enter an order after a hearing within 60 days, the Court asks that the parties send an inquiry/notice to the judicial assistant by email advising that the motion remains unresolved by the Court.
Notes re Discovery under Amended Rules
Discovery relates to pending claims and defenses &em; not for potential claims.
Proportionality applies to all discovery. Proportionality begins with relevance to pending claims and may no longer include everything that is relevant if not proportionate to needs of the case.
"Staged" or "staggered" discovery is encouraged. Discovery rulings are always without prejudice unless otherwise stated. Put simply, core discovery may go first and then, with evidence, fringe discovery may follow if proportionate to case needs.
Objections to discovery must be timely, specific and detailed or they are waived. The Court encourages setting objections for a hearing as opposed to motions with legal briefs in support and opposition that embellish on the objections.
Documents not subject to objection must be produced, even if objections are made to others.
Initial discovery disclosures are required in all cases filed after December 31, 2024. A party may not seek additional discovery until that party’s initial disclosure obligations are satisfied. Rule 1.280(a),(k), (f)
Supplemental discovery is required in all pending cases, no matter when filed. Parties now have an ongoing duty to timely supplement and correct discovery. Rule 1.280(g), (k)
All discovery disclosures, requests, responses, and objections must be certified by an attorney or self-represented party. If a certification violates the Rule without substantial justification, the Court must impose sanctions. Rule 1.280(k)
If a discovery motion is granted/denied, the Court must award “reasonable expenses” to the prevailing party unless the Court finds substantial justification or other circumstances that make an award unjust. Rule 1.380(a)(4)
If a party fails to provide information or identify a witness as required by the discovery rules, the party is not allowed to use that information or witness to supply evidence on a motion, at a hearing, or at a trial, unless the failure was substantially justified or is harmless. In addition to or instead of this sanction, the court, on motion and after giving an opportunity to be heard: (1) may order payment of the reasonable expenses, including attorneys' fees, caused by the failure; (2) may inform the jury of the party's failure; and (3) may impose other appropriate sanctions. Rule 1.380(d)
Mandatory Compliance with Conferral Rules
Meet and Confer Required
Before
Filing of Motions
In an effort to eliminate unnecessary hearings, mandatory compliance with Rule 1.202 and
Local Rule #4 (PDF)
is strictly enforced.
Before filing a non-dispositive motion, movants must confer with opposing parties in a good faith effort to resolve the issues raised in the motion.
As required under Rule 1.202, all hearing notices
must
include a certificate of conferral certifying that counsel for the movant has discussed the relief requested with opposing counsel, or certify that the opposing party did not respond describing with particularity all of the efforts undertaken to accomplish dialogue with the opposing party prior to filing the motion, or that the rules do not apply to their motion.
At the hearing, counsel who requested the hearing must be prepared to detail efforts made to speak to opposing counsel in a good faith effort to resolve or narrow the issues raised. As directed under Rule 1.202(d), the purposeful evasion of communication under the rules may result in an appropriate sanction.
The Court expects counsel to re-confer after all responses and replies have been filed, to ensure that only those issues which require Court resolution are set for hearing.
Failure to comply with the requirements of Rule 1.202 and
Local Rule #4 (PDF)
may result in sanctions against the non-compliant party, including denial of the motion without prejudice. See Rule 1.202(d).
Stipulations for Substitution of Counsel
Stipulations for substitution of counsel must comply with Florida Rules of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.505(e) and (f).
The written consent of the client must be included.
As long as there is no objection and there is written client consent, a hearing is not necessary. Submit the order for signature by the judge via the Online Scheduling System and attach a copy of the signed stipulation and written client consent as supporting documents.
Withdrawal of Counsel
All motions to withdraw must be set for a UMC hearing, with proper notice to the client, in accordance with Florida Rules of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.505(f) and (i), and all parties/attorneys. The Court strongly encourages counsel to ensure that their clients attend the hearing so that the Court may advise them of the ramifications of the withdrawal of counsel.

Motions to Compel Discovery

. The moving attorney must submit the order for signature by the judge and provide a copy of the motion as an attachment via the Online Scheduling System.

Motions for clarification
Motions for new trial
File the motion with the Clerk and provide a copy with supporting authority via email to
CAD-DivisionAI@pbcgov.org
for review by Judge Curley.
The judge will review the motion and determine whether to rule on the motion, order a response, or set the motion for hearing.
Daubert
Motions
Any party seeking to exclude expert testimony under
Daubert
shall file a motion with the Court specifically identifying the basis for the challenge. Written responses to any
Daubert
motion are strongly encouraged and should be filed ten (10) days after the motion is filed.
Please be mindful of the court-ordered deadlines in the DCMO for disclosing experts and expert opinions, and for filing
Daubert
motions. As required under Rule 1.200(e) (1), deadlines in the DCMO are strictly enforced unless modified by the Court.
Requests to extend the deadlines for the filing of
Daubert
motions must be filed prior to the deadlines and set for hearing. Failure to timely file a
Daubert
motion may constitute grounds for denial of the motion.
Motions in Limine and Deposition Designations
The Court will not entertain boilerplate, non-case-specific motions in limine prior to trial. These include motions which do no more than require the Court and opposing counsel to follow the law, or seek an order prohibiting counsel from violating the rules of evidence, making "Golden Rule" arguments during closing argument, or expressing personal beliefs. If these issues arise during trial, they may be raised contemporaneously via objection.
All case-specific motions in limine as well as objections to deposition designations shall be scheduled and heard in compliance with the deadlines in the DCMO, and prior to calendar call.
Self-Represented Litigants
Self-represented, pro se litigants are required to comply with all relevant procedural rules and substantive law as are attorneys, both in Court and in their written submissions to the Court. These include standards of professionalism and courtesy.
The judicial assistant is not permitted to give legal advice.
Self-represented litigants may go to the
Palm Beach County Clerk's website
to seek information on locations of Self-Help Centers and other resources to assist with understanding the Court's procedures and obtaining proper forms and information on filing the proper motion.
Self-represented litigants may also contact Legal Aid of Palm Beach County
(561) 655-8944
or the Palm Beach County Bar Association
(561) 687-2800
for possible assistance with legal matters.
ADA Accommodations:
If you need an ADA accommodation, please contact the ADA Coordinator at
(561) 355-4380
or email
ADA@pbcgov.org
.
Information on ADA accommodations can be found on the
Court's ADA Information page
.
Court Reporters
Court reporters are not provided by the Court for civil matters.
It is up to the parties to arrange for court reporters, if they wish.
As required under the DCMO, the moving party shall be the party responsible for securing the presence of a court reporter. The moving party shall advise all parties in writing in advance of the hearing or trial of the arrangements made, if any, for the presence of a court reporter, or shall advise all parties in advance of the hearing or trial that the moving party has chosen not to obtain a court reporter.
The court reporter is required to file the “Court Reporter Appearance” form. See
Administrative Order 2.504-1/25
.
IMPORTANT NOTE:
In the event that a party is appearing in person in the courtroom, the court reporter must be present in the courtroom as well.
Interpreters
As required under the DCMO, any party needing the services of an interpreter, or calling a witness that may need the services of an interpreter, is responsible for ensuring a competent interpreter is present for any hearing or trial.
Next Generation Lawyers
Judge Curley has a strong commitment to supporting the development of our next generation of lawyers. The Court encourages parties and senior attorneys to allow less-experienced practitioners the opportunity to argue in court. Lead counsel should advise the Court prior to the beginning of a hearing if a lawyer of seven (7) or fewer years of experience will be arguing a matter. Ordinarily, only one lawyer for each party may argue at a hearing. In the event a less-experienced lawyer is presenting, the Court will allow multiple lawyers to argue on an issue.

items.summary: Division AI's instructions, marked updated October 27, 2026, describe new scheduling services for registered Online Scheduling users: text/email alerts for available hearing slots, a court-approved priority standby list for earlier dates, and downloadable calendar appointments. Standby offers contain a one-time scheduling link; declining an offer leaves the hearing on the standby list. Parties seeking hearing time should use Online Scheduling first, then contact the judicial assistant, and then seek a case-management conference if necessary. For ongoing scheduling difficulties, the revised instructions permit a unilateral case-management conference with at least five business days' notice; the prior instructions specified six coordination attempts over at least two weeks. Trial-continuance motions, including agreed motions, are now directed to UMC rather than the previously preferred dedicated DCM conference slots. The revised exhibit instructions allow Digital Evidence Portal uploads for evidentiary hearings and nonjury trials and require hard-copy exhibits and a sequentially numbered exhibit list at least 48 hours beforehand. The new text expressly conditions remote jury-trial witness appearances on counsel's agreement. The judge, judicial assistant, telephone, email and ordinary calendar-call location remain unchanged.

three (3) business days
before the hearing, through e-courtesy on the

Case Management Conference (CMC):
Pursuant to 15th Judicial Circuit Admin. Order 3.110-12/24*, and as directed by the Florida Supreme Court, at the time of filing, all non-exempt cases are automatically designated to one of three tracks:
Case Management Tracks and Track Changes
General Track: Circuit Civil Jury cases will be assigned to a General Track with deadlines established to ensure that cases are disposed of within 18 months after service on the last defendant or 120 days after commencement of the action, whichever occurs first. A Uniform Differentiated Case Management Order and Order Setting Trial
(DCMGJT)
will be issued upon filing.
Streamlined Track: Circuit Civil Non-Jury cases will be assigned to a Streamlined Track with deadlines established to ensure that cases are disposed of within 12 months after service on the last defendant or 120 days after commencement of the action, whichever occurs first. A Uniform Differentiated Case Management Order and Order Setting Trial
(DCMSNT)
will be issued upon filing.
Expedited Track: Circuit Civil Foreclosure cases will be assigned to an Expedited Track and scheduled for disposition within 12 Months from the date of filing. A Uniform Differentiated Case Management Order and Order Setting Trial
(DCMENT)
will be issued upon filing.
A fourth track, the
Complex Track
, contemplates disposition within 30 months after service on the last defendant or 120 days after commencement of the action. The Complex Track involves those cases with extraordinary complexity as to require or benefit from early intervention and individual judicial management. Complex cases are defined by Rule 1.201. Cases will not be automatically designated as complex, nor can they be designated as complex solely on agreement of the parties. Cases may only be assigned to the Complex Track in one of two ways:
Motion or stipulation by the parties
with court approval
. Rule 1.201(a); or
Designation by the Court on its own Motion following a case review. Rule 1.201. Cases will be reassigned tracks only under very limited circumstances. Re-designation is not for merely modifying deadlines or obtaining continuances. See 15th Judicial Circuit
Administrative Order 3.110 12/24* (PDF)
.

does not

. Parties may schedule a Case Management Conference on the UMC docket or, if more time is needed, as a Special Set Hearing.

identify the specific issues to be addressed during the Case Management Conference; and
must provide a list of all pending motions.
During a Case Management Conference, the Court may address all scheduling issues, including requests to amend the case management order, and other issues that may impact trial of the case.
Attorneys and self-represented litigants who appear at a Case Management Conference must be prepared on the pending matters in the case, be prepared to make decisions about future progress and conduct of the case, and have authority to make representations to the court and enter into binding agreements concerning motions, issues, and scheduling. If a party is represented by more than one attorney, the attorney(s) present at a Case Management Conference must be prepared with all attorneys' availability for future events. Rule 1.200(j)(3)
On failure of a party's counsel or a self-represented litigant to attend a Case Management Conference, the Court may dismiss the action, strike the pleadings, limit proof or witnesses, or take any other appropriate action against a party failing to attend. Rule 1.200(j)(6).
Represented parties (as opposed to counsel or self-represented parties) are not required to attend Case Management Conferences unless the Court specifically orders such.

Your DCMO is your Trial Order.
The DCMO or any amended DCMO serves both as a Case Management Order and a Trial Order.
Each of the DCMOs contains a schedule with an E-calendar call date, an actual trial period, and pretrial deadlines.
These are firm deadlines that will be strictly enforced. Rule 1.200(e)(1).

CAD-DivisionAN@pbcgov.org

The following requirements are consistent with those set forth under the DCMO's, 15th Judicial Circuit
Administrative Order 3.110 12/24* (PDF)
, and Rule 1.200(e). The parties must strictly follow the directives in these Rules and Orders. Deadlines in a case management order will be strictly enforced unless changed by court order.
The parties are expected to actively manage their case and to confer early and often to ensure compliance and the timely resolution of their case.
All motions to extend deadlines must be filed prior to the deadline.
Untimely motions will be denied absent compelling circumstances and a showing of good cause. If any party is unable to meet the deadlines set forth in a DCMO for any reason, including unavailability of hearing time, the affected party must promptly set a Case Management Conference.
Notices of unavailability have no effect on the deadlines set by the case management order. Rule 1.200(f).
Any motion to extend a deadline or amend a case management order, must specify:
the basis of the need for the extension, including when the basis became known to the movant;
whether the motion is opposed;
the specific date to which the movant is requesting the deadline be extended, and whether that date is agreed by all parties; and
the action and specific dates for the action that will enable the movant to meet the proposed new deadline, including, but not limited to, confirming the specific date any required participants such as third-party witnesses or experts are available.
Rule 1.200(e)(3)
If the parties agree, and the extension or modification will not prevent the case from being trial ready by the original E-Calendar Call date, the parties may file a motion and submit for the Court's consideration an agreed Amended DCMO order. An agreed Amended DCMO does not need to cut and paste from the original DCMO, but must contain:
the current remaining deadlines;
agreed-upon dates for all remaining deadlines;

Florida Supreme Court Extends Deadlines After Flood Closures –
AOSC26-59
Heavy rain and flooding closed the courts in Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, and St. Lucie Counties on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. On November 6, 2026, the Florida Supreme Court issued Administrative Order AOSC26-59 to give relief to attorneys and litigants in pending cases.
What the order does
Deadlines extended:
In these four counties, time limits set by rule of procedure, court order, statutes that apply to court proceedings, or anything else related to court proceedings are extended from close of business on Monday, November 2, 2026, until close of business on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. This applies only when the last day of a time period falls within that window.
Speedy trial suspended:
Speedy trial time limits in criminal and juvenile cases are suspended for the same period. The days in that period are added back to the speedy trial timeline.
What you should do
Read the full order and check your deadlines. Attorneys should check how the order affects their pending matters. Self-represented litigants who have questions about their own case can contact the Clerk of Court in their county or speak with an attorney. Court staff cannot give legal advice.
View Administrative Order AOSC26-59 (PDF)
Constitution Day 2026
On Wednesday, September 16 and Thursday, September 17, more than 100 students from four St. Lucie County high schools took part in the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit’s annual Constitution Day program, stepping into the roles of attorneys and jurors for a mock trial based on the landmark case
Elonis v. United States
.
View Event
Florida Rural Legal Services, Inc. (FRLS) Relocates Fort Pierce Office to Port St. Lucie
Florida Rural Legal Services, Inc. (FRLS), a non-profit law firm, has relocated its former Fort Pierce office to Port St. Lucie, located at 10570 S. U.S. Highway 1, Third Floor, Port St. Lucie, FL., 34952.
FRLS provides free civil legal aid to eligible individuals, families, and vulnerable communities across 13 Florida counties, as well as farmworkers statewide. Since 1966, FRLS has helped clients navigate civil legal issues like landlord-tenant disputes, disaster-related legal issues, public benefits denials, and more.
In addition, FRLS’s Pro Bono Program offers law students, active attorneys, and retired legal practitioners’ opportunities to volunteer, virtually or in person, to help expand access to justice for those most in need.
Learn More (link to FRLS.org)
Judge Jennifer Alcorta Waters Honored with Community Service Award
The Nineteenth Judicial Circuit is proud to share that Judge Jennifer Alcorta Waters was recognized last Saturday by the Palm City Chamber of Commerce with the Michelle Radcliffe Dutro Memorial Award.
Established in 2014, the Michele Radcliffe Dutro Memorial Award honors exceptional service and lasting community impact. This year’s recipient, Judge Waters, is recognized for her dedication to public service and leadership in Mental Health Court.
Read More
Indian River County Courts Mark Historic All Women Bench
History was made in the 19th Judicial Circuit as Indian River County’s entire bench, including both County and Circuit Courts, is now comprised of women. From the first female judge sworn in within the circuit in 1989 to today’s six experienced jurists serving the community, this milestone reflects decades of progress in Florida’s judiciary.
These judges bring diverse backgrounds in criminal, civil, family, juvenile, and probate law, along with a shared commitment to fairness, service, and improving access to justice.
Read more on our Events page to learn about the judges and the path that led to this historic moment.

Practical effect: civil litigants with deadlines ending November 2 through November 4 in the four counties receive relief per the order; the page directs practitioners to read the full order and check their deadlines.

Beginning December 11, 2026 all Calendar Calls will be via ZOOM. Orders will be sent out for the upcoming Calendar Call set on December 11, 2026 for all OPEN cases, if you do not receive an order please contact the division at
CAD-DivisionAA@pbcgov.org

Senior Judges and other divisional judges will continue to cover all hearings and trials and matters will continue to be set on the docket and scheduled. Additional UMC dates have been released in OLS and are available for scheduling. All requests for special set hearings, case management conferences, or other scheduling matters should be sent to the Divisional CAD email CAD-DivisionAA@pbcgov.org. Last updated 10/28/2026

A. Communications with the Judicial Office
Method of Communication
:
The best way to contact the Judicial Assistant is via email to
CAD-DivisionAA@pbcgov.org
When the judicial assistant is out of the office, there will be an alternate contact for immediate assistance.
All communications to the judicial office must be submitted by e-mail to
CAD-DivisionAA@pbcgov.org
, the dedicated divisional e-mail account. The subject line of any e-mail to the judicial office must contain the case number, case name, and relevant matter (e.g., 2026CA000111 – Smith v. Jones – 2-Hour Hearing Requested).
Unless otherwise specifically directed by the Court, communication with chambers on case-related matters is limited to scheduling hearings and related issues.
All communications must be via email to
CAD-DivisionAA@pbcgov.org
, with all parties copied and otherwise in accord with the instructions on setting hearings set forth below. The Court does not accept ex parte communications via email or by telephone. The judicial assistant will direct anyone who contacts chambers ex parte to send an e-mail with all parties copied.
The judicial assistant cannot give legal advice regarding how to proceed with your case. All substantive issues are handled by the Court via motion. Please file a motion and set the appropriate hearing. Do not contact the judicial assistant about any substantive matters.
Self-represented (pro se) parties needing assistance can contact the Self-Help Center at
(561) 355-6781
located on the first floor of the Main West Palm Beach Courthouse or visit the self-service center in the clerk's office in the Satellite Courthouses.
Ex parte Communications:
All communications with the judicial office must comply with Canon 3 of the Code of Judicial Conduct, which prohibits a judge from initiating, permitting, or considering ex parte communications and from considering other communications outside the presence of the parties concerning a pending or impending proceeding, unless authorized by law. All parties must be copied on any e-mail directed to the judicial office, unless an ex parte communication is authorized by law.
Unsolicited Communications:
Parties may only contact the judicial office in accordance with these practices and procedures.
Unsolicited communications from non-parties will not be considered by the Court.
Do not include the court’s divisional e-mail on contentious, back-and-forth e-mail exchanges between parties. This type of communication will not be considered by the Court.
Substantive matters are handled by properly filed motions and not via e-mail. If you are requested to remove the court’s e-mail address from your e-mail thread, please do so promptly.
E-Filing Portal Contact Information:
All attorneys and self-represented litigants must make and receive service by e-mail, which is generally through the Florida Courts E-Filing Portal, unless excused. Florida Rules of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.516.
All attorneys and self-represented litigants must provide an e-mail address to receive signed orders electronically, unless excused. Florida Rules of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.516. It is the responsibility of attorneys and self-represented litigants to update their contact information using Form 2.603 any time there is a change in the e-mail account registered for electronic service.
B. Scheduling Procedures
Court Schedule:
Case Management Conferences (CMC):
Any Party may request a CMC when a case requires.
The court strongly encourages the early use of CMCs in more complex cases, multiple-party litigation, or any case that might benefit from court intervention. Cases assigned to the complex track will be set for routine case management conferences.
Unless excused by the court in advance, all CMCs are mandatory for attorneys and self-represented litigants. Parties represented by counsel are not required to appear at a CMC.
Any request for a CMC or status conference must articulate the reasons for the necessity of the conference.
Trials
Trials are conducted Monday through Thursday. Fridays are reserved for special set hearings.
Division AA Calendar call is no longer by E-Calendar Call, Calendar Call, beginning December 11, 2026 will be held on ZOOM at 9:00 A.M
Pursuant to the 15th Judicial Circuit's Administrative Order 3.110 (as amended 12/24) at the time of filing cases that are not exempt under the administrative order will be automatically designated to one of three tracks. Cases will receive one of the three Uniform Differentiated Case Management Order and Order Setting Trial (DCM) orders below:
The General Track (DCMGJT) is for JURY TRIALS. Time to disposition is within 18 months.
The Streamlined Track (DCMSNT) is for NON-JURY TRIALS. Time to disposition is within 12 months.
The Expedited Track (DCMENT) is for FORECLOSURE TRIALS. Time to disposition is within 12 months.
The Complex Track. Cases will not be automatically designated as complex. A motion must be filed and set for hearing. The Court will determine if a case is eligible to be designated as complex. Time to disposition is within 30 months.
Cases will be reassigned tracks only under very limited circumstances. Re-designation is not for modifying deadlines or obtaining continuances. See Part 4 of Administrative Order 3.110.
THE DCM ORDER IS YOUR TRIAL ORDER. Notices for trial are not necessary.
Every DCMO contains a schedule with a calendar call date and pretrial deadlines. These are firm deadlines. Cases must be ready for trial by the calendar call date.
Deadlines may be modified by agreement of the parties with submission of an agreed case management order
as long as the case remains on the same assigned trial docket.
If parties disagree about deadlines or the new deadlines take the case out of the assigned trial docket, a hearing must be set.
Prior to calendar call, counsel must have
:
participated in mediation,
held a pretrial conference,
exchanged exhibit and witness lists,
agreed on the length of time the trial will take, including jury selection where applicable,
agreed on time periods during the upcoming trial docket when all counsel are available,
filed the pretrial stipulation,
collaborated on proposed jury instructions, providing trial clerk with a single copy, noting the parties differences, if any, on any specific provision,
pre-marked the exhibits in accordance with instructions of the clerk and comptroller, and
scheduled for hearing prior to trial any motion in limine or other pretrial motion.
Uniform Motion Calendar
Uniform Motion Calendar ("UMC") hearings are held Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday at
8:30 A.M.
REMOTELY (via the ZOOM platform) and are set through Court Online Services. Scheduling is solely between the parties. Please do not call the Judicial Assistant to schedule or cancel a UMC hearing.
UMC is strictly for non-evidentiary motions which can be heard in a total of 10 minutes (5 minutes per side). Motions for attorney's fees, summary judgment, and any evidentiary matters are NOT appropriate for UMC and should be specially set for hearing. Please Note: Default Final Judgments and uncontested Motions for Summary Judgment may be set on the Uniform Motion Calendar.
A separate motion is not required. Before scheduling, attorneys/pro se parties must first file a motion and notice of hearing (including complete ZOOM information on the Notice) with the Clerk's office and give opposing side(s) at least five (5) business days' notice, unless the parties have agreed to the short notice. Attorneys should always attempt to clear a date chosen with opposing counsel. Mandatory compliance with Local Rule #4 is strictly enforced. Attorneys are required to "make reasonable efforts to actually speak to one another and engage in reasonable compromises to resolve or narrow the disputes before seeking court intervention." Prior to scheduling, the "attorney noticing the motion shall attempt to resolve the matter and shall certify to the Court the good faith attempt to resolve."
The Court reviews all motions prior to the hearing. A copy of the Notice of Hearing and the Motion or other pertinent pleadings must be sent to chambers in advance, via regular mail, express mail or courier. Proposed Orders shall be uploaded to the online system AFTER the hearing takes place. Do not submit proposed orders in advance of the hearing to the Online Scheduling System. They will be rejected and returned unsigned.
Cancellation of UMC Hearings
To cancel a hearing scheduled for UMC, the scheduling attorney's office must file a Notice of Cancellation and submit it to the Court via
CAD-DivisionAA@pbcgov.org
. In addition, that attorney's office must log in to the 15th Judicial Circuit's Online Scheduling System, select "Uniform Motion Calendar "UMC" Scheduling; select "Cancel Hearings" and follow the directions on the screen.
Specially Set Hearings
All emails requesting hearing time must include:: case number and style, specific motion(s) requesting to be heard, amount of time being requested, if the hearing will be evidentiary, the names and contact information for all parties, and must note if the matter is on a trial docket.
The judicial assistant will provide five dates of availability. If the parties cannot agree on any of those dates, the Court will unilaterally set the matter for hearing.
15 and 30 Minute Hearings
: Special Set Hearing time is available through the Court's Online Services in blocks of 15 and 30 minutes. If agreeable hearing time is unavailable on OLS, the parties shall email the judicial assistant
CAD-DivisionAA@pbcgov.org
requesting available dates.
Parties are not permitted to stack hearing times on OLS to create a hearing slot that is more than 30 minutes.
Greater than 30 Minute Hearings
: Hearings of more than 30 minutes must be scheduled by e-mailing the judicial assistant at
CAD-CAD-DivisionAA@pbcgov.org
and copying opposing counsel and any self-represented litigant. Parties should not copy the court on their conferral emails when scheduling a hearing. Copy the court only on the request for dates and once the parties have agreed on a date. The subject line of any e-mail to the judicial office must contain the case number, case name, and relevant matter (e.g., 2026CA000111 – Smith v. Jones – 2-Hour Hearing Requested).
Special Set Hearings may not be cancelled without prior permission.
Hearings will be on ZOOM unless all parties agree to a live hearing.  The Order setting hearing should reflect whether it will be live or on ZOOM.
Notices of Hearing:
For Hearings longer than 30 minutes, a notice of hearing must be filed and served immediately after reserving hearing time.
When special set hearings are scheduled through OLS, an order setting hearing is automatically generated for entry by the court.
UMC hearings set through OLS do not automatically generate orders, so notices must be served by the setting party.
A notice of hearing involving any remote appearance must list the division's Zoom information.
All notices of hearing must contain the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) notification required by Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.540.
When scheduling hearings through OLS please include the docket entry number of the motion to be heard.
Meet and Confer Required
To eliminate unnecessary hearings, mandatory compliance with Rule 1.202 and
Local Rule #4 (PDF)
is strictly enforced. Before filing a non-dispositive motion, movants must confer with opposing parties in a good faith effort to resolve the issues raised in the motion. Attorneys must "make reasonable efforts to actually speak to one another and engage in reasonable compromises to resolve or narrow the disputes before seeking court intervention." Prior to filing, the "attorney noticing the motion shall attempt to resolve the matter and shall certify to the Court the good faith attempt to resolve." Rule 1.202(b)
All hearing notices must include a certificate of conferral certifying that counsel for the movant has discussed the relief requested with opposing counsel, or certify that the opposing party did not respond, describing with particularity all of the efforts undertaken to accomplish dialogue with the opposing party prior to filing the motion, or that the rules do not apply to their motion. Rule 1.202
In addition, the parties should reconfer after all responses and replies have been filed to ensure that only issues requiring Court resolution are set for hearing.
Failure to comply with the requirements of Rule 1.202 and Local Rule 4 may result in sanctions against the non-compliant party, including denial of the motion without prejudice. Rule 1.202(d)
Submission Deadlines:
The court must receive any materials for the hearing no later than three (3) business days before the hearing. Hearing materials may be sent by mail or delivered to the Judge's mail box at the security desk.
Order of Proceedings:
Matters will generally be heard in the order in which they appear on the docket, but the court reserves the right to call matters on UMC out of order.
Continuance Procedure:
Motions for continuance must state with specificity:
the basis of the need for the continuance, including when the basis became known to the movant;
whether the motion is opposed;
the action and specific dates for the action that will enable the movant to be ready, including, but not limited to, confirming the specific date any required participants are available; and
the proposed date by which the case will be ready to proceed and whether that date is agreed by all parties. Except for good cause shown, the motion must be signed by the party requesting the continuance, as required by Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.545(e).
Return to TOC
C. Remote Appearance
Remote Electronic Appearance Procedure:
The court maintains both a live and virtual courtroom, allowing parties to appear either in person or remotely for non-evidentiary hearings, as provided by Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.530. Requests to use communication technology for an appearance must be made by motion if the hearing has been set as a live hearing. In emergencies, the party requesting a remote proceeding must immediately file a motion and contact the Judicial Assistant at
CAD-DivisionAA@pbcgov.org
so the matter may be promptly addressed.
Evidentiary hearings, trials, and hearings in Excess of 60 minutes are in person, though witnesses may appear via ZOOM by proper motion or agreement of all parties, such that all parties appear live in court. Requests for a Hybrid hearing must be made by a properly filed motion.
Show Cause hearings that expressly require in-person attendance in the Order will not be heard via ZOOM
Most SPECIAL SET hearings as agreed to by the parties are conducted remotely using the ZOOM platform. If a live, in-person appearance is preferred, all parties must agree, and that agreement must be reflected in the order setting the hearing.
All UMC hearings are conducted remotely via Zoom or by telephone conference.
Motions for trial testimony by Zoom must be filed before the pre-trial conference, though the parties can agree to it at any time.
Court reporters must be present in the courtroom for in-person hearings. The court does not allow court reporters to appear by Zoom for matters set for in-person hearings because microphone placement is difficult.
Platform Used:
The court uses Zoom for remote hearings.
Anyone appearing remotely must be in a private, quiet location free from distractions. Under no circumstances will a participant be permitted to appear remotely from a moving vehicle.
Any person appearing remotely must dress and behave professionally, as if physically present in the courtroom.
Any person appearing remotely must mute their microphone when joining the proceeding and keep it off until the court instructs otherwise.
If a witness appears remotely, the party calling the witness must ensure the witness has a functioning camera and microphone and has tested the internet connection before the hearing. The oath will be administered in accordance with Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.530.
